title: Alexander the Great conquers Bactria
summary: Alexander of Macedon overruns Bactria and the lands of modern Afghanistan in a gruelling campaign, leaving Greek garrisons and settlers that seeded later Hellenistic kingdoms.

title: The Greco-Bactrian kingdom
summary: Diodotus I breaks Bactria away from the Seleucid empire to found the independent Greco-Bactrian kingdom, a Hellenistic state that fused Greek and local traditions north of the Hindu Kush.

title: The Kushan empire and Gandhara art
summary: Under rulers such as Kanishka the Kushans build an empire across Bactria and Gandhara, spreading Buddhism along the Silk Road and giving rise to the Greco-Buddhist Gandhara school of sculpture.

title: The Bamiyan Buddhas carved
summary: Monks carve two colossal Buddhas, about 55 and 38 metres high, into the cliffs of the Bamiyan Valley, a great centre of Buddhist pilgrimage on the routes through the Hindu Kush.

title: Arab conquest and the coming of Islam
summary: Arab Muslim forces take Herat in the wake of the conquest of Persia, beginning the gradual and long-contested Islamisation of the Afghan lands.

title: Mahmud of Ghazni and the Ghaznavid empire
summary: Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni builds a vast empire from Afghanistan into Iran and India and turns his capital Ghazni into a centre of Islamic culture and learning.

title: The Ghurids sack Ghazni
summary: The Ghurids of central Afghanistan overthrow Ghaznavid power, sacking Ghazni and extending Muslim rule into northern India; their Minaret of Jam survives as a UNESCO World Heritage site.

title: Herat, capital of the Timurid renaissance
summary: Shah Rukh moves the Timurid capital to Herat, where he and Queen Gawhar Shad make the city a dazzling centre of architecture, poetry and miniature painting.

title: Ahmad Shah Durrani founds the Afghan state
summary: A jirga at Kandahar elects Ahmad Shah Durrani ruler after Nadir Shah's death; the Durrani Empire he founds is regarded as the origin of the modern Afghan state.

title: First Anglo-Afghan War
summary: Britain invades to install a friendly ruler but is overwhelmed; a British-Indian force is destroyed during its disastrous 1842 retreat from Kabul, an early clash of the Great Game.

title: Second Anglo-Afghan War and the Treaty of Gandamak
summary: Britain invades again over fears of Russian influence; the 1879 Treaty of Gandamak gives Britain control of Afghan foreign affairs in return for subsidy and protection.

title: The Durand Line drawn
summary: Amir Abdur Rahman Khan agrees the Durand Line with British India, fixing a frontier that divides Pashtun communities and remains a source of dispute with Pakistan to this day.

title: Independence and the Treaty of Rawalpindi
summary: Amir Amanullah Khan repudiates British control of foreign affairs and, after the Third Anglo-Afghan War, secures the Treaty of Rawalpindi (8 August 1919) recognising Afghan control of its own foreign relations.

title: Amanullah's reforms collapse
summary: Sweeping modernising reforms provoke tribal and religious revolt; Amanullah Khan abdicates and flees into exile in January 1929, plunging the country briefly into civil strife.

title: The long reign of Zahir Shah
summary: Mohammad Zahir Shah rules for four decades of cautious modernisation and neutrality, introducing in 1964 a constitution that opens a brief era of parliamentary politics.

title: Daoud Khan founds the republic
summary: Mohammad Daoud Khan overthrows his cousin Zahir Shah in a bloodless coup, abolishes the monarchy and proclaims Afghanistan a republic with himself as president.

title: The Saur Revolution
summary: The communist PDPA overthrows and kills President Daoud Khan, seizing power in the Saur Revolution and imposing radical reforms that ignite armed rebellion across the country.

title: The Soviet invasion
summary: Soviet forces invade on 24 December 1979, kill the Afghan leader Hafizullah Amin and install Babrak Karmal, beginning a decade-long war against the US-backed mujahideen.

title: Soviet withdrawal
summary: Under the 1988 Geneva Accords the Soviet Union pulls out; the last troops leave on 15 February 1989 after a war that killed huge numbers of Afghans and displaced millions.

title: Collapse of the communist government and civil war
summary: Najibullah's government falls in 1992 and rival mujahideen factions turn on one another, devastating Kabul in a civil war that opens the way for the Taliban.

title: The Taliban capture Kabul
summary: The Taliban, led by Mullah Omar, seize Kabul and proclaim the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, imposing a severe religious order and isolating the country internationally.

title: Destruction of the Bamiyan Buddhas
summary: The Taliban dynamite the colossal sixth-century Buddhas of Bamiyan as idolatrous, destroying a unique monument of world heritage months before their own fall.

title: US-led intervention topples the Taliban
summary: After the 11 September attacks a US-led coalition and the Northern Alliance overthrow the Taliban; the Bonn Agreement of December 2001 installs Hamid Karzai's interim government.

title: Taliban return to power
summary: Following the 2020 Doha agreement and the withdrawal of foreign forces, the Afghan government collapses and the Taliban retake Kabul on 15 August 2021, re-establishing the Islamic Emirate.

title: Portuguese reach the Kingdom of Kongo
summary: The navigator Diogo Cão reached the mouth of the Congo River and made contact with the Kingdom of Kongo, opening relations between this powerful Central African monarchy and Portugal.

title: Kongo adopts Christianity
summary: The Kongo ruler was baptised and, under his son Afonso I, the kingdom embraced Catholicism, literacy and sustained diplomatic ties with Portugal and the papacy.

title: Rise of Ndongo under the ngola
summary: The Kimbundu-speaking Kingdom of Ndongo grew in strength under its ruler the ngola, asserting independence from Kongo; the title would give the future colony its name.

title: Ovimbundu and Lunda states take shape
summary: In the central highlands the Ovimbundu kingdoms emerged, while in the east the Lunda states built a wide commercial and political network across the interior savanna.

title: Portuguese found Luanda
summary: Paulo Dias de Novais established São Paulo da Assunção de Loanda on the Angolan coast, creating the base from which Portuguese power and the slave trade would expand.

title: Founding of Benguela
summary: The Portuguese established the port of Benguela to the south, which would become a second major outlet for the export of enslaved Africans to the Americas.

title: Njinga becomes queen of Ndongo
summary: After leading a diplomatic mission to the Portuguese in 1621, Njinga Mbande took the throne of Ndongo, beginning a decades-long struggle against Portuguese expansion.

title: Njinga rules from Matamba
summary: Driven from Ndongo by the Portuguese, Njinga rebuilt her power in the eastern kingdom of Matamba, from which she resisted, raided and negotiated with the colonisers until peace in 1656.

title: Atlantic slave trade at its height
summary: Luanda became the leading slave-trading port of the entire Atlantic, funnelling vast numbers of captives seized in interior wars to the Americas, overwhelmingly to Brazil.

title: Portugal abolishes the slave trade
summary: Portugal formally outlawed the transatlantic slave trade, ending Luanda's centuries as a slaving port, though clandestine traffic and later forced labour persisted in Angola.

title: Berlin Conference and the Scramble
summary: The Berlin Conference required Portugal to demonstrate effective occupation of Angola, spurring the military campaigns that would subdue the independent interior kingdoms.

title: Conquest of the Ovimbundu kingdoms
summary: Portuguese forces conquered the Ovimbundu kingdoms of the central highlands, bringing one of Angola's largest peoples under colonial control.

title: Battle of the Cunene
summary: Heavy fighting against the Kwanhama (Ovambo) in the south marked the violent and protracted character of the Portuguese conquest of Angola's interior frontier.

title: Effective occupation completed
summary: Only in the early twentieth century, with pacification campaigns continuing into the 1920s, did Portugal establish effective control over the whole of Angola.

title: Revolt breaks out
summary: The Baixa de Cassanje cotton workers' revolt, the 4 February attack on a Luanda prison, and the UPA's 15 March uprising in the north marked the start of Angola's war of independence against Portugal.

title: Founding of UNITA
summary: Jonas Savimbi founded the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola, drawing support from the Ovimbundu and creating the third of the rival liberation movements alongside the MPLA and FNLA.

title: Carnation Revolution in Portugal
summary: A military coup overthrew Portugal's dictatorship, and the new government moved to decolonise, opening the path to Angolan independence.

title: Alvor Agreement
summary: Portugal, the MPLA, the FNLA and UNITA signed the Alvor Agreement, providing for a transitional government and independence, but trust between the movements quickly collapsed into open conflict.

title: Independence proclaimed
summary: As the Portuguese departed, the MPLA proclaimed the People's Republic of Angola in Luanda under Agostinho Neto, marking the country's independence amid a contest with the rival movements.

title: Cold War intervention
summary: As civil war erupted, South Africa invaded the south and Cuba sent troops to support the MPLA, turning Angola into a major proxy battleground between the superpower blocs.

title: Battle of Cuito Cuanavale
summary: Cuban, Angolan and South African forces fought a major conventional battle around Cuito Cuanavale, a turning point that helped lead to negotiated foreign troop withdrawals.

title: Bicesse Accords
summary: A ceasefire under the Bicesse Accords legalised UNITA as a party and set the stage for multiparty elections, briefly raising hopes of an end to the war.

title: Disputed elections and renewed war
summary: The MPLA's dos Santos led UNITA's Savimbi in Angola's first multiparty elections, but Savimbi rejected the result and returned to war, plunging the country back into conflict.

title: Death of Savimbi ends the war
summary: Jonas Savimbi was killed in an ambush by government forces; within weeks UNITA and the MPLA signed the Luena Memorandum, ending the twenty-seven-year civil war.

title: Reconstruction and the oil boom
summary: Peace allowed Angola to rebuild on the back of surging oil revenues, driving rapid growth in the 2000s amid persistent inequality and corruption.

title: Angola joins OPEC
summary: Angola became a member of OPEC, underscoring its standing as one of Africa's leading oil producers and the centrality of crude oil to its economy.

title: Lourenço succeeds dos Santos
summary: After thirty-eight years in power, José Eduardo dos Santos stepped down and João Lourenço became president, with the MPLA retaining control of the government.

title: Illyrian and Greek Butrint
summary: Illyrian tribes inhabited the eastern Adriatic coast, where Greek colonists from about the eighth century BCE helped develop the settlement of Buthrotum (Butrint) into a flourishing city.

title: Roman conquest of Illyria
summary: Rome conquered the Illyrians in the second century BCE and absorbed their lands; Butrint flourished under Roman rule with a forum, aqueduct and public buildings.

title: Byzantine rule begins
summary: After the division of the Roman Empire the Albanian lands passed to the Byzantine Empire, remaining a contested Christian borderland for much of the following eight centuries.

title: Early Christian Butrint
summary: Butrint became an episcopal seat with an early Christian basilica and a baptistery whose mosaic floor survives, marking the spread of Christianity in the region under Byzantium.

title: Ottoman invasion of Albania
summary: The Ottoman Turks invaded Albania in 1388 and, over the following decades, brought most of the divided and contested country under their control, largely completing the conquest by about 1430.

title: Skanderbeg's revolt and the return to Kruje
summary: Gjergj Kastrioti (Skanderbeg) broke with the Ottomans after 1443, reconverted to Christianity and seized his ancestral fortress of Kruje, launching a national revolt against Ottoman rule.

title: League of Lezhe
summary: Skanderbeg united Albanian princes in the League of Lezhe to coordinate resistance, giving the scattered lordships a measure of common purpose against the Ottoman Empire.

title: The sieges of Kruje
summary: From his stronghold at Kruje Skanderbeg withstood repeated Ottoman sieges, including those of 1450 and 1466-67, keeping much of Albania free for some twenty-five years.

title: Death of Skanderbeg
summary: Skanderbeg died at Lezhe in 1468; without his leadership Albanian resistance collapsed, and the Ottomans took Kruje in 1478 and Shkoder in 1479, completing the conquest.

title: Albania within the Ottoman Empire
summary: Following the fall of Kruje and Shkoder, Albania was incorporated into the Ottoman Empire, beginning nearly five centuries of rule during which most Albanians converted to Islam.

title: Ottoman towns of Berat and Gjirokastra
summary: The towns of Berat and Gjirokastra developed the distinctive Ottoman-era urban architecture, including fortified citadels and tall stone houses, that later earned them UNESCO World Heritage status.

title: The Rilindja national awakening
summary: A cultural and political revival, the Rilindja, promoted the Albanian language, literature and a distinct national identity, led by writers and patriots such as the poet Naim Frasheri.

title: League of Prizren
summary: Founded at Prizren in response to the Congress of Berlin, the Albanian League sought to unify the Albanian lands into one autonomous unit and to resist their partition among neighbouring states.

title: Declaration of independence at Vlore
summary: An assembly at Vlore led by Ismail Qemali proclaimed Albania an independent state and raised the national flag, breaking from the Ottoman Empire during the First Balkan War.

title: Conference of London and the borders
summary: The Great Powers recognised an autonomous Albania but, pressed by its neighbours, drew borders leaving about half the Albanian-populated lands, including Kosovo, outside the state, creating the Albanian national question.

title: The rise of Zog
summary: Ahmed Zogu consolidated power, becoming president in 1925 and in 1928 proclaiming himself King Zog I, ruling an authoritarian monarchy increasingly dependent on Fascist Italy.

title: Italian invasion of Albania
summary: Fascist Italy invaded Albania on 7 April 1939; King Zog fled into exile and the Italian king Victor Emmanuel III was proclaimed king of Albania, ending its independence.

title: Communist victory and Hoxha in power
summary: As German forces withdrew, the communist-led partisans took Tirana and formed a provisional government under Enver Hoxha, who would rule Albania for over four decades.

title: Breaks with Yugoslavia and the USSR
summary: Hoxha broke with Tito's Yugoslavia in 1948 and allied with the Soviet Union, then ruptured with Moscow in 1961 over de-Stalinisation, turning instead to Maoist China.

title: Albania declared an atheist state
summary: The Hoxha regime launched a campaign against religion, closing mosques and churches and proclaiming Albania the world's first officially atheist state.

title: Rupture with China and total isolation
summary: Hoxha broke with post-Maoist China in the late 1970s, leaving Albania almost completely isolated, its borders sealed and its economy self-reliant by decree.

title: Death of Enver Hoxha
summary: Hoxha died in 1985 after ruling for over forty years, leaving the most tightly controlled society in Europe to his successor Ramiz Alia.

title: End of one-party rule
summary: After the Tirana student protests of December 1990, Albania held its first multiparty elections in March 1991, and the Party of Labour's monopoly on power ended with the 1992 elections.

title: US-Albania relations resumed
summary: The United States and Albania resumed diplomatic relations on 15 March 1991 after a break of more than half a century dating to the Italian takeover of 1939.

title: Pyramid scheme collapse and unrest
summary: The collapse of fraudulent pyramid investment schemes in early 1997 wiped out the savings of many Albanians and triggered armed unrest that brought the state close to anarchy before order was restored.

title: Kosovo declares independence
summary: Kosovo, whose population is overwhelmingly ethnic Albanian and which was left outside Albania in 1913, declared independence on 17 February 2008, recognised the next day by the United States.

title: Albania joins NATO
summary: Albania, with Croatia, formally joined NATO on 1 April 2009 as the alliance's 27th and 28th members, completing its strategic reorientation toward the West.

title: EU candidate status
summary: Albania, which applied for membership in April 2009, was granted European Union candidate status in June 2014; accession negotiations were formally opened in July 2022.

title: The Charlemagne tradition and the Marca Hispanica
summary: Andorran tradition, recalled in the anthem 'El Gran Carlemany', credits Charlemagne with freeing the valleys from the Moors and granting their charter; the region lay within the Carolingian frontier zone of the Marca Hispanica.

title: Christianity and Carolingian order
summary: As part of the Carolingian frontier, the valleys were integrated into Latin Christendom, with the church of Urgell emerging as the dominant local authority over the centuries that followed.

title: Lordship of the Bishop of Urgell
summary: The Bishop of Urgell consolidated lordship over the Andorran valleys, entrusting their defence to secular protectors, among them the powerful counts of Foix.

title: The first paréage
summary: A feudal charter signed at Lleida ended the dispute between the Bishop of Urgell and the Count of Foix by placing Andorra under their joint suzerainty, creating the co-principality.

title: The second paréage
summary: A second charter settled questions of justice and defence left open in 1278; together the two paréages formed Andorra's first basic law and constitutional foundation until 1993.

title: The questia tribute and neutrality
summary: Andorra rendered a symbolic annual tribute, the questia, to each co-prince as an act of homage; the settlement was understood to recognise the valleys' neutrality.

title: Self-government within divided lordship
summary: Because neither co-prince could rule alone, Andorrans gained latitude to govern their own valleys, developing assemblies of the parishes that prefigured a national council.

title: Founding of the Consell de la Terra
summary: The co-princes allowed Andorrans to create the Council of the Land, drawn from heads of households of the parishes, one of Europe's oldest representative assemblies and the ancestor of today's parliament.

title: The French crown becomes co-prince
summary: After the rights of Foix passed through Navarre to Henry IV, an edict confirmed the King of France and the Bishop of Urgell as Andorra's co-princes; the French role later passed to the head of state.

title: The Casa de la Vall
summary: The Andorran council established its seat and court at the Casa de la Vall in Andorra la Vella, long the symbolic home of the valleys' self-government.

title: Neutrality through revolution and war
summary: Through the French Revolution and Napoleonic Wars the co-principality survived; the French co-princely role transferred to each new French regime while Andorra guarded its neutrality.

title: The New Reform
summary: A reform led by syndic Guillem d'Areny-Plandolit and decreed by the episcopal co-prince broadened the Council and regularised elections, modernising Andorra's institutions while keeping the co-principality.

title: Neutral through the First World War
summary: Andorra remained outside the fighting of the Great War; an anomaly of its undefined status was that it was reportedly omitted from the peace settlement and stayed nominally at war for decades.

title: Boris Skossyreff, 'King Boris I'
summary: A Russian-born adventurer briefly induced the Andorran council to proclaim him king during a period of unrest over voting rights; he was arrested and expelled within about two weeks.

title: Neutral in the Second World War
summary: Andorra preserved its neutrality through the Second World War, its mountain passes serving as a quiet crossing-point between Vichy France and Spain.

title: The first written constitution
summary: Andorrans approved by referendum a constitution that made Andorra a sovereign parliamentary democracy, with the two co-princes reduced to constitutional heads of state and power vested in an elected government and council.

title: Admission to the United Nations
summary: Andorra was admitted as a member state of the United Nations, taking its place in the international community as a fully recognised sovereign state.

title: Member of the Council of Europe
summary: Andorra joined the Council of Europe, committing the new democracy to European standards of human rights and the rule of law.

title: Madriu-Perafita-Claror Valley inscribed by UNESCO
summary: Andorra's only World Heritage Site, the Madriu-Perafita-Claror Valley, was inscribed as a cultural landscape, recognised for its high-Pyrenean pastoralism and a communal land-ownership system surviving from the 13th century.

title: Monetary agreement and the euro
summary: Andorra signed a monetary agreement with the European Union allowing it to use the euro as its official currency and to issue its own euro coins.

title: Association agreement with the EU
summary: After concluding negotiations in 2023, the European Commission in 2024 proposed an association agreement to give Andorra (with San Marino) deep access to the EU single market, comparable to the European Economic Area.

title: Hafit-period tombs near Jebel Hafit
summary: Beehive-shaped stone tombs of the Hafit period appear on the slopes of Jebel Hafit near Al Ain, the earliest monumental architecture of the region and a marker of settled life at the desert's edge.

title: The Umm an-Nar culture flourishes
summary: Named for an island off Abu Dhabi, the Umm an-Nar culture built circular communal tombs, fortified towers and agricultural settlements at Hili, trading copper and goods with Mesopotamia and the Indus valley.

title: The aflaj irrigation system at Hili
summary: Hili preserves one of the oldest known examples of the aflaj, underground channels that carried mountain groundwater to oasis date gardens, sustaining agriculture in an arid land.

title: Islam reaches the lower Gulf coast
summary: Islam spread to southeastern Arabia during the lifetime of the Prophet Muhammad, drawing the coastal communities into the new faith and the trade networks of the Muslim world.

title: The Battle of Dibba in the Ridda Wars
summary: After the Prophet's death, a campaign by the first caliph Abu Bakr against apostate tribes culminated in a battle at Dibba on the east coast, securing the region within the Islamic order.

title: Portuguese seize control of the coast
summary: Portuguese naval expansion fortified Gulf ports to dominate the spice and pearl trade, beginning two centuries of European and Omani contest over the region's sea lanes.

title: Britain breaks the Qasimi sea power
summary: After repeated clashes over Gulf shipping, British forces subdued the Qasimi dynasty and razed Ras al-Khaimah, ending the maritime dominance of the Qawasim in the lower Gulf.

title: The General Treaty of Peace
summary: The coastal sheikhs signed the General Treaty of Peace with Britain, limiting maritime aggression and initiating the series of agreements that established British paramountcy over the future emirates.

title: The Perpetual Maritime Truce
summary: The Treaty of Maritime Peace in Perpetuity committed the rulers to a permanent truce at sea, giving the coast the name Trucial Coast and its statelets the name Trucial States.

title: The Exclusive Agreement with Britain
summary: The Trucial rulers agreed to cede no territory and form no foreign relations except through Britain, in return for British protection, making the coast in effect a British protected zone.

title: Collapse of the pearl trade
summary: The Great Depression and the Japanese cultured pearl destroyed the natural-pearl economy that had sustained the Trucial Coast, bringing years of poverty and hunger.

title: Abu Dhabi exports its first oil
summary: After commercial oil was struck in Abu Dhabi from 1958-1960, the first cargo of crude was exported from Das Island in 1962, beginning the transformation of the emirates' fortunes.

title: Sheikh Zayed becomes ruler of Abu Dhabi
summary: Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan succeeded his brother Shakhbut as ruler of Abu Dhabi and began directing oil revenue into the building of a modern state.

title: Britain announces withdrawal from the Gulf
summary: The British government declared it would withdraw its forces and end its treaty role in the Gulf by the end of 1971, prompting the Trucial rulers to plan a federation.

title: The United Arab Emirates is founded
summary: The rulers of Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah, Ajman, Umm al-Quwain and Fujairah proclaimed the United Arab Emirates, with Sheikh Zayed as first president and Sheikh Rashid as vice president.

title: Ras al-Khaimah joins the federation
summary: The seventh emirate, Ras al-Khaimah, acceded to the union in February 1972, completing the United Arab Emirates as a federation of seven emirates.

title: A common currency and federal integration
summary: The federation introduced the UAE dirham and advanced reforms to unify infrastructure and government, knitting the seven emirates into a single modern state.

title: The Burj Khalifa opens in Dubai
summary: Dubai inaugurated the Burj Khalifa, the tallest building in the world, a symbol of the emirate's wager on trade, real estate and tourism rather than oil.

title: The Hope probe reaches Mars
summary: The UAE's Hope spacecraft entered orbit around Mars, making the country the first Arab nation and the fifth worldwide to reach the planet.

title: Mohamed bin Zayed elected president
summary: Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan was elected president of the United Arab Emirates, succeeding his late brother Khalifa and continuing the Al Nahyan leadership of the federation.

title: Ancient peopling of the land
summary: Hunter-gatherer peoples occupy the Pampas, Patagonia and the Andean northwest over many millennia, leaving sites such as the painted hands of the Cueva de las Manos.

title: Diaguita and Guarani societies
summary: Settled Diaguita farmers flourish in the northwest within the Andean world, while Guarani-speaking peoples cultivate the riverine northeast.

title: Spanish reach the Rio de la Plata
summary: European expeditions begin to explore the great estuary of the Rio de la Plata, opening the region to Spanish ambitions.

title: First founding of Buenos Aires
summary: Pedro de Mendoza founds a first settlement on the Rio de la Plata, soon abandoned amid famine and Indigenous resistance, its survivors retreating to Asuncion.

title: Refounding of Buenos Aires
summary: Juan de Garay leads an expedition from Asuncion and permanently re-establishes Buenos Aires, fixing the future capital on the estuary.

title: Jesuit missions among the Guarani
summary: The Jesuit Order founds mission towns among the Guarani that flourish until the order's expulsion from Spanish lands in 1767.

title: Viceroyalty of the Rio de la Plata created
summary: Charles III establishes the new viceroyalty with Buenos Aires as capital, routing Potosi silver through the port and spurring its rise.

title: Free trade reforms
summary: Bourbon commercial reforms loosen Spain's trade monopoly, allowing Buenos Aires to trade more freely and accelerating its growth as an Atlantic port.

title: British invasions repelled
summary: British forces seize Buenos Aires twice and are twice expelled by local militias, kindling creole self-confidence and a taste for autonomy.

title: The May Revolution
summary: An open cabildo in Buenos Aires deposes the viceroy and forms the Primera Junta, the first home government, launching the war of independence.

title: Belgrano raises the flag
summary: Manuel Belgrano first flies the light-blue-and-white flag at Rosario; it is adopted by the Congress of Tucuman in 1816.

title: Declaration of Independence at Tucuman
summary: The Congress of Tucuman declares independence from Spain as the United Provinces of South America, signed by twenty-nine delegates under the presidency of Laprida.

title: San Martin crosses the Andes
summary: San Martin leads the Army of the Andes over the cordillera and defeats royalist forces at Chacabuco, opening the liberation of Chile.

title: Collapse of central authority
summary: The United Provinces fragment as central government breaks down and provincial caudillos contend for power, beginning decades of civil war.

title: The rule of Rosas
summary: The Federalist caudillo Juan Manuel de Rosas dominates Argentina as governor of Buenos Aires until his fall, a period of strongman rule and conflict.

title: Battle of Caseros
summary: Justo Jose de Urquiza defeats Rosas at Caseros, opening the way to the constitutional organisation of the country.

title: The National Constitution
summary: A constituent congress at Santa Fe sanctions the Constitution of 1853, establishing a federal, representative and republican state.

title: The Conquest of the Desert
summary: Military campaigns led by Julio Argentino Roca seize the Pampas and northern Patagonia from the Mapuche and other peoples through killing, subjugation and displacement.

title: Mass European immigration
summary: Some four million immigrants, chiefly Italians and Spaniards, arrive to settle and work the land, so that by 1914 nearly a third of Argentines are foreign-born.

title: First election under universal male suffrage
summary: Hipolito Yrigoyen of the Radical Civic Union wins the presidency in the first vote under the secret universal male ballot of 1912.

title: The first military coup
summary: Amid the Great Depression the army overthrows Yrigoyen, opening the fraud-ridden Infamous Decade and a century of military intervention.

title: Peron elected president
summary: Juan Peron wins the presidency with broad working-class support, launching the Peronist movement that will dominate Argentine politics.

title: Peron overthrown
summary: The Revolucion Libertadora ousts Peron, who goes into an exile of nearly two decades while Peronism is banned at home.

title: Peron's return and death
summary: Peron returns from exile and is re-elected president in 1973, but dies on 1 July 1974, leaving power to his wife Isabel amid deepening crisis.

title: Military coup and the Dirty War
summary: The armed forces seize power and launch the National Reorganization Process, a dictatorship whose Dirty War forcibly disappears thousands of people; from 1977 the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo march weekly to demand their return.

title: The Falklands/Malvinas War
summary: Argentina invades the Falklands/Malvinas on 2 April; after ten weeks of war its forces surrender to Britain on 14 June, discrediting the junta.

title: Return to democracy
summary: Raul Alfonsin is inaugurated president, restoring civilian democratic rule after seven years of dictatorship.

title: Nunca Mas and the Trial of the Juntas
summary: Following the CONADEP report Nunca Mas, civilian courts try and convict the junta leaders for the crimes of the Dirty War.

title: Economic and political crisis
summary: A severe financial collapse forces a sovereign default and topples several presidents in days, the gravest crisis of the democratic era.

title: Founding of Erebuni
summary: The Urartian king Argishti I founded the fortress of Erebuni on the site of present-day Yerevan, one of the oldest continuously inhabited city sites in the world.

title: Urartu at its height
summary: In the 9th and 8th centuries BCE the kingdom of Urartu, centred on Lake Van, became a major power of the Middle East before being succeeded in the region by the Armenians.

title: Reign of Tigranes the Great
summary: Tigranes II expanded Armenia until it briefly stretched from the Caspian toward the Mediterranean, taking the title 'king of kings' and making Armenia the strongest state in the Roman East before Roman armies forced his retreat.

title: End of the Armenian monarchy
summary: The Sasanian Persians abolished the Arsacid kingdom of Armenia and ruled the territory through appointed officials, ending the ancient Armenian monarchy.

title: Armenia adopts Christianity
summary: King Tiridates III proclaimed Christianity the religion of his kingdom after his conversion by Gregory the Illuminator, making Armenia the first nation to adopt Christianity as its state religion.

title: Mother Cathedral of Echmiatsin
summary: The earliest of Armenia's great domed churches, the Mother Cathedral of Echmiatsin, was traditionally built by Tiridates III and Gregory the Illuminator; it remains the seat of the Armenian Apostolic Church.

title: Mesrop Mashtots creates the Armenian alphabet
summary: The scholar Mesrop Mashtots devised the 36-letter Armenian alphabet, enabling Scripture and literature in Armenian and launching a 5th-century golden age of writing and translation.

title: Bagratid kingdom restored
summary: Ashot I of the Bagratuni dynasty was recognised as king of Armenia by both the caliph and the Byzantine emperor, reviving an independent Armenian monarchy.

title: Ani becomes the Bagratid capital
summary: King Ashot III moved the capital to Ani, which flourished as a major medieval city known as the 'city of a thousand churches' for its cathedral and monastic architecture.

title: Kingdom of Cilician Armenia
summary: Leo II was crowned king Leo I, raising the Armenian principality in Cilicia to a kingdom that, allied with the Crusaders, lasted until its conquest by the Mamluks in 1375.

title: Fall of Cilician Armenia
summary: The Mamluks of Egypt conquered the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia, extinguishing the last independent medieval Armenian state.

title: Russia annexes eastern Armenia
summary: Following war with Persia, Russia annexed the eastern (Persian) Armenian lands, dividing the Armenian homeland between the Russian and Ottoman empires.

title: The Armenian Genocide
summary: From 24 April 1915 the Ottoman Young Turk government deported and massacred the empire's Armenian population in death marches toward the Syrian desert; widely recognised as the first genocide of the 20th century, with deaths estimated from roughly 600,000 to as many as 1.5 million.

title: First Republic of Armenia
summary: As the Russian Empire collapsed, Armenians of the Caucasus declared an independent Republic of Armenia with its capital at Yerevan, the first modern Armenian state.

title: Sovietisation of Armenia
summary: Squeezed between Turkish nationalist forces and the advancing Red Army, the First Republic fell and Armenia was Sovietised, ending its short-lived independence.

title: Armenian SSR established
summary: The Transcaucasian federation was dissolved and Armenia became a separate union republic of the U.S.S.R., the Armenian Soviet Socialist Republic.

title: Nagorno-Karabakh dispute erupts
summary: The regional legislature of Nagorno-Karabakh, an Armenian-majority enclave within Soviet Azerbaijan, voted to join Armenia, triggering a conflict that escalated into open war.

title: Spitak earthquake
summary: A catastrophic earthquake struck northern Armenia around Spitak and Gyumri, killing tens of thousands and leaving hundreds of thousands homeless in the final Soviet years.

title: Independence from the Soviet Union
summary: Armenians approved independence by referendum and the Supreme Council declared secession from the U.S.S.R.; the United States recognised Armenia on 25 December 1991.

title: First Nagorno-Karabakh War ceasefire
summary: After fighting that left roughly 30,000 dead (estimate) and hundreds of thousands displaced, a 1994 ceasefire left Armenian forces in de facto control of Nagorno-Karabakh and adjacent districts.

title: The Velvet Revolution
summary: A peaceful protest movement led by Nikol Pashinyan brought down the governing elite and installed a new reform government, with Pashinyan elected prime minister.

title: Second Nagorno-Karabakh War
summary: In a 44-day war Azerbaijan retook much of the territory around Nagorno-Karabakh; a Russian-brokered ceasefire on 9 November 2020 ended the fighting, with heavy casualties on both sides (estimates).

title: Azerbaijani offensive and the Karabakh exodus
summary: An Azerbaijani offensive brought Nagorno-Karabakh fully under its control; within about a week well over 100,000 ethnic Armenians fled to Armenia, and the enclave's authorities were dissolved by 1 January 2024.

title: Aboriginal peoples settle the continent
summary: Aboriginal peoples reached Australia at least 65,000 years ago, crossing from Southeast Asia to the joined landmass of Sahul and beginning the world's oldest continuous human occupation of a single territory.

title: Settlement across the whole continent
summary: Within tens of thousands of years, Aboriginal peoples had spread across the entire continent, from tropical north to the cold south, developing diverse cultures adapted to every environment.

title: Hundreds of nations and languages
summary: By the time of European contact the continent was home to hundreds of distinct nations speaking around 250 languages, sustaining complex law, kinship, trade, art, and spiritual systems centred on connection to Country.

title: Cook charts and claims the east coast
summary: Lieutenant James Cook charted the eastern coast of the continent aboard HMB Endeavour and claimed it for Britain as New South Wales, opening the way to British colonisation.

title: The First Fleet founds the penal colony
summary: Captain Arthur Phillip's First Fleet established a British penal colony at Sydney Cove, beginning permanent European settlement and the dispossession of Aboriginal peoples of the Sydney region.

title: Smallpox devastates Aboriginal peoples
summary: A smallpox epidemic spread among Aboriginal peoples around Sydney, killing a large proportion of the Eora and neighbouring peoples and compounding the impact of land seizure and conflict.

title: The frontier wars
summary: Across the continent, the expansion of pastoral settlement met Aboriginal resistance in a long, dispersed frontier conflict of raids, reprisals, and massacres that, with introduced disease, devastated Aboriginal peoples and dispossessed them of their land.

title: Gold rushes begin
summary: Discoveries of gold in New South Wales and Victoria triggered rushes that drew hundreds of thousands of migrants, transforming the colonies' population, economy, and society within a decade.

title: Eureka Stockade
summary: Goldminers at Ballarat rebelled against oppressive licensing and the denial of political rights; troops stormed their stockade, killing more than twenty, but the revolt helped secure democratic reforms.

title: Federation creates the Commonwealth of Australia
summary: Six self-governing colonies federated under a written Constitution to form the Commonwealth of Australia, a new federal nation with a parliament in which power was shared between the Commonwealth and the states.

title: Immigration Restriction Act and 'White Australia'
summary: One of the new parliament's first laws established the cornerstone of the 'White Australia' policy, using a dictation test to exclude non-European migrants and keep the nation overwhelmingly white and British.

title: Women win the federal vote
summary: The Commonwealth Franchise Act gave most (non-Aboriginal) women the right to vote and to stand for the federal parliament, making Australia one of the first nations to enfranchise women nationally.

title: Gallipoli landing and the Anzac legend
summary: Australian and New Zealand troops landed at Gallipoli in a costly campaign that, despite ending in withdrawal, became a foundational national story commemorated each year on Anzac Day.

title: The Stolen Generations
summary: Under official assimilation policies, governments and churches forcibly removed many thousands of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from their families over decades, causing profound and lasting harm.

title: Bombing of Darwin
summary: Japanese aircraft bombed Darwin during the Second World War, the largest attack ever mounted on Australia, prompting Australia to turn increasingly toward the United States for security.

title: Post-war mass immigration
summary: A large post-war immigration programme brought millions of migrants, first from Europe and later from Asia and beyond, transforming Australia into a far more diverse society.

title: The 1967 referendum
summary: Australians voted by nearly 91 per cent to let the Commonwealth make laws for Aboriginal people and to include them in the census, a landmark in the struggle for Aboriginal rights and recognition.

title: Australia Act and full legal independence
summary: The Australia Act 1986, building on the Statute of Westminster adopted in 1942, ended the British Parliament's power to legislate for Australia and abolished appeals to the Privy Council, completing Australia's legal independence.

title: Mabo decision overturns terra nullius
summary: The High Court ruled in Mabo v Queensland that the continent had not been terra nullius and that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples could hold native title, leading to the Native Title Act 1993.

title: National Apology to the Stolen Generations
summary: Prime Minister Kevin Rudd delivered a formal apology in parliament to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, and especially to the Stolen Generations harmed by past policies of forced child removal.

title: Voice to Parliament referendum
summary: Australians voted against a constitutional amendment to recognise First Peoples and establish an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Voice to Parliament, leaving questions of recognition and reconciliation unresolved.

title: The Eastern March granted to the Babenbergs
summary: The marchia orientalis, a frontier march of the Holy Roman Empire on the Danube, was entrusted to Count Liutpold of the Bavarian house of Babenberg, beginning their long rule over the future Austria.

title: First mention of 'Ostarrîchi'
summary: A charter of Emperor Otto III used the word 'Ostarrîchi', the 'eastern realm', the earliest recorded form of the name Österreich (Austria), referring to the Babenberg march.

title: The Privilegium Minus raises Austria to a duchy
summary: Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa's Privilegium Minus elevated Austria from a march to a duchy and detached it from Bavaria, granting the Babenbergs wide hereditary rights; Vienna became their seat.

title: End of the Babenberg line
summary: Duke Frederick II 'the Quarrelsome' was killed fighting the Hungarians, leaving no male heir; the extinction of the Babenbergs left the duchy of Austria contested among neighbouring powers.

title: Battle of the Marchfeld
summary: Rudolf I of Habsburg defeated and killed the Bohemian king Ottokar II near Dürnkrut on the Marchfeld, seizing the Austrian lands; in 1282 he enfeoffed his sons with them, founding Habsburg rule in Austria.

title: First Ottoman siege of Vienna
summary: The army of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent besieged Vienna for three weeks in the autumn of 1529 before withdrawing, the first great Ottoman assault on the Habsburg capital.

title: Second Ottoman siege and the relief of Vienna
summary: An Ottoman army under Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa besieged Vienna until a relief force led by Charles V of Lorraine and King Jan III Sobieski of Poland routed it on 12 September 1683, a turning point against Ottoman expansion.

title: Prince Eugene and the conquest of Hungary
summary: After Vienna's deliverance, Prince Eugene of Savoy won victories such as Zenta (1697) and the capture of Belgrade (1717); the Peace of Karlowitz (1699) secured Habsburg control of Hungary and Transylvania.

title: Reign of Maria Theresa
summary: Inheriting the Habsburg lands under the Pragmatic Sanction, Maria Theresa survived the War of the Austrian Succession and reformed the administration, army and education across her dominions.

title: The Empire of Austria proclaimed
summary: In response to Napoleon's imperial coronation, Franz II issued a patent assuming the hereditary title of Emperor of Austria as Franz I, formally constituting the Habsburg lands as an empire.

title: Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire
summary: Franz II laid down the crown of the Holy Roman Empire, which was dissolved after some thousand years, leaving the Habsburg ruler as Emperor of Austria alone.

title: Revolution and the accession of Franz Joseph
summary: The revolutions of 1848 shook the Austrian Empire, drove the chancellor Metternich into exile and brought the eighteen-year-old Franz Joseph to the throne, where he would remain until 1916.

title: The Austro-Hungarian Compromise
summary: The Ausgleich of 1867 reorganised the empire into the Dual Monarchy of Austria-Hungary, two states sharing a common monarch, foreign policy, finance and army; Franz Joseph was crowned king of Hungary on 8 June.

title: Assassination at Sarajevo
summary: Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne, and his wife Sophie were assassinated in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip, the spark that led Austria-Hungary to war.

title: Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia
summary: After the July Crisis, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, triggering a chain of alliances that plunged Europe into the First World War.

title: Collapse of Austria-Hungary and the First Republic
summary: As the war was lost the empire disintegrated; Emperor Karl I renounced participation in government on 11 November and the Republic of German-Austria was proclaimed on 12 November 1918, ending Habsburg rule.

title: Treaty of Saint-Germain
summary: Signed for Austria by Karl Renner, the treaty confirmed the breakup of Austria-Hungary, forbade union with Germany without League of Nations approval, limited Austria's army and ceded South Tyrol to Italy.

title: South Tyrol ceded to Italy
summary: Under Saint-Germain the German-speaking southern part of historic Tyrol was awarded to Italy, placing a large German-speaking population under Italian rule and creating a lasting territorial grievance.

title: Dollfuss and the corporate state
summary: Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss suspended parliament and established an authoritarian 'corporate state'; he was assassinated by Austrian Nazis in July 1934, deepening the First Republic's crisis.

title: The Anschluss
summary: German troops entered Austria on 12 March 1938 and on 13 March a law proclaimed reunification with the Reich; Austrian independence ended and a manipulated April plebiscite recorded near-total approval.

title: The Austrian State Treaty
summary: Signed at the Belvedere in Vienna by the four occupying powers and foreign minister Leopold Figl, the treaty restored Austria's full sovereignty and ended the four-power occupation; it came into force on 27 July 1955.

title: Declaration of permanent neutrality
summary: After the last occupation troops left, the Austrian parliament passed a constitutional law declaring the republic's permanent neutrality, the condition on which the Soviet Union had agreed to withdraw.

title: Gruber-De Gasperi Agreement on South Tyrol
summary: Austrian foreign minister Karl Gruber and Italian premier Alcide De Gasperi signed an accord committing Italy to grant autonomy and language and education rights to South Tyrol's German-speaking population.

title: South Tyrol's Second Autonomy Statute
summary: After the dispute reached the UN (Resolutions 1497 of 1960 and 1661 of 1961) and the 'Package' of 1969, the Second Autonomy Statute took effect in 1972, granting real autonomy to the province of Bolzano.

title: Accession to the European Union
summary: Following a referendum on 12 June 1994 in which about two-thirds voted in favour, Austria joined the European Union on 1 January 1995, integrating the neutral republic into the European mainstream.

title: The rock art of Gobustan
summary: On a plateau south of Baku, prehistoric peoples carved more than 6,000 engravings of hunters, animals and boats, leaving a record of roughly 40,000 years of human activity later inscribed by UNESCO.

title: The kingdom of Caucasian Albania
summary: The Caucasian Albanians established a kingdom in the eastern Caucasus, much of which overlaps present-day Azerbaijan, before falling under the suzerainty of the Sasanian Persian Empire.

title: Caucasian Albania adopts Christianity
summary: King Urnayr made Christianity the state religion of Caucasian Albania, which kept its own church and alphabet as a Sasanian province until the Arab conquests.

title: Arab conquest and the coming of Islam
summary: Arab armies brought the eastern Caucasus under Muslim rule, introducing Islam in the seventh century and beginning some four centuries of Arab control over the region.

title: Seljuk invasions and Turkic settlement
summary: The Seljuk Turks invaded the Caucasus, changing the population and establishing the dominance of Oghuz Turkic, the basis of the modern Azerbaijani language.

title: The Shirvanshahs make Baku their capital
summary: The Shirvanshahs, who had held Baku since the 11th century, made it their capital, walling the inner city and raising the Maiden Tower.

title: The Palace of the Shirvanshahs
summary: The Shirvanshahs built their palace complex in Baku's inner city — reception hall, mosque, mausoleum and bath-house — later inscribed with the walled city by UNESCO in 2000.

title: Ismail I and the Safavid empire
summary: Crowned shah at Tabriz with his base in Azerbaijan, Ismail I founded the Safavid dynasty and made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion, binding the land to Persia.

title: Treaty of Gulistan
summary: Ending the Russo-Persian war of 1804–13, Persia ceded to Russia the eastern Caucasus khanates from Lankaran to Derbent, including Baku, Shirvan, Ganja and Karabakh.

title: Treaty of Turkmenchay
summary: The second Russo-Persian war ended with Turkmenchay, confirming Russian rule and adding Nakhichevan and Yerevan, fixing the Aras-river border that still divides the two Azerbaijans.

title: The Baku oil boom begins
summary: Modern commercial oil extraction began in Baku in 1872; by 1900 the Abşeron field was the largest in the world, turning the city into a global energy capital.

title: Azerbaijan Democratic Republic declared
summary: On 28 May 1918 Azerbaijan declared independence under Musavat leadership, founding the first secular parliamentary republic in the Muslim world, with Mammad Amin Rasulzade among its leaders.

title: Soviet annexation
summary: The Red Army entered Baku in April 1920 against little resistance, ending the democratic republic and bringing Azerbaijan under Soviet rule.

title: Azerbaijan SSR established
summary: Following the Red Army's entry into Baku, the Azerbaijan Soviet Socialist Republic was formed, becoming a full union republic of the USSR from 1936.

title: Nagorno-Karabakh autonomous oblast created
summary: The Armenian-majority mountainous region of Nagorno-Karabakh was constituted as an autonomous oblast within Soviet Azerbaijan, freezing a contested status that would later erupt.

title: Karabakh dispute reignites
summary: Under perestroika, Nagorno-Karabakh's Armenian majority demonstrated for transfer to Armenia, triggering intercommunal violence that grew into open conflict as the Soviet Union collapsed.

title: Azerbaijan declares sovereignty
summary: Azerbaijan declared its sovereignty in 1989 as Soviet authority weakened, a first step toward the restoration of independence two years later.

title: Independence restored
summary: Azerbaijan adopted the Constitutional Act on State Independence, declaring itself successor to the 1918 republic; the US recognised it on 25 December 1991.

title: First Karabakh war ends in ceasefire
summary: A 1994 ceasefire halted the first Nagorno-Karabakh war, leaving Armenian forces in de facto control of the region and surrounding districts, with large displacement on both sides (figures are estimates).

title: Ilham Aliyev succeeds his father
summary: On the death of the gravely ill Heydar Aliyev, his son Ilham Aliyev became president, continuing a family-led order built on Caspian oil and gas wealth.

title: Second Nagorno-Karabakh war
summary: In a 44-day war Azerbaijani forces retook much of Nagorno-Karabakh, capturing Shusha before a ceasefire on 9 November 2020; casualty figures are estimates.

title: Azerbaijan takes full control of Nagorno-Karabakh
summary: A September 2023 offensive brought all of Nagorno-Karabakh under Azerbaijani control and dissolved the self-declared republic; by estimates over 100,000 of about 120,000 ethnic Armenians fled.

title: Foundation under Ntare Rushatsi
summary: By tradition Ntare Rushatsi (Ntare I) founds the dynasty of the Kingdom of Burundi; oral histories credit him with ending a famine and unifying competing centres of power.

title: Expansion under Ntare IV Rugamba
summary: The kingdom roughly doubles in size under Mwami Ntare IV Rutaganzwa Rugamba; by mid-century its borders broadly match those of present-day Burundi.

title: First European contact
summary: European explorers and missionaries reach the Lake Tanganyika region for the first time, beginning sustained outside contact with the kingdom.

title: Burundi assigned to German East Africa
summary: Burundi is incorporated into German East Africa; Germany rules indirectly through the mwami while establishing military posts over the following years.

title: Belgian conquest of Urundi
summary: Belgian forces invade Urundi during the First World War, ending German control and beginning Belgian administration of the territory.

title: League of Nations mandate of Ruanda-Urundi
summary: Belgium receives Ruanda-Urundi as a mandate; rule through Tutsi-favouring indigenous hierarchies deepens ethnic stratification. The mandate became a UN Trust Territory in 1946.

title: Assassination of Prince Louis Rwagasore
summary: Weeks after UPRONA's electoral victory, Prime Minister Prince Louis Rwagasore, the independence hero and son of Mwami Mwambutsa IV, is shot dead; the killing is later traced to rival politicians with foreign involvement.

title: Independence under the monarchy
summary: Burundi becomes independent from Belgium as a constitutional monarchy under Mwami Mwambutsa IV, separating from Rwanda and retaining its throne.

title: Assassination of PM Pierre Ngendandumwe
summary: Hutu prime minister Pierre Ngendandumwe is assassinated, deepening the political crisis that followed independence.

title: Failed Hutu coup and reprisals
summary: A Hutu-led coup attempt fails and is followed by army reprisals, foreshadowing later cycles of violence.

title: Monarchy abolished; republic declared
summary: Mwami Mwambutsa IV is deposed in July; his son reigns briefly as Ntare V before Captain Michel Micombero overthrows him in November, abolishes the monarchy and proclaims a republic.

title: Micombero's military republic
summary: Michel Micombero installs a Tutsi-dominated military republic, concentrating power in the army and state.

title: Insurrection and the killing of Ntare V
summary: A Hutu-led insurrection erupts in southern Burundi; on 29 April the deposed king Ntare V is killed in Gitega, and large-scale state reprisals begin.

title: The Ikiza mass killings
summary: State and army reprisals kill an estimated 100,000–300,000 people, overwhelmingly Hutu, with educated Hutu deliberately targeted; many scholars regard the events as a genocide. Hundreds of thousands flee abroad.

title: Bagaza seizes power
summary: Colonel Jean-Baptiste Bagaza overthrows Micombero in a bloodless coup and pursues limited liberalisation through the late 1970s and early 1980s.

title: Buyoya takes power
summary: Major Pierre Buyoya deposes Bagaza in a bloodless coup, becoming president and later steering the country toward reform.

title: Ntega and Marangara killings
summary: Ethnic violence in the northern communes of Ntega and Marangara kills thousands, pressuring Buyoya to begin national reconciliation and democratisation.

title: Multiparty constitution
summary: A new constitution approved by referendum and promulgated in 1992 opens the way to multiparty competition under President Buyoya.

title: Ndadaye elected first Hutu president
summary: Melchior Ndadaye of FRODEBU defeats Buyoya to become Burundi's first democratically elected and first Hutu head of state.

title: Assassination of Ndadaye; civil war begins
summary: Ndadaye is assassinated by soldiers after months in office, igniting reciprocal massacres and a civil war that would kill an estimated 300,000 people.

title: Arusha Peace Agreement
summary: The Arusha Peace and Reconciliation Agreement, mediated by Nyerere and then Mandela, sets out ethnic power-sharing and a path out of the war.

title: CNDD-FDD joins the peace process
summary: The main rebel movement, the CNDD-FDD, agrees to the peace process and ceasefires; the war winds down toward the 2005 transition.

title: CNDD-FDD wins power; Nkurunziza president
summary: Following the Arusha settlement, the former rebel CNDD-FDD wins the 2005 elections and Pierre Nkurunziza becomes president.

title: Third-term crisis
summary: Nkurunziza's bid for a disputed third term triggers mass protests, a failed May coup and a deadly crackdown; over a thousand are killed and hundreds of thousands flee.

title: Constitutional referendum
summary: A 2018 referendum amends the constitution and resets presidential term limits, potentially allowing Nkurunziza to remain in power until 2034.

title: Succession to Ndayishimiye
summary: Nkurunziza declines to run; Évariste Ndayishimiye wins the May 2020 election. Nkurunziza dies on 8 June and Ndayishimiye is sworn in on 18 June 2020.

title: Battle of the Golden Spurs
summary: A Flemish town militia, mostly craft guildsmen, destroyed a French army of knights near Courtrai, collecting the golden spurs of the slain nobles and asserting the independence of the Flemish towns.

title: The Flemish cloth boom
summary: Importing English wool, Bruges, Ghent and Ypres became among the richest cloth-producing cities in Europe, with Bruges the leading port and financial centre of the north.

title: Foundation of the beguinages
summary: Communities of beguines, women living a religious life without taking monastic vows, established enclosed beguinages in the Flemish towns; thirteen survive as a UNESCO World Heritage site bearing witness to this medieval tradition.

title: Flanders passes to Burgundy
summary: On the death of the last count, the County of Flanders was inherited by Philip the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, beginning the gathering of the Low Countries under a single dynasty.

title: The Habsburg inheritance
summary: After Charles the Bold of Burgundy was killed, his daughter Mary married the Habsburg archduke Maximilian of Austria, passing the Low Countries to the Habsburg dynasty.

title: Abdication of Charles V in Brussels
summary: The emperor Charles V, born in Ghent, abdicated the Netherlands to his son Philip II in Brussels in 1555, and the provinces passed under the rule of Habsburg Spain.

title: Union of Arras and the split of the Low Countries
summary: The Catholic southern provinces reaffirmed loyalty to Spain in the Union of Arras while the northern provinces formed the Union of Utrecht, beginning the permanent division of the Low Countries into Belgium and the Netherlands.

title: Fall of Antwerp
summary: After a siege of over a year, the Spanish commander Alessandro Farnese took the great Protestant port of Antwerp, confirming Spanish control of the southern Netherlands and driving its merchants and craftsmen north.

title: From Spanish to Austrian Netherlands
summary: By the Treaty of Utrecht ending the War of the Spanish Succession, the southern Netherlands passed from Spain to the Austrian Habsburgs, becoming the Austrian Netherlands.

title: French annexation of the southern Netherlands
summary: Revolutionary France annexed the Austrian Netherlands and the prince-bishopric of Liège, ending Habsburg rule and governing the region directly from Paris for twenty years.

title: Union with the Netherlands
summary: After Napoleon's defeat at Waterloo on Belgian soil, the Congress of Vienna merged the southern provinces with the Dutch into the United Kingdom of the Netherlands under William I, as a buffer against France.

title: The Belgian Revolution
summary: Rebellion in Brussels drove out the Dutch garrison; a National Congress proclaimed independence and adopted a liberal constitution, breaking the southern provinces away from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands.

title: Leopold I, first King of the Belgians
summary: The German prince Leopold of Saxe-Coburg was installed as the first king and took his constitutional oath on 21 July 1831, a date still observed as Belgium's national day.

title: Treaty of London guarantees Belgian neutrality
summary: Austria, Britain, France, Prussia, Russia and the Netherlands recognised Belgium as an independent and perpetually neutral state and guaranteed its neutrality, the treaty later cited by Britain to enter the First World War.

title: Accession of Leopold II
summary: Leopold II succeeded Leopold I as King of the Belgians, ruling an industrialising kingdom while pursuing his own colonial ambitions in central Africa.

title: Foundation of the Congo Free State
summary: After winning recognition at the Berlin Conference, Leopold II proclaimed the Congo Free State as his private possession, a regime whose forced labour and atrocities caused massive loss of life.

title: Annexation of the Congo by Belgium
summary: Under international pressure over the atrocities, Leopold II was forced to cede his private colony to the Belgian state, which took it over as the Belgian Congo.

title: Neutral Moresnet
summary: Unable to agree on ownership of a village and its zinc mine, the powers created Neutral Moresnet, a tiny condominium of about 3.5 square kilometres jointly administered by Prussia and the Netherlands, then Prussia and Belgium, until the Treaty of Versailles awarded it to Belgium.

title: The Baarle enclaves take shape
summary: Medieval land deals between the lords of Breda and the dukes of Brabant scattered sovereignty across Baarle, leaving the Belgian Baarle-Hertog as a cluster of enclaves inside the Netherlands, some containing Dutch counter-enclaves.

title: Germany invades neutral Belgium
summary: Executing the Schlieffen Plan, Germany invaded Belgium after King Albert I refused free passage; the violation of the 1839 neutrality treaty, dismissed as a 'scrap of paper', brought Britain into the First World War.

title: The Battle of the Yser
summary: Falling back behind the river Yser, the Belgian army opened the sluices and flooded the polders to halt the German advance, holding a last strip of free Belgium around Nieuwpoort and Diksmuide for the rest of the war.

title: Versailles: Eupen-Malmedy and the end of Moresnet
summary: The Treaty of Versailles ended Belgian neutrality, abolished Neutral Moresnet and transferred Eupen, Malmedy and Sankt Vith from Germany to Belgium, giving the kingdom a German-speaking minority after a much-criticised popular consultation in 1920.

title: Second German invasion
summary: Germany again invaded neutral Belgium on 10 May 1940, this time thrusting through the Ardennes, and rapidly overwhelmed the defending Belgian, French and British forces.

title: Surrender of King Leopold III
summary: After eighteen days of fighting Leopold III surrendered the Belgian army without consulting his government, beginning four years of German occupation and a political crisis over the king's conduct.

title: Founding member of NATO
summary: Belgium was one of twelve states that signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington on 4 April 1949; NATO headquarters later moved to Brussels in 1967.

title: Founding the European Community
summary: Belgium was one of the six founders of the European Coal and Steel Community in 1951 and the European Economic Community by the Treaty of Rome in 1957, with Brussels becoming the centre of European integration.

title: Independence of the Congo
summary: The Belgian Congo became the independent Democratic Republic of the Congo, ending Belgium's central African colony amid turmoil and a swift descent into crisis.

title: The linguistic frontier fixed
summary: Language laws drew a fixed border between Dutch-, French- and German-speaking areas and created four language regions, entrenching the divide between Belgium's communities.

title: Belgium becomes a federal state
summary: The fourth state reform amended the constitution to declare Belgium a federal state composed of Communities and Regions, completing the devolution of the once-unitary kingdom.

title: Aja migrations from Tado
summary: Aja-speaking peoples spread, by oral tradition, eastward from Tado on the Mono River across the coastal plain of southern Benin, founding a cluster of kin-based kingdoms including Allada.

title: Rise of the Kingdom of Allada
summary: Allada (Great Ardra) emerged as the leading Aja kingdom of the coastal region and the dynastic source from which the kingdoms of Dahomey and Porto-Novo would branch.

title: Founding of Porto-Novo
summary: The prince Te-Agbanlin, of the Allada royal house, founded the lagoon settlement of Hogbonu (Ajashe), later named Porto-Novo, which grew into a coastal port-kingdom of mixed Aja and Yoruba population.

title: Foundation of Dahomey at Abomey
summary: Fon rulers established the Kingdom of Dahomey on the Abomey plateau; King Houegbadja is credited with beginning the Royal Palaces of Abomey and building a strongly centralised monarchy.

title: Dahomey conquers Allada
summary: King Agaja's army overran Allada, the parent kingdom of the Fon dynasty, beginning Dahomey's drive toward the coast and the Atlantic trade.

title: Conquest of Ouidah (Whydah)
summary: Agaja seized the major slaving port of Whydah (Ouidah), giving Dahomey direct control of one of the busiest points of embarkation on the Slave Coast.

title: Tributary to the Oyo Empire
summary: Dahomey's expansion brought it into conflict with the Yoruba empire of Oyo to the east, to which it became tributary for much of the eighteenth century.

title: The Royal Palaces of Abomey
summary: A line of kings built earthen palaces decorated with polychrome bas-reliefs within a single great enclosure at Abomey; the complex was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985.

title: Ouidah and the Atlantic slave trade
summary: The port of Ouidah served for nearly two centuries as a leading point of embarkation on the Slave Coast, through which more than a million enslaved Africans are estimated to have been deported across the Atlantic.

title: Ghezo seizes the throne
summary: Ghezo overthrew his brother Adandozan with the support of the Brazilian slave trader Francisco Félix de Sousa, beginning a reign that would expand Dahomey's army and its female Agojie regiment.

title: Dahomey breaks free of Oyo
summary: Ghezo defeated the weakened Yoruba empire of Oyo, ending the tributary status Dahomey had borne since the early eighteenth century and asserting full independence.

title: British blockade of Dahomey's ports
summary: Britain imposed a naval blockade to force Dahomey to end the slave trade; Ghezo agreed in 1852 but soon resumed slaving, as palm oil rose to become the kingdom's chief legitimate export.

title: First written record of the women warriors
summary: European observers recorded Dahomey's distinctive all-female troops — the Agojie or Mino, later called the 'Amazons' — who would become an elite, high-status corps of the royal army.

title: First Franco-Dahomean War
summary: King Behanzin's forces clashed with the French around Cotonou; though repelled by superior French weaponry, the war marked the opening of Dahomey's struggle against French expansion.

title: French conquest of Dahomey
summary: A French expedition under Colonel Alfred-Amédée Dodds advanced on Abomey; Behanzin burned the capital rather than surrender it, and after further resistance capitulated in January 1894.

title: Behanzin deposed and exiled
summary: France deposed the last independent king of Dahomey and exiled him to Martinique and later Algeria, where he died in 1906; the kingdom passed under French control.

title: Colony of French Dahomey
summary: Dahomey was organised as a French colony with its capital at Porto-Novo and incorporated into the federation of French West Africa, where it remained for six decades.

title: Independence as the Republic of Dahomey
summary: Dahomey became a fully independent state on 1 August 1960, with Hubert Maga as its first president, ending French colonial rule.

title: The cycle of coups begins
summary: General Christophe Soglo deposed President Hubert Maga in Dahomey's first military coup, opening more than a decade of chronic instability and repeated seizures of power.

title: Kérékou seizes power
summary: Major Mathieu Kérékou overthrew the Presidential Council in the last of Dahomey's coups, ending the era of regional deadlock and establishing a durable military government.

title: Adoption of Marxism-Leninism
summary: Kérékou proclaimed Marxism-Leninism as the official ideology of the state, nationalising key sectors and aligning the country with the Eastern bloc.

title: Dahomey renamed Benin
summary: Kérékou renamed the country the People's Republic of Benin, after the Bight of Benin, formally retiring the name Dahomey inherited from the precolonial Fon kingdom.

title: Collapse of the Marxist state
summary: Amid economic ruin, unpaid wages and mass protest, Kérékou renounced Marxism-Leninism, setting the stage for a negotiated transition to democracy.

title: The National Conference
summary: A sovereign National Conference of the nation's 'living forces' met in Cotonou, stripped Kérékou of power and launched a transitional government — a pioneering model of peaceful democratic transition for Africa.

title: Multiparty constitution adopted
summary: Voters approved a new democratic constitution by referendum, establishing a multiparty presidential republic and ending the Marxist one-party state.

title: Soglo defeats Kérékou at the polls
summary: Nicéphore Soglo won the presidential election, and Kérékou peacefully handed over power — a rare democratic alternation in the Africa of the time.

title: Kérékou returns by election
summary: Having peacefully left office, Mathieu Kérékou returned to the presidency by winning the 1996 election, serving until term limits obliged him to step down in 2006.

title: France returns the Abomey treasures
summary: France formally returned 26 royal artworks looted from the palaces of Abomey during the 1892 conquest, a landmark act of cultural restitution to be displayed in Benin.

title: Foundation of the Mossi states
summary: Tradition attributes the Mossi kingdoms of Tenkodogo, Ouagadougou and Yatenga to the line of Ouédraogo, son of the princess Yennenga; the dating is uncertain and some accounts place the origins earlier.

title: Songhai campaigns against the Mossi
summary: The Songhai emperor Askia Muhammad I campaigns against the non-Muslim Mossi, defeating Mossi of Yatenga but failing to subdue the kingdoms, which retain their religion and independence.

title: Yatenga becomes independent of Ouagadougou
summary: As central authority weakens, the kingdom of Yatenga, with its capital at Ouahigouya, breaks free of Ouagadougou's overlordship.

title: Loropéni's gold-trade fortresses flourish
summary: The stone enclosures of the Lobi country, including Loropéni, reach their height as the trans-Saharan gold trade peaks; the settlements are linked to the Lohron and Kulango peoples.

title: Loropéni settlement abandoned
summary: The fortified settlement at Loropéni is abandoned, for reasons still debated by archaeologists.

title: Loropéni inscribed by UNESCO
summary: The Ruins of Loropéni are added to the UNESCO World Heritage List, becoming Burkina Faso's first such site.

title: French conquest of the Mossi
summary: France claims the Volta region and occupies Ouagadougou; Mossi resistance collapses and the Mogho Naba Wobgo goes into exile.

title: Colony of Upper Volta created
summary: France establishes the separate colony of Upper Volta (Haute-Volta) within French West Africa.

title: Upper Volta partitioned
summary: The colony is dismembered for economic reasons and divided among Côte d'Ivoire, French Sudan and Niger.

title: Upper Volta reconstituted
summary: After the war and Mossi pressure, Upper Volta is re-established within its former boundaries as a French West African territory.

title: Independence of Upper Volta
summary: Upper Volta gains full independence from France; Maurice Yaméogo becomes its first president.

title: Fall of Yaméogo; Lamizana takes power
summary: A popular revolt against austerity forces President Yaméogo to resign; Lieutenant Colonel Sangoulé Lamizana leads the army into government.

title: Coup brings Saye Zerbo to power
summary: Colonel Saye Zerbo overthrows Lamizana, continuing the pattern of military seizures of power.

title: Jean-Baptiste Ouédraogo takes over
summary: A further coup ousts Zerbo and installs Major Jean-Baptiste Ouédraogo, in whose government radical young officers, including Thomas Sankara, gain influence.

title: Sankara seizes power
summary: Captain Thomas Sankara comes to power in a coup, beginning a radical revolution oriented toward self-reliance and the rural poor.

title: Upper Volta renamed Burkina Faso
summary: On the first anniversary of the revolution, the country is renamed Burkina Faso — 'land of upright (honest) people' — with a new flag and anthem.

title: Agacher Strip war with Mali
summary: A brief border conflict, the 'Christmas War', is fought with Mali over the mineral-rich Agacher Strip before regional mediation ends it.

title: Assassination of Thomas Sankara
summary: Sankara and twelve others are killed in a coup led by his comrade Blaise Compaoré, who takes the presidency.

title: Murder of Norbert Zongo
summary: The investigative journalist Norbert Zongo is killed, a case that becomes a symbol of repression under Compaoré and triggers mass protests.

title: Popular uprising ousts Compaoré
summary: Protests against Compaoré's bid to extend his rule culminate in the storming of the National Assembly; he resigns after 27 years and flees to Côte d'Ivoire.

title: Jihadist insurgency spreads to Burkina Faso
summary: Sahelian jihadist groups linked to al-Qaeda and the Islamic State, alongside the homegrown Ansarul Islam, escalate attacks, killing thousands and displacing more than a million people.

title: Coup ousts President Kaboré
summary: Citing the government's failure to halt the insurgency, the military under Lieutenant Colonel Paul-Henri Damiba removes elected president Roch Marc Christian Kaboré.

title: Second 2022 coup brings Ibrahim Traoré to power
summary: Captain Ibrahim Traoré overthrows Damiba in a second coup, becoming transitional leader as jihadist violence continues to spread.

title: Gopala founds the Pala dynasty
summary: Gopala is raised to power amid disorder and founds the Pala dynasty, a Buddhist imperial line that would rule Bengal and Bihar for some four centuries and spread Buddhism as far as Tibet.

title: Somapura Mahavihara built at Paharpur
summary: The Pala king Dharmapala builds the great monastery of Somapura at Paharpur, one of the largest Buddhist viharas south of the Himalayas and a centre of learning for centuries; today a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: Turkish conquest ends Sena rule
summary: The general Bakhtiyar Khalji conquers Bengal, ending the Hindu Sena dynasty and inaugurating centuries of Muslim rule in the delta.

title: Iliyas Shah founds the Bengal Sultanate
summary: Shamsuddin Iliyas Shah unifies Bengal's principalities and establishes the independent Iliyas Shahi Sultanate at Lakhnauti, beginning more than two centuries of sovereign Muslim rule.

title: Reign of Husain Shah
summary: Alauddin Husain Shah presides over a golden age of the Bengal Sultanate, patronising Bengali literature and extending the kingdom's frontiers.

title: Mughal conquest of Bengal
summary: Akbar's forces defeat the last independent sultan at the Battle of Rajmahal, ending the Bengal Sultanate and absorbing the delta into the Mughal Empire.

title: Dhaka becomes the Mughal capital of Bengal
summary: The Mughal governor establishes Dhaka as the capital of the Bengal subah, and the city grows into a hub of administration, military power and the global muslin trade.

title: Dhaka muslin and the wealth of Bengal
summary: Mughal Bengal becomes the world's foremost exporter of fine muslin and a leading source of European trade with Asia, making the province the richest in the empire.

title: The nawabs of Bengal become autonomous
summary: As Mughal central power fades after Aurangzeb's death, the governors of Bengal rule as near-independent nawabs over the empire's wealthiest province.

title: Battle of Plassey
summary: Robert Clive's East India Company forces defeat Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah after the betrayal of Mir Jafar, beginning British political control of Bengal and, in time, of India.

title: The Great Bengal Famine
summary: An estimated ten million people — about a third of Bengal's population — die as monsoon failure compounds the East India Company's insistence on collecting land revenue from a starving peasantry.

title: First Partition of Bengal
summary: Viceroy Lord Curzon divides Bengal into a Muslim-majority east (capital Dacca) and a Hindu-majority west, sparking the Swadeshi movement; the partition is annulled in 1911.

title: Partition creates East Pakistan
summary: The partition of British India makes Muslim-majority eastern Bengal into East Pakistan, a wing of the new state separated from its western half by a thousand miles of India.

title: The Bengali Language Movement
summary: Students in Dhaka demanding that Bengali be a state language of Pakistan are shot by police; the martyrs become foundational to Bengali nationalism and, later, to UNESCO's International Mother Language Day.

title: The Awami League's Six-Point demand
summary: Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's Awami League issues a six-point programme for the political and economic autonomy of East Pakistan, the charter of Bengali self-determination.

title: Awami League wins the election
summary: The Awami League secures 167 of the 169 East Pakistani seats and a National Assembly majority; West Pakistan's refusal to hand over power ignites the crisis that leads to war.

title: Declaration of independence
summary: After the Pakistani army launches Operation Searchlight on 25 March, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman proclaims Bangladesh's independence on 26 March, beginning the Liberation War.

title: Victory and the birth of Bangladesh
