summary: After a nine-month war in which possibly a million Bengalis were killed and ten million fled to India, Indian forces intervene and the Pakistani army surrenders at Dhaka, founding the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

title: Assassination of Mujib and military rule
summary: Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and most of his family are killed in a coup; a counter-coup brings Ziaur Rahman to power, beginning fifteen years of military-dominated rule.

title: The 2024 uprising and Hasina's fall
summary: A student-led mass uprising over a civil-service job-quota system forces Sheikh Hasina to resign after fifteen years and flee to India; the Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus is appointed to head an interim government.

title: Thracian royal tombs of Kazanlak and Sveshtari
summary: The painted tholos tomb at Kazanlak and the richly sculpted tomb at Sveshtari, among the finest monuments of the Thracian civilisation, were later inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1979 and 1985.

title: Foundation of the First Bulgarian Empire
summary: Khan Asparukh defeated the army of Emperor Constantine IV and forced Byzantium to recognise a Bulgar realm south of the Danube, with its capital at Pliska, the act conventionally regarded as the birth of the Bulgarian state.

title: Christianization under Boris I
summary: Boris I adopted Eastern Orthodox Christianity for his court and people, anchoring Bulgaria to Constantinople and providing his Slav and Bulgar subjects with a unifying faith and church.

title: Cyrillic and the Preslav and Ohrid schools
summary: Boris I gave refuge to the disciples of Saints Cyril and Methodius, who in the literary schools of Preslav and Ohrid developed the Cyrillic script and a Slavonic Christian literature that spread across the Orthodox Slavic world.

title: The golden age of Simeon the Great
summary: Tsar Simeon I expanded Bulgaria toward three seas, took the title of tsar and raised the church to a patriarchate, presiding over a cultural golden age centred on his capital, Great Preslav.

title: Byzantine conquest of the First Empire
summary: After long wars the Byzantine emperor Basil II, the 'Bulgar-Slayer', destroyed Bulgarian resistance and annexed the realm, ending the First Bulgarian Empire and absorbing it into Byzantium.

title: Revolt of Asen and Peter restores the state
summary: The boyar brothers Asen and Peter rose against Byzantine rule and within a year won recognition of a restored Bulgarian realm, founding the Second Bulgarian Empire with its capital at Tarnovo.

title: Ivan Asen II and the Second Empire's apogee
summary: Under Tsar Ivan Asen II Bulgaria reached its greatest extent and prosperity, dominating the Balkans and patronising an Orthodox cultural flowering centred on Tarnovo.

title: The frescoes of the Boyana Church
summary: The second-layer frescoes of the Boyana Church near Sofia, painted in 1259, rank among the masterpieces of medieval European art and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: Fall of Tarnovo to the Ottomans
summary: The Ottoman army captured the Bulgarian capital of Tarnovo, breaking the heart of the Second Empire as the Ottomans absorbed the Bulgarian lands.

title: Ottoman conquest completed
summary: With the subjection of the last Bulgarian territories by 1396, the Second Bulgarian Empire ended and Bulgaria passed under Ottoman rule that would last nearly five centuries.

title: Nearly five centuries of Ottoman rule
summary: Bulgaria was governed for almost five hundred years as an Ottoman province, its medieval state destroyed but its language and identity preserved chiefly through the Orthodox Church and its monasteries.

title: Paisius of Hilendar and the National Revival
summary: The monk Paisius of Hilendar completed his 'Slavonic-Bulgarian History', a passionate call to national pride conventionally taken as the start of the Bulgarian National Revival.

title: Creation of the Bulgarian Exarchate
summary: An Ottoman decree established an autonomous Bulgarian Exarchate, separating the national church from Greek ecclesiastical control and giving institutional form to the awakening nation.

title: The April Uprising and the 'Bulgarian Horrors'
summary: A rising organised by Bulgarian revolutionaries was crushed with massacres of civilians at Batak and elsewhere; reported across Europe as the 'Bulgarian Horrors', it inflamed opinion and helped precipitate the Russo-Turkish War.

title: Russo-Turkish War and liberation
summary: Russia's war against the Ottoman Empire ended Ottoman rule over Bulgaria; the Treaty of San Stefano of 3 March 1878 restored a Bulgarian state, a date Bulgarians commemorate as Liberation Day.

title: Treaty of San Stefano creates 'Greater Bulgaria'
summary: The Russo-Ottoman treaty created a large autonomous Bulgarian principality reaching from the Danube to the Aegean and embracing most of Macedonia, an expansive state soon known as Greater Bulgaria.

title: Treaty of Berlin dismembers the state
summary: The Congress of Berlin revised San Stefano, splitting Greater Bulgaria into a small autonomous principality, the separate province of Eastern Rumelia, and Macedonia left under Ottoman rule, the foundational grievance of Bulgarian nationalism.

title: Unification with Eastern Rumelia
summary: A bloodless revolution united the autonomous province of Eastern Rumelia with the Principality of Bulgaria; Bulgaria secured the union by defeating Serbia in the ensuing war, recovering part of the San Stefano territory.

title: Diplomatic relations with the United States
summary: The United States established diplomatic relations with Bulgaria in 1903, the first US diplomatic agent presenting his credentials in Sofia on 19 September of that year.

title: Proclamation of independence
summary: Prince Ferdinand proclaimed Bulgaria's full independence at Tarnovo and took the title of tsar, ending Ottoman suzerainty; the United States recognised the kingdom's independence in 1909.

title: First Balkan War
summary: Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece and Montenegro of the Balkan League drove the Ottoman Empire almost entirely out of Europe, with Bulgarian armies bearing the heaviest fighting in Thrace.

title: Second Balkan War and the loss of Macedonia
summary: Bulgaria attacked its former allies over the division of Macedonia and was crushed by Serbia, Greece, Romania and the Ottomans; the Treaty of Bucharest left most of Macedonia to its rivals and Southern Dobruja to Romania.

title: Treaty of Craiova returns Southern Dobruja
summary: By the Treaty of Craiova, Romania ceded Southern Dobruja back to Bulgaria, restoring the 1912 frontier, the one Axis-era border change that was not reversed after the Second World War.

title: Bulgaria joins the Axis
summary: Bulgaria adhered to the Tripartite Pact in March 1941 and joined the German-led attack on Yugoslavia and Greece, occupying parts of Macedonia and Thrace it had long claimed.

title: Deportations and the rescue of Bulgaria's Jews
summary: Bulgaria deported over 11,000 Jews from occupied Thrace and Macedonia to Treblinka, but protests led by Dimitar Peshev and the Orthodox Church forced Tsar Boris III to cancel the deportation of the roughly 48,000 Jews of Bulgaria proper, who survived.

title: Communist seizure of power
summary: As Soviet forces entered Bulgaria, a Communist-led Fatherland Front took power, beginning the communist era and the country's incorporation into the Soviet sphere.

title: People's Republic proclaimed
summary: A referendum abolished the monarchy and Bulgaria was proclaimed a People's Republic, a one-party communist state allied to the Soviet Union.

title: Fall of Todor Zhivkov
summary: The veteran communist leader Todor Zhivkov was ousted by his own party amid the collapse of the Soviet bloc, opening the way to a multi-party system and Bulgaria's first free elections in 1990.

title: Accession to NATO
summary: Bulgaria became a member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation in the alliance's largest wave of enlargement, anchoring the country in the Euro-Atlantic security community.

title: Accession to the European Union
summary: Bulgaria joined the European Union on 1 January 2007, completing its return to Europe after the fall of communism and the hardships of transition.

title: Lucayan settlement of the islands
summary: The Lucayans, a Taíno (Arawakan) people, migrated from Hispaniola and Cuba and settled the Bahamian archipelago, eventually numbering perhaps 40,000 across dozens of islands.

title: Columbus's first landfall at Guanahani
summary: Christopher Columbus made his first landfall in the Americas at the Lucayan island of Guanahani, which he renamed San Salvador and claimed for Castile, opening the European encounter with the New World.

title: Spanish enslavement of the Lucayans
summary: Spanish raiders began systematically seizing Lucayans as forced labour for the mines and pearl fisheries of the Greater Antilles and Venezuela, devastating the islands' population.

title: Depopulation of the Bahamas
summary: By about 1520 enslavement and disease had all but exterminated the Lucayans; the islands were left effectively abandoned for more than a century.

title: The Eleutheran Adventurers settle Eleuthera
summary: English Puritans led by William Sayle left Bermuda seeking religious freedom and founded the first lasting English settlement in the Bahamas on the island they named Eleuthera ("freedom").

title: Grant to the Lords Proprietors of Carolina
summary: The Bahamas were granted to the Lords Proprietors of Carolina, though their rule proved weak and largely nominal, leaving the scattered islands poorly governed.

title: Nassau becomes a pirate haven
summary: Amid a collapse of royal authority, Nassau became the base of a loose pirate republic, home to Blackbeard, Charles Vane, Anne Bonny and others who preyed on Atlantic shipping.

title: Woodes Rogers ends the pirate republic
summary: Royal governor Woodes Rogers arrived at Nassau with the King's Pardon, accepted the surrender of many pirates, drove out the rest and restored Crown authority under the motto "Pirates Expelled, Commerce Restored".

title: Spain cedes the Bahamas to Britain
summary: Under the Treaty of Paris of 1783 Spain ceded the Bahamas to Britain, securing the colony's future under the Crown after years of contest and a brief Spanish occupation.

title: American Loyalists and enslaved Africans arrive
summary: Loyalist refugees from the new United States emigrated to the Bahamas after the American Revolution, bringing thousands of enslaved Africans and roughly trebling the colony's population.

title: The failed cotton plantations
summary: Loyalists planted cotton on the "Cotton Islands", but exhausted soils and pests ruined the crop within a couple of decades, collapsing the plantation economy.

title: Slavery Abolition Act takes effect
summary: The British Slavery Abolition Act came into force in the Bahamas on 1 August 1834, beginning emancipation; after an apprenticeship period, full freedom followed in 1838.

title: An economy of wrecking and sponging
summary: The poor post-emancipation colony lived largely on salvaging shipwrecks, sponge-fishing and salt, with wrecking for a time its single largest source of income.

title: Civil War blockade-running boom
summary: During the American Civil War, Nassau became the chief hub for running the Union blockade, shipping arms to the Confederacy and cotton out, and growing fabulously wealthy in the process.

title: Collapse of the blockade boom
summary: The defeat of the Confederacy in 1865 ended blockade-running overnight and plunged Nassau back into economic depression.

title: Prohibition-era rum-running
summary: American Prohibition turned the Bahamas into a base for smuggling liquor across the Gulf Stream, enriching the colony until repeal in 1933 ended the trade.

title: Founding of the Progressive Liberal Party
summary: Bahamians opposed to UBP and "Bay Street" dominance founded the Progressive Liberal Party, which became the vehicle of the movement for majority rule.

title: Internal self-government
summary: A new constitution granted the Bahamas internal self-government with a cabinet and a first premier, while Britain retained defence and external affairs.

title: Majority rule — the Quiet Revolution
summary: Lynden Pindling's PLP gained power after the 1967 election, making him the first Black premier and ending the long political dominance of the white "Bay Street" elite.

title: Independence of The Bahamas
summary: The Commonwealth of The Bahamas became independent of the United Kingdom on 10 July 1973 under Prime Minister Lynden Pindling, remaining a Commonwealth realm and joining the United Nations.

title: First peaceful change of government
summary: Hubert Ingraham's Free National Movement defeated the PLP in 1992, ending Lynden Pindling's twenty-five years in power in the country's first democratic alternation of government.

title: Hurricane Dorian devastates Abaco and Grand Bahama
summary: Category 5 Hurricane Dorian stalled over the northern Bahamas, killing scores, leaving hundreds missing and causing about US$3.4 billion in damage — roughly a quarter of GDP.

title: Philip Davis and the PLP return to power
summary: Philip Davis led the Progressive Liberal Party to victory in the 2021 general election, becoming prime minister, in another peaceful transfer of power.

title: Charter of Ban Kulin
summary: Ban Kulin granted the merchants of Dubrovnik (Ragusa) freedom to trade across Bosnia; the document is one of the oldest state charters of the South Slavs and a landmark of early Bosnian statehood.

title: Stjepan Kotromanić expands Bosnia
summary: Ban Stjepan Kotromanić of the Kotromanić dynasty enlarged Bosnia southward, incorporating the principality of Hum, the territory later known as Herzegovina.

title: Coronation of Tvrtko I
summary: Tvrtko I was crowned king, raising Bosnia from a banate to a kingdom; under him it reached the Dalmatian coast and became, briefly, the most powerful state in the western Balkans.

title: The stećci tombstones
summary: Across medieval Bosnia, communities raised monumental carved limestone tombstones known as stećci; sites in Bosnia and neighbouring lands were inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage in 2016.

title: Ottoman conquest of Bosnia
summary: The armies of Sultan Mehmed II conquered most of Bosnia in 1463, ending the medieval kingdom and beginning more than four centuries of Ottoman rule.

title: Bosnia incorporated into the Ottoman Empire
summary: Following the conquest, Bosnia became an Ottoman province; the settlement of Vrhbosna was developed into Sarajevo, the future provincial capital.

title: Islamization and a multi-confessional society
summary: Over generations much of Bosnia's Slavic population converted to Islam, creating, alongside Orthodox, Catholic and Jewish communities, the uniquely interwoven multi-confessional society that defines the country.

title: The Mehmed Paša Sokolović Bridge, Višegrad
summary: The eleven-arch Ottoman bridge over the Drina at Višegrad was built to designs by the imperial architect Sinan; it was inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage in 2007.

title: The Old Bridge at Mostar (Stari Most)
summary: The single-arch Old Bridge over the Neretva, a masterpiece of Ottoman engineering, gave Mostar its name; the Old City of Mostar was inscribed by UNESCO in 2005 after the bridge's wartime destruction and reconstruction.

title: Herzegovinian uprising and the Eastern Crisis
summary: A peasant revolt in Herzegovina widened into a great-power crisis over the 'Eastern Question', ending Ottoman rule and leading to Austro-Hungarian occupation in 1878.

title: Austro-Hungarian occupation
summary: The Congress of Berlin authorised Austria-Hungary to occupy and administer Bosnia and Herzegovina, ending effective Ottoman rule while leaving nominal sovereignty in Istanbul.

title: Annexation by Austria-Hungary
summary: Vienna formally annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina, triggering a European diplomatic crisis and inflaming South Slav nationalist opposition to Habsburg rule.

title: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
summary: In Sarajevo, Gavrilo Princip of the Young Bosnia movement shot dead Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie, the act that triggered the outbreak of the First World War.

title: Bosnia joins the Yugoslav kingdom
summary: With Austria-Hungary's collapse, Bosnia was incorporated into the new Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, later renamed Yugoslavia, losing its separate administrative identity.

title: Axis invasion and the NDH
summary: The Axis dismembered Yugoslavia and incorporated Bosnia into the Ustaša-led Independent State of Croatia, whose terror against Serbs, Jews and Roma helped ignite a brutal multi-sided civil war.

title: First session of ZAVNOBiH
summary: At Mrkonjić Grad the anti-fascist council ZAVNOBiH proclaimed Bosnia and Herzegovina a federal unit of its equal peoples, ensuring it would be restored as a distinct republic within Yugoslavia.

title: Bosnia a republic of socialist Yugoslavia
summary: After the Partisan victory, Bosnia and Herzegovina became one of the six federal republics of Tito's socialist Yugoslavia, with its multi-ethnic society constitutionally recognised.

title: Sarajevo Winter Olympics
summary: Sarajevo hosted the 1984 Winter Olympic Games, a high point of confidence for the multi-ethnic socialist republic less than a decade before war engulfed the city.

title: Independence referendum
summary: Bosnians voted overwhelmingly for independence in a referendum largely boycotted by Serbs; the country was recognised internationally and joined the UN on 22 May 1992.

title: Siege of Sarajevo begins
summary: Bosnian Serb forces encircled and shelled the capital from the surrounding hills; lasting about 1,425 days, it became the longest siege of a capital city in modern history.

title: Ethnic cleansing and the Bosnian War
summary: Campaigns to expel and destroy rival communities through killings, deportation, detention camps and sexual violence devastated Bosnia, crimes later prosecuted before the ICTY.

title: The Srebrenica genocide
summary: After overrunning the UN 'safe area', Bosnian Serb forces under Ratko Mladić executed up to 8,000 Bosniak men and boys; the ICTY and ICJ ruled the killings genocide.

title: ICJ Genocide judgment (Bosnia v. Serbia)
summary: The International Court of Justice held that genocide was committed at Srebrenica and that Serbia had violated the Genocide Convention by failing to prevent it and to cooperate with the ICTY.

title: Dayton Agreement initialled
summary: After negotiations led by Richard Holbrooke, the General Framework Agreement for Peace was initialled at Dayton, Ohio, ending the Bosnian War.

title: Dayton Agreement signed in Paris
summary: The peace agreement was formally signed in Paris, preserving a single Bosnian state divided into two entities, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, with an Office of the High Representative.

title: Brčko District established
summary: Binding arbitration under Annex 2 created the Brčko District, a self-governing unit held in condominium by both entities under the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

title: EU candidate status granted
summary: The European Council granted Bosnia and Herzegovina the status of EU candidate country, conditional on reforms to the rule of law and the constitutional and electoral system.

title: Rise of the Principality of Polotsk
summary: The Krivichi formed a principality around Polotsk on the Western Dvina, the oldest centre of statehood on Belarusian soil and an early constituent of Kievan Rus with a strong tradition of autonomy.

title: Christianization of the Rus lands
summary: The conversion of Kievan Rus to Orthodox Christianity in the late tenth century bound Polotsk and the Belarusian lands to Byzantine Christendom and its written, ecclesiastical culture.

title: Vseslav of Polotsk seizes Kiev
summary: Prince Vseslav of Polotsk, the principality's most celebrated ruler, briefly held the throne of Kiev itself, a measure of Polotsk's ambition and its rivalry with the senior princes of Rus.

title: The Mongol invasion of Rus
summary: The Mongol onslaught destroyed Kievan Rus and shattered the old federation of principalities; the western Belarusian lands, comparatively sheltered, were soon drawn into the orbit of rising Lithuania.

title: Belarusian lands within the Grand Duchy
summary: Over the 150 years after the Mongol invasion the Grand Duchy of Lithuania expanded to absorb the Belarusian lands, whose Ruthenian (Old Belarusian) tongue became the chancery language of the state.

title: Skaryna prints the first East Slavic book
summary: Francysk Skaryna, born in Polotsk, issued his Psalter from his press in Prague, the first book printed in an East Slavic language, followed by further biblical books in 1517-1519.

title: A printing press in Vilnius
summary: Moving his workshop to Vilnius, capital of the Grand Duchy, Skaryna produced the Little Travel Book and later The Apostle, the first books printed within the Grand Duchy of Lithuania itself.

title: Mir Castle and the Radziwiłł magnates
summary: The Gothic castle at Mir, begun in the 1520s and rebuilt in Renaissance style under the Radziwiłł family, became one of the great fortified residences of the Grand Duchy and is now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

title: Union of Lublin and the Commonwealth
summary: The Union of Lublin merged Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania into the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, placing the Belarusian lands at the heart of a vast federal state and accelerating the Polonisation of their elites.

title: Partitions of Poland and Russian annexation
summary: In three partitions Russia, Prussia and Austria divided the Commonwealth; Russia took most of the Belarusian lands, and after 1795 all of Belarus was ruled by the Russian Empire.

title: Suppression of the Uniate Church and Russification
summary: The Uniate (Greek Catholic) Church was abolished and absorbed into Russian Orthodoxy, part of a sustained imperial policy of Russification that discouraged the Belarusian language and name.

title: The Struve Geodetic Arc
summary: Five of the surviving station points of the Struve Geodetic Arc, the first accurate measurement of a long meridian segment carried out across the empire between 1816 and 1855, lie in Belarus and are inscribed by UNESCO.

title: Nasha Niva and the national awakening
summary: The newspaper Nasha Niva, published in Vilnius from 1906, became the platform of the Belarusian national revival, carrying the early work of the poets Yanka Kupala and Yakub Kolas.

title: Belarusian People's Republic proclaimed
summary: Under German occupation, the Rada in Minsk proclaimed the independence of the Belarusian People's Republic, the first modern declaration of Belarusian statehood, though it never controlled the territory and was soon driven into exile.

title: Founding of the Byelorussian SSR
summary: As the Germans withdrew, the Bolsheviks announced the Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic; in 1922 it became one of the four founding republics of the Soviet Union.

title: Treaty of Riga partitions Belarus
summary: The treaty ending the Polish-Soviet War divided Belarus between Poland and Soviet Russia along the line of the first partition; western Belarus went to Poland and the east became the Byelorussian SSR.

title: Stalinist terror and Kurapaty
summary: Amid forced collectivisation, the NKVD carried out mass executions of Belarusians at Kurapaty near Minsk between 1937 and 1941; the mass graves, revealed in 1988, became the emblem of Soviet repression in Belarus.

title: Reunification of western Belarus
summary: Following the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact and the German invasion of Poland, Soviet forces entered eastern Poland and western Belarus was annexed to the Byelorussian SSR, reuniting the Belarusian lands.

title: Nazi occupation and mass death
summary: The German occupation killed a quarter to a third of the population; the people of Belarus fell from about 9.2 million before the war to roughly 6.3 million by late 1944, with cities like Minsk left in ruins.

title: The Khatyn massacre
summary: German forces and auxiliaries burned the village of Khatyn with its inhabitants, one of hundreds of Belarusian villages annihilated in anti-partisan reprisals and a lasting symbol of the occupation's brutality.

title: Founding member of the United Nations
summary: In recognition of the Belarusian people's role in defeating fascism, the Byelorussian SSR signed the UN Charter at San Francisco in 1945, becoming a founding member of the United Nations despite not being an independent state.

title: The Chernobyl disaster
summary: The reactor explosion at Chernobyl in Ukraine sent about 70 percent of its radioactive fallout onto Belarus, contaminating nearly a quarter of the country's territory and affecting some 2.2 million people.

title: Independence of Belarus
summary: After declaring sovereignty on 27 July 1990, the Supreme Soviet gave the declaration constitutional force on 25 August 1991 in the wake of the Moscow coup, proclaiming the independent Republic of Belarus.

title: Belavezha Accords dissolve the USSR
summary: In the Belavezha forest in Belarus, part of the UNESCO-listed Belovezhskaya Pushcha, the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus, including Stanislau Shushkevich, signed accords declaring that the USSR had ceased to exist and founding the Commonwealth of Independent States.

title: Lukashenka elected president
summary: Alyaksandr Lukashenka won Belarus's first presidential election on an anti-corruption platform and went on to consolidate authoritarian rule and forge ever-deeper ties with Russia.

title: Treaty on the Union State with Russia
summary: Lukashenka and Yeltsin signed a Treaty on the Creation of a Union State, a blueprint for deep Russian-Belarusian integration that has bound the two countries ever closer.

title: Disputed election and mass protests
summary: Lukashenka's claimed landslide re-election sparked the largest protests in Belarusian history; the EU declared the vote neither free nor fair and refused to recognise his mandate, while he held on with Russian support.

title: Maya settlement of the lowlands
summary: Maya-speaking peoples settled the lowland forests and river valleys of present-day Belize, founding farming villages that over centuries grew into towns and cities across the heart of the Maya world.

title: Caracol defeats Tikal
summary: Caracol, allied with Calakmul, won a decisive "Star War" victory over Tikal in 562 CE; the defeated city carved no monuments for over a century, marking Caracol's rise as a great power of the southern lowlands.

title: Height of the Classic Maya cities
summary: Caracol, Xunantunich, Lamanai, Altun Ha and others flourished as ceremonial and political centres, with monumental architecture, hieroglyphic inscriptions and populations in the tens of thousands sustained by intensive agriculture.

title: The Classic Maya collapse
summary: From the late eighth century the southern lowland cities ceased raising monuments and were abandoned, in a prolonged collapse attributed to drought, environmental stress and warfare — though Lamanai and scattered Maya communities endured.

title: British woodcutters settle the coast
summary: English and Scottish buccaneers and logwood cutters began settling the coast of present-day Belize, beyond effective Spanish control; calling themselves the Baymen, they cut logwood for the European dye trade.

title: Enslaved Africans imported for the timber trade
summary: From the early 1700s the Baymen imported enslaved Africans, many via Jamaica and Bermuda, to cut and haul logwood and then mahogany — the labour on which the settlement's forest economy rested.

title: Spain concedes cutting rights
summary: By the treaties of Paris (1763) and Versailles (1783) Spain granted British subjects the right to cut logwood — and after 1786 the more valuable mahogany — within defined limits, while reserving sovereignty over the territory.

title: Battle of St. George's Caye
summary: In engagements off St. George's Caye, the outnumbered Baymen, a small British force and enslaved Africans repelled a Spanish fleet from the Yucatán; the Spanish withdrew on 10 September, ending the last attempt to expel the settlers.

title: The Garifuna reach the southern coast
summary: The Garifuna (Garinagu), deported by the British from St. Vincent, settled the southern coast around Stann Creek and Punta Gorda; their arrival on 19 November is marked as Garifuna Settlement Day, a national holiday from 1941.

title: Emancipation completed
summary: Following abolition across the British Empire from 1834, the apprenticeship system ended in British Honduras on 1 August 1838, freeing the enslaved; the freed African population formed the core of the colony's Creole society.

title: Caste War refugees swell the population
summary: The Caste War of Yucatán drove thousands of Maya and Spanish-speaking Mestizo refugees into the colony's north and west, adding to the Creole and Garifuna populations and deepening Belize's plural society.

title: The Anglo-Guatemalan boundary treaty
summary: Britain and Guatemala signed a treaty fixing the settlement's limits from the Río Hondo to the Sarstoon; the unfulfilled Article 7, promising a means of communication never built, became the root of Guatemala's later claim.

title: The Colony of British Honduras
summary: The settlement was formally declared the Colony of British Honduras under a lieutenant-governor subordinate to Jamaica; it became a separate Crown Colony in 1871 and was made independent of Jamaica under its own governor in 1884.

title: The People's United Party founded
summary: Amid anger over the 1949 currency devaluation, the People's United Party was founded and soon led by George Cadle Price; it championed democratic rights and self-rule and would dominate Belizean politics for decades.

title: Universal adult suffrage
summary: Britain granted universal adult suffrage to British Honduras in 1954; the PUP won the ensuing elections, beginning a long run of electoral dominance that carried Price's party toward self-government and independence.

title: Internal self-government
summary: Under a new constitution Britain granted internal self-government, retaining only defence and foreign affairs; George Price became premier, with Belizeans now running their own domestic affairs.

title: British Honduras renamed Belize
summary: In June 1973 the colony's name was officially changed from British Honduras to Belize, an assertion of national identity adopted eight years before formal independence.

title: Independence as Belize
summary: Belize became an independent state within the Commonwealth on 21 September 1981 with George Price as first prime minister — the last British colony on the Central American mainland to win independence, its frontier still claimed by Guatemala.

title: Recognition and an embassy
summary: Five weeks after independence the United States raises its consulate general to embassy status, recognising Belize and establishing diplomatic relations on the same day.

title: Barrier Reef made a World Heritage site
summary: UNESCO inscribed the Belize Barrier Reef Reserve System — seven protected areas including the Blue Hole and Half Moon Caye — as a World Heritage site, recognising the largest reef in the Atlantic-Caribbean and second-largest on Earth.

title: Special Agreement on the dispute
summary: Belize and Guatemala signed a Special Agreement committing to submit Guatemala's territorial, insular and maritime claim to the International Court of Justice, subject to approval by referendum in each country.

title: Belize votes to go to the ICJ
summary: After Guatemalans approved referral on 15 April 2018, Belizeans voted on 8 May 2019 to submit the dispute to the International Court of Justice; the Court was seised of the case on 7 June 2019.

title: Pleadings before the World Court
summary: Guatemala and Belize filed written pleadings before the International Court of Justice in the case "Guatemala's Territorial, Insular and Maritime Claim (Guatemala/Belize)", moving toward a final, binding judgment on the century-old dispute.

title: A nation of 419,000
summary: The Statistical Institute of Belize puts the mid-year population at 418,982 — a country the size of Wales with fewer people than a mid-sized city, holding the Atlantic's largest reef and some of the Maya world's greatest cities.

title: Tiwanaku reaches its apogee
summary: The city of Tiwanaku near Lake Titicaca flourishes as the spiritual and political centre of a powerful Andean culture, building the monumental complex later inscribed by UNESCO.

title: The Aymara lordships
summary: After Tiwanaku's decline, Aymara-speaking kingdoms dominate the highlands around Lake Titicaca until the rise of the Inca.

title: Inca conquest of the highlands
summary: The Inca empire expands south into the region the Spanish would call Charcas, absorbing the Aymara lands while permitting them their language and identity.

title: Spanish conquest of Charcas
summary: Spanish forces subdue the highlands of Upper Peru, organising them as the Audiencia of Charcas within the Viceroyalty of Peru.

title: Silver discovered at Cerro Rico
summary: The discovery of immense silver deposits in the mountain above Potosi sets off a boom that makes the city one of the largest and richest in the world.

title: Toledo systematises the mita
summary: Viceroy Francisco de Toledo organises the mita, a forced labour draft that compels indigenous men across the Andes to work the deadly mines and mercury refineries of Potosi.

title: Potosi feeds the Spanish empire
summary: Potosi's silver becomes the principal source of bullion for the Spanish crown, financing its empire while consuming the lives of indigenous mitayos.

title: Tupac Katari besieges La Paz
summary: The Aymara leader Tupac Katari, part of the great Andean rebellion begun by Tupac Amaru II, lays siege to La Paz before being captured and executed.

title: Uprisings at Chuquisaca and La Paz
summary: Revolts in Upper Peru in 1809, sparked by the Spanish crisis under Napoleon, are remembered among the first independence movements in the Americas.

title: Battle of Ayacucho
summary: Antonio Jose de Sucre routs the last great royalist army at Ayacucho, sealing the independence of Spanish South America and opening the way to liberate Charcas.

title: Republic of Bolivia proclaimed
summary: A congress at Chuquisaca declares the independence of Upper Peru as a republic named Bolivia in honour of Simon Bolivar, with Sucre soon its first president.

title: War of the Pacific
summary: Chile defeats Bolivia and its ally Peru and annexes Bolivia's coast; Bolivia loses its Pacific province of Antofagasta and becomes landlocked.

title: Treaty confirms the loss of the coast
summary: A treaty between Bolivia and Chile formally cedes the Pacific coast to Chile, fixing Bolivia's landlocked status and a lasting national grievance.

title: The age of the tin barons
summary: Tin replaces silver as Bolivia's great export, making a handful of mine owners enormously rich while the indigenous mine workers labour in poverty.

title: The Chaco War with Paraguay
summary: Bolivia is defeated by Paraguay in a brutal war over the Gran Chaco, losing most of the disputed land and discrediting the old governing order.

title: The National Revolution
summary: A popular insurrection brings the MNR and Victor Paz Estenssoro to power, launching reforms that reshape Bolivia.

title: Tin nationalised, suffrage and land reform
summary: The revolutionary government nationalises the tin mines, grants universal suffrage to the indigenous majority, and decrees a sweeping agrarian reform.

title: Military coup ends the revolution
summary: The armed forces overthrow Paz Estenssoro, ending the revolutionary era and beginning eighteen years of military rule.

title: Death of Che Guevara
summary: The revolutionary Ernesto Che Guevara is captured and killed by the Bolivian army while leading a failed guerrilla campaign in the southeast.

title: Return to democracy
summary: After years of military rule and the violent Garcia Meza regime, the armed forces cede power to Congress, which makes Hernan Siles Zuazo president.

title: Hyperinflation and stabilisation
summary: Amid catastrophic hyperinflation, a returning Paz Estenssoro imposes a drastic stabilisation programme that ends the crisis but brings severe austerity.

title: Evo Morales takes office
summary: Evo Morales, leader of the MAS, becomes Bolivia's first indigenous president, beginning an era of indigenous-majority politics and hydrocarbon nationalisation.

title: Plurinational constitution
summary: A new constitution refounds Bolivia as a plurinational state recognising its indigenous nations and expanding their rights.

title: Disputed election and Morales's resignation
summary: After a contested October vote that an OAS audit found marred by irregularities, weeks of protest and the loss of military and police support lead Morales to resign and go into exile.

title: Return of the MAS under Arce
summary: Luis Arce wins the presidency for the MAS, returning the party to power a year after Morales's fall.

title: Turn to the centre-right
summary: Amid economic crisis and a split between Arce and Morales, the centrist Rodrigo Paz wins the presidency, ending nearly twenty years of MAS rule.

title: Ancient settlement of the land
summary: Hunter-gatherer peoples occupy what is now Brazil over many millennia, leaving rock art and ancient sites across the interior and the northeast.

title: Tupi-Guarani expansion
summary: Tupi-Guarani-speaking peoples spread across the Atlantic coast and into the interior, developing the farming and village societies later encountered by Europeans.

title: Complex Amazonian societies
summary: Riverine peoples of Amazonia sustain substantial settled populations, managing forests and soils on a scale long underestimated by outsiders.

title: Some thousand nations at contact
summary: On the eve of European arrival, perhaps two to four million people in hundreds of distinct nations inhabit the territory of present-day Brazil.

title: Cabral claims Brazil for Portugal
summary: Pedro Alvares Cabral makes landfall on the coast near present-day Porto Seguro and claims the land for the Portuguese crown.

title: The sugar economy
summary: Sugar plantations and mills worked by enslaved labour rise in Pernambuco and Bahia, making Brazil a leading producer and the colony's chief source of wealth.

title: Transatlantic slave trade
summary: Brazil becomes the largest single destination of the Atlantic slave trade, receiving roughly 4.8-5 million enslaved Africans over more than three centuries.

title: Gold rush in Minas Gerais
summary: The discovery of gold in the interior sets off a vast rush, founding towns such as Ouro Preto and shifting the colony's centre southward.

title: The court moves to Rio
summary: Fleeing Napoleon, the Portuguese royal court relocates to Rio de Janeiro, which becomes the seat of the empire and is opened to wider trade.

title: Independence and the Empire
summary: Dom Pedro proclaims independence at the Cry of Ipiranga and is acclaimed Emperor Pedro I, founding the Empire of Brazil.

title: Reign of Pedro II begins
summary: Pedro II assumes personal rule, beginning a long reign that brings political stability and the rise of the coffee economy.

title: War of the Triple Alliance
summary: Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay defeat Paraguay in the deadliest war in South American history, at enormous human and financial cost.

title: Abolition of slavery
summary: Princess Isabel signs the Lei Aurea, abolishing slavery without compensation; Brazil is the last country in the Americas to do so.

title: Proclamation of the Republic
summary: A military coup led by Marshal Deodoro da Fonseca deposes Pedro II and proclaims the Republic, ending the monarchy.

title: First republican constitution
summary: The Constitution of 1891 establishes a federal republic with strong states, modelled in part on the United States.

title: War of Canudos
summary: The army crushes a large millenarian community in the Bahian backlands, exposing the gulf between the republican coast and the impoverished interior.

title: Mass immigration
summary: Millions of immigrants, especially Italians, Portuguese, Spaniards, and Japanese, arrive to work coffee and settle the south, reshaping Brazilian society.

title: Revolution of 1930
summary: A disputed election amid the Depression brings down the Old Republic, and Getulio Vargas takes power, beginning a new era.

title: The Estado Novo
summary: Vargas imposes a centralised dictatorship, ruling by decree, banning parties, and censoring the press until his ouster in 1945.

title: Inauguration of Brasilia
summary: The purpose-built modernist capital, designed by Lucio Costa and Oscar Niemeyer, is inaugurated in the interior, shifting Brazil's centre of gravity inland.

title: Military coup
summary: The armed forces overthrow President Joao Goulart and seize power, beginning twenty-one years of military dictatorship.

title: Institutional Act Number Five
summary: AI-5 suspends habeas corpus and civil liberties, opening the regime's most repressive phase of censorship, torture, and disappearances.

title: Return to civilian rule
summary: After a gradual political opening, the military hands power back to civilians, ending the dictatorship.

title: The Citizen Constitution
summary: A new constitution restores full democracy and enshrines an expansive charter of civil, political, and social rights.

title: Plano Real ends hyperinflation
summary: A new currency and stabilisation plan tame runaway inflation, reshaping the economy and politics of the 1990s.

title: Lula and social inclusion
summary: Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's governments expand social programmes during a commodities boom, lifting millions out of poverty.

title: Impeachment amid Lava Jato
summary: President Dilma Rousseff is impeached as the sweeping Car Wash corruption investigation reshapes Brazilian politics.

title: Brasilia attacked, democracy holds
summary: Supporters of the defeated president storm the Congress, presidential palace, and Supreme Court; the institutions withstand the assault.

title: Brunei trades with China as Po-ni
summary: Chinese sources record a trading kingdom on the north coast of Borneo, called Po-ni, exchanging tribute and goods with the Chinese empire from around the 6th century.

title: Boni described as a wealthy maritime kingdom
summary: A Chinese account portrays Boni as a prosperous state with a fleet to protect its trade in camphor, spices, and forest products drawn from the Bornean interior.

title: Tributary ties to Majapahit
summary: Brunei comes under the cultural and political influence of the Hindu Javanese empire of Majapahit, to which it pays tribute, while maintaining its long-standing relationship with China.

title: Conversion to Islam and the first sultan
summary: Awang Alak Betatar embraces Islam, takes the title Sultan Muhammad Shah, and becomes the first sultan of Brunei, refounding the state as an Islamic sultanate.

title: Founding of the ruling dynasty
summary: The line descended from Muhammad Shah, later the House of Bolkiah, establishes itself as Brunei's royal house, beginning a continuous monarchy that endures to the present.

title: Accession of Sultan Bolkiah
summary: Bolkiah, the fifth sultan, comes to the throne and presides over Brunei's golden age, expanding the sultanate's dominion across Borneo and the surrounding seas.

title: Empire at its zenith
summary: Under Bolkiah, Brunei's power extends over the whole of Borneo, the Sulu Archipelago, and into the Philippines, with Bruneian influence reaching as far as Manila.

title: Magellan's expedition reaches Brunei
summary: The ships of Ferdinand Magellan's circumnavigation anchor off Brunei and record a wealthy capital ruled by the great Bolkiah, who controls Borneo and neighbouring islands.

title: Spanish attack on the capital
summary: A Spanish expedition from the Philippines briefly captures Brunei's capital during a war with the sultanate before being forced to withdraw, signalling the new European challenge.

title: Cession of Sarawak to James Brooke
summary: After helping put down a revolt, the English adventurer James Brooke is made rajah of Sarawak, founding the White Rajah dynasty and beginning the dismemberment of Brunei's territory.

title: Labuan ceded to Britain
summary: Brunei cedes the island of Labuan in Brunei Bay to Great Britain, which establishes it as a crown colony, further reducing the sultanate's holdings.

title: Brunei becomes a British protectorate
summary: Sultan Hashim signs a treaty placing Brunei under British protection, transferring control of its foreign affairs to Britain while preserving the sultanate from absorption.

title: British Residency system imposed
summary: A supplementary agreement installs a British Resident to advise the sultan on all matters but Malay custom and Islam; in practice the Resident comes to run the administration.

title: Oil struck at Seria
summary: The British Malayan Petroleum Company, a Shell enterprise, makes the first commercial oil discovery at Seria, launching the petroleum industry that would make Brunei rich.

title: Japanese occupation begins
summary: Japanese forces land at Kuala Belait and quickly occupy Brunei, seizing the strategically vital Seria oil fields; the occupation lasts until 1945.

title: Allied liberation
summary: Australian troops land in Brunei Bay during the Borneo Campaign, ending the Japanese occupation; the capital and much of the country lie in ruins from the fighting and must be rebuilt after the war.

title: Constitution grants self-government
summary: A written constitution gives Brunei internal self-government and ends the British Residency, with Britain keeping control of defence and foreign affairs.

title: The Brunei revolt
summary: The Parti Rakyat Brunei's armed wing launches an uprising against the sultanate and the Malaysia plan; British forces crush it within days, and the party is banned.

title: Brunei stays out of Malaysia
summary: Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddien III decides not to join the new Federation of Malaysia, keeping Brunei on a separate course toward eventual independence.

title: Accession of Hassanal Bolkiah
summary: Omar Ali Saifuddien III abdicates in favour of his son Hassanal Bolkiah, who becomes the 29th sultan and would go on to be the world's longest-reigning living monarch.

title: Full independence and Malay Islamic Monarchy
summary: Brunei resumes full sovereignty from Britain; the sultan becomes prime minister and proclaims Melayu Islam Beraja, the Malay Islamic Monarchy, as the national philosophy.

title: Sharia penal code phased in
summary: Brunei begins implementing a strict Sharia penal code in stages, with later phases drawing international condemnation, while pursuing the Wawasan 2035 plan to diversify beyond oil.

title: First Buddhist temples founded
summary: Tibetan tradition credits King Songtsen Gampo with building the earliest Buddhist temples in the Bhutanese valleys, including Kyichu Lhakhang at Paro, as Buddhism spread south from Tibet.

title: Guru Rinpoche brings Buddhism to Bhutan
summary: The tantric master Guru Padmasambhava (Guru Rinpoche) is said to have travelled into Bhutan, blessing sites such as Bumthang and the Taktsang cliff at Paro and marking the proper advent of Buddhism in the country.

title: Drukpa Kagyu tradition takes root
summary: The Drukpa ('Dragon') Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism spreads into the southern valleys and becomes the dominant religious tradition, lending Bhutan its name Druk Yul, the Land of the Thunder Dragon.

title: Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal arrives in Bhutan
summary: Fleeing a sectarian dispute in Tibet, the Drukpa Kagyu lama Ngawang Namgyal enters western Bhutan and is recognised as the Zhabdrung, beginning the unification of the country.

title: Punakha Dzong founded
summary: The Zhabdrung begins building Punakha Dzong at the confluence of two rivers as his capital, one of a network of fortress-monasteries that became the seats of Bhutan's temporal and religious power.

title: Dual system of government established
summary: The Zhabdrung institutes the chhoesi dual system, splitting power between a spiritual Je Khenpo and a secular Druk Desi; his death around this time is concealed to preserve the fledgling state.

title: A Chinese imperial army enters Bhutan
summary: Qing forces invade and briefly establish control — the first of three outside powers to reach into the valleys within two centuries.

title: The first British intervention
summary: A century before the Duar War, British forces intervene in Bhutan — the beginning of the Raj's long pressure on its southern frontier.

title: The Duar War with British India
summary: After a failed British mission and disputes over the southern duars, Britain and Bhutan fight a five-month war that ends in Bhutanese defeat.

title: Treaty of Sinchula
summary: Bhutan cedes the Bengal and Assam duars to British India in exchange for an annual subsidy, fixing its modern southern border and binding it to the Raj.

title: Treaty of Punakha
summary: Revising the Sinchula terms, Britain increases Bhutan's subsidy and pledges non-interference in internal affairs while guiding its foreign relations, securing Bhutan's continued independence.

title: Ugyen Wangchuck crowned first king
summary: An assembly at Punakha Dzong unanimously elects Ugyen Wangchuck, penlop of Tongsa, as the first hereditary Druk Gyalpo, ending the dual system and founding the Wangchuck dynasty.

title: Accession of the second king
summary: On Ugyen Wangchuck's death the crown passes peacefully to his son Jigme Wangchuck, confirming the stability of the new hereditary monarchy.

title: The treaty with independent India
summary: Delhi guarantees non-interference in Bhutan's internal affairs while retaining influence over its foreign relations — the terms of British Punakha, inherited by a new republic.

title: National Assembly established
summary: King Jigme Dorji Wangchuck creates the Tshogdu, Bhutan's National Assembly, beginning the reform of the country's institutions alongside the abolition of serfdom and land redistribution.

title: Bhutan joins the United Nations
summary: Bhutan is admitted as the 128th member of the United Nations, a milestone in its emergence from isolation and its assertion of full sovereignty.

title: Gross National Happiness proclaimed
summary: On acceding to the throne, the young fourth king Jigme Singye Wangchuck advances Gross National Happiness as Bhutan's guiding measure of development, valuing well-being and culture over GDP alone.

title: Slavery abolished
summary: The third king abolishes slavery and serfdom, one of the first acts of a reign that would open a closed kingdom deliberately and slowly.

title: The first foreign tourists
summary: Bhutan admits its first tourists — a controlled opening, priced and permitted rather than free, and still the model today.

title: The census and the citizenship rules
summary: A census brands many ethnic Nepalis illegal immigrants, and measures stressing Tibetan-derived Bhutanese culture antagonise the Lhotshampa; violent unrest follows in the south in 1990.

title: Exodus of the Lhotshampa
summary: Amid 'one nation, one people' measures and stricter citizenship rules, tens of thousands of southern Bhutanese of Nepali origin leave or are expelled, and more than 100,000 end up in UNHCR camps in eastern Nepal.

title: Resettlement of Bhutanese refugees
summary: A multinational programme led by UNHCR and IOM resettles over 100,000 Bhutanese refugees from Nepal to countries including the United States, Canada, Australia and Europe.

title: Television and the internet arrive
summary: Limited television and internet services are permitted and several dozen political prisoners released, a decade after the kingdom tightened.

title: The treaty with India revised
summary: A new agreement gives Bhutan more say over its own foreign and defence policy, loosening a constraint carried from 1910 through 1949.

title: Constitution and democratic monarchy
summary: Following the country's first parliamentary elections, Bhutan's written Constitution comes into force, transforming the kingdom into a democratic constitutional monarchy with Gross National Happiness as a goal of the state.

title: Coronation of the fifth king
summary: Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck is formally enthroned as the fifth Druk Gyalpo, his coronation timed to the centenary of the Wangchuck monarchy and the inauguration of democratic rule.

title: A prime minister questions Gross National Happiness
summary: Tshering Tobgay says the concept is overused and masks real problems — rising debt, chronic unemployment, poverty and corruption.

title: Rock art at Tsodilo Hills
summary: San hunter-gatherers paint the Tsodilo Hills; some images are dated to around 24,000 years before present, part of a record of over 4,500 paintings.

title: Herders and farmers arrive
summary: Peoples bringing cattle, sheep and pottery move into present-day Botswana, beginning the long shift from hunter-gathering toward herding and farming societies.

title: Early Bantu settlement
summary: Bantu-speaking settlers, among them the ancestors of the Kalanga, establish farming and cattle-keeping communities in the eastern part of the region.

title: Rise of the Tswana merafe
summary: The Bangwaketse form the first major Tswana state in the region, followed by the Bakwena, Bangwato and Batawana, cattle-keeping chiefdoms ruled by dikgosi.

title: The difaqane convulses the region
summary: Wars and forced migrations linked to the wider mfecane/difaqane disrupt Tswana society, bringing raiding, displacement and famine.

title: Sebego expels the Kololo
summary: Sebego, regent of the Bangwaketse, raises some 4,000 men and permanently drives the invading Kololo out of the region.

title: Ndebele raids under Mzilikazi
summary: Mzilikazi's Ndebele raid Tswana communities through the 1830s, capturing cattle, women and children before migrating north across the Limpopo.

title: London Missionary Society arrives
summary: LMS missionaries reach the Tswana lands; Robert Moffat later founds Kuruman and translates the Bible into Setswana.

title: Livingstone founds Kolobeng
summary: David Livingstone establishes the Kolobeng mission among the Bakwena near Kgosi Sechele, his only church and the source of his single convert.

title: Boer attack on the Bakwena
summary: Transvaal Boers attack Sechele's Bakwena and sack Livingstone's Kolobeng mission, part of mounting pressure from the Transvaal on Tswana land.

title: Khama III becomes kgosi of the Bangwato
summary: The Christian reformer Khama III takes the Bangwato chieftainship, banning liquor and aligning his powerful morafe with the missionaries.

title: Bechuanaland Protectorate declared
summary: After Sir Charles Warren's expedition, Britain proclaims a protectorate over the territory north of the Molopo to check Boer and German expansion.

title: The three kings' mission to Britain
summary: Khama III, Sebele I and Bathoen I travel to Britain and persuade the government to keep the protectorate out of Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company.

title: Capital moved to Mafeking
summary: The protectorate's administration is seated at Mafeking, a town outside the territory's own borders, where it remains until the 1960s.

title: Seretse Khama marries Ruth Williams
summary: Bangwato heir Seretse Khama marries Englishwoman Ruth Williams in London, igniting a crisis with apartheid South Africa and Britain.

title: Exile and return of Seretse Khama
summary: Britain exiles Seretse and Ruth to appease South Africa; he is allowed home in 1956 after renouncing the Bangwato throne, fuelling nationalism.

title: BDP wins the first general election
summary: Seretse Khama's Bechuanaland Democratic Party wins self-government elections; Gaborone is built as the new capital.

title: Independence of Botswana
summary: The protectorate becomes the Republic of Botswana with Seretse Khama as first president, entering nationhood as one of the world's poorest states.

title: Diamonds discovered at Orapa
summary: De Beers geologists locate a major diamond kimberlite pipe at Orapa, the find that would transform Botswana's economy.

title: Debswana partnership formed
summary: Botswana and De Beers form a 50-50 joint venture to mine diamonds, securing for the state a direct share of mineral wealth.

title: Death of Seretse Khama
summary: Botswana's founding president dies in office; power passes peacefully to Vice-President Quett Masire, confirming the country's democratic stability.

title: The megaliths of Bouar are raised
summary: Farmers near Bouar in the west erected multi-ton standing stones (tazunu), among the most important prehistoric monuments in Central Africa and evidence of organised Neolithic communities.

title: Ironworking and migration
summary: Ubangian, Central Sudanic and Bantu-speaking peoples settled the watershed and ironworking spread, laying down the ethnic patchwork of Gbaya, Banda, Zande, Nzakara and others.

title: Zande and Bandia kingdoms expand
summary: Under the Avongara nobility the Zande spread across the south-east, while the Bandia clan founded Ubangi River states including the Nzakara kingdom and the sultanate of Bangassou.

title: Dar al-Kuti founded under Wadai
summary: The sultanate of Dar al-Kuti was established as a tributary of Dar Runga and ultimately of Wadai, becoming a staging ground for slave raids into the Banda and Nzakara lands to the south.

title: Al-Zubayr installs al-Sanusi at Dar al-Kuti
summary: The Sudanese warlord Rabih az-Zubayr (al-Zubayr) deposed Kobur and installed Muhammad al-Sanusi, who from his base at Ndélé intensified the razzias that depopulated much of the Ubangi region.

title: France founds Bangui
summary: French forces established a post at Bangui on the Ubangi River, the base from which they extended control over the territory that became the colony of Ubangi-Shari.

title: Concessionary companies take over
summary: France leased huge tracts of Ubangi-Shari to private companies such as the Company of the Upper Ubangi Sultanates, whose militias exacted rubber and ivory through brutal forced labour.

title: Death of al-Sanusi of Dar al-Kuti
summary: French forces killed Muhammad al-Sanusi at Ndélé, ending the slave-raiding sultanate of Dar al-Kuti; his successor's resistance was suppressed by 1912.

title: Kongo-Wara rebellion
summary: The Gbaya prophet Karinou led a mass revolt against forced labour and railway recruitment; the French killed him in December 1928 and crushed the uprising by 1931, with thousands dead.

title: Boganda founds MESAN
summary: Barthélemy Boganda, the territory's first deputy to the French National Assembly, founded the Movement for the Social Evolution of Black Africa, the engine of Central African nationalism.

title: Death of Boganda
summary: Boganda, who had proclaimed the autonomous republic in December 1958 and championed a 'United States of Latin Africa', died in a plane crash months before independence; David Dacko succeeded him.

title: Independence from France
summary: The Central African Republic became fully independent, with David Dacko as its first president and Bangui as its capital.

title: Ubangi-Shari joins French Equatorial Africa
summary: The dependency France set up in 1894 is folded into the federation governed from Brazzaville, a structure that lasted until independence.

title: An assembly, and a seat in Paris
summary: The territory gains its own assembly and representation in the French parliament; Barthélemy Boganda becomes the first Central African elected to it.

title: Self-government under Boganda
summary: Ubangi-Shari achieves self-government within French Equatorial Africa with Boganda as prime minister, months before his death in an air crash.

title: Bokassa seizes power
summary: Army commander Jean-Bédel Bokassa overthrew President David Dacko in the Saint-Sylvestre coup, beginning more than a decade of personal rule.

title: Coronation of Emperor Bokassa I
summary: Having declared the Central African Empire in 1976, Bokassa crowned himself emperor in a lavish ceremony costing about US$20 million while the country remained among the world's poorest.

title: Killing of schoolchildren
summary: Protests against compulsory school uniforms ended in the massacre of scores of detained children and students in Bangui, an atrocity widely linked to Bokassa that hastened the end of his rule.

title: France overthrows Bokassa
summary: A French military operation (Barracuda) deposed Bokassa and restored David Dacko; Bokassa fled into exile and was later tried and convicted.

title: Bozizé seizes power
summary: After coups by André Kolingba (1981) and an elected interlude under Ange-Félix Patassé, army chief François Bozizé overthrew Patassé, continuing the cycle of armed takeovers.

title: Patassé ends twelve years of military rule
summary: Ange-Félix Patassé wins the presidency in elections that close the era opened by Bokassa and continued by his successors.

title: Séléka captures Bangui
summary: The Séléka rebel coalition seized the capital and ousted President Bozizé; its leader Michel Djotodia declared himself president, the country's first Muslim head of state.

title: Sectarian civil war erupts
summary: Reprisals between Séléka and the anti-balaka militias spiralled into sectarian massacres; attacks in Bangui in early December 2013 killed more than a thousand civilians.

title: UN establishes MINUSCA
summary: After French and African Union deployments, the UN Security Council authorised the MINUSCA peacekeeping mission in April 2014; it assumed responsibility in September, alongside interim president Catherine Samba-Panza.

title: Khartoum peace agreement
summary: President Touadéra's government and fourteen armed groups signed a peace accord in Khartoum, but implementation was partial and fighting soon resumed.

title: CPC offensive and Wagner
summary: A rebel coalition (the CPC) attacked around the December 2020 elections; the government, increasingly backed by Russian Wagner Group mercenaries deployed from 2018, pushed it back with MINUSCA's help.

title: Peopling of the continent
summary: The ancestors of First Nations were established across the Americas by the end of the last Ice Age, developing diverse societies, languages, and economies over thousands of years before European contact.

title: Norse arrival at L'Anse aux Meadows
summary: Norse explorers established a short-lived base at L'Anse aux Meadows on the northern tip of Newfoundland around the year 1000 — the first known European presence in the Americas, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: John Cabot reaches the Atlantic coast
summary: Sailing for England, John Cabot reached the coast of present-day Atlantic Canada in 1497, beginning the sustained European interest in the region's fisheries and lands that would follow.

title: Jacques Cartier explores the St. Lawrence
summary: Jacques Cartier explored the Gulf of St. Lawrence and claimed the region for France, opening the way for later French interest in the fur trade and settlement.

title: Champlain founds Quebec
summary: Samuel de Champlain established Quebec as a fortified trading post on the St. Lawrence, founding the colony of New France and anchoring the French fur trade in alliance with Indigenous nations.

title: Founding of Montreal
summary: French missionaries and settlers founded Ville-Marie, the future Montreal, as a mission and trading settlement that became a hub of the fur trade and a gateway to the interior.

title: Battle of the Plains of Abraham
summary: British forces defeated the French outside Quebec City in the decisive Battle of the Plains of Abraham, the turning point of the Seven Years' War in North America that led to the fall of New France.

title: Treaty of Paris cedes New France to Britain
summary: The Treaty of Paris ended the Seven Years' War, with France ceding its North American mainland territories to Britain and bringing the French Catholic population of Canada under British rule.

title: Quebec Act
summary: The Quebec Act restored French civil law, guaranteed freedom of Catholic worship, and enlarged Quebec's boundaries, securing the loyalty of French Canadians while inflaming the Thirteen Colonies.

title: Constitutional Act divides the Canadas
summary: The Constitutional Act split Quebec into Upper Canada and Lower Canada, creating separate English- and French-majority colonies each with an elected assembly.

title: Rebellions in Upper and Lower Canada
summary: Armed uprisings against oligarchic colonial rule in both Canadas were suppressed but led to Lord Durham's report and, ultimately, to responsible government.

title: Confederation — the Dominion of Canada
summary: The British North America Act united Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick into the self-governing Dominion of Canada, with Sir John A. Macdonald as first prime minister.

title: Red River Resistance and Manitoba
summary: Métis led by Louis Riel resisted the transfer of Rupert's Land to Canada, securing rights that shaped the creation of the province of Manitoba in 1870.

title: The Indian Act
summary: The Indian Act consolidated federal control over the lives, lands, and governance of First Nations peoples, becoming a central instrument of assimilation and dispossession that remains in force in amended form.

title: Canadian Pacific Railway completed
summary: The driving of the last spike at Craigellachie completed the transcontinental Canadian Pacific Railway, binding the new nation together and fulfilling a promise made to British Columbia at Confederation.

title: North-West Resistance and the execution of Riel
summary: Métis and First Nations grievances on the prairies erupted in the North-West Resistance; its defeat and the hanging of Louis Riel deepened the divide between French and English Canada.

title: Canada in the First World War
summary: Canada fought in the First World War as part of the British Empire but as a distinct national force; the costly victory at Vimy Ridge in 1917 became a symbol of emerging nationhood.

title: Conscription Crisis
summary: The imposition of compulsory military service deeply divided English and French Canada, becoming one of the most divisive episodes in Canadian political history.

title: Statute of Westminster
summary: The Statute of Westminster granted Canada legislative independence from the British Parliament, a landmark in its evolution toward full sovereignty.

title: Canada in the Second World War
summary: Canada entered the Second World War by its own parliamentary decision and mobilised on a vast scale, contributing major forces to the Allied victory and emerging more industrialised and autonomous.

title: A new national flag and a maturing identity
summary: Canada adopted the red-and-white maple leaf flag in 1965, a symbol of a distinct national identity as the post-war country built a welfare state and universal health care.

title: Official multiculturalism policy
summary: Canada became the first country to adopt multiculturalism as official government policy, within a bilingual framework, recognising the contributions of diverse cultural communities.

title: Patriation of the Constitution
summary: The Constitution Act, 1982, patriated Canada's constitution, entrenched the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, recognised Aboriginal rights, and ended the need for British legislation — completing Canada's path to full sovereignty.

title: Quebec sovereignty referendum
summary: Quebec voters narrowly rejected sovereignty in the 1995 referendum, the closest of two votes on independence, underlining the enduring tension over the place of Quebec within Canada.

title: Truth and Reconciliation Commission reports
summary: After years of survivor testimony, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission documented the harms of the residential school system, described it as cultural genocide, and issued 94 Calls to Action for reconciliation.

title: The Federal Charter of the forest cantons
summary: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden sealed a charter of mutual aid against outside lords, refusing foreign judges and pledging to keep the peace; later regarded as the founding act of the Swiss Confederation and its oldest constitutional document.

title: Battle of Morgarten
summary: Men of Schwyz and Uri ambushed and destroyed a Habsburg army of knights under Duke Leopold I at Morgarten, the first great victory of the Confederation and a celebrated triumph of foot soldiers over mounted nobility.

title: Battle of Sempach
summary: The Confederates routed a Habsburg army at Sempach and killed Duke Leopold III of Austria, breaking Habsburg power in the region and confirming the Confederacy as a serious military force.

title: The Burgundian Wars
summary: Swiss and allied armies defeated Charles the Bold of Burgundy at Grandson and Murten in 1476 and at Nancy in 1477, where Charles fell; victory destroyed Burgundy as a power and made Swiss pikemen the most feared infantry in Europe.

title: The Confederacy of thirteen cantons
summary: With the accession of Appenzell the league reached its early-modern form of thirteen cantons, a loose alliance of self-governing communities bound by oath rather than ruled by a single sovereign.

title: Battle of Marignano
summary: A French army under Francis I decisively defeated the Swiss near Milan, the first great Swiss defeat in two hundred years; the Confederates withdrew from Italy, a retreat traditionally seen as the dawn of Swiss neutrality.

title: Zwingli's Reformation in Zürich
summary: Huldrych Zwingli began preaching reform from the Grossmünster in Zürich, launching the Swiss Reformation; the movement won over several cities while the inner cantons remained Catholic, dividing the Confederation by confession.

title: Calvin and the Reformation in Geneva
summary: John Calvin began the work that made Geneva the international centre of Reformed Protestantism, deepening the confessional division between the Protestant west and Catholic centre of Switzerland.

title: Peace of Westphalia: independence from the Empire
summary: The settlement ending the Thirty Years' War formally recognised the Swiss Confederation's exemption from the Holy Roman Empire, confirming in law the independence the cantons had long held in fact.

title: French invasion and the Helvetic Republic
summary: Revolutionary France conquered Switzerland and replaced the old Confederation with the Helvetic Republic, a centralised unitary state that abolished cantonal sovereignty and the privileges of the patrician towns.

title: Napoleon's Act of Mediation
summary: After years of factional strife Napoleon imposed the Act of Mediation, restoring a confederal system and creating six new full cantons, including Vaud and Ticino, while keeping Switzerland tied to France.

title: Congress of Vienna recognises permanent neutrality
summary: The European powers declared the perpetual neutrality of Switzerland to be in Europe's interest and guaranteed its territory; confirmed by the Treaty of Paris later that year, this made armed neutrality the foundation of Swiss policy.

title: The borders of modern Switzerland fixed
summary: The Vienna settlement restored the cantons and set the Confederation's external borders, which have remained almost unchanged since, leaving curiosities such as the foreign enclaves of Büsingen and Campione d'Italia.

title: The Sonderbund War
summary: After seven Catholic cantons formed the separatist Sonderbund, the federal army under General Dufour defeated it in under a month with fewer than a hundred deaths, ending Switzerland's last civil war.

title: The Federal Constitution
summary: Switzerland adopted a federal constitution that turned the loose confederation into a modern federal state with a Federal Assembly, a collegial executive and a single market, while preserving the cantons; the assembly first met in Bern in November 1848.

title: Dunant at the Battle of Solferino
summary: The Geneva businessman Henri Dunant witnessed the carnage of Solferino and organised relief for the wounded, an experience that inspired his 1862 book A Memory of Solferino and his call for protection of war victims.

title: Founding of the Red Cross (ICRC)
summary: A committee of five Genevans took up Dunant's proposals and formed the body that became the International Committee of the Red Cross, adopting the red cross on white — the inverse of the Swiss flag — as the emblem of neutral medical aid.

title: The first Geneva Convention
summary: A diplomatic conference convened by the Swiss government adopted the first Geneva Convention for the protection of the wounded in war, the foundation of modern international humanitarian law, of which Switzerland remains depositary.

title: Joining the League of Nations
summary: Switzerland joined the new League of Nations, headquartered in Geneva, on terms that its permanent neutrality would be respected, confirming Geneva's role as a centre of international diplomacy.

title: Armed neutrality in the Second World War
summary: Encircled by the Axis, Switzerland mobilised under General Henri Guisan, who rallied the army on the Rütli and adopted the Alpine Réduit defence; the country stayed unoccupied but later faced reckoning over refugees and looted assets.

title: Women win the federal vote
summary: A referendum in 1971 finally granted Swiss women the right to vote and stand in federal elections, one of the last democracies in Europe to do so; the final canton was compelled to follow only in 1990.

title: Switzerland joins the United Nations
summary: After rejecting membership in 1986, Swiss voters narrowly approved joining the UN in a referendum on 3 March 2002, and Switzerland became the 190th member state that September, while still standing outside the European Union.

title: A neutral federal republic in the heart of Europe
summary: Switzerland remains a federal republic of twenty-six cantons and four languages, neutral and outside the EU yet enclosing the foreign enclaves of Büsingen and Campione d'Italia, with Geneva a global hub of diplomacy and humanitarian law.

title: Ancient peopling of the land
summary: Hunting and gathering peoples settle the long territory between the Andes and the Pacific over many millennia, the deep ancestors of the Mapuche and the Andean peoples of the north.

title: The moai of Rapa Nui
summary: On Easter Island, the Polynesian society of Rapa Nui carves and raises some 900 colossal stone moai on hundreds of ceremonial platforms, an unrivalled monumental tradition later recognised by UNESCO.

title: Inca expansion reaches the Maule
summary: The Inca empire extends its influence into northern and central Chile but is unable to subdue the Mapuche, whose resistance checks imperial control near the Maule River.

title: Almagro's expedition turns back
summary: Diego de Almagro leads the first Spanish entry into Chile as far as the Maule River; finding no gold or empire, the expedition returns to Peru, but the Spanish first clash with the Araucanians.

title: Founding of Santiago
summary: Pedro de Valdivia founds Santiago de Nueva Extremadura in the central valley, the nucleus of Spanish Chile and its future capital.

title: Conquest reaches the Biobio
summary: Valdivia extends Spanish rule south of the Biobio and founds Concepcion, pushing into the Mapuche heartland and igniting lasting resistance.

title: Mapuche defeat and kill Valdivia
summary: At Tucapel, Mapuche forces led by Lautaro destroy a Spanish column and capture Valdivia, who is executed; the disaster opens the long Arauco War.

title: The frontier Captaincy General
summary: Chile is governed as a poor, militarised captaincy general of the Spanish empire, its southern frontier held against an independent Mapuche nation that the conquest never subdued.

title: First national junta
summary: Creole leaders in Santiago form a governing junta after the fall of the Spanish king, the founding act of Chilean self-government and the national day.

title: Crossing the Andes and Chacabuco
summary: San Martin's Army of the Andes crosses the cordillera and defeats the royalists at Chacabuco, opening the road to Santiago and the liberation of Chile.

title: The Battle of Maipu
summary: Patriot forces under San Martin, with O'Higgins, crush the Spanish royalists near Santiago, sealing Chilean independence on the mainland weeks after its formal declaration.

title: The Constitution of 1833
summary: A conservative constitution shaped by Diego Portales establishes a strong centralised presidency, anchoring decades of unusual political stability.

title: The War of the Pacific
summary: A dispute over nitrate taxes leads Chile to war with Peru and Bolivia; Chilean victories win the nitrate-rich Atacama and leave Bolivia landlocked.

title: Pacification of Araucania
summary: After three centuries of independence, the Chilean state subdues the Mapuche south of the Biobio by military campaign and opens their territory to settlement.

title: Neruda wins the Nobel Prize
summary: Pablo Neruda, poet, diplomat and senator, is awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature, crowning Chile's golden age of letters.

title: Election of Salvador Allende
summary: The Marxist Salvador Allende of the Popular Unity coalition wins a narrow plurality and is confirmed by Congress, the first freely elected Marxist head of state in the Americas.

title: The military coup
summary: The armed forces under General Augusto Pinochet overthrow President Salvador Allende, who dies as troops storm La Moneda, ending Chile's democratic experiment.

title: The Pinochet dictatorship
summary: Pinochet's regime represses opponents through detention, torture, killing and forced disappearance while imposing free-market reforms; the abuses are later documented by the Rettig and Valech commissions.

title: The 1980 Constitution
summary: A constitution drafted under the dictatorship is approved in a controlled plebiscite, entrenching military prerogatives and remaining, much amended, in force for decades.

title: The 'No' plebiscite
summary: Asked to extend Pinochet's rule, Chileans vote No by 55 to 43 percent, compelling the open presidential election that opens the path back to democracy.

title: Return to democracy
summary: Patricio Aylwin is inaugurated president, restoring civilian democratic rule and soon creating the Rettig Commission to investigate the dictatorship's crimes.

title: Pinochet arrested in London
summary: Augusto Pinochet is detained in London on a foreign warrant for human-rights crimes, a landmark in the pursuit of accountability before his death in 2006.

title: The 'estallido social' protests
summary: A metro fare rise in Santiago ignites the largest protests since the dictatorship, broadening into demands for reform of pensions, health, education and the constitution.

title: New constitution rejected
summary: After a 2020 vote to rewrite the charter, Chileans reject a sweeping progressive draft 62 to 38 percent, a major blow to President Gabriel Boric; a later attempt also fails.

title: Shang dynasty rules the Yellow River valley
