summary: The Shang, the first Chinese dynasty with historical records, governs from cities such as Anyang and produces ritual bronzes and the oracle-bone script, the earliest known Chinese writing.

title: Oracle-bone divination records
summary: Shang diviners inscribe questions to ancestors and deities on ox bones and turtle shells; these inscriptions are the oldest unambiguous Chinese writing and a primary source for early history.

title: Zhou conquest and the Mandate of Heaven
summary: King Wu of Zhou defeats the Shang at the Battle of Muye and founds the Zhou dynasty, justifying the overthrow with the Mandate of Heaven, a doctrine of morally conditional rule that endures for millennia.

title: Western Zhou collapses; Eastern Zhou begins
summary: Nomadic invasions force the Zhou court to flee east to Luoyang in 771 BCE, beginning the Eastern Zhou and a long decline of royal authority into the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods.

title: Lifetime of Confucius
summary: Confucius (551-479 BCE) teaches that social order rests on moral cultivation, ritual, and proper human relationships; his thought becomes the dominant ethical tradition of imperial China.

title: Qin unifies China; the First Emperor is proclaimed
summary: Qin completes its conquest of the Warring States and its king takes the title Shi Huangdi, founding the first unified Chinese empire and the centralized bureaucratic system that defines imperial China.

title: Frontier walls joined into the Great Wall
summary: Under the First Emperor, earlier northern fortifications are connected into a unified defense against steppe invasions, the origin of the Great Wall that later dynasties would expand.

title: Death of the First Emperor and the terracotta army
summary: Qin Shi Huang dies and is entombed near Xi'an in a colossal mausoleum guarded by roughly 8,000 terracotta warriors, rediscovered in 1974 and now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

title: Han dynasty consolidates the empire
summary: After the Qin collapse, the Han dynasty (206 BCE-220 CE) institutionalizes Confucian-trained bureaucracy and the civil service, giving China its enduring model of imperial government and the name of its majority people.

title: Silk Road trade routes open under Emperor Wu
summary: Emperor Wu's campaigns against the Xiongnu and missions into Central Asia open the overland Silk Road, linking China to India, Persia, and the Mediterranean in exchange of goods and ideas.

title: Collapse of the Han and centuries of division
summary: The Han empire fragments into the Three Kingdoms and successive Northern and Southern Dynasties, a long era of disunion during which Buddhism takes deep root in China.

title: Sui dynasty reunifies China
summary: The Sui (581-618) reunite north and south and build the Grand Canal, restoring a centralized empire after centuries of division and setting the stage for the Tang golden age.

title: Tang dynasty and a cosmopolitan golden age
summary: The Tang dynasty (618-907) builds a vast, outward-looking empire centered on Chang'an, refining the examination system and producing a flowering of poetry; woodblock printing and gunpowder first appear.

title: Song dynasty and a commercial revolution
summary: The Song dynasty (960-1279) presides over an economic and technological boom, introducing movable-type printing, government paper money, the navigational compass, and gunpowder weapons.

title: Kublai Khan founds the Mongol Yuan dynasty
summary: Kublai Khan declares the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and completes the conquest of the Song by 1279, ruling China from Dadu (Beijing) as the first foreign-led dynasty to govern all of China.

title: Ming dynasty restores Han rule
summary: Zhu Yuanzhang overthrows the Yuan and founds the Ming dynasty (1368-1644), which rebuilds the Great Wall in stone, constructs the Forbidden City, and revives Han Chinese imperial governance.

title: Zheng He's maritime voyages
summary: The Ming admiral Zheng He leads seven vast treasure-fleet expeditions across Southeast Asia, the Indian Ocean, and the coast of Africa, projecting Chinese power before the dynasty turns inward.

title: Manchus establish the Qing dynasty
summary: The Manchus capture Beijing and found the Qing dynasty (1644-1912), China's last imperial dynasty, which expands the empire to its greatest extent under the Kangxi and Qianlong emperors.

title: First Opium War and the 'unequal treaties'
summary: War with Britain over the opium trade ends in Qing defeat and the Treaty of Nanjing (1842), ceding Hong Kong and opening treaty ports, the start of a century of foreign encroachment China calls its century of humiliation.

title: Xinhai Revolution erupts
summary: The Wuchang Uprising of 10 October 1911 sparks the Xinhai Revolution against the Qing, rapidly spreading across the provinces and bringing down China's last imperial dynasty.

title: Republic of China founded; last emperor abdicates
summary: Sun Yat-sen becomes provisional president of the Republic of China on 1 January 1912, and on 12 February the child emperor Puyi abdicates, ending more than two millennia of imperial rule.

title: Warlord Era of political fragmentation
summary: The death of Yuan Shikai in 1916 plunges China into the Warlord Era, with regional militarists ruling much of the country until the Nationalists reassert partial unity by 1928.

title: Second Sino-Japanese War and the Nanjing Massacre
summary: Japan's full-scale invasion from July 1937 brings catastrophic violence, including the December 1937 Nanjing Massacre, in which Japanese forces murdered many tens of thousands of civilians and prisoners and committed mass rape.

title: Chinese Civil War resumes; Communist victory
summary: After Japan's surrender, full-scale civil war between Nationalists and Communists resumes, ending in 1949 with Communist victory and the retreat of Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist government to Taiwan.

title: People's Republic of China proclaimed
summary: Mao Zedong proclaims the People's Republic of China from the Tiananmen gate in Beijing on 1 October 1949, with Zhou Enlai as premier, after Communist victory in the civil war.

title: Great Leap Forward and the great famine
summary: Mao's Great Leap Forward forces rapid collectivization and crude industrialization, causing a famine from 1959 to 1961 that killed an estimated 15 million to tens of millions of people.

title: Cultural Revolution
summary: Mao launches the Cultural Revolution, a decade of political persecution, purges, and social upheaval that convulses Chinese society until his death in 1976.

title: Deng Xiaoping launches reform and opening
summary: Under Deng Xiaoping, China begins 'reform and opening' in 1978, decollectivizing agriculture and embracing markets and foreign investment, igniting decades of rapid economic growth.

title: Tiananmen Square crackdown
summary: The army violently suppresses pro-democracy demonstrations centered on Beijing's Tiananmen Square in June 1989, killing many protesters and reasserting tight Communist Party political control.

title: The savannas join the trans-Saharan trade
summary: As the Ghana and Mali empires expanded southward, the northern peoples of the region — Senufo and Mandé — were drawn into trans-Saharan commerce, exchanging forest kola nuts for salt, cloth, and gold.

title: Dyula merchants found northern trading towns
summary: Mandé-speaking Muslim merchants, the Dyula, established trading and Islamic centres such as Kong, Bondoukou, Bouna, and Begho, linking the rainforest to the markets of the Sahel.

title: Seku Watara founds the Empire of Kong
summary: Seku Watara united the Dyula of Kong into a state, often called the Wattara Empire, that grew rich controlling the gold and kola trade and reached into present-day Burkina Faso, Mali, and Ghana.

title: Kong expands northward
summary: Under Seku Watara and his kin the empire of Kong extended its reach, conquering toward Bobo-Dioulasso and cementing its dominance over the regional trade routes before central authority weakened after his death about 1745.

title: Akan states form on the eastern frontier
summary: As the Asante Empire rose in present-day Ghana, Akan groups such as the Abron founded states near the eastern edge of modern Côte d'Ivoire, beginning a long era of Akan migration into the region.

title: The Baoulé migrate under Queen Abla Pokou
summary: By tradition, Queen Abla Pokou broke from the Asante after a succession struggle and led her people west across the Comoé River, founding the Baoulé kingdom around Sakasso — the largest people of modern Côte d'Ivoire.

title: The Agni kingdoms of Indénié and Sanwi
summary: Other Akan groups fleeing the Asante established the Agni (Anyi) kingdoms of Indénié and Sanwi in the south-east, near the lagoons and the Gold Coast, extending Akan institutions across the forest zone.

title: Earliest recorded French voyage to the coast
summary: French mariners reached the West African coast; over the following centuries European traders worked the shore for ivory, gold, and other goods, giving the Ivory Coast its lasting name, though its surf-bound coast limited permanent contact.

title: France signs treaties on the lagoon coast
summary: The naval officer Bouët-Willaumez concluded treaties with rulers around Grand-Bassam and Assinie, securing the first durable French trading footholds on the coast of present-day Côte d'Ivoire.

title: France constitutes the colony of Côte d'Ivoire
summary: After protectorate treaties negotiated by Binger and Treich-Laplène, France formally established the colony of Côte d'Ivoire on 10 March 1893, naming Louis-Gustave Binger its first governor.

title: Capture of Samori Touré ends northern resistance
summary: The Mandé empire-builder Samori Touré, who had resisted the French for years and sacked Kong, was captured at Guélémou on 29 September 1898 and exiled to Gabon, breaking organised resistance in the savanna.

title: Côte d'Ivoire joins French West Africa
summary: The colony became a constituent territory of the Federation of French West Africa, governed from Dakar, and was developed as a source of cocoa, coffee, and timber for the metropole.

title: Head tax and forced labour
summary: France imposed a head tax in 1900 and a forced-labour regime that compelled African men to work without pay on infrastructure and plantations, drawing recruits from the lands later organised as Upper Volta and provoking repeated revolts.

title: Houphouët-Boigny founds the African Agricultural Union
summary: Félix Houphouët-Boigny organised African cocoa and coffee planters into the Syndicat Agricole Africain to win them the rights enjoyed by European growers — the start of his rise to political leadership.

title: Forced labour abolished
summary: On a bill closely associated with Houphouët-Boigny, the French parliament abolished forced labour throughout the empire in 1946; the same year he helped found the inter-territorial RDA and its Ivorian party, the PDCI.

title: Independence under Houphouët-Boigny
summary: After choosing autonomy within the French Community in a 1958 referendum, Côte d'Ivoire became a fully independent republic on 7 August 1960, with Félix Houphouët-Boigny as its first president.

title: The 'Ivorian miracle'
summary: Liberal, export-led growth built on cocoa and coffee and close ties to France made Côte d'Ivoire one of the most prosperous states in sub-Saharan Africa, with Abidjan a thriving commercial hub.

title: Commodity slump ends the boom
summary: A collapse in world cocoa and coffee prices ended the era of rapid growth, leaving heavy debt and rising discontent that would strain the one-party system.

title: Capital moved to Yamoussoukro
summary: Houphouët-Boigny designated his birthplace, Yamoussoukro, the official political capital, though Abidjan remained the economic and administrative centre.

title: Basilica of Our Lady of Peace consecrated
summary: The vast basilica at Yamoussoukro, modelled on St Peter's in Rome and recognised as the largest church in the world, was consecrated by Pope John Paul II amid controversy over its enormous cost.

title: First multiparty election
summary: Under domestic and international pressure Houphouët-Boigny legalised opposition parties and won the country's first multiparty presidential election against the historian Laurent Gbagbo.

title: Death of Houphouët-Boigny
summary: The country's founding president died in office after more than three decades in power, leaving a celebrated record of stability and growth but no clearly prepared successor.

title: The politics of 'Ivoirité'
summary: President Bédié promoted 'Ivoirité', a doctrine of authentic Ivorian belonging used to exclude rivals such as Alassane Ouattara and to question the citizenship of northerners and immigrants, deepening a north–south rift.

title: The first coup d'état
summary: General Robert Guéï overthrew President Henri Konan Bédié in the country's first military coup, ending the PDCI's unbroken hold on power since independence.

title: Civil war divides the country
summary: An army mutiny grew into a rebellion that split Côte d'Ivoire between a government-held south and a rebel-held north under the Forces Nouvelles, drawing in French and UN peacekeepers.

title: Ouagadougou Political Agreement
summary: A peace accord brokered through regional mediation brought rebel leader Guillaume Soro into a unity government and set a path toward reunification and elections, easing the first civil war.

title: Post-election crisis
summary: After the disputed November 2010 runoff, Gbagbo refused to cede to Ouattara; the standoff became open conflict that killed about 3,000 people before pro-Ouattara forces, backed by France and the UN, captured Gbagbo on 11 April 2011.

title: Recovery under Ouattara
summary: Alassane Ouattara took office and presided over a return to rapid growth; he was re-elected in 2015 and won a contested third term in 2020 that opponents argued was unconstitutional.

title: Rise of the Sao culture
summary: South of Lake Chad the Sao began building walled towns and producing distinctive terracotta and bronze artwork, forming one of the earliest known complex societies in the region.

title: The Bantu expansion begins
summary: The Grassfields of the Cameroon-Nigeria borderlands are widely held to lie near the homeland of the Bantu languages, whose speakers spread from this region across central and southern Africa.

title: Height of the Sao city-states
summary: The Sao settlements of the Lake Chad basin reached their apex between roughly the ninth and fifteenth centuries before being absorbed by neighbouring states and peoples such as the Kotoko.

title: Portuguese name the river of prawns
summary: Portuguese sailors reaching the Wouri estuary named it Rio dos Camaroes, the river of prawns, after its abundant crustaceans; the name later evolved into Kamerun, Cameroun, and Cameroon.

title: Founding of the Bamum kingdom
summary: The Bamum dynasty was founded by Nshare Yen, who established Foumban as the capital of a Grassfields kingdom that grew through conquest and diplomacy.

title: Modibo Adama founds the Adamawa Emirate
summary: Acting under Usman dan Fodio, the Fulani leader Modibo Adama launched a jihad into Fombina and established the Adamawa Emirate, spreading Islam and Fulani rule across the north as part of the Sokoto Caliphate.

title: King Njoya devises the Bamum script
summary: King Ibrahim Njoya of Bamum and his palace circle created an original writing system, the Bamum script, and the Shumom language, used to record the kingdom's history, laws, and knowledge.

title: Douala treaty and German protectorate
summary: The Douala kings Bell and Akwa signed a treaty of protection with German agents; Gustav Nachtigal then proclaimed a German protectorate over Kamerun, beginning colonial rule.

title: France cedes Neukamerun
summary: Under the Treaty of Fez ending the Agadir crisis, France ceded the large territory of Neukamerun to Germany, expanding the colony eastward.

title: The Kamerun campaign
summary: British, French, and Belgian forces invaded German Kamerun from August 1914; after a prolonged campaign the last German garrison surrendered in early 1916.

title: Partition into French and British mandates
summary: The League of Nations divided the former German colony between France, which took the larger French Cameroun, and Britain, which administered the Northern and Southern Cameroons alongside Nigeria.

title: Founding of the UPC
summary: Ruben Um Nyobe and others founded the Union des Populations du Cameroun, a nationalist party demanding immediate independence and the reunification of French and British Cameroon.

title: The UPC is banned
summary: After waves of unrest, the French administration outlawed the UPC, pushing the movement underground and into an armed insurgency.

title: Killing of Ruben Um Nyobe
summary: The UPC leader Ruben Um Nyobe was tracked down and shot by a French-led military unit; repression of the insurgency continued in the Bassa and Bamileke regions with heavy loss of life.

title: Independence of French Cameroun
summary: The UN trusteeship administered by France ended and French Cameroun became an independent republic, with Ahmadou Ahidjo as its first president.

title: The British Cameroons plebiscite
summary: In a UN-supervised vote the Northern Cameroons chose to join Nigeria while the Southern Cameroons chose to reunite with the Republic of Cameroon.

title: Reunification and federation
summary: The Southern Cameroons joined the republic to form the Federal Republic of Cameroon, uniting francophone East Cameroon and anglophone West Cameroon following the Foumban Conference.

title: From federation to unitary state
summary: A referendum abolished the two-state federation in favour of a centralised United Republic of Cameroon, ending West Cameroon's separate autonomy.

title: Ahidjo resigns; Biya succeeds
summary: Ahmadou Ahidjo unexpectedly resigned the presidency and was succeeded by his prime minister, Paul Biya.

title: Failed coup against Biya
summary: An attempted coup by elements loyal to former president Ahidjo was suppressed within days, after which Biya tightened his hold on power.

title: Return to multiparty politics
summary: Biya legalised opposition parties in 1990 and held the first multiparty presidential election in 1992, which he won amid allegations of irregularities.

title: Anglophone protests begin
summary: Lawyers and teachers in the North-West and South-West regions launched protests against the marginalisation of English-speaking Cameroonians; a security crackdown followed.

title: Escalation into armed conflict
summary: The protests gave way to an armed insurgency as separatists proclaimed the independent state of Ambazonia; the conflict has since killed thousands and displaced hundreds of thousands.

title: Biya re-elected at 92
summary: Paul Biya won a further presidential term, extending a tenure begun in 1982; opposition figures disputed the official results.

title: Kingdom of Kongo founded
summary: Lukeni lua Nimi establishes the kingdom of Kongo on the lower Congo River, ruling from Mbanza Kongo.

title: Kongo's king baptised as João I
summary: After Diogo Cão's 1483 landfall, King Nzinga a Nkuwu accepts Catholic baptism, taking the name João I and opening close ties with Portugal.

title: Afonso I protests the slave trade
summary: King Afonso I (Nzinga Mbemba) writes to João III of Portugal complaining that traders are illegally enslaving his subjects, even as the Atlantic trade expands.

title: Kuba kingdom unified by Shyaam
summary: Shyaam a-Mbul a Ngoong founds the Bushong dynasty, uniting chiefdoms between the Sankuru and Kasai into the Kuba kingdom famed for its art.

title: Battle of Mbwila breaks Kongo
summary: Portuguese forces defeat Kongo and kill King António I at Mbwila (Ambuila); the kingdom splinters into rival factions and a long civil war.

title: Atlantic slave trade at its height
summary: Central African captives are funnelled in vast numbers into the transatlantic trade, hollowing out communities across the lower Congo.

title: Tippu Tip's eastern slaving state
summary: Swahili-Arab trader Tippu Tip builds a domain around Kasongo in Maniema, raiding the eastern Congo for ivory and slaves.

title: Stanley descends the Congo River
summary: Henry Morton Stanley completes the first European traverse of the Congo from interior to the Atlantic, mapping the basin for would-be colonisers.

title: Leopold hires Stanley for the Congo
summary: King Leopold II commissions Stanley to build stations and obtain treaties from local chiefs, laying the basis for a private colonial claim.

title: Congo Free State proclaimed
summary: Following the Berlin Conference, Leopold II establishes the Congo Free State as his personal possession, recognised by the European powers.

title: The rubber regime and the Force Publique
summary: Monopoly decrees and rubber quotas, enforced by the Force Publique through hostage-taking and mutilation, drive a system of forced labour and mass death.

title: The Casement Report
summary: British consul Roger Casement publishes a report documenting atrocities; E. D. Morel's Congo Reform Association amplifies the outcry.

title: Belgium annexes the Belgian Congo
summary: Under international pressure, Belgium takes the territory from Leopold II, ending the Free State and creating the Belgian Congo colony.

title: Belgian Congo established
summary: The colony is administered by Belgium for half a century, its economy built on Katangan copper and other minerals.

title: Independence from Belgium
summary: The Congo becomes independent with Lumumba as prime minister and Kasa-Vubu as president.

title: Katanga secedes; the Congo Crisis
summary: An army mutiny and Moïse Tshombe's Belgian-backed secession of Katanga plunge the new state into crisis and UN intervention.

title: Assassination of Lumumba
summary: Captured and transferred to Katanga, Patrice Lumumba is killed; Belgian officers were present and foreign involvement is widely documented.

title: Mobutu seizes power
summary: Colonel Joseph-Désiré Mobutu takes full control in a military coup, beginning a three-decade dictatorship.

title: Congo renamed Zaire
summary: Under his 'authenticité' campaign, Mobutu renames the country Zaire and adopts the name Mobutu Sese Seko.

title: Rwandan refugee crisis in the Kivus
summary: The Rwandan genocide drives over a million refugees into eastern Zaire, destabilising the Kivu provinces.

title: First Congo War
summary: A Rwanda- and Uganda-backed rebellion under Laurent-Désiré Kabila advances across the country against the collapsing Mobutu regime.

title: Mobutu falls; Kabila takes power
summary: Mobutu flees into exile and dies months later; Kabila seizes Kinshasa and restores the name Democratic Republic of the Congo.

title: Second Congo War begins
summary: Kabila breaks with Rwanda and Uganda; nine nations and many militias are drawn into 'Africa's World War,' the deadliest conflict since 1945.

title: Laurent Kabila assassinated
summary: President Laurent-Désiré Kabila is shot dead in Kinshasa; his son Joseph Kabila succeeds him and seeks peace.

title: Peace agreements end the war
summary: The 2002 Sun City and Pretoria accords and a transitional government formally end the Second Congo War in 2003.

title: M23 rebellion seizes Goma
summary: The M23 rebel movement briefly captures Goma in North Kivu before being pushed back; conflict festers across the east.

title: M23 retakes Goma
summary: After re-emerging in 2021, M23 — with Rwandan backing — captures Goma again in early 2025, deepening the humanitarian crisis.

title: Bantu peoples settle the region
summary: Bantu-speaking farmers and ironworkers settled the forests and savannas of the modern Congo over the first millennium CE, founding the Kongo, Teke, Vili, Mboshi and other communities that make up the country's peoples.

title: Rise of the Kingdom of Loango
summary: The Vili built the Kingdom of Loango on the Atlantic coast, with its capital at Buali; ruled by the maloango, it became a producer of cloth and a centre of trade in copper, ivory and enslaved people.

title: The Teke (Anziku) kingdom inland
summary: North of the Congo River the Teke (Bateke), organised as the Anziku or Tio kingdom under a sacred king titled the makoko, controlled the interior plateaus and trade routes; the northern reaches of Kongo also touched the region.

title: Loango becomes a hub of the Atlantic trade
summary: The Loango coast, with markets at Loango Bay, Malemba and Cabinda, grew into a major export point for ivory, copper and enslaved people; Vili middlemen linked interior caravan networks to European ships offshore.

title: Peak of the slave trade through Loango
summary: By the eighteenth century the Loango ports were embarking large numbers of enslaved Africans each year, bound mainly for the Caribbean and the Americas, drawing the coastal kingdoms ever deeper into the Atlantic economy.

title: Succession crisis weakens Loango
summary: A succession crisis after the death of the king recorded as Buatu, together with the growing power of provincial governors and traders, undermined the maloango's central authority and began Loango's long decline.

title: Decline as the slave trade is suppressed
summary: The European suppression of the Atlantic slave trade undercut the Loango coast's economy; the kingdom fragmented into small chieftaincies and had effectively ceased to exist as a unified state by the early 1880s.

title: Brazza's treaty with Makoko
summary: In September 1880 Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza signed a treaty with the Teke ruler Makoko Iloo I, placing his lands under French protection and securing France's claim to the north bank of the Congo River.

title: Founding of Brazzaville at Nkuna
summary: Brazza founded a French post at the village of Nkuna (Mfoa) on the north bank of Stanley Pool on 10 September 1880; held by Sergeant Malamine Camara, it was named Brazzaville and became the centre of French rule.

title: Berlin Conference divides the two Congos
summary: The Berlin Conference recognised French claims north of the Congo River and assigned the south bank to Leopold II's Congo Free State, fixing the lasting division between the Republic of the Congo and the future Democratic Republic.

title: Middle Congo joins French Equatorial Africa
summary: France reorganised its Central African colonies in 1910 into French Equatorial Africa — Gabon, Middle Congo, Ubangi-Shari and Chad — governed from Brazzaville, which became the federation's federal capital.

title: Building the Congo-Ocean Railway
summary: The Congo-Ocean Railway was built from 1921 to 1934 by the Société de Construction des Batignolles to link Brazzaville to Pointe-Noire; forced labourers conscripted across French Equatorial Africa died in the thousands, an estimate commonly placed above 17,000.

title: Railway completed; Pointe-Noire opens as port
summary: The roughly 512-kilometre railway was completed in 1934, establishing Pointe-Noire as the colony's Atlantic ocean terminal and the backbone of the export economy that bypassed the lower Congo rapids.

title: Brazzaville, capital of Free France
summary: After French Equatorial Africa rallied to General de Gaulle in 1940, Brazzaville became the effective capital of Free France, a base for organising resistance against Vichy and the Axis powers.

title: The Brazzaville Conference
summary: De Gaulle convened the Brazzaville Conference in early 1944, which promised post-war colonial reforms — ending the harshest forced labour, granting African representation and citizenship — while explicitly rejecting independence.

title: Autonomy within the French Community
summary: Following the September 1958 referendum, Middle Congo became the autonomous Republic of the Congo within the French Community, a self-governing step short of full sovereignty.

title: Independence under Fulbert Youlou
summary: The Republic of the Congo became independent on 15 August 1960 with the Abbé Fulbert Youlou as its first president, a pro-Western leader who kept close ties to France.

title: The Trois Glorieuses topple Youlou
summary: A three-day popular uprising in August 1963, led by trade unions and youth, forced Youlou's resignation; Alphonse Massamba-Débat took power and steered the country toward one-party "scientific socialism."

title: People's Republic of the Congo proclaimed
summary: Marien Ngouabi, who had seized power in 1968, proclaimed the People's Republic of the Congo in 1969 — Africa's first Marxist-Leninist state — with the Congolese Labour Party (PCT) as the sole legal party.

title: Assassination of Marien Ngouabi
summary: President Marien Ngouabi was assassinated in Brazzaville on 18 March 1977; a military committee took power, and after a brief interim under General Yhombi-Opango leadership passed to Denis Sassou Nguesso in 1979.

title: Sassou Nguesso takes power
summary: Colonel Denis Sassou Nguesso became president in 1979, leading the PCT one-party state through the 1980s while petroleum became the mainstay of the economy and ties to France and Western oil firms deepened.

title: National conference opens democracy
summary: After the PCT dropped Marxism-Leninism in 1990, a sovereign national conference in 1991 stripped Sassou Nguesso of executive power, made him a ceremonial head of state and set the Congo on a path to multiparty elections.

title: Lissouba wins multiparty election
summary: Pascal Lissouba of UPADS won the Congo's first multiparty presidential election in August 1992, ending the PCT's monopoly and inaugurating a brief democratic period.

title: Militia clashes over disputed elections
summary: Disputes over the 1993 legislative elections sparked armed clashes between political militias in Brazzaville, fracturing the new democracy along factional and regional lines.

title: Civil war returns Sassou Nguesso to power
summary: Civil war erupted in June 1997 between forces of President Lissouba and former president Sassou Nguesso; backed by Angolan troops, Sassou Nguesso's forces prevailed by October, Lissouba fled into exile, and Sassou Nguesso declared himself president.

title: New constitution; Sassou Nguesso elected
summary: A new constitution adopted in 2002 entrenched Sassou Nguesso's presidency; he won the presidential election that year and was re-elected in 2009 amid opposition complaints.

title: Referendum removes term limits
summary: A constitutional referendum in October 2015, reported as overwhelmingly approved on a disputed turnout, scrapped presidential term limits and the age ceiling, clearing the way for Sassou Nguesso to seek further terms; he was re-elected in 2016 and 2021.

title: San Agustin megaliths
summary: In the upper Magdalena valley, the San Agustin culture carves the largest assemblage of monumental religious statuary in South America, later a UNESCO World Heritage site.

title: Tierradentro tombs
summary: The people of Tierradentro hew vast painted underground burial chambers into the mountains, a unique record of a developed pre-Hispanic Andean society.

title: Rise of the Muisca
summary: The Muisca chiefdoms flourish on the high plateau around Bogota and Tunja, celebrated for goldwork, salt, and trade across the Andes.

title: The El Dorado tradition
summary: At Lake Guatavita, Muisca ritual offerings of gold to the waters give rise to the legend of El Dorado that would lure Spanish expeditions inland.

title: Founding of Bogota
summary: Gonzalo Jimenez de Quesada founds Santa Fe de Bogota after subduing the Muisca, establishing the capital of the New Kingdom of Granada.

title: Audiencia of Bogota
summary: The crown establishes a royal court and administrative tribunal at Bogota, opening the formal colonial era in New Granada.

title: Cartagena fortified
summary: Cartagena de Indias is built into the most complete fortified port in South America, guarding the empire's wealth against repeated pirate and naval assaults.

title: Viceroyalty of New Granada
summary: Spain governs the territory through the Viceroyalty of New Granada, capital Bogota, encompassing modern Colombia, Panama, Ecuador, and Venezuela.

title: The Comunero revolt
summary: A popular rising against new Bourbon taxes sweeps the interior, an early sign of the unrest that would lead to the independence movement.

title: Cry of independence
summary: A junta seizes power in Bogota, beginning the New Granadan independence movement amid the crisis of Spanish royal authority.

title: Battle of Boyaca
summary: Bolivar and Santander rout the royalist army at the Boyaca bridge, securing the liberation of New Granada and opening the road to Bogota.

title: Congress of Cucuta
summary: The republic of Gran Colombia is formally organised, uniting New Granada, Venezuela, and Ecuador under Bolivar's presidency.

title: Breakup of Gran Colombia
summary: Venezuela and Ecuador secede and Bolivar dies near Santa Marta; the union dissolves, leaving New Granada as a separate state.

title: United States of Colombia
summary: A Liberal-led federal constitution reorganises the country as the loosely united States of Colombia, intensifying partisan and regional rivalry.

title: The Constitution of 1886
summary: A Conservative-led charter creates a centralised Republic of Colombia with a strong presidency and a renewed alliance with the Catholic Church.

title: War of a Thousand Days
summary: Liberals and the Conservative government fight Colombia's deadliest civil war, with an estimated 100,000 dead, leaving the country ruined.

title: Separation of Panama
summary: Backed by U.S. warships, Panama secedes after Colombia rejects the canal treaty; the United States recognises it and secures the canal zone.

title: Assassination of Gaitan and the Bogotazo
summary: The killing of Liberal leader Jorge Eliecer Gaitan triggers the Bogotazo riots that devastate Bogota and ignite a decade of bloodshed.

title: La Violencia
summary: Partisan warfare between Liberals and Conservatives ravages the countryside, killing an estimated two hundred thousand or more Colombians.

title: The National Front
summary: Liberals and Conservatives agree to alternate the presidency and share offices, ending partisan war but closing politics to other movements.

title: Garcia Marquez and Macondo
summary: The journalist and novelist Gabriel Garcia Marquez gives literary form to Colombia's history of violence and wonder, later winning the 1982 Nobel Prize.

title: FARC formally established
summary: The Southern Bloc guerrillas adopt the name Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) at their second conference, formalising the organization that becomes the country's largest leftist insurgency.

title: Cartels and paramilitaries
summary: Cocaine cartels and right-wing paramilitary forces intensify the conflict with assassinations, bombings, kidnappings, and massacres of civilians.

title: Peace accord with the FARC
summary: After four years of talks in Havana, the Santos government and the FARC sign a peace agreement; Santos receives the Nobel Peace Prize.

title: Truth Commission report
summary: The official Truth Commission estimates about 450,000 killed in 1985-2018 and millions displaced, the great majority of the dead civilians.

title: Election of Gustavo Petro
summary: Colombia elects Gustavo Petro, a former guerrilla, as its first leftist president, pledging a policy of total peace with remaining armed groups.

title: Earliest settlement of the islands
summary: Austronesian seafarers and Bantu-speaking peoples from the African mainland settle the archipelago, occupying the islands no later than the eighth century CE and embedding them in Swahili-coast networks.

title: Dembeni phase and Indian Ocean trade
summary: The Dembeni-phase settlement flourishes as one of the richest sites of its age in the region, trading rock crystal and other goods with the Abbasid and Fatimid worlds and importing Persian and Chinese ceramics.

title: Islam takes root
summary: Islam, carried by Indian Ocean merchants and migrants, becomes established across the islands, tying the Comoros to the religious culture of the Swahili coast.

title: Rise of the island sultanates
summary: Muslim sultanates of Swahili culture emerge on the islands, with ruling houses claiming Arab, Persian (Shirazi) and Hadhrami descent to legitimise their authority.

title: Portuguese and European contact
summary: Portuguese navigators reach the islands in the early sixteenth century; the Comoros become a provisioning station for ships crossing the western Indian Ocean.

title: Malagasy slaving raids
summary: Sakalava and Betsimisaraka war-fleets from Madagascar raid the Comoros for captives over several decades, devastating communities across the archipelago.

title: Slave society on the islands
summary: The slave trade and plantation labour expand greatly, and by the mid-nineteenth century enslaved people are estimated to make up a very large proportion of the islands' population.

title: Mayotte ceded to France
summary: The ruler of Mayotte cedes the island to France, giving France its first foothold in the Comoro archipelago.

title: Protectorates over the three islands
summary: France establishes protectorates over Grande Comore, Anjouan and Mohéli, dealing with sultans including Said Ali bin Said Omar of Grande Comore.

title: Annexation and administration via Madagascar
summary: The islands are formally brought under French possession and attached to the colony of Madagascar; the last sultan relinquishes power by 1912.

title: Plantation economy
summary: Colonial rule reorganises the economy around export crops—vanilla, cloves, copra and especially ylang-ylang—making the Comoros a leading supplier of perfume essence.

title: Separate overseas territory
summary: The Comoros are detached from Madagascar and constituted as a distinct French overseas territory, beginning to acquire their own institutions.

title: Overseas territory with representation
summary: The Comoros are confirmed as a French overseas territory and given representation in the French Parliament and a local assembly.

title: Internal autonomy granted
summary: A year after Madagascar's independence, the Comoros are granted internal autonomy, with their own governing council and capital at Moroni.

title: Independence referendum
summary: Voters back independence by about 95 per cent across the archipelago, but on Mayotte a majority of roughly 63 per cent votes to remain French, splitting the islands.

title: Unilateral declaration of independence
summary: The Chamber of Deputies in Moroni, led by Ahmed Abdallah, declares the Comoros independent, claiming all four islands; Abdallah becomes first president.

title: Admitted to the United Nations
summary: The Comoros joins the UN under General Assembly resolution 3385 (XXX), which reaffirms the territorial integrity of the archipelago including Mayotte.

title: Abdallah overthrown
summary: A coalition aided by mercenaries led by Bob Denard ousts President Ahmed Abdallah weeks after independence, beginning a long era of coups.

title: Ali Soilih's revolution
summary: Radical leftist Ali Soilih takes power and launches a confrontational revolution against the sultans, religious notables and old order, alienating France and the elite.

title: Denard restores Abdallah
summary: Bob Denard returns with mercenaries, overthrows Soilih—who is soon killed—and restores Ahmed Abdallah; the state becomes the Federal Islamic Republic of the Comoros.

title: Assassination of Ahmed Abdallah
summary: President Abdallah is shot dead in his office in Moroni in disputed circumstances; Denard is widely suspected but later acquitted, and is pressured to leave.

title: Operation Kaskari and French intervention
summary: Bob Denard seizes Moroni with mercenaries in his final coup attempt; France intervenes in 'Operation Azalée' and removes him within days.

title: Anjouan and Mohéli secede
summary: Anjouan and Mohéli declare separation from the Comoros; a federal attempt to retake Anjouan by force is defeated, pushing the archipelago towards fragmentation.

title: Azali Assoumani seizes power
summary: Army chief Azali Assoumani takes power in a coup amid the secession crisis, casting himself as the guarantor of national unity.

title: Union constitution and rotating presidency
summary: Following the Fomboni accords, a new constitution approved by referendum creates the Union of the Comoros, giving each island autonomy and rotating the Union presidency among the three islands.

title: Mayotte votes to become a French department
summary: In a referendum, Mayotte votes overwhelmingly to become a fully integrated French department, a status it assumes in 2011 as France's 101st department.

title: UN affirms Comorian sovereignty over Mayotte
summary: The UN General Assembly has repeatedly affirmed Comorian sovereignty over Mayotte and the archipelago's territorial integrity; the Comoros claims the island while France administers it.

title: The medinas of the sultanates inscribed
summary: The Medinas of the Historic Sultanates of the Comoros become the archipelago's first World Heritage site — the stone towns of the pre-colonial sultanates recognised on criteria (iii) and (iv).

title: Portuguese reach the uninhabited islands
summary: Sailing for Prince Henry the Navigator, the Venetian captain Alvise Cadamosto and others made landfall on the empty Cape Verde archipelago; further islands were charted over the next decade by Diogo Gomes and António de Noli.

title: Ribeira Grande founded on Santiago
summary: Portuguese settlers established Ribeira Grande (today Cidade Velha) on Santiago — the first permanent European city in the tropics — drawing Portuguese, Genoese and Flemish settlers, convicts and Sephardic Jews.

title: Trading privileges over the Guinea coast
summary: The Portuguese crown granted Santiago's settlers the right to trade in the "Rivers of Guinea" on the West African mainland, anchoring the colony's economy to commerce with the coast.

title: The Nossa Senhora do Rosário church
summary: Construction of the church of Nossa Senhora do Rosário at Ribeira Grande, among the oldest surviving colonial churches anywhere, reflected the town's new role as a bishopric and religious centre of the islands.

title: A sorting-house of the slave trade
summary: Ribeira Grande became a major entrepôt where enslaved Africans from the Upper Guinea coast were held, baptised, taxed and re-exported to the Americas, with thousands passing through annually by mid-century.

title: Drake sacks Ribeira Grande
summary: The English privateer Sir Francis Drake attacked and sacked the wealthy port of Ribeira Grande, one of several corsair raids that beset the islands during the era of the Iberian Union.

title: Cassard's French raid destroys the city
summary: The French corsair Jacques Cassard stormed and looted Ribeira Grande, stripping its churches and houses; the coastal town, already declining, never recovered from the assault.

title: Capital moves to Praia
summary: As the slave trade waned and Ribeira Grande lay in ruins, administration shifted to the more defensible plateau of Praia, which became the capital in 1770 and remains so today.

title: Mindelo becomes an Atlantic coaling station
summary: The deep harbour of Porto Grande at Mindelo on São Vicente was developed as a coaling station for transatlantic steamships and later a submarine-cable relay, briefly making the port cosmopolitan and prosperous.

title: Slavery abolished
summary: Portugal abolished slavery in its territories in 1869, ending the legal trade that had built the islands' early wealth, though forced and contract labour systems persisted afterward.

title: Famines kill at least 100,000
summary: Recurrent droughts produced a series of catastrophic famines; during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries at least 100,000 people died of starvation and disease, amid an inadequate colonial response.

title: The twentieth-century famines
summary: Two further droughts brought famines that together killed tens of thousands; starving refugees were interned in camps outside Praia, and survivors emigrated in growing numbers, deepening the diaspora.

title: The morna and Creole letters
summary: The poet Eugénio Tavares of Brava elevated the morna to a literary art in Cape Verdean Creole; the song-form of love, parting and sodade would later be carried worldwide by Cesária Évora.

title: Cabral founds the PAIGC
summary: Amílcar Cabral and a small group founded the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde, conceiving the two Portuguese territories as one nation to be liberated together.

title: Armed struggle begins on the mainland
summary: Because the islands were unsuited to guerrilla war, the PAIGC waged its armed campaign on the Guinea-Bissau mainland from 1963, while Cape Verdean cadres filled the party's leadership.

title: Cabral assassinated in Conakry
summary: Amílcar Cabral was shot dead at a PAIGC roadblock in Conakry by a party member and others, in a plot widely linked to Portuguese agents, two years before the islands gained independence.

title: The Carnation Revolution
summary: A military coup in Lisbon overthrew Portugal's Estado Novo dictatorship, worn down by its colonial wars, opening the way to decolonisation and negotiations on Cape Verde's independence.

title: Independence of Cape Verde
summary: The Republic of Cape Verde declared independence from Portugal on 5 July 1975 under the PAIGC, with Aristides Pereira as first president; the United States recognised the new state the same day.

title: Bissau coup ends the union
summary: A coup in Guinea-Bissau led by João Bernardo "Nino" Vieira overthrew President Luís Cabral and shattered the planned union with Cape Verde, whose PAIGC branch broke away to form the separate PAICV.

title: The PAICV and a one-party state
summary: Cape Verde's branch of the PAIGC was reconstituted as the African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde (PAICV), which governed the islands as a pragmatic one-party state through the 1980s.

title: End of one-party rule
summary: Amid rising pressure for pluralism, the opposition Movement for Democracy (MpD) formed in April 1990 and the National Assembly abolished single-party rule that September, clearing the way for free elections.

title: First multiparty elections
summary: In Cape Verde's first free elections the MpD won a parliamentary majority, and António Mascarenhas Monteiro defeated President Aristides Pereira with about 73 per cent of the vote; the PAICV ceded power peacefully.

title: Peaceful alternation of power
summary: The PAICV returned to government in the 2001 elections and Pedro Pires won the presidency, confirming a pattern of peaceful, competitive transfers of power between rival parties.

title: Cesária Évora and morna go global
summary: Cesária Évora, the "barefoot diva", won a Grammy for the album Voz d'Amor, the high point of a career that carried Cape Verdean morna and its Creole longing to audiences worldwide.

title: Graduation from least-developed status
summary: Buoyed by tourism, remittances and stable governance, Cape Verde graduated from the UN list of least-developed countries — a rare achievement for an African state — confirming its development progress.

title: Cidade Velha named a World Heritage Site
summary: UNESCO inscribed Cidade Velha, the Historic Centre of Ribeira Grande — the first European city in the tropics — as Cape Verde's only World Heritage Site, recognising its role in the Atlantic slave trade and colonial expansion.

title: Morna inscribed as intangible heritage
summary: UNESCO added morna, the Cape Verdean musical practice of love, parting and sodade, to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, honouring the islands' best-known cultural expression.

title: Diquis chiefdoms and the stone spheres
summary: Chiefdom societies in the Diquis delta carve more than 300 near-perfect stone spheres and build settlements of mounds and paved precincts.

title: UNESCO World Heritage inscription
summary: The Diquis settlements with their stone spheres become Costa Rica's first cultural World Heritage Site, recognised as unique evidence of pre-Columbian chiefdom societies.

title: Columbus reaches the Rich Coast
summary: On his fourth voyage Columbus lands on the Caribbean coast; gifts of gold inspire the name Costa Rica, the Rich Coast.

title: Founding of Cartago
summary: The Spanish establish Cartago in the Central Valley as the colonial capital, which it remains until 1823.

title: Independence from Spain
summary: Central America, Costa Rica included, declares independence from Spain; the province soon joins the Mexican Empire and then a regional federation.

title: Coffee arrives from Cuba
summary: Thirteen years before independence, coffee is introduced and becomes the principal crop of a province that had never had one — a dominance lasting into the 20th century.

title: Juan Mora Fernandez, first head of state
summary: Costa Rica's first elected head of state founds schools and courts and promotes coffee planting through free land grants.

title: Withdrawal from the federation
summary: Disenchanted with the strife of the United Provinces of Central America, Costa Rica severs its federal ties and charts an independent course.

title: Costa Rica declares itself sovereign
summary: A decade after leaving the federation, the republic formally declares independence and notifies Washington on 5 September.

title: US recognition — on paper
summary: Washington recognises Costa Rican independence by empowering its charge d'affaires in Guatemala, who never visits the country and reaches no agreement by post.

title: Diplomatic relations established
summary: Costa Rican minister Felipe Molina presents his credentials in Washington; a US consulate opens in San Jose the following year.

title: National War against William Walker
summary: Costa Rica joins Central America in defeating the American filibuster William Walker; the soldier Juan Santamaria becomes a national hero.

title: Minor Keith and the banana railways
summary: Minor C. Keith begins building railways and planting bananas, ventures that in 1899 merge into the United Fruit Company and reshape the Caribbean coast.

title: First free election in Central America
summary: Costa Rica holds what is regarded as the first free and honest election in Central America, beginning a long democratic tradition.

title: Disputed election sparks civil war
summary: The annulment of the 1948 election to bar president-elect Otilio Ulate triggers a brief but bloody civil war.

title: Figueres leads the civil war
summary: Jose Figueres Ferrer leads an armed uprising in support of president-elect Ulate; the two-month war kills about 2,000 people before the government surrenders.

title: Constitution abolishes the army
summary: Figueres's junta promulgates a new constitution that bans a standing army, grants women the vote, and nationalises the banks, then hands power to Ulate.

title: National park system created
summary: Costa Rica establishes a national park system that grows to protect roughly a quarter of the country, anchoring its conservation and ecotourism economy.

title: Oscar Arias wins the Nobel Peace Prize
summary: President Oscar Arias Sanchez is awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for the Central American peace plan signed by the region's leaders in August 1987.

title: A country without an army raises a force
summary: After clashes with Sandinista troops across the San Juan, a US-trained anti-guerrilla force begins operating — the limits of demilitarisation in a region at war.

title: San Juan navigation dispute settled
summary: Costa Rica and Nicaragua resolve a long-standing quarrel over navigation on the river that forms their border.

title: Recognition switches from Taipei to Beijing
summary: Costa Rica transfers diplomatic recognition to the People's Republic of China in pursuit of investment.

title: Laura Chinchilla, first woman president
summary: Costa Rica elects its first female head of state.

title: Diquis spheres named World Heritage
summary: UNESCO inscribes the Diquis chiefdom settlements and their stone spheres as Costa Rica's first cultural World Heritage Site.

title: The Hague settles Isla Portillos
summary: The International Court of Justice rules that sovereignty over the disputed San Juan wetland belongs to Costa Rica — a demilitarised state settling its border in court.

title: Columbus reaches Cuba
summary: On his first voyage Christopher Columbus anchors off the northern coast of Cuba and claims the island for Spain, his first encounter with the Taino there.

title: Spanish conquest begins
summary: Diego Velazquez leads the conquest of Cuba, founding Baracoa as the first Spanish settlement; further towns follow within a few years.

title: Collapse of the Taino
summary: Forced labour, starvation, and Old World disease all but extinguish the indigenous Taino, prompting the import of enslaved Africans.

title: Founding of Havana
summary: The Spanish found Havana, whose harbour becomes an obligatory stop on the route to the New World and the most heavily fortified port of the Caribbean.

title: The fortifications of Havana
summary: Construction of the Castillo de la Real Fuerza and, later, the Morro and La Cabana fortresses makes Havana the fortified key to the Indies.

title: Sugar-and-slavery boom
summary: Cuba becomes the world's leading sugar producer, importing over 600,000 enslaved Africans; by 1860 it makes nearly a third of the world's sugar.

title: Grito de Yara
summary: Carlos Manuel de Cespedes frees his slaves and proclaims independence at La Demajagua, beginning the Ten Years' War against Spain.

title: Marti's War of Independence
summary: Jose Marti orders the resumption of war and lands in Cuba, dying at Dos Rios on 19 May; the rising continues under Gomez and Maceo.

title: Sinking of the USS Maine
summary: The U.S. battleship Maine explodes in Havana harbour, propelling the United States toward war with Spain over Cuba.

title: Spanish-American War ends Spanish rule
summary: After Spain's defeat, the Treaty of Paris ends Spanish dominion over Cuba; the Teller Amendment had disclaimed U.S. annexation.

title: The Platt Amendment
summary: The U.S. Congress conditions withdrawal on the Platt Amendment, reserving a right of intervention and a naval base at Guantanamo Bay; Cuba writes it into its constitution.

title: Republic of Cuba proclaimed
summary: The United States ends its occupation and the Republic of Cuba is installed under Tomas Estrada Palma, its first president.

title: Fall of Machado
summary: Amid depression and unrest the army forces dictator Gerardo Machado to flee, opening the era of Fulgencio Batista.

title: Batista's coup
summary: Anticipating electoral defeat, Fulgencio Batista seizes power in a bloodless coup and rules as dictator, provoking armed opposition.

title: Triumph of the Revolution
summary: Batista flees and the 26th of July Movement takes power; Fidel Castro soon leads the new government, which turns toward socialism.

title: Bay of Pigs invasion
summary: A brigade of U.S.-backed Cuban exiles lands at the Bay of Pigs in an attempt to overthrow Castro and is defeated within days.

title: U.S. embargo made comprehensive
summary: President Kennedy expands the trade embargo to cover nearly all commerce with Cuba and makes it permanent.

title: Cuban Missile Crisis
summary: Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba trigger a thirteen-day confrontation; a U.S. quarantine and a Soviet agreement to withdraw the missiles avert nuclear war.

title: The Special Period begins
summary: The Soviet collapse ends Cuba's subsidies and trade; Castro declares a special period of rationing and austerity as GDP contracts sharply.

title: Raul Castro assumes the presidency
summary: An ailing Fidel Castro hands power to his brother Raul, who introduces gradual economic reforms.

title: Thaw with the United States
summary: Obama and Raul Castro announce normalisation; diplomatic relations are restored and embassies reopen in 2015, though the embargo remains.

title: Leadership beyond the Castros
summary: Miguel Diaz-Canel becomes president in 2018 and Communist Party leader in 2021, the first non-Castro to hold the top posts since 1959.

title: Ottoman conquest of Cyprus
summary: An Ottoman army took Cyprus from Venice, capturing Nicosia and Famagusta and beginning more than three centuries of Ottoman rule that settled a Muslim Turkish-Cypriot community on the island.

title: Emergence of the Turkish-Cypriot community
summary: Muslim settlers, many from Anatolia, established a distinct Turkish-Cypriot community alongside the Greek-Cypriot majority, while the Orthodox Church regained authority over Greek Cypriots under the millet system.

title: British administration of Cyprus begins
summary: Under the Cyprus Convention the Ottoman Empire transferred the administration of Cyprus to Britain, which annexed the island in 1914 and made it a Crown colony in 1925.

title: EOKA campaign for enosis
summary: The guerrilla organisation EOKA, backed by Archbishop Makarios, fought British rule in pursuit of enosis (union with Greece); Turkish Cypriots opposed enosis and called for taksim (partition).

title: Zürich and London agreements
summary: Britain, Greece, and Turkey, with Greek-Cypriot and Turkish-Cypriot leaders, agreed terms for an independent bicommunal republic, barring both enosis and partition and naming the three powers as guarantors.

title: Britain annexes Cyprus
summary: After more than three centuries of Ottoman rule and thirty-six years of British administration, Britain annexes the island outright on entering the First World War against the Ottoman Empire.

title: Independence of the Republic of Cyprus
summary: Cyprus became an independent bicommunal republic under a power-sharing constitution, with Makarios III as president and Fazıl Küçük as Turkish-Cypriot vice-president, and Britain retaining sovereign base areas.

title: Breakdown of power-sharing and intercommunal violence
summary: After President Makarios proposed constitutional amendments curtailing Turkish-Cypriot safeguards, the partnership collapsed and intercommunal violence broke out; Turkish Cypriots withdrew from the bicommunal state into enclaves.

title: UN peacekeeping force (UNFICYP) established
summary: By Resolution 186 the UN Security Council created UNFICYP to prevent renewed fighting and restore normal conditions; the force has remained deployed in Cyprus ever since.

title: Coup against Makarios
summary: Greek-Cypriot nationalists in the National Guard, backed by the military junta in Athens, overthrew President Makarios in pursuit of enosis and installed Nikos Sampson.

title: Turkish military intervention
summary: Invoking its guarantor role under the 1960 treaty, Turkey landed forces in Cyprus; described by Turkey as a peace operation and by the Republic of Cyprus as an invasion, it ended with Turkish control of the northern third of the island.

title: Turkish Federated State of Cyprus proclaimed
summary: The Turkish-Cypriot leadership under Rauf Denktaş proclaimed a 'Turkish Federated State of Cyprus' in the north, presented as a building block for a future federation rather than a separate sovereign state.

title: Security Council Resolution 353
summary: The Council calls on all states to respect the sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity of Cyprus, demands an immediate ceasefire and an end to foreign military intervention, and demands the withdrawal of foreign military personnel not authorised by international agreements.

title: Declaration of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus
summary: The Turkish-Cypriot assembly under Rauf Denktaş unilaterally declared the independent Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus in the island's north, presenting it as an act of self-determination.

title: UN Security Council Resolution 541
summary: The Security Council deplored the declaration, considered it legally invalid, called for its withdrawal, and called on all states not to recognise any Cypriot state other than the Republic of Cyprus.

title: UN Security Council Resolution 550
summary: The Security Council reaffirmed Resolution 541, condemned secessionist actions including the exchange of ambassadors with Turkey, and addressed the status of the fenced town of Varosha.

title: The Committee on Missing Persons is established
summary: The leaders of the two communities set up a bicommunal committee, with United Nations participation, to recover and identify the remains of the missing — a joint list of 2,002 people, 492 Turkish Cypriots and 1,510 Greek Cypriots.

title: Crossing points open along the Green Line
summary: For the first time in decades, crossing points in the UN buffer zone were opened, allowing movement between north and south and easing the communities' separation without settling the dispute.

title: Annan Plan referendums fail
summary: The UN reunification plan was approved by a majority of Turkish Cypriots but rejected by a large majority of Greek Cypriots in simultaneous referendums, so it was not implemented.

title: Republic of Cyprus joins the European Union
summary: Cyprus acceded to the EU as a divided island; EU law applies in full only in the south and is suspended in the north pending a political settlement.

title: Crans-Montana talks collapse
summary: UN-brokered reunification negotiations at Crans-Montana ended without agreement, after which Turkish-Cypriot leaders increasingly pressed for a two-state solution rejected by the Republic of Cyprus and the UN.

title: The peacekeeping mandate rolls on
summary: The Security Council renews a mission begun in 1964; some 2,400 peacekeepers patrol the buffer zone between the two communities.

title: Ledra Street reopens
summary: The crossing in the heart of walled Nicosia, closed since 1964, is reopened — the most symbolically charged of the openings along the buffer zone.

title: The eurozone crisis reaches the island
summary: The Republic of Cyprus negotiates a deal to extricate its financial sector from the eurozone debt crisis; the north, outside the EU and using the Turkish lira, is affected differently.

title: New crossings at Deryneia and Lefke
summary: The first new buffer-zone crossings in eight years open in the east and the west of the island.

title: The Neolithic settlement of Choirokoitia
summary: A farming community of round stone dwellings flourished at Choirokoitia, one of the best-preserved and most important prehistoric sites in the eastern Mediterranean, illuminating the early evolution of human society in the region.

title: Greek settlement and the city-kingdoms
summary: After the collapse of Mycenaean Greece, Greek-speaking settlers established the city-kingdoms of Cyprus, among them Salamis, Kition and Paphos, making Greek the island's predominant language.

title: The sanctuary of Aphrodite at Paphos
summary: Old Paphos became the principal centre of the worship of Aphrodite, whose temple bore witness to one of the oldest Mycenaean settlements and drew pilgrims from across the Greek world.

title: Assyrian, Egyptian and Persian overlordship
summary: The Cypriot kingdoms paid tribute successively to the Assyrian, Egyptian and Persian empires, sharing in the wider Greek world's long struggle against Persian domination.

title: Ptolemaic rule
summary: Following Alexander the Great's conquests, Cyprus passed to the Hellenistic Ptolemies of Egypt, who abolished the independent city-kingdoms and governed the island as a province until Rome took it in 58 BCE.

title: Rome annexes Cyprus
summary: Cyprus was annexed by Rome and organised as a province; under Roman rule the island prospered, with Nea Paphos as its capital and a centre of the celebrated mosaic art later inscribed by UNESCO.

title: Paul and Barnabas convert the proconsul
summary: On their journey across Cyprus the apostles Paul and Barnabas reached the Roman proconsul Sergius Paulus at Paphos, an early instance of a senior Roman official embracing Christianity.

title: An autocephalous Church
summary: The Church of Cyprus was recognised as self-governing (autocephalous), free from the authority of any neighbouring patriarch, a distinction its archbishops have defended throughout the island's history.

title: Arab raids and a contested frontier
summary: From the mid-seventh century Cyprus suffered repeated Arab naval raids and for some three centuries lay as a contested zone between Byzantium and the Caliphate before Byzantine rule was firmly restored in 965.

title: The painted churches of the Troödos
summary: The mountain region of Troödos accumulated one of the largest groups of Byzantine churches and monasteries, richly decorated with murals later inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

title: Richard the Lionheart seizes Cyprus
summary: En route to the Third Crusade, King Richard I of England captured Cyprus from its Byzantine governor, ending Byzantine rule and opening the island to Latin Crusader control.

title: The Lusignan Kingdom of Cyprus
summary: Guy de Lusignan, former king of Jerusalem, took possession of Cyprus, founding a French feudal dynasty that ruled the island as a Latin Crusader kingdom for nearly three centuries.

title: Cyprus ceded to Venice
summary: Caterina Cornaro, widow of the last Lusignan king, ceded Cyprus to the Republic of Venice, which ruled it as a fortified colonial outpost and bulwark against the Ottomans.

title: Ottoman conquest of Cyprus
summary: An Ottoman army invaded in 1570, taking Nicosia, and after a long siege captured Famagusta in 1571, ending Venetian rule and beginning more than three centuries of Ottoman administration.

title: Two communities take shape
summary: Under Ottoman rule the Orthodox Church was restored and its archbishop made leader of the Greek Cypriots, while Muslim settlement established the Turkish Cypriot community alongside it.

title: Britain takes over Cyprus
summary: Under the Cyprus Convention, Britain assumed the administration of Cyprus from the Ottoman Empire, which retained nominal sovereignty, gaining a strategic Mediterranean base near the route to India.

title: British annexation
summary: When the Ottoman Empire joined the First World War against Britain, Britain annexed Cyprus; Turkey renounced its claim to the island in the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne.

title: Cyprus made a Crown Colony
summary: Cyprus was formally declared a British Crown Colony, consolidating colonial administration over the island.

title: The énosis plebiscite
summary: The Orthodox Church organised a plebiscite in which the overwhelming majority of Greek Cypriots voted for union with Greece; Britain refused, and Turkish Cypriots opposed it, sharpening communal division.

title: EOKA launches its armed campaign
summary: EOKA, led by Colonel Georgios Grivas with the support of Archbishop Makarios III, began an armed struggle against British rule in pursuit of énosis, opening four years of insurgency and repression.

title: The Zürich-London Agreements
summary: Greece and Turkey reached a compromise at Zürich, endorsed in London by Britain and Cypriot leaders, setting the terms for an independent Cyprus that excluded both énosis and partition.

title: Independence and the Treaty of Guarantee
summary: The Republic of Cyprus became independent under a Greek-Turkish power-sharing constitution; the Treaty of Guarantee bound Britain, Greece and Turkey to its independence and territorial integrity, and Britain kept two Sovereign Base Areas.

title: Breakdown and the Green Line
summary: After President Makarios proposed constitutional changes, intercommunal violence broke out in December 1963; Turkish Cypriots withdrew from government and a ceasefire line dubbed the 'Green Line' was drawn through Nicosia.

title: UN Security Council Resolution 186 establishes UNFICYP
summary: The Security Council unanimously recommended, with the consent of the Government of Cyprus, the creation of the UN Peace-keeping Force in Cyprus to prevent a recurrence of fighting and help restore order; UNFICYP became operational on 27 March 1964.

title: A UN mediator for the Cyprus question
summary: Resolution 186 also recommended that the Secretary-General designate a mediator to promote a peaceful and agreed settlement, beginning the long international effort to resolve the dispute.

title: The Greek-junta-backed coup
summary: The military junta ruling Greece, through the Cypriot National Guard, overthrew President Makarios in pursuit of énosis; Makarios escaped abroad and a hardline nationalist was installed.

title: Turkish military intervention
summary: Invoking its guarantor rights under the 1960 Treaty of Guarantee, Turkey landed forces on 20 July 1974 and in a second August offensive took the northern third of the island, partitioning Cyprus and displacing both communities; UNFICYP was thereafter tasked with supervising the ceasefire lines and the buffer zone.

title: Declaration of the 'TRNC' and UN Resolution 541
summary: The Turkish Cypriot leadership proclaimed the 'Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus' on 15 November 1983; on 18 November the Security Council, in Resolution 541, considered the declaration legally invalid and called on all states not to recognise any Cypriot state other than the Republic of Cyprus.

title: The Annan Plan referendums
summary: A UN reunification plan was put to simultaneous referendums; Turkish Cypriots approved it but about three-quarters of Greek Cypriots voting rejected it, leaving the island divided on the eve of EU membership.

title: Accession to the European Union
summary: The Republic of Cyprus joined the EU; the whole island is EU territory, but the application of EU law is suspended in the northern areas not under the government's effective control.

title: Mission of Cyril and Methodius to Great Moravia
summary: At the request of Prince Rostislav, the Byzantine brothers Cyril and Methodius came to Great Moravia, translated the liturgy into Old Church Slavonic and devised the Glagolitic alphabet, bringing Christianity to the Slavs.

title: Fall of Great Moravia
summary: Weakened by internal division and overwhelmed by the Magyars, Great Moravia disintegrated in the early tenth century, and leadership of the western Slavs shifted to the Premyslid dukes of Bohemia.

title: Martyrdom of Saint Wenceslas
summary: Wenceslas (Vaclav), Premyslid duke of Bohemia and promoter of Christianity, was murdered by his brother and was at once venerated as a martyr, becoming the patron saint of the Czech nation.

title: Golden Bull of Sicily and the Kingdom of Bohemia
summary: The Golden Bull of Sicily, issued by Emperor Frederick II, confirmed the royal title of the Premyslid rulers as hereditary, formally raising Bohemia from a duchy to a kingdom within the Holy Roman Empire.

title: End of the Premyslid dynasty
summary: The murder of Wenceslas III extinguished the male line of the Premyslids; after a brief contest the Bohemian crown passed to the House of Luxembourg, the dynasty of Charles IV.

title: Foundation of Charles University
summary: Charles IV founded the university in Prague that bears his name, the first university in central Europe, endowed with the same rights and liberties as the universities of Paris and Bologna.

title: Charles IV crowned Holy Roman Emperor
summary: Already king of Bohemia, Charles was crowned Holy Roman Emperor in Rome in 1355, making Prague the principal residence of the Empire and the centre of European politics and culture.

title: Building of Charles Bridge and Gothic Prague
summary: Charles IV laid the foundation of the stone bridge over the Vltava and advanced St Vitus Cathedral and the New Town, creating the Gothic core of Prague later recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage site.

title: Jan Hus preaches at the Bethlehem Chapel
summary: Appointed preacher at the Bethlehem Chapel in Prague, Hus began to denounce church corruption and indulgences and to champion reform and vernacular preaching, drawing on the ideas of John Wycliffe.

title: Jan Hus burned at the Council of Constance
summary: Condemned as a heretic despite a promise of safe conduct, Hus was burned at the stake at Constance on 6 July 1415, becoming a martyr whose death set off the Hussite movement.

title: The Hussite Wars
summary: Followers of Hus fought a series of wars against the Catholic crown and papal crusades; under Jan Zizka the Hussite armies proved nearly invincible before the conflict ended in compromise.

title: Compact of Iglau
summary: The moderate Utraquist Hussites secured a peace settlement, the Compact of Iglau, that granted communion in both kinds and an independent Bohemian Catholic church, ending the main phase of the wars.

title: Bohemia under the Habsburgs
summary: The Bohemian estates elected Ferdinand I of Habsburg as king, binding the kingdom to the Habsburg monarchy and to Austria and Hungary for nearly four centuries.

title: Defenestration of Prague
summary: Protestant nobles threw two Catholic imperial regents and their secretary from a window of Prague Castle, sparking the Bohemian revolt against Ferdinand II and helping to launch the Thirty Years' War.

title: Battle of White Mountain
summary: Imperial and Catholic League armies crushed the Bohemian rebels at White Mountain near Prague, ending Czech estates' power and ushering in Habsburg absolutism and forced Counter-Reformation.

title: The Czech National Revival
summary: From the late 18th century, scholars led by the historian Frantisek Palacky rebuilt and codified the Czech language and national history, transforming a cultural awakening into a political movement within Austria-Hungary.

title: Foundation of Czechoslovakia
summary: With Austria-Hungary collapsing, independence was proclaimed in Prague on 28 October 1918; Tomas Garrigue Masaryk became the first president of the new multi-ethnic democratic republic.

title: The Munich Agreement
summary: Germany, Italy, Britain and France agreed at Munich that Czechoslovakia must cede the German-majority Sudetenland to Nazi Germany; Czechoslovakia was not a party and yielded under Anglo-French pressure.

title: German annexation of the Sudetenland
summary: Following the Munich Agreement, German forces occupied the Sudetenland, stripping Czechoslovakia of its border defences and around three million inhabitants in its German-speaking borderlands.

title: Occupation and the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia
summary: In breach of Munich, Germany occupied the Czech lands on 15 March 1939 and proclaimed the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia, while a separate Slovak state was set up under German control.

title: Expulsion of the Sudeten Germans
summary: Under the Benes decrees and Allied agreement at Potsdam, Czechoslovakia stripped the citizenship and property of its Germans and expelled some three million Sudeten Germans, the largest forced migration in the history of the Czech lands.

title: Communist coup
summary: In February 1948 the Communist Party seized full power in Czechoslovakia, ending postwar democracy and bringing the country firmly into the Soviet bloc for the next four decades.

title: Prague Spring crushed by Warsaw Pact
summary: Alexander Dubcek's reforms of 'socialism with a human face' were ended when roughly half a million Warsaw Pact troops, led by the Soviet Union, invaded Czechoslovakia in August 1968.

title: The Velvet Revolution
summary: A suppressed student march in Prague on 17 November 1989 set off mass protests that toppled the communist regime within weeks; Vaclav Havel was elected president on 29 December.

title: The Velvet Divorce and birth of the Czech Republic
summary: After a 1992 vote to divide, Czechoslovakia split peacefully on 1 January 1993 into the Czech Republic and Slovakia; the Czech Republic later joined NATO in 1999 and the EU in 2004.

title: Battle of the Teutoburg Forest
summary: Germanic tribes under Arminius destroyed three Roman legions commanded by Varus, ending Roman attempts to conquer Germania east of the Rhine and securing the river as a permanent frontier.

title: Coronation of Charlemagne
summary: Pope Leo III crowned the Frankish king Charlemagne Emperor of the Romans in Rome, reviving the western imperial title and binding the German lands into a renewed Christian empire.

title: Treaty of Verdun
summary: Charlemagne's grandsons divided the Carolingian empire into three kingdoms. East Francia, the German-speaking eastern share, became the foundation of the future Kingdom of Germany.

title: Otto I crowned emperor
summary: Pope John XII crowned Otto I of East Francia emperor in Rome, uniting the German and Italian kingdoms and founding the Holy Roman Empire that would frame German political life for over 800 years.

title: Luther's Ninety-five Theses
summary: Martin Luther issued his Ninety-five Theses against the sale of indulgences, sparking the Protestant Reformation that split Western Christianity and reshaped German society and language.

title: Peace of Augsburg
summary: The imperial diet established the first lasting legal coexistence of Lutheranism and Catholicism, letting each prince set his territory's religion under the principle cuius regio, eius religio.

title: The Thirty Years' War and the Peace of Westphalia
summary: A devastating European war fought largely in Germany ended with the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, which confirmed the autonomy of the empire's states and entrenched German fragmentation.

title: Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire
summary: Under pressure from Napoleon, Emperor Francis II abdicated the imperial crown and dissolved the Holy Roman Empire, ending the medieval framework of German statehood after more than eight centuries.

title: Congress of Vienna and the German Confederation
summary: After Napoleon's defeat, the Congress of Vienna created a loose confederation of German states dominated by Austria and Prussia, leaving national unity unfulfilled.

title: The Revolutions of 1848
summary: Liberal and nationalist uprisings swept the German states, and the Frankfurt Parliament drafted a constitution for a united Germany, but the movement collapsed when the Prussian king refused its imperial crown.

title: Proclamation of the German Empire
summary: Following victory in the Franco-Prussian War, the German states united as the German Empire, proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles with Wilhelm I as Emperor and Bismarck as Chancellor.

title: The Bismarckian empire and industrial rise
summary: Under Bismarck's chancellorship the empire industrialised rapidly and introduced the world's first national social insurance, while maintaining a careful balance of power in Europe.

title: German colonial expansion
summary: Germany acquired colonies in Africa and the Pacific, a latecomer's empire whose rule, including the genocide of the Herero and Nama in South West Africa, left a brutal legacy.

title: The First World War
summary: Germany fought the First World War as the principal Central Power. Four years of total war devastated a generation and ended in German defeat.

title: Abdication of Wilhelm II
summary: Amid military collapse and revolution, Emperor Wilhelm II abdicated and a republic was proclaimed in Berlin; the armistice followed two days later, ending the war and the monarchy.

title: The Weimar Republic and its constitution
summary: Germany's first democracy adopted the Weimar Constitution in 1919, establishing a parliamentary republic that would be undermined by economic crisis and political extremism.

title: Hitler appointed chancellor
