summary: Hungary lost about two-thirds of its territory and population, leaving roughly three million ethnic Hungarians outside the new borders in Romania, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia and elsewhere; the trauma shaped Hungarian politics for a century.

title: First Vienna Award
summary: Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy awarded Hungary parts of southern Slovakia from Czechoslovakia, the first of the revisionist gains that drew Hungary toward the Axis.

title: Second Vienna Award
summary: Germany and Italy awarded Hungary northern Transylvania from Romania, deepening Hungary's dependence on the Axis powers in its quest to reverse Trianon.

title: Hungary enters the war as an Axis ally
summary: Seeking to keep and extend the lands restored by the Vienna Awards, Hungary joined Germany's war and took part in the invasion of the Soviet Union.

title: German occupation of Hungary
summary: German forces occupied Hungary to keep it in the war and to deport its Jews, then the largest surviving Jewish community in Europe, numbering some 760,000 to 780,000 people.

title: Deportation of the Hungarian Jews
summary: Between 15 May and 9 July 1944 about 437,000 Jews were deported, mostly to Auschwitz-Birkenau, where some three-quarters were murdered on arrival; Horthy halted the trains on 7 July.

title: The Arrow Cross seizure of power
summary: After Horthy's attempt to leave the war, Germany installed the fascist Arrow Cross, which murdered thousands more Jews in Budapest before the Soviet conquest of the city.

title: The siege of Budapest
summary: The months-long battle for the capital between German-Hungarian and Soviet forces destroyed much of historic Budapest, including the castle and the Danube bridges, as the Red Army completed its conquest of Hungary.

title: The Hungarian People's Republic
summary: Backed by the Soviet Union, the communists seized total power and proclaimed a one-party People's Republic, imposing Stalinist terror, show trials and forced collectivisation under Mátyás Rákosi.

title: The Hungarian Revolution of 1956
summary: A nationwide rising under premier Imre Nagy declared Hungary's withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact; the Soviet army crushed it on 4 November, killing some 2,500 Hungarians and driving about 200,000 into exile.

title: 'Goulash communism' and the New Economic Mechanism
summary: János Kádár's reforms admitted limited market forces and private enterprise, giving Hungarians a relative prosperity and freedom unusual in the Soviet bloc.

title: The Pan-European Picnic and the opening of the border
summary: A border gate opened near Sopron let some 700 East Germans flee west; Hungary's subsequent full opening of its frontier breached the Iron Curtain and helped bring down the Berlin Wall.

title: Proclamation of the republic
summary: On the anniversary of the 1956 rising Hungary proclaimed itself a free republic, ending four decades of communist rule and beginning its transition to democracy.

title: Accession to NATO and the European Union
summary: Having joined NATO on 12 March 1999, Hungary acceded to the European Union on 1 May 2004 in the bloc's largest single enlargement, completing its return to the West.

title: Rise of the Srivijaya thalassocracy
summary: From its base at Palembang in Sumatra, the Buddhist kingdom of Srivijaya comes to dominate maritime trade through the Straits of Malacca and Sunda and becomes a renowned centre of Buddhist scholarship.

title: Construction of Borobudur
summary: Under the Sailendra dynasty in central Java the great Buddhist monument of Borobudur is built; the world's largest Buddhist temple, it is today a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: Founding of the Majapahit empire
summary: Raden Wijaya establishes Majapahit in eastern Java, which grows into the most powerful Hindu-Buddhist empire of the archipelago.

title: Majapahit's golden age under Hayam Wuruk
summary: Under King Hayam Wuruk and his prime minister Gajah Mada, Majapahit reaches its height, projecting power and trade across much of the archipelago.

title: Islam takes root in northern Sumatra
summary: The early Muslim sultanate of Samudera Pasai in northern Sumatra marks the establishment of Islam in the archipelago, spread by traders along the maritime routes.

title: Rise of the Demak Sultanate on Java
summary: Demak emerges as the first major Islamic state on Java and a base from which Islam spreads across the island as Majapahit's power collapses.

title: Spice sultanates of Ternate, Tidore and Aceh flourish
summary: Muslim sultanates controlling the clove, nutmeg and pepper trade grow rich and powerful, making the archipelago the hub of a global spice economy.

title: Portuguese capture of Malacca
summary: Afonso de Albuquerque seizes the trading city of Malacca, beginning sustained European involvement in the archipelago's spice trade.

title: Founding of the Dutch East India Company (VOC)
summary: The Dutch Republic charters the VOC with sweeping powers to trade, wage war and govern, launching nearly two centuries of company rule in the Indies.

title: Founding of Batavia
summary: Governor-General Jan Pieterszoon Coen storms Jayakarta and builds Batavia (modern Jakarta) as the VOC's Asian headquarters.

title: The Banda massacre
summary: To enforce the nutmeg monopoly, Coen's forces kill, starve, enslave or deport almost the entire population of the Banda Islands, an atrocity that destroys Bandanese society.

title: Dissolution of the VOC
summary: Bankrupt after decades of war, debt and corruption, the VOC is dissolved and its possessions pass to the Dutch state, ushering in direct colonial rule.

title: The Cultivation System
summary: The Dutch impose the Cultuurstelsel, forcing Javanese peasants to grow export crops for the colonial state; it enriches the Netherlands while causing widespread hardship and local famines.

title: Founding of Budi Utomo
summary: The cultural society Budi Utomo is founded, widely regarded as the start of organised Indonesian nationalism and the National Awakening.

title: Sukarno founds the Indonesian National Party
summary: Sukarno establishes the PNI, demanding full independence and giving the nationalist movement a charismatic mass leader.

title: The Youth Pledge (Sumpah Pemuda)
summary: Young nationalists vow to recognise one Indonesian motherland, nation and language, a foundational moment in forging a unified national identity.

title: Japanese occupation of the Indies
summary: Japan conquers the Dutch East Indies, ending Dutch rule; its occupation brings forced labour and hardship but also mobilises and arms Indonesian nationalists.

title: Proclamation of Independence
summary: Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta proclaim Indonesia an independent republic in Jakarta, days after Japan's surrender; they become president and vice-president the next day.

title: The Indonesian National Revolution
summary: Indonesians wage a four-year armed and diplomatic struggle against Dutch attempts to reimpose colonial rule, enduring two major Dutch offensives and heavy losses.

title: Recognition of sovereignty
summary: Following the Round Table Conference in The Hague, the Netherlands formally transfers sovereignty and recognises the independence of Indonesia.

title: The anti-communist mass killings
summary: Following the 30 September coup attempt blamed on the PKI, an army-led purge kills an estimated 500,000 to over a million suspected communists and others, a vast atrocity that paves Suharto's path to power.

title: Suharto's New Order
summary: Suharto formally becomes president and rules for over three decades, delivering growth and stability through authoritarian control, military dominance and pervasive corruption.

title: Fall of Suharto and Reformasi
summary: Amid economic collapse and mass protests, Suharto resigns after 32 years in power, launching the Reformasi era of democratic reform and decentralisation.

title: First direct presidential election
summary: Indonesians directly elect their president for the first time, consolidating one of the world's largest democracies after the authoritarian New Order.

title: Mature urban phase of the Indus cities
summary: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro and hundreds of other settlements reach their peak, with grid-planned streets, advanced drainage and standardised weights across a vast trading network.

title: Mohenjo-daro flourishes
summary: Mohenjo-daro, on the Indus in modern Pakistan, becomes one of the civilisation's largest cities and is today a UNESCO World Heritage Site renowned for its Great Bath and citadel.

title: Decline of the Harappan cities
summary: The major cities are gradually abandoned as weakening monsoons and shifting rivers undermine the agricultural base, marking the end of the civilisation's urban phase.

title: Composition of the Rigveda
summary: The Rigveda, the oldest Vedic text and a foundational scripture of Hinduism, is composed in early Sanskrit and preserved through oral tradition.

title: Rise of the Buddha and Mahavira
summary: Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha) founds Buddhism and Mahavira reforms Jainism, launching two enduring religions amid a wider questioning of Vedic ritual.

title: Chandragupta Maurya founds the Maurya Empire
summary: Chandragupta Maurya overthrows the Nanda dynasty and builds the first empire to unify most of the subcontinent, with its capital at Pataliputra.

title: Ashoka's conquest of Kalinga and conversion
summary: After the devastating Kalinga war, Emperor Ashoka embraces Buddhism, renounces conquest, and spreads an ethic of dharma through inscribed edicts across his vast empire.

title: Gupta golden age
summary: The Gupta Empire presides over a classical flowering of Sanskrit literature, mathematics and astronomy, including the works of Kalidasa and Aryabhata and the maturing of the decimal system.

title: Founding of the Delhi Sultanate
summary: Qutb al-Din Aibak establishes independent rule at Delhi, beginning a 320-year succession of Islamic dynasties that reshape the politics and culture of northern India.

title: Babur founds the Mughal Empire
summary: Babur defeats Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat, ending the Delhi Sultanate and establishing the Mughal Empire, which would rule much of the subcontinent for over two centuries.

title: Reign of Akbar
summary: Akbar the Great consolidates and expands the empire, reforms its administration with the mansabdari system, and pursues a policy of religious tolerance and cultural synthesis.

title: Death of Aurangzeb and Mughal decline
summary: Aurangzeb dies after extending the empire to its greatest extent; his costly wars and religious policies leave the Mughal state weakened, and its authority rapidly fragments thereafter.

title: Battle of Plassey
summary: Robert Clive's East India Company forces defeat the Nawab of Bengal, marking the beginning of British political and military dominance in India.

title: British Crown rule begins
summary: After the suppression of the 1857 rebellion, the Crown abolishes East India Company rule and assumes direct governance of India, beginning the British Raj.

title: The Salt March
summary: Gandhi leads a 24-day march to the sea to make salt in defiance of the British salt monopoly, galvanising mass non-violent resistance against colonial rule.

title: Bengal famine
summary: An estimated two to three million people die in Bengal in a man-made famine driven by wartime inflation, export priorities and colonial policy rather than any major shortfall in food production.

title: Independence and Partition
summary: India becomes independent from Britain under Prime Minister Nehru as the subcontinent is partitioned into India and Pakistan, unleashing mass migration and communal violence.

title: Partition violence and mass migration
summary: Up to 12–20 million people are uprooted and an estimated one to two million die in massacres and forced migration along the new India–Pakistan border.

title: Constitution and the Republic
summary: The Constitution of India comes into force, making India a sovereign democratic republic with universal suffrage and fundamental rights; the day is celebrated as Republic Day.

title: Palladius sent to the Irish
summary: Pope Celestine I commissioned the bishop Palladius as the first bishop 'to the Irish believing in Christ', marking the formal arrival of organised Christianity on the island.

title: The mission of St Patrick
summary: The British-born missionary Patrick, traditionally active from the 430s, evangelised much of Ireland, secured toleration for Christians and fostered a native clergy and monasticism; his feast is 17 March.

title: Columba founds Iona
summary: The Irish monk Columba established the monastery of Iona off western Scotland, a launching point for the spread of Christianity and Irish learning into Scotland and Northumbria.

title: The monastic golden age
summary: Monasteries such as Clonard, Clonmacnoise and Bangor became renowned centres of learning whose scribes copied Western literature and produced illuminated manuscripts, while Irish missionaries evangelised Europe.

title: First Viking raids on Ireland
summary: Scandinavian raiders struck Rathlin Island in 795, beginning decades of assaults on the rich coastal monasteries recorded with alarm in the Irish annals.

title: Founding of Dublin as a longphort
summary: The Vikings built a fortified ship-camp (longphort) at Dublin in 841 and overwintered there, founding what would become Ireland's most important town and a hub of Norse trade.

title: Brian Boru becomes High King
summary: Brian Boru of the Dál Cais of Munster made himself High King of Ireland around 1002, the most powerful ruler the island had known and a claimant to authority over all of Ireland.

title: Battle of Clontarf
summary: On Good Friday 1014 Brian Boru's army defeated the Norse of Dublin and the men of Leinster near Dublin, breaking Viking political power in Ireland; Brian was killed in the battle.

title: Anglo-Norman landing in Ireland
summary: At the invitation of the exiled Leinster king Diarmait Mac Murchada, Anglo-Norman, Welsh and Flemish forces landed in Wexford in 1169, beginning centuries of English involvement in Ireland.

title: Henry II and the Lordship of Ireland
summary: Henry II landed at Waterford in 1171, the first English king in Ireland, and established the Lordship of Ireland; in 1177 he made his son John 'Lord of Ireland'.

title: Flight of the Earls and the Plantation of Ulster
summary: After the Gaelic earls fled Ireland in 1607, King James I planted English and Scottish Protestant settlers across confiscated lands in Ulster from 1609, embedding a lasting religious and political division.

title: Cromwellian conquest
summary: Oliver Cromwell's parliamentary army stormed Drogheda and Wexford with notorious massacres; the conquest was followed by the 1652 Act for the Settlement of Ireland and the mass confiscation of Catholic land.

title: Williamite victory and the Penal era
summary: The Protestant William III defeated the Catholic James II at the Boyne in 1690 and Limerick in 1691, after which the Protestant Ascendancy entrenched its rule through the anti-Catholic Penal Laws.

title: Act of Union
summary: The Act of Union merged the Kingdom of Ireland with Great Britain into the United Kingdom on 1 January 1801, abolishing the Irish Parliament and placing Ireland under direct rule from Westminster.

title: The Great Famine (An Gorta Mór)
summary: Potato blight destroyed Ireland's staple crop from 1845; about a million people died and a million more emigrated, and the population fell sharply even as food continued to be exported amid an inadequate British relief effort.

title: The Land League and the Land War
summary: The Irish National Land League, founded in 1879 with Charles Stewart Parnell as president, mobilised tenant farmers against landlordism, opening the 'Land War' over rents and ownership.

title: The Home Rule bills
summary: Under Parnell's pressure the Liberal government introduced Home Rule bills in 1886 and 1893 to give Ireland self-government within the UK; both were defeated, but Home Rule became the central Irish demand.

title: The Easter Rising
summary: Republicans seized the General Post Office and other Dublin sites and proclaimed an Irish Republic; the rising was suppressed within a week, but the execution of its leaders turned opinion towards independence.

title: War of Independence
summary: After Sinn Féin's 1918 victory and the first Dáil in 1919, the IRA waged a guerrilla war against British forces until a truce on 11 July 1921 opened the way to negotiations.

title: Anglo-Irish Treaty
summary: The Treaty signed in London created the Irish Free State as a dominion within the British Empire and confirmed the partition of Ireland, leaving six northern counties in the United Kingdom.

title: Civil War over the Treaty
summary: The Treaty split the movement: pro-Treaty forces under Michael Collins fought anti-Treaty republicans under Éamon de Valera in a civil war that the Free State won at heavy cost.

title: Declaration of the Republic
summary: The Republic of Ireland Act, signed 21 December 1948 and in force from 18 April 1949, declared the twenty-six-county state a republic, removed the King's last role and left the Commonwealth.

title: UK annexes Rockall
summary: British Royal Marines landed on the uninhabited Atlantic islet of Rockall in 1955 and claimed it for the United Kingdom; it was declared part of Scotland by the Island of Rockall Act 1972.

title: Accession to the European Communities
summary: After a 1972 referendum carried by over 80 per cent, Ireland joined the European Economic Community on 1 January 1973, beginning a transformation from an agricultural economy to a modern European state.

title: The Celtic Tiger
summary: From the mid-1990s, foreign direct investment and the single market fuelled rapid growth, the 'Celtic Tiger', turning one of western Europe's poorer countries into one of its most prosperous.

title: Good Friday (Belfast) Agreement
summary: The 1998 Agreement settled the conflict over Northern Ireland on the principle of consent and created power-sharing institutions; Ireland amended Articles 2 and 3 of its Constitution to replace its territorial claim with a peaceful aspiration to unity.

title: UK–Ireland continental shelf agreement
summary: Ireland and the United Kingdom agreed a delimitation of the continental shelf between them; Ireland maintained that Rockall, an uninhabitable rock, generates no continental shelf or exclusive economic zone.

title: The kingdom of Elam and the city of Susa
summary: Elam, one of the earliest civilisations of the region, flourishes around its capital Susa in south-western Iran, trading and warring with Mesopotamia until Susa is sacked by the Assyrians around 647 BCE.

title: Cyrus the Great founds the Achaemenid Empire
summary: Cyrus II overthrows the Median king Astyages and unites the Medes and Persians, founding the Achaemenid (Persian) Empire — the first Persian world empire.

title: Conquest of Babylon and the Cyrus Cylinder
summary: Cyrus captures Babylon and issues the Cyrus Cylinder, a Babylonian cuneiform document recording his restoration of temples and return of deported peoples, often hailed as an early charter of tolerance.

title: Darius I builds Persepolis
summary: Darius the Great organises the empire into satrapies, builds the Royal Road and standardised coinage, and begins the magnificent ceremonial capital of Persepolis, today a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: Alexander conquers Persia and burns Persepolis
summary: After defeating Darius III at Gaugamela (331 BCE), Alexander the Great enters and burns Persepolis and the last Achaemenid king is killed, ending the empire in 330 BCE.

title: The Parthian (Arsacid) Empire
summary: Arsaces I founds the Parthian Empire in north-eastern Iran, reviving Persian traditions and becoming Rome's chief rival in the East for nearly five centuries.

title: Ardashir I founds the Sasanian Empire
summary: Ardashir I overthrows the last Parthian king and establishes the Sasanian Empire, the last great pre-Islamic Persian state, with its capital at Ctesiphon.

title: Zoroastrianism as state religion
summary: The Sasanian kings establish Zoroastrianism, the faith attributed to the prophet Zoroaster, as the official religion of Iran, supported by a powerful priesthood and network of fire temples.

title: Exhausting wars with Byzantium
summary: The last great Byzantine–Sasanian war drains both empires militarily and economically, leaving Persia dangerously weakened on the eve of the Arab conquest.

title: Battle of Nahavand — the 'Victory of Victories'
summary: Arab Muslim forces crush the Sasanian army at Nahavand, breaking organised Persian resistance; the empire finally collapses with the death of Yazdegerd III in 651 CE.

title: Islamisation of Persia begins
summary: With the Sasanian state destroyed, Iran is incorporated into the Islamic caliphate; over the following centuries most of its people convert to Islam while retaining the Persian language and much of their culture.

title: Abbasid Revolution and the rise of Baghdad
summary: Backed by support from Persian Khorasan, the Abbasids overthrow the Umayyads and found Baghdad, drawing heavily on Persian administrative and intellectual traditions.

title: Persia at the heart of the Islamic golden age
summary: In the House of Wisdom and beyond, Persian scholars such as Avicenna, al-Khwarizmi and Omar Khayyam advance medicine, mathematics and astronomy during the Islamic golden age.

title: Ferdowsi completes the Shahnameh
summary: The poet Ferdowsi finishes the Shahnameh, the 'Book of Kings', an epic of some 50,000 couplets that preserves Iran's mythic and pre-Islamic history and anchors the Persian language.

title: Mongol invasion of Iran
summary: Genghis Khan's armies invade Iran, devastating its cities; his grandson Hulagu completes the conquest, taking Alamut in 1256 and destroying Baghdad in 1258, and founds the Ilkhanate.

title: Timur and the Timurid era
summary: Timur (Tamerlane) conquers the lands of the former Ilkhanate, founding the Timurid empire whose courts become celebrated centres of Persianate art and learning.

title: Ismail I founds the Safavid dynasty and Shia Iran
summary: Ismail I captures Tabriz, proclaims himself shah, and declares Twelver Shia Islam the state religion, setting Iran apart from its Sunni neighbours and shaping its identity to the present day.

title: Shah Abbas moves the capital to Isfahan
summary: At the height of Safavid power, Shah Abbas the Great relocates the capital to Isfahan and builds the grand Naqsh-e Jahan (Imam) Square, a UNESCO World Heritage masterpiece of urban design.

title: Afghan sack of Isfahan and Safavid decline
summary: Afghan invaders besiege and sack Isfahan, shattering Safavid power; the dynasty formally ends in 1736, opening a period of instability before the rise of the Qajars.

title: Persian Constitutional Revolution
summary: After mass protests, Mozaffar al-Din Shah grants a constitution and the first Majles (parliament), a pioneering experiment in constitutional government in the Middle East.

title: Discovery of oil
summary: Oil is struck in south-western Iran, making the country a strategic prize and tying its economy to foreign-controlled concessions for decades to come.

title: Reza Khan founds the Pahlavi dynasty
summary: Having seized power in a 1921 coup, Reza Khan deposes the last Qajar shah and is crowned Reza Shah Pahlavi, launching an authoritarian drive to modernise and centralise Iran.

title: The CIA-backed coup against Mosaddegh
summary: Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh, who had nationalised the oil industry, is overthrown in August 1953 in a coup organised by the CIA and British intelligence, restoring the shah's power.

title: The Islamic Revolution
summary: The shah flees in January 1979 and Ayatollah Khomeini returns from exile; the monarchy collapses on 11 February, ending some 2,500 years of Iranian kingship.

title: Proclamation of the Islamic Republic
summary: After a referendum on 30–31 March approves the change by an overwhelming majority, Khomeini proclaims the Islamic Republic of Iran on 1 April 1979.

title: US embassy seized and hostage crisis
summary: Militant students storm the US embassy in Tehran, holding 52 Americans for 444 days and setting the new republic on a long course of confrontation with the West.

title: The Iran–Iraq War
summary: Iraq invades in September 1980, igniting a devastating eight-year war; Iran accepts UN Security Council Resolution 598 and a ceasefire takes effect on 20 August 1988.

title: The Sumerians invent cuneiform writing
summary: In the Sumerian city of Uruk, scribes develop cuneiform — wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay — first to keep accounts and then to record law, literature and history, making Mesopotamia the cradle of the written word.

title: Sargon founds the Akkadian Empire
summary: Sargon of Akkad unites the Sumerian city-states under one ruler, creating what is often called history's first empire, with its capital at Akkad and a Semitic-speaking dynasty.

title: Hammurabi issues his law code
summary: Hammurabi, sixth king of Babylon, unifies much of Mesopotamia and promulgates the Code of Hammurabi, 282 laws inscribed on a diorite stela — one of the most complete legal collections of the ancient world.

title: Fall of Nineveh and the Assyrian Empire
summary: A coalition of Babylonians and Medes besieges and destroys Nineveh, capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire whose first capital, Ashur, is now a UNESCO World Heritage site, ending Assyrian power and clearing the way for the Neo-Babylonian Empire.

title: Babylon at its height under Nebuchadnezzar II
summary: The Neo-Babylonian Empire reaches its zenith under Nebuchadnezzar II, who rebuilds Babylon with the Ishtar Gate and great walls; the ruined city, associated with the Hanging Gardens, is today a UNESCO World Heritage site.

title: Cyrus the Great captures Babylon
summary: The Persian king Cyrus the Great takes Babylon, ending the Neo-Babylonian Empire and bringing Mesopotamia into the Achaemenid Persian realm as one of its richest provinces.

title: Hatra, capital of an Arab kingdom
summary: Under Parthian influence the fortified city of Hatra flourishes as the capital of a small Arab kingdom, twice withstanding Roman sieges before falling in the 3rd century; its ruins are now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

title: Mesopotamia under the Sasanians
summary: The Sasanian dynasty replaces the Parthians and rules Mesopotamia from Ctesiphon, making the fertile 'Sawad' the agricultural and administrative core of the Sasanian Empire for four centuries.

title: Battle of al-Qadisiyyah and the Arab conquest
summary: Arab Muslim armies of the Rashidun Caliphate defeat the Sasanians at al-Qadisiyyah near al-Hira and take Ctesiphon, ending Persian rule in Mesopotamia and beginning the region's Islamisation.

title: Al-Mansur founds Baghdad
summary: The Abbasid caliph al-Mansur founds Baghdad on the Tigris as his 'City of Peace', a circular capital that swiftly becomes one of the world's largest and wealthiest cities.

title: The House of Wisdom and the Golden Age
summary: Under Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun, Baghdad's scholars — associated with the Bayt al-Hikmah, the 'House of Wisdom' — translate and advance Greek, Persian and Indian learning during the Islamic Golden Age.

title: Samarra becomes the Abbasid capital
summary: The caliphs move their capital upriver to Samarra, building immense palaces and the Great Mosque with its spiral Malwiya minaret, today a UNESCO World Heritage site.

title: The Mongol sack of Baghdad
summary: The Mongol forces of Hulagu Khan besiege and storm Baghdad, executing the last Abbasid caliph al-Musta'sim and destroying the city; the sack ends the Abbasid Caliphate and devastates the region.

title: Ottoman conquest of Baghdad
summary: The Ottoman Empire takes definitive control of Baghdad from Safavid Persia, ruling Mesopotamia for nearly three centuries as the provinces of Mosul, Baghdad and Basra.

title: British mandate and the Iraqi revolt
summary: After capturing Baghdad in 1917, Britain is granted a League of Nations mandate over Iraq; a widespread anti-British revolt in 1920 pushes Britain toward installing an Arab monarchy.

title: Faisal I crowned king of Iraq
summary: Britain installs the Hashemite prince Faisal I, a leader of the wartime Arab Revolt, as king of the new Iraqi state, creating a monarchy and parliament under British supervision.

title: Independence and entry into the League of Nations
summary: The British mandate ends and the Kingdom of Iraq is admitted to the League of Nations as an independent state — the first League mandate anywhere to achieve independence.

title: Republican coup ends the monarchy
summary: Army officers led by Abd al-Karim Qasim overthrow the Hashemite monarchy in a predawn coup; King Faisal II is killed and the Republic of Iraq is proclaimed.

title: Saddam Hussein assumes the presidency
summary: After years consolidating power within the Ba'ath Party, Saddam Hussein formally becomes president of Iraq in July 1979 and establishes a brutal one-man dictatorship.

title: The Iran–Iraq War
summary: Iraq invades Iran in September 1980, beginning an eight-year war of attrition that kills an estimated several hundred thousand to over a million people on both sides before a UN-mediated ceasefire takes effect in 1988.

title: Invasion of Kuwait and the Persian Gulf War
summary: Iraq invades and annexes Kuwait in August 1990; a United States-led coalition of many nations expels Iraqi forces in early 1991, after which Iraq is placed under severe international sanctions.

title: US-led invasion topples Saddam Hussein
summary: A United States-led coalition invades Iraq and overthrows Saddam Hussein's government within weeks; Saddam is captured in December 2003 and later executed in 2006.

title: New constitution and sectarian war
summary: Iraq adopts a federal, power-sharing constitution, but a Sunni-led insurgency and, after the 2006 al-Askari shrine bombing, brutal Shiʿi–Sunni sectarian violence engulf the country.

title: ISIS seizes Mosul and proclaims a caliphate
summary: The jihadist group ISIS sweeps across northern Iraq, captures Mosul, and declares a 'caliphate', imposing extreme violence and destroying heritage sites including parts of Hatra, Ashur and Nimrud.

title: Liberation of Mosul and defeat of ISIS
summary: Backed by a US-led coalition, Iraqi forces retake Mosul in July 2017 after months of urban warfare, and Iraq declares victory over ISIS in December 2017, ending its territorial control.

title: Ingólfr Arnarson settles Reykjavík
summary: By tradition the first permanent settler, Ingólfr Arnarson, came from Norway around 874 and established his homestead at the site he named Reykjavík, opening the age of settlement, the Landnám.

title: The Landnám (Age of Settlement)
summary: Within roughly sixty years hundreds of Norse settlers, many by way of the Norse colonies in the British Isles, claimed Iceland's habitable land, as recorded in Íslendingabók and Landnámabók.

title: Founding of the Althing at Þingvellir
summary: The settlers established a general assembly, the Althing, on the plain of Þingvellir, where law was recited from the Law Rock; it is one of the oldest parliaments in the world and the centre of the Icelandic Commonwealth.

title: The Icelandic Commonwealth
summary: A stateless society of chieftains and farmers governed itself for over three centuries through the Althing and its law council, without a king or central executive.

title: The Althing adopts Christianity
summary: Faced with a split between pagans and Christians, the Althing entrusted the decision to the lawspeaker Þorgeir, who ruled that Iceland should become Christian; the conversion was achieved by compromise, without bloodshed.

title: Snorri Sturluson and the sagas
summary: Chieftain and twice lawspeaker, Snorri Sturluson wrote the Prose Edda and the Heimskringla, central works of the saga age that preserved the mythology and history of the Norse world.

title: The Age of the Sturlungs
summary: Rivalry among a few powerful families, above all the Sturlungs, brought decades of feud, killing and burning, fatally weakening the Commonwealth's institutions of consensus.

title: The Old Covenant (Gamli sáttmáli)
summary: Worn down by civil strife and pressed by King Haakon IV, the Icelandic chieftains swore allegiance to the Norwegian crown, ending the independent Commonwealth and beginning centuries of foreign rule.

title: Execution of Bishop Jón Arason
summary: Jón Arason, bishop of Hólar and the last Catholic bishop in Iceland, was beheaded with his two sons at Skálholt for resisting the Danish-imposed Reformation, after which Iceland became fully Lutheran.

title: The Danish trade monopoly
summary: The Danish crown confined all Icelandic trade to a small group of licensed Danish merchants, depressing prices and returns and impoverishing the island for nearly two centuries.

title: The Laki eruption
summary: The Laki fissure erupted for eight months from June 1783, producing about 14.7 cubic kilometres of lava and immense quantities of toxic gas that poisoned the land and spread a haze across Europe.

title: The Móðuharðindin famine
summary: Fallout from Laki killed most of Iceland's livestock; the ensuing 'famine of the mist' killed roughly a fifth of the population, the worst disaster in the country's history.

title: The Althing restored
summary: A royal decree of 1843 revived the Althing, which first met again on 1 July 1845 as an advisory assembly, reviving in modern form the institution founded in 930.

title: Constitution on the settlement millennium
summary: On the thousandth anniversary of the settlement, Denmark granted Iceland a constitution and increased control over domestic affairs, though executive power remained with the crown.

title: Home Rule
summary: Iceland gained Home Rule, with an Icelandic minister resident in Reykjavík and answerable to the Althing, a major step toward full self-government.

title: The Act of Union and the Kingdom of Iceland
summary: The Danish-Icelandic Act of Union made Iceland a sovereign state in personal union with the Danish crown, with Denmark retaining foreign affairs and the union open to termination after twenty-five years.

title: British occupation of Iceland
summary: After Germany occupied Denmark, British forces occupied strategically vital Iceland in May 1940 to forestall a German move, severing Iceland's last constitutional ties to its monarch.

title: United States assumes Iceland's defence
summary: By agreement with the Icelandic government, the United States took over the island's defence in 1941, building a substantial military presence in the North Atlantic.

title: Founding of the Republic at Þingvellir
summary: After an overwhelming referendum, Icelanders proclaimed a republic at Þingvellir, ending the union with Denmark; Sveinn Björnsson became the first president and 17 June became the national day.

title: Iceland a founding member of NATO
summary: Abandoning neutrality, Iceland joined NATO as a founding member in 1949, a state with no army, on the understanding it would not host foreign troops in peacetime; the decision provoked a riot at the Althing.

title: First Cod War (12 nautical miles)
summary: Iceland extended its fishery limit from four to twelve nautical miles in 1958; after confrontations at sea Britain acknowledged the twelve-mile limit, the first of Iceland's victories over the Royal Navy.

title: Second Cod War (50 nautical miles)
summary: Iceland extended its limit to fifty miles from September 1972; its coast guard cut dozens of British trawl nets before a NATO-mediated interim agreement was reached in November 1973.

title: Third Cod War (200 nautical miles)
summary: Iceland claimed a 200-mile zone in 1975; after clashes and a threat to close the Keflavík NATO base, Britain recognised the 200-mile limit in an agreement of 2 June 1976.

title: The 200-mile limit and the EEZ
summary: Iceland's successful assertion of a 200-mile fishing zone helped establish the Exclusive Economic Zone in international law, later codified in the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.

title: Collapse of the banks
summary: The three big Icelandic banks, whose assets dwarfed the economy, failed within days in October 2008 in the largest banking collapse relative to GDP in history; the state passed emergency laws and turned to the IMF before recovering.

title: Legendary foundation of Rome
summary: Roman tradition, fixed by the scholar Varro, dates the founding of the city to 753 BCE, with Romulus as first king. The date is legendary, but it long anchored Rome's sense of its own origins.

title: Greek colonies of Magna Graecia
summary: From around the 8th century BCE Greek city-states founded colonies across southern Italy and Sicily, from Cumae to Tarentum, creating the prosperous Hellenic world of Magna Graecia.

title: Etruscan ascendancy in central Italy
summary: The Etruscans developed a sophisticated urban civilization in central Italy and, by tradition, supplied Rome with several of its kings before being gradually absorbed by the Roman state.

title: Founding of the Roman Republic
summary: Tradition holds that the Romans expelled their last king and established a republic governed by elected magistrates and the Senate, conventionally dated to 509 BCE.

title: The Punic Wars and Mediterranean supremacy
summary: In three wars against Carthage, Rome destroyed its great rival and became the dominant power of the western Mediterranean, beginning its rise to imperial dominion.

title: Augustus and the founding of the Principate
summary: The Senate granted Octavian the title Augustus, marking the start of the Roman Empire. As first emperor he established the Principate and ushered in the Pax Romana.

title: Completion of the Colosseum
summary: The Flavian Amphitheatre, the Colosseum, was inaugurated in Rome, a monument to the engineering and civic spectacle of the imperial city.

title: Edict of Milan and the rise of Christianity
summary: Constantine and Licinius granted toleration to Christianity, beginning its transformation from a persecuted faith into the dominant religion of the Roman world.

title: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
summary: The Germanic leader Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus, traditionally regarded as the last Western Roman emperor, ending Roman imperial rule in Italy.

title: Lombard invasion of Italy
summary: The Lombards swept into Italy, fragmenting the peninsula into a patchwork of Lombard duchies and Byzantine territories and shaping its long political division.

title: Charlemagne crowned emperor in Rome
summary: Pope Leo III crowned the Frankish king Charlemagne emperor in Rome, binding Italy to the Frankish and later Holy Roman imperial order and to the papacy.

title: Roger II crowned King of Sicily
summary: Norman conquests in the south were united when Roger II was crowned King of Sicily, creating a wealthy multicultural kingdom of Latins, Greeks and Arabs.

title: Lombard League defeats Frederick Barbarossa at Legnano
summary: The allied northern communes defeated the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa at Legnano, securing recognition of communal liberties in northern Italy.

title: Competition for the Florence Baptistery doors
summary: The famous contest for the bronze doors of the Florence Baptistery, won by Lorenzo Ghiberti, is often taken as a symbolic opening of the artistic Renaissance.

title: Medici ascendancy in Florence
summary: Cosimo de' Medici returned to dominate Florentine politics, beginning the family's long patronage of art and learning that helped define the Renaissance.

title: French invasion and the Italian Wars
summary: The French invasion of 1494 opened decades of warfare in which France and Spain fought for control of Italy, exposing the weakness of its divided states.

title: Michelangelo paints the Sistine Chapel ceiling
summary: Commissioned by the papacy in Rome, Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel ceiling became one of the supreme achievements of High Renaissance art.

title: Napoleonic reorganization of Italy
summary: Napoleon's campaigns swept aside the old states and spread revolutionary, legal and national ideas across Italy, before the powers restored the former rulers in 1815.

title: Garibaldi's Expedition of the Thousand
summary: Giuseppe Garibaldi's volunteers conquered Sicily and southern Italy, bringing down the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies and clearing the way for unification.

title: Proclamation of the Kingdom of Italy
summary: The first Italian parliament in Turin proclaimed Victor Emmanuel II King of Italy, the founding act of the unified Italian state and climax of the Risorgimento.

title: Capture of Rome
summary: Italian troops breached the Aurelian Walls at Porta Pia and took Rome from the Papal States; after a plebiscite, Rome became Italy's capital, completing unification.

title: March on Rome and Mussolini's rise to power
summary: After the Fascist March on Rome, King Victor Emmanuel III appointed Mussolini prime minister, beginning the transition to a Fascist dictatorship.

title: Fascist racial laws
summary: Mussolini's government enacted antisemitic racial laws that stripped Italian Jews of rights and citizenship, foreshadowing later deportations under German occupation.

title: Italy enters the Second World War
summary: Italy declared war on Britain and France, entering the Second World War as Germany's Axis ally, a decision that brought defeat, occupation and devastation.

title: Mussolini's fall and the armistice
summary: Mussolini was ousted in July 1943 and Italy signed an armistice with the Allies on 8 September; Germany then occupied the north, and a violent civil war and Resistance followed.

title: Birth of the Italian Republic
summary: In a referendum, Italians voted to abolish the monarchy and establish a republic; the new democratic constitution took effect on 1 January 1948.

title: Taino settlement of Xaymaca
summary: Arawak-speaking peoples settle the island they call Xaymaca, building villages led by caciques and farming cassava and corn.

title: Columbus reaches Jamaica
summary: On his second voyage Christopher Columbus arrives off the north coast, claiming the island for Spain and naming a harbour Santa Gloria.

title: Sevilla la Nueva founded
summary: Spain establishes its first permanent settlement on the north coast, beginning a colonial era that all but exterminates the Taino.

title: English conquest
summary: An English force under Penn and Venables seizes the island for Cromwell, launching the sugar-and-slavery plantation economy.

title: Port Royal earthquake
summary: A powerful earthquake and tsunami sink much of the buccaneer city of Port Royal, killing thousands and ending its golden age.

title: Maroon treaties
summary: Treaties with Cudjoe's Leeward Maroons and Nanny's Windward Maroons end the First Maroon War, granting them land and autonomy.

title: Tacky's Revolt
summary: A major slave rebellion led by the Akan leader Tacky sweeps the island before being crushed with the aid of the Maroons.

title: The Baptist War
summary: Samuel Sharpe leads a Christmas rebellion of tens of thousands; its suppression hastens the end of slavery in the empire.

title: Emancipation
summary: After the Abolition Act of 1833 and a period of apprenticeship, the enslaved people of Jamaica gain full freedom.

title: Morant Bay rebellion
summary: Paul Bogle's uprising is brutally crushed; Bogle and George William Gordon are executed, and Jamaica becomes a crown colony.

title: Garvey founds the UNIA
summary: Marcus Garvey establishes the Universal Negro Improvement Association, building the largest Pan-African movement of its age.

title: Birth of Rastafari
summary: The Rastafari movement emerges in Jamaica after the crowning of Haile Selassie I, drawing on Garvey's vision of African redemption.

title: Labour rebellions
summary: Island-wide worker uprisings give rise to Bustamante's union and Manley's PNP, founding modern Jamaican party politics.

title: Universal adult suffrage
summary: A new constitution grants every adult the vote, the first in the British Caribbean, and Jamaica holds its first elections under it.

title: West Indies Federation
summary: Jamaica joins the federation of British Caribbean colonies as its largest member, an experiment in regional union.

title: Referendum to leave the federation
summary: Jamaicans vote to withdraw from the West Indies Federation, dooming it and opening the way to separate independence.

title: Independence
summary: Jamaica becomes an independent nation within the Commonwealth, with Alexander Bustamante as its first prime minister.

title: Two-party democracy
summary: Independent Jamaica settles into a competitive democracy contested by the JLP and the PNP, with peaceful alternations of power.

title: Reggae goes global
summary: Bob Marley and the Wailers bring reggae and the Rastafari message to a worldwide audience, making Jamaica a cultural superpower.

title: Bolt's sprinting dynasty
summary: Usain Bolt wins the 100m and 200m at three straight Olympics, cementing Jamaica's dominance of world sprinting.

title: World Heritage inscription
summary: The Blue and John Crow Mountains, refuge of the Maroons, become Jamaica's first UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: Ammon, Moab and Edom emerge
summary: As the Iron Age began, three settled kingdoms took shape on the plateau east of the Jordan, each with its own capital, language and national god, controlling the caravan trade of the King's Highway.

title: Ammon regains its independence
summary: According to the biblical account, the kingdom of Ammon, centred on Rabbath Ammon (modern Amman), reasserted its independence after the death of the Israelite king David.

title: The Mesha Stele of Moab
summary: King Mesha of Moab erected a stone inscription recording his wars and building works, one of the earliest royal inscriptions from the lands east of the Jordan.

title: Alexander the Great and the end of Persian rule
summary: The conquests of Alexander brought the region into the Hellenistic world, hastening the eclipse of the old Iron Age kingdoms and opening the way to Greek and later Roman cities.

title: The Nabataeans resist the Greeks at Petra
summary: The Nabataean Arabs, established around Petra, repelled campaigns by the Hellenistic successors of Alexander, marking their emergence as a distinct desert power controlling the caravan trade.

title: Petra reaches its golden age
summary: At the height of the incense trade the Nabataeans carved Petra's monumental tomb-temples and engineered an elaborate system of dams, channels and cisterns to sustain a great city in the desert.

title: Rome annexes the Nabataean kingdom
summary: The emperor Trajan absorbed the Nabataean realm as the province of Arabia Petraea, ending Nabataean independence as Roman power extended across the region.

title: Petra inscribed as a World Heritage Site
summary: UNESCO inscribed Petra on the World Heritage List as a unique artistic achievement and an outstanding architectural ensemble of the early centuries BCE and CE.

title: Pompey creates the Decapolis
summary: Rome's reorganisation of the East grouped Gerasa (Jerash) and neighbouring Greek-style cities into the Decapolis, a league of self-governing towns that prospered under Roman rule.

title: Jerash flourishes as a Roman city
summary: Gerasa was rebuilt with colonnaded streets, an oval forum, temples and theatres, becoming one of the wealthiest cities of the Roman Near East and leaving ruins still visible today.

title: Christian Byzantium and the mosaics of Um er-Rasas
summary: Under Byzantine rule Christianity spread across the plateau and church floors were laid with elaborate mosaics, preserved most fully at Um er-Rasas, later a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: The Battle of the Yarmuk
summary: Muslim Arab armies decisively defeated the Byzantines near the Yarmuk River, ending Roman rule over the region and bringing the lands east of the Jordan into the new Islamic world.

title: Umayyad rule and the desert castles
summary: Governing from Damascus, the Umayyad caliphs built fortified desert residences across the eastern plateau, including Quseir Amra with its celebrated frescoes of early Islamic secular art.

title: Quseir Amra is built
summary: An Umayyad prince raised the bath-house and pleasure palace of Quseir Amra, whose figurative murals make it one of the most important survivals of early Islamic art; UNESCO inscribed it in 1985.

title: The Ottomans conquer the region
summary: After defeating the Mamluks, the Ottoman Turks absorbed the lands east of the Jordan into their empire as part of the province of Syria, ruling for four centuries.

title: The Hejaz Railway crosses the plateau
summary: The Ottomans completed the Hejaz Railway through the territory, linking Damascus toward the holy cities and binding the region more tightly to the empire on the eve of the Arab Revolt.

title: The Great Arab Revolt begins
summary: Sharif Hussein of Mecca, supported by Britain, launched the Arab Revolt against the Ottoman Empire; his sons Faisal and Abdullah led its forces toward Syria, aided by T. E. Lawrence.

title: Abdullah founds the Emirate of Transjordan
summary: After the Cairo Conference, Abdullah ibn Hussein formed a government east of the Jordan under British mandate, establishing Hashemite rule and the Emirate of Transjordan.

title: Independence of the Hashemite Kingdom
summary: Following the Treaty of London, the British mandate ended and Transjordan became a fully independent kingdom, with Abdullah re-designated as king; 25 May is celebrated as Independence Day.

title: Annexation of the West Bank
summary: After his Arab Legion occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem in the 1948 war, King Abdullah formally annexed the territory and renamed the enlarged state the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan.

title: Assassination of King Abdullah I
summary: Abdullah I was shot dead on the steps of the al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem by a Palestinian gunman, opening a brief succession crisis before his grandson Hussein came to the throne.

title: King Hussein assumes power
summary: After his father Talal was declared unfit to rule, the young Hussein bin Talal took full constitutional powers, beginning a reign of nearly half a century that shaped the modern kingdom.

title: The Six-Day War and loss of the West Bank
summary: In the war with Israel, Jordan lost the West Bank and East Jerusalem, and a fresh wave of Palestinian refugees fled into the East Bank, deepening the kingdom's demographic transformation.

title: Black September
summary: King Hussein's army moved against armed Palestinian factions that had built a state within the state; after intense fighting and a brief Syrian incursion, the guerrillas were expelled by July 1971.

title: Peace treaty with Israel
summary: King Hussein signed the Wadi Araba treaty with Israel, ending the state of war and making Jordan the second Arab country, after Egypt, to conclude a formal peace with Israel.

title: Abdullah II succeeds his father
summary: On the death of King Hussein, his son Abdullah II ascended the throne, going on to promote economic reform while steering Jordan through war in Iraq, the Arab Spring and a vast refugee influx.

title: The Arab Spring and Syrian refugees
summary: Protests during the regional uprisings of 2011 prompted reforms from Abdullah II, while the Syrian civil war soon drove hundreds of thousands of refugees into Jordan, straining its economy.

title: Rise of the Yamato state
summary: Clan leaders on the Yamato plain consolidate power, build monumental kofun tombs, and establish the imperial lineage claiming descent from the sun goddess Amaterasu.

title: Introduction of Buddhism
summary: Buddhism reaches Japan from the Korean kingdom of Baekje, traditionally dated to 552; it is championed by the Soga clan over conservative opposition.

title: Prince Shotoku's Seventeen-Article Constitution
summary: As regent, Prince Shotoku promulgates a set of Confucian and Buddhist moral precepts for government and intensifies the adoption of Chinese institutions.

title: The Taika Reform
summary: A court coup destroys Soga dominance and inaugurates reforms reorganizing land and administration along centralized Chinese lines, the basis of the ritsuryo state.

title: Capital established at Nara
summary: The court founds Japan's first permanent capital, Heijo-kyo (Nara), modeled on the Tang Chinese capital, beginning the Nara period.

title: Capital moved to Heian-kyo (Kyoto)
summary: Emperor Kanmu relocates the capital to Heian-kyo, the site of Kyoto, opening the Heian period and a long era of aristocratic court culture.

title: The Tale of Genji
summary: The court lady Murasaki Shikibu completes The Tale of Genji, widely regarded as the world's first full-length novel and the summit of Heian literature.

title: Genpei War
summary: Civil war between the Taira and Minamoto warrior clans ends with Minamoto victory at Dan-no-ura in 1185, shattering court supremacy and ushering in warrior rule.

title: Minamoto Yoritomo becomes shogun
summary: Yoritomo is appointed shogun, formalizing the Kamakura shogunate and a system of warrior government that would last, in varying forms, until 1868.

title: Mongol invasions repelled
summary: Kublai Khan's Yuan forces twice attempt to invade Japan; both fleets are wrecked by typhoons later mythologized as the kamikaze, or divine winds.

title: Ashikaga Takauji founds the Muromachi shogunate
summary: Takauji establishes the second shogunate, ruling from Kyoto's Muromachi district and presiding over a brilliant if unstable cultural era.

title: Onin War
summary: A succession dispute ignites a decade of warfare that devastates Kyoto, cripples shogunal authority, and tips Japan into the fragmented Sengoku era.

title: Arrival of Europeans and firearms
summary: Portuguese traders reach Japan, introducing firearms and, soon after, Christianity, adding new pressures to the Sengoku wars.

title: Hideyoshi completes unification
summary: Toyotomi Hideyoshi brings the last domains under central control, finishing the reunification of Japan begun by Oda Nobunaga.

title: Battle of Sekigahara
summary: Tokugawa Ieyasu defeats a rival coalition in the decisive battle that makes him master of Japan and clears the path to the shogunate.

title: Tokugawa shogunate founded
summary: Ieyasu is appointed shogun and establishes his government at Edo, beginning the Tokugawa (Edo) period of long internal peace.

title: Sakoku: national seclusion
summary: A series of edicts seals Japan from most foreign contact, banning Christianity and overseas travel and restricting trade to Nagasaki for over two centuries.

title: Meiji Restoration
summary: A coup ends the Tokugawa shogunate and restores direct imperial rule under Emperor Meiji, launching rapid modernization and Westernization.

title: Meiji Constitution promulgated
summary: Japan adopts a Western-influenced constitution establishing a constitutional monarchy with an imperial parliament, the Diet.

title: Russo-Japanese War
summary: Japan's victory over Russia marks the first modern defeat of a European power by an Asian state and confirms Japan as a major power.

title: Attack on Pearl Harbor
summary: Japan attacks the U.S. fleet at Pearl Harbor, bringing the United States into World War II and opening the Pacific War.

title: Atomic bombings and surrender
summary: The United States drops atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki on August 6 and 9; Japan announces surrender, formalized on September 2, ending World War II.

title: Pacifist constitution takes effect
summary: Japan's postwar constitution establishes democracy and popular sovereignty, makes the emperor a symbol of the state, and renounces war under Article 9.

title: Treaty of San Francisco and end of occupation
summary: Signed in 1951 and effective in 1952, the peace treaty restores Japanese sovereignty and ends the Allied occupation.

title: Postwar economic miracle
summary: Hosting the Tokyo Olympics symbolizes Japan's recovery as it becomes an industrial powerhouse during decades of rapid, sustained growth.

title: Tohoku earthquake and Fukushima disaster
summary: A magnitude-9.0 earthquake and tsunami devastate northeastern Japan and trigger meltdowns at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant.

title: The Saka 'Golden Man' of Issyk
summary: A high-status Saka warrior is buried in the Issyk kurgan near Almaty in a costume of thousands of gold plaques, a celebrated emblem of the Iron Age nomad cultures that dominated the Kazakh steppe in the first millennium BCE.

title: Turkic khaganates dominate the steppe
summary: Turkic-speaking confederations, beginning with the Türk (Göktürk) Khaganate and later the Karakhanids, take control of the region; Zhetysu becomes a heartland of the Western Turkic realm, fixing the Turkic language and spreading Islam.

title: Silk Road towns of the south flourish
summary: Caravan cities such as Otrar, Taraz, Sauran, and Yasi prosper on the trade between China and the Mediterranean, becoming centres of commerce, craft, and Islamic learning along the southern Kazakh steppe.

title: Mongol conquest of the Syr Darya and Khwarezm
summary: Provoked by the killing of his envoys at Otrar, Genghis Khan storms the Silk Road towns and overruns Khwarezm; Otrar falls after a months-long siege, and the steppe is absorbed into the Mongol empire.

title: The Golden Horde rules the western steppe
summary: The lands of present-day Kazakhstan pass to the line of Jochi, forming the western wing of the Mongol empire known as the Golden Horde, where Turks outnumber Mongols and Islam becomes the prevailing faith.

title: Timur builds the Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi
summary: At Yasi (Turkestan) Timur orders a monumental mausoleum over the tomb of the Sufi master Khoja Ahmed Yasawi; left unfinished at Timur's death in 1405, it became a masterpiece of Timurid architecture and a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003.

title: Foundation of the Kazakh Khanate
summary: The Jochid sultans Janibek and Kerei break with Abu'l-Khayr Khan and lead their followers into Zhetysu, founding the Kazakh Khanate, the realm Kazakhs regard as the root of their nation and statehood.

title: The three jüz take shape
summary: Kazakh society organises into three hordes, the Great, Middle, and Little jüz, each a confederation of tribes with its own pastures, united by language, Islam, and descent and headed by Genghisid khans.

title: The 'Great Disaster' of the Dzungar wars
summary: Devastating invasions by the Buddhist Dzungar confederation drive Kazakhs from their pastures with great loss of life, an episode remembered as the Aktaban Shubyryndy that gravely weakens the khanate.

title: The Little Horde accepts Russian protection
summary: Abu'l-Khayr Khan of the Little Horde swears allegiance to the Russian Empire for protection against the Dzungars; the Middle Horde follows in 1740 and part of the Great Horde in 1742, opening the steppe to Russian power.

title: Ablai Khan elected ruler of the Kazakhs
summary: Ablai (Abylai) is elected khan of the Kazakhs and balances between the Russian and Qing empires to preserve a degree of independence; he endures as a national symbol of Kazakh sovereignty.

title: Russia abolishes the Kazakh khanates
summary: To end Kazakh autonomy, Russia abolishes the khanate of the Middle Horde in 1822, the Little Horde in 1824, and the Great Horde in 1848, dismantling the political structure of the Kazakh Khanate.

title: Kenesary Kasymov's revolt
summary: Kenesary Kasymov, a grandson of Ablai Khan, leads the largest Kazakh uprising against Russian rule, fighting to restore the independent khanate until he is killed in 1847.

title: The Kazakh famine (Asharshylyk)
summary: Forced collectivisation and the settling of nomads under Filipp Goloshchekin produce a man-made famine that kills an estimated 1.5 million people, around a third of all Kazakhs, the deadliest catastrophe in Kazakh history; the toll is an estimate.

title: Kazakh S.S.R. becomes a union republic
summary: Kazakhstan, an autonomous republic since 1920 and renamed the Kazak A.S.S.R. in 1925, is raised to a full constituent republic of the Soviet Union under the 1936 constitution.

title: Semipalatinsk nuclear test site
summary: The Soviet Union conducts some 456 nuclear tests at the Semipalatinsk site in northeastern Kazakhstan between 1949 and 1989, exposing local populations to radioactive fallout with severe long-term health effects.

title: Khrushchev's Virgin Lands campaign
summary: Nikita Khrushchev's drive to plough up the northern Kazakh steppe for grain brings hundreds of thousands of mostly Slavic settlers, transforming the republic's demography so that Kazakhs become a minority in Kazakhstan.

title: Kazakhstan declares independence
summary: Kazakhstan proclaims itself a sovereign, independent state, the last of the Soviet republics to declare independence, with Nursultan Nazarbayev as president; the USSR formally dissolves days later.

title: Capital moved to Astana
summary: Nazarbayev relocates the capital from Almaty to Akmola on the northern steppe; renamed Astana ('capital') in 1998, it is rebuilt as a planned showcase city of modern architecture.

title: Nazarbayev resigns; Tokayev succeeds
summary: After nearly three decades in power, Nazarbayev steps down as president, handing office to Kassym-Jomart Tokayev while retaining major influence; the capital is briefly renamed Nur-Sultan in his honour.

title: 'Bloody January' unrest
summary: Protests over fuel prices spread nationwide and turn violent; Tokayev declares a state of emergency, summons CSTO troops, and authorises lethal force, with about 227 deaths reported, then sidelines Nazarbayev's allies to consolidate power.

title: Turkana Boy lives near Lake Turkana
summary: A Homo erectus youth, later catalogued KNM-WT 15000, lives near what is now the Nariokotome River; his fossilised skeleton would become the most complete of its species ever recovered.

title: Hominins at Koobi Fora
summary: The Koobi Fora deposits east of Lake Turkana preserve fossils of Paranthropus boisei and early Homo, making the area one of the world's leading sites for the study of human evolution.

title: Cushitic pastoralists enter the north
summary: Southern Cushitic-speaking herders move into the arid lands of northern Kenya, among the earliest food-producing communities in the region.

title: Olorgesailie tool traditions and the Stone Age
summary: Sites such as Olorgesailie in the Rift Valley preserve vast accumulations of hand-axes and other tools, documenting hundreds of thousands of years of Stone Age life in Kenya.

title: Bantu expansion reaches western Kenya
summary: Iron-using Bantu-speaking farmers spread into western Kenya, part of the wider Bantu expansion that reshaped much of eastern and southern Africa.

title: Rise of the Swahili coast
summary: Coastal Bantu communities trading across the Indian Ocean develop the Swahili language and an Afro-Islamic urban culture, founding settlements that grow into city-states.

title: Ibn Battuta visits Mombasa
summary: The traveller Ibn Battuta describes Mombasa and Kilwa as prosperous, pious Muslim trading towns, attesting to the wealth of the medieval Swahili coast.

title: Zheng He's fleet reaches Malindi
summary: Vessels of the Chinese admiral Zheng He's treasure fleet are recorded reaching Malindi, marking the eastern extent of the Indian Ocean trade that linked the Swahili coast to China.

title: Southern Luo migrate into western Kenya
summary: Nilotic-speaking Luo communities move into the Lake Victoria basin of western Kenya, the last major wave of the migrations that formed the country's peoples.

title: Vasco da Gama reaches the Kenyan coast
summary: The Portuguese navigator Vasco da Gama calls at Mombasa and Malindi en route to India, beginning a century of Portuguese involvement on the Swahili coast.

title: Portuguese build Fort Jesus
summary: The Portuguese construct Fort Jesus at Mombasa to a Renaissance design by Giovanni Battista Cairati, anchoring their control of the coast and the Indian Ocean trade routes.

title: Omani Arabs capture Fort Jesus
summary: After a siege of some thirty-three months, Omani forces take Fort Jesus, ending Portuguese dominance and bringing the Kenyan coast, Zanzibar and Pemba under Omani Arab control.

title: Zanzibar becomes the Omani capital
summary: Sultan Seyyid Said moves the Omani capital from Muscat to Zanzibar, making the island the centre of a commercial empire to which the Kenyan coast was bound.

title: Fort Jesus inscribed by UNESCO
summary: Fort Jesus is added to the UNESCO World Heritage List as an outstanding example of sixteenth-century military architecture and a witness to the contest for the Indian Ocean trade.

title: East Africa Protectorate established
summary: Britain proclaims the East Africa Protectorate over the territory that would become Kenya, beginning nearly seven decades of formal British rule.

title: The Uganda Railway is built
summary: The 'Lunatic Line' is driven from Mombasa to Lake Victoria, built largely by indentured Indian labourers; it reaches Nairobi in 1899 and opens the interior to settlement.

title: Kenya Colony created
summary: The protectorate's interior becomes the Crown colony of Kenya, while a coastal strip leased from the sultan of Zanzibar remains a protectorate.

title: Harry Thuku founds early protest
summary: Harry Thuku establishes the Young Kikuyu Association, one of the first organised African political movements against colonial land and labour policies.

title: Kenyatta leads the Kenya African Union
summary: Jomo Kenyatta, back from years in Britain, becomes president of the Kenya African Union, the leading vehicle of African nationalist demands.

title: State of emergency declared
summary: As the Mau Mau revolt spreads, the colonial government declares a state of emergency that lasts until 1960, ushering in mass detentions and a brutal counter-insurgency.

title: Jomo Kenyatta convicted
summary: Kenyatta is tried and imprisoned for allegedly directing the Mau Mau, in proceedings later widely denounced as a sham; he is freed in 1961.

title: Lancaster House conferences
summary: Three constitutional conferences in London negotiate Kenya's path to independence amid rivalry between KANU and the federalist KADU.

title: Internal self-government (Madaraka)
summary: Kenya attains internal self-government under a KANU government led by Kenyatta, six months before full independence.

title: Kenya becomes independent
summary: Kenya gains independence from the United Kingdom with Jomo Kenyatta as prime minister; one year later, on 12 December 1964, it becomes a republic.

title: Moi succeeds Kenyatta
summary: On Kenyatta's death, Vice-President Daniel arap Moi becomes president, beginning a 24-year tenure that formalises the one-party state.

title: Failed coup attempt
summary: Air-force officers attempt to overthrow Moi; the coup is crushed and followed by tighter political control and a constitutionally entrenched one-party state.

title: Return to multiparty politics
summary: Under domestic and international pressure, Kenya amends its constitution to legalise opposition parties, paving the way for the multiparty elections of 1992.

title: Kibaki ends KANU rule
summary: Mwai Kibaki wins the presidency, ending nearly four decades of unbroken KANU government since independence.

title: Post-election violence
summary: Kibaki's disputed re-election sparks ethnic and political violence that kills more than 1,100 people; a power-sharing deal brokered by Kofi Annan is signed on 28 February 2008.

title: New constitution adopted
summary: Kenyans approve a new constitution that limits presidential power, expands rights, and devolves authority to 47 county governments.

title: The Yenisei Kyrgyz destroy the Uyghur Khaganate
summary: The Yenisei Kyrgyz overthrew the Uyghur Khaganate and sacked its capital Ordu-Baliq, briefly making the Kyrgyz the dominant power of the eastern steppe and driving the Uyghurs out of Mongolia.

title: Transmission of the epic of Manas
summary: The Kyrgyz preserved the vast oral epic of Manas, recited by bards (manaschi), telling of the legendary hero who united the Kyrgyz tribes; it remains the cornerstone of Kyrgyz cultural memory.

title: Manas trilogy recognized by UNESCO
summary: UNESCO inscribed the Kyrgyz epic trilogy of Manas, Semetey and Seytek on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, recognizing one of the world's longest oral epics.

title: Karakhanid Balasagun and the Burana tower
summary: Under the Karakhanid dynasty, the first Turkic Muslim power in Central Asia, Balasagun in the Chüy valley flourished as a capital; its minaret, the Burana tower, survives as the best-known monument of northern Kyrgyzstan.

title: Mongol conquest of Central Asia
summary: The empire of Genghis Khan overran Central Asia, drawing the Kyrgyz lands into the Mongol world and, after the empire's division, into the Chagatai realm and its successor states.

title: Kyrgyz consolidate in the Tian Shan
summary: Through the upheavals of the post-Mongol centuries the Kyrgyz tribes settled in the Tian Shan, living as mountain nomads organized in tribes and clans, the homeland they hold to this day.

title: Sulaiman-Too inscribed by UNESCO
summary: The sacred mountain of Sulaiman-Too above Osh, with its petroglyphs, places of worship and reconstructed 16th-century mosques, became Kyrgyzstan's first UNESCO World Heritage Site, recognized for its blend of pre-Islamic and Islamic belief.

title: Kyrgyz under the Khanate of Kokand
summary: The Khanate of Kokand extended its rule over the Kyrgyz tribes, building the fortress of Pishpek (later Bishkek) to control the Chüy valley and recruiting Kyrgyz fighters, though its rule was widely resisted.

title: Russia annexes Kokand; Kyrgyzstan under imperial rule
summary: After suppressing an uprising, the Russian Empire abolished the Khanate of Kokand and annexed its lands as the Fergana Province, bringing the Kyrgyz country under direct Russian colonial rule.

title: The 1916 revolt (Urkun)
summary: A decree conscripting Central Asians for wartime labour triggered a revolt across Russian Turkestan; in the Kyrgyz lands it was suppressed with great violence, and tens of thousands fled toward China, with heavy loss of life. Casualty figures remain estimates.

title: Kara-Kyrgyz Autonomous Oblast created
summary: In the Soviet national-territorial delimitation of Central Asia, the Kyrgyz lands were organized as the Kara-Kyrgyz Autonomous Oblast within the Russian SFSR, giving the Kyrgyz their own named territory for the first time.

title: The Kirghiz SSR becomes a union republic
summary: Kyrgyzstan was elevated to the Kirghiz Soviet Socialist Republic, a full constituent republic of the Soviet Union, with its capital at Frunze (formerly Pishpek, today Bishkek).

title: Chingiz Aitmatov wins the Lenin Prize
summary: The Kyrgyz writer Chingiz Aitmatov was awarded the Lenin Prize for 'Tales of the Mountains and Steppes', bringing Kyrgyz literature to a worldwide audience and becoming the republic's most celebrated cultural figure.

title: Akayev chosen to lead the republic
summary: Amid Gorbachev's reforms and rising ethnic tension in the south, the physicist Askar Akayev was elected head of the Kirghiz SSR, the leader who would guide the republic to independence.

title: Kyrgyzstan declares independence
summary: As the Soviet Union collapsed, the Supreme Soviet of the republic declared Kyrgyzstan's independence; Askar Akayev became the first president of the sovereign state, with its capital at Bishkek.

title: U.S. recognition and diplomatic relations
summary: The United States established diplomatic relations with independent Kyrgyzstan on 25 December 1991, opening its embassy in Bishkek in February 1992 as the Soviet Union was dissolved.

title: The Tulip Revolution
summary: Allegations of fraud in the parliamentary elections and of pervasive corruption sparked mass demonstrations that forced President Akayev to flee the country, in the first of Kyrgyzstan's post-Soviet revolutions.

title: The 2010 revolution ousts Bakiyev
summary: A violent uprising in Bishkek over corruption and rising prices forced President Kurmanbek Bakiyev to flee; an interim government under Roza Otunbayeva took power and prepared a new constitution.

title: Ethnic violence in the south
summary: Clashes between ethnic Kyrgyz and Uzbeks in Osh and Jalal-Abad erupted into days of communal violence, killing several hundred people — figures are estimates and remain contested — and displacing hundreds of thousands.

title: Parliamentary republic and the first peaceful transfer
summary: A new constitution made Kyrgyzstan a parliamentary republic, a rarity in Central Asia; the 2011 election that followed Otunbayeva's interim presidency was the country's first peaceful handover of power.

title: Japarov and the return to presidential rule
summary: After 2020 protests over disputed elections, Sadyr Japarov rose from prison to the presidency, winning election in January 2021; constitutional referendums then restored a strong presidential system.

title: Rise of Funan
summary: Funan emerges around the Mekong delta as the first major Hinduized kingdom of Southeast Asia, prospering on maritime trade between India and China.

title: Chenla supplants Funan
summary: Chenla, ruled by princes descended from the kings of Funan, absorbs Funan's territory and becomes the dominant power in the region.

title: Fragmentation of Chenla
summary: Chenla splits into a Land Chenla and a Water Chenla and loses cohesion, leaving the Khmer lands divided on the eve of the Angkorian unification.

title: Jayavarman II founds the Khmer Empire
summary: Jayavarman II is consecrated as devaraja and universal ruler on Mahendraparvata, asserting Khmer independence and inaugurating the empire of Angkor.

title: Suryavarman II and Angkor Wat
summary: Suryavarman II reunites the empire and begins Angkor Wat, dedicated to Vishnu and the largest religious structure in the world, completed after his death.

title: Jayavarman VII rebuilds Angkor Thom and the Bayon
summary: After repelling a Cham invasion, Jayavarman VII embraces Mahayana Buddhism, expands the empire to its greatest extent, and builds Angkor Thom and the Bayon.

title: Thai capture of Angkor
summary: After repeated Tai attacks, Angkor is captured in 1431 and subsequently abandoned as a capital, marking the end of the imperial era.

title: French protectorate established
summary: King Norodom signs a treaty placing Cambodia under French protection to fend off Siamese and Vietnamese pressure; Siam acknowledges the protectorate by 1867.

title: Cambodia joined to French Indochina
summary: Cambodia is incorporated into the colonial federation of French Indochina, its monarchy preserved as a figurehead while the French administer the country.

title: Japan ends French rule; Sihanouk proclaims independence
summary: Japan removes the French administration in the closing months of the war, and King Sihanouk briefly proclaims Cambodian independence before France returns.

title: Full independence declared
summary: After Sihanouk's Royal Crusade for Independence, France transfers sovereignty and King Norodom Sihanouk declares Cambodia's full independence in Phnom Penh.

title: Lon Nol coup and the Khmer Republic
summary: While Sihanouk is abroad, the National Assembly removes him and Lon Nol takes power, abolishing the monarchy, proclaiming the Khmer Republic, and joining the war on the U.S. side.

title: Khmer Rouge capture Phnom Penh
summary: Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge seize the capital, empty the cities, rename the country Democratic Kampuchea, and abolish money, markets, religion, and private life.

title: The Cambodian genocide
summary: Under the Khmer Rouge an estimated 1.5 to 3 million people, about a quarter of the population, die from execution, forced labour, starvation, and disease.

title: Vietnamese intervention ends the regime
summary: Vietnam invades Cambodia, captures Phnom Penh in January 1979, ousts the Khmer Rouge, and ends the genocide, beginning a decade-long occupation.

title: Paris Peace Agreements signed
summary: The Cambodian factions sign the Paris Agreements on a Comprehensive Political Settlement, ending the war and delegating transitional authority to the United Nations.

title: UNTAC mission
summary: The UN Transitional Authority in Cambodia repatriates over 300,000 refugees and organizes national elections, one of the largest peacekeeping operations of its era.

title: Constitutional monarchy restored
summary: UN-supervised elections produce a new constitution restoring the kingdom, and Norodom Sihanouk returns to the throne as constitutional monarch.

title: Death of Pol Pot and collapse of the Khmer Rouge
summary: The Khmer Rouge insurgency disintegrates and Pol Pot dies, ending the movement responsible for the genocide of the 1970s.

title: Cambodia joins ASEAN
summary: Cambodia becomes a member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, marking its reintegration into regional and international affairs after decades of war and isolation.

title: Opposition dissolved, CPP entrenched
summary: With the main opposition party dissolved by the courts, Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party wins every National Assembly seat, consolidating one-party dominance.

title: Khmer Rouge tribunal concludes
summary: The UN-backed Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia convicts senior Khmer Rouge leaders of crimes against humanity and genocide before concluding its work.

title: Hun Manet succeeds his father
summary: After 38 years in power, Hun Sen hands the premiership to his son Hun Manet, who is sworn in on 22 August 2023 in a dynastic succession.

title: Legendary founding of Gojoseon
summary: According to the Samguk yusa, the mythical Dangun establishes Gojoseon, traditionally regarded as the first Korean kingdom; the date is commemorated as National Foundation Day.

title: Fall of Gojoseon to Han China
summary: The Han dynasty conquers Gojoseon and establishes commanderies in the north, fragmenting the peninsula into smaller competing states.

title: Emergence of the Three Kingdoms
summary: Silla, Goguryeo, and Baekje take shape as the three dominant kingdoms of the peninsula, each later adopting Buddhism and centralized rule.

title: Introduction of Buddhism
summary: Buddhism is officially adopted in Goguryeo and spreads through the kingdoms, becoming a major force in art, statecraft, and religious life.

title: Silla unifies the peninsula
summary: Allied with Tang China, Silla conquers Baekje in 660 and Goguryeo in 668, then expels the Tang, achieving the first unification of Korea under native rule.

title: Bulguksa and Seokguram built
summary: Unified Silla constructs the Bulguksa temple and the Seokguram grotto near Gyeongju, masterpieces of Buddhist art later inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage.

title: Wang Geon founds Goryeo
summary: The general Wang Geon establishes the Goryeo dynasty at Kaesong; by 936 he reunifies the peninsula, giving rise to the Western name Korea.

title: Mongol invasions begin
summary: Mongol armies invade Goryeo; after prolonged resistance from Ganghwa Island, Korea submits to Yuan overlordship for roughly a century.

title: Tripitaka Koreana completed
