summary: Goryeo Buddhists carve the entire Buddhist canon onto more than 80,000 woodblocks as a prayer for deliverance from the Mongols, a printing landmark preserved at Haeinsa.

title: Fall of Goryeo
summary: Weakened by factionalism and Mongol decline, Goryeo is overthrown by the general Yi Seong-gye, who founds the Joseon dynasty.

title: Joseon dynasty founded
summary: Yi Seong-gye establishes the Joseon dynasty, adopts Neo-Confucianism as state ideology, and soon moves the capital to Hanyang (Seoul).

title: Creation of hangul
summary: King Sejong the Great sponsors the Korean alphabet, completed in 1443 and promulgated in 1446 to make literacy accessible to ordinary people.

title: Japanese (Imjin) invasions repelled
summary: Toyotomi Hideyoshi's forces invade Korea; resistance led by Admiral Yi Sun-sin and his turtle ships, with Ming Chinese aid, ultimately drives them out.

title: Korea made a Japanese protectorate
summary: After defeating Russia, Japan imposes a protectorate treaty stripping Korea of its diplomatic sovereignty, a prelude to full annexation.

title: Japanese annexation of Korea
summary: Japan formally annexes Korea, ending the Joseon dynasty and more than five centuries of Korean monarchy and beginning 35 years of colonial rule.

title: Annexation and colonial government
summary: Japan installs a Government-General in Seoul, ruling Korea through military and police power and beginning systematic economic exploitation.

title: March First Movement
summary: A Declaration of Independence sparks nationwide demonstrations by some two million Koreans; the peaceful protests are violently suppressed with thousands killed.

title: Korean Provisional Government formed
summary: Korean nationalists establish a Provisional Government in exile in Shanghai to coordinate the independence struggle against Japanese rule.

title: Forced labor and wartime mobilization
summary: As the Pacific War expands, Japan conscripts hundreds of thousands of Koreans for forced labor and military service and coerces women into sexual slavery.

title: Liberation from Japan
summary: Japan's surrender ends 35 years of colonial rule; Koreans celebrate Gwangbokjeol, the Restoration of Light, even as foreign occupation and division loom.

title: Division at the 38th parallel
summary: The peninsula is split into Soviet and American occupation zones along the 38th parallel, setting the stage for two rival Korean states.

title: Republic of Korea proclaimed
summary: South Korea is established under President Syngman Rhee after a constitution is promulgated and UN-observed elections held; the DPRK is founded in the north weeks later.

title: The Korean War
summary: North Korea invades the South; a US-led UN force and Chinese intervention turn the war into a grinding stalemate that devastates the peninsula and kills millions.

title: Korean War armistice
summary: An armistice halts the fighting near the 38th parallel and creates the Demilitarized Zone; no peace treaty is signed, freezing the division to the present day.

title: Park Chung-hee's military coup
summary: General Park Chung-hee seizes power and launches state-led, export-driven industrialization, the Miracle on the Han River, alongside authoritarian repression.

title: Gwangju Uprising
summary: A pro-democracy uprising in Gwangju is crushed by the military with heavy loss of life, becoming a catalyst and symbol for South Korea's democracy movement.

title: June Democratic Struggle
summary: Millions protest nationwide, forcing the regime to grant direct presidential elections and democratic reform, founding the present Sixth Republic.

title: Seoul Summer Olympics
summary: Seoul hosts the Summer Olympics, showcasing South Korea's recovery and helping cement its turn toward democracy and global engagement.

title: Asian financial crisis and IMF rescue
summary: A regional financial crisis forces South Korea to seek a major IMF bailout; sweeping reforms follow under President Kim Dae-jung.

title: First inter-Korean summit
summary: President Kim Dae-jung meets North Korea's Kim Jong-il in Pyongyang under the Sunshine Policy; Kim Dae-jung receives the Nobel Peace Prize that year.

title: Rome annexes Dardania
summary: The kingdom of the Dardani in the central Balkans was absorbed by Rome and incorporated into the province of Moesia, with towns such as Ulpiana, Scupi and Naissus as regional centres.

title: Province of Dardania
summary: In the administrative reorganisation of the later Roman Empire, the region was constituted as a province again bearing the ancient name of Dardania, within the diocese of Moesia.

title: Slavic settlement of the interior
summary: As the Danube frontier collapsed, Slavic peoples settled widely across the Balkan interior under and after Byzantine authority, transforming the population of the future Kosovo.

title: Byzantine and Bulgarian borderland
summary: The region passed between the Byzantine Empire, the First Bulgarian Empire and rising Serbian principalities, a contested frontier of the medieval Balkans before the Nemanjic ascendancy.

title: Nemanjic rule and the Serbian Church
summary: The Nemanjic dynasty consolidated its hold over the region, which became a centre of the medieval Serbian state and of the autocephalous Serbian Orthodox Church seated at the Patriarchate of Pec.

title: Gracanica and Visoki Decani built
summary: The monastery of Gracanica was founded in 1321 and Visoki Decani built in the mid-14th century for King Stefan Decanski; with other churches they form the UNESCO Medieval Monuments in Kosovo, later placed on the List of World Heritage in Danger.

title: The Battle of Kosovo
summary: At Kosovo Polje, the Field of Blackbirds, the Serbian prince Lazar and his allies fought the Ottoman sultan Murad I; both rulers died and the Ottoman victory led to the eventual subjugation of Serbia.

title: Ottoman conquest completed
summary: By the mid-15th century the Ottomans had established direct rule over all of Serbia, including Kosovo, ending the medieval Serbian state in the region.

title: Ottoman administration of Kosovo
summary: For roughly four and a half centuries Kosovo was ruled as part of the Ottoman Empire, governed through the Balkan provinces and, latterly, the vilayet of Kosovo.

title: Migrations and a shifting population
summary: Over the Ottoman centuries many Orthodox Serbs emigrated and parts of the population converted to Islam, while the Albanian-speaking share grew, probably forming a majority by the 18th century.

title: The League of Prizren
summary: Albanian leaders founded the League of Prizren in Kosovo, the first Albanian nationalist organisation, seeking to unite Albanian-inhabited lands and promote the Albanian language amid the Congress of Berlin's partition plans.

title: Suppression of the League
summary: After resisting territorial transfers to Montenegro and Greece, the League of Prizren was suppressed by the Ottoman authorities, but it had laid the foundation of the Albanian national movement.

title: Balkan Wars bring Kosovo into Serbia
summary: The Balkan Wars ended Ottoman rule, and Kosovo was incorporated into the Kingdom of Serbia, later part of the Yugoslav state.

title: Wide autonomy under the Yugoslav constitution
summary: The 1974 Yugoslav constitution gave Kosovo broad self-government as an autonomous province within Serbia, with its own assembly, courts and a veto, making it nearly a republic in practice.

title: Pristina student protests
summary: Student demonstrations in Pristina demanding republic status for Kosovo grew into wider unrest, which the Yugoslav authorities suppressed, exposing deep tensions over the province's status.

title: Milosevic revokes Kosovo's autonomy
summary: Under Slobodan Milosevic, the Serbian assembly stripped Kosovo of most of the autonomy granted in 1974, returning police, courts, education and language policy to Belgrade and igniting Albanian resistance.

title: The Albanian parallel state
summary: Led by Ibrahim Rugova and the Democratic League of Kosovo, Kosovo's Albanians boycotted Serbian institutions and ran their own parallel schools, clinics and administration in a decade of nonviolent resistance.

title: KLA insurgency and Serbian crackdown
summary: The Kosovo Liberation Army's insurgency against Serbian rule met an escalating campaign by Serbian and Yugoslav forces, killing many Albanians and displacing hundreds of thousands during 1998.

title: NATO air campaign begins
summary: After the failure of talks at Rambouillet, NATO launched Operation Allied Force against Yugoslav forces on 24 March 1999, a 78-day air campaign intended to halt the humanitarian catastrophe in Kosovo.

title: Mass expulsion of Kosovo Albanians
summary: Serbian and Yugoslav forces forcibly expelled some 862,000 ethnic Albanians from Kosovo, uprooting more than 80 percent of the population, with thousands killed in a systematic campaign later prosecuted as war crimes.

title: UN Resolution 1244 and UNMIK
summary: The Security Council adopted Resolution 1244, ending the war, placing Kosovo under UN interim administration (UNMIK) with a NATO-led KFOR security force, while reaffirming Yugoslav sovereignty and deferring final status.

title: Constitutional Framework for self-government
summary: UNMIK established a Constitutional Framework for Provisional Self-Government, creating an assembly, presidency and government for Kosovo while final status and ultimate authority remained with the UN administration.

title: Declaration of independence
summary: The Assembly of Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in Pristina, proclaiming the Republic of Kosovo; the United States recognised it the next day, followed by many other states.

title: ICJ advisory opinion
summary: Responding to the UN General Assembly, the International Court of Justice advised that the 2008 declaration of independence did not violate general international law or Resolution 1244.

title: Brussels Agreement
summary: Under EU facilitation, Belgrade and Pristina reached the First Agreement of Principles Governing the Normalisation of Relations, addressing the integration of Serb-majority areas and a planned association of Serb municipalities in northern Kosovo.

title: Ohrid agreement on normalisation
summary: At Ohrid the parties reached an EU-facilitated Agreement on the Path to Normalisation, committing to good-neighbourly relations and mutual recognition of documents and symbols, though Serbia did not recognise Kosovo's statehood.

title: An unresolved status
summary: Recognised by around a hundred states but not by Serbia, Russia, China or several EU members, Kosovo remains outside the UN, with the Serb-majority north around Mitrovica its most contested question.

title: Dilmun settlement on Failaka
summary: Failaka island became a flourishing outpost of the Bronze Age Dilmun trading culture, with a town, temple, palace, and one of the largest concentrations of Dilmun seals known.

title: Alexander's fleet names the island Ikaros
summary: During the exploration of the Gulf by Alexander the Great's navy, the admiral Nearchus is credited with naming Failaka 'Ikaros' after an Aegean island.

title: A Seleucid Greek fortress rises on Ikaros
summary: Under the Seleucid successors of Alexander, a fortified Greek settlement with stone walls and two temples was built on Failaka, the only standing Hellenistic stronghold in the Gulf.

title: A Greek inscription confirms Ikaros
summary: A Danish archaeological expedition uncovered a forty-four-line Greek inscription on Failaka, settling the identification of the island with the Ikaros of ancient sources.

title: The Bani Utub settle the bay
summary: Clans of the Bani Utub, part of the Anizah confederation, migrated from the Arabian interior to the Gulf coast and founded the town of Kuwait around its sheltered bay.

title: Sabah I becomes the first Al Sabah ruler
summary: The Bani Utub chose Sabah ibn Jabir, founder of the Al Sabah dynasty, to be their sheikh, beginning a line of rulers that continues to the present day.

title: A pearling and trade entrepot
summary: Kuwait grew wealthy as a maritime port, its dhows trading to India and Africa, its shipyards renowned, and its pearling fleets diving the Gulf oyster beds each summer.

title: Mubarak Al-Sabah seizes power
summary: Mubarak took control of Kuwait in a palace coup in which the ruling sheikh and his brother were killed, beginning a reign that would shape the modern state.

title: The Anglo-Kuwaiti agreement
summary: Mubarak signed a secret treaty placing Kuwait's foreign relations under British control in exchange for protection, making the sheikhdom a British protectorate and shielding it from the Ottomans.

title: Kuwait's separate status confirmed
summary: Anglo-Ottoman negotiations recognized Kuwait as an autonomous district under British protection, distinguishing it from the Ottoman territories that would later form Iraq.

title: The oil concession is granted
summary: Sheikh Ahmad al-Jabir Al-Sabah granted a concession to the Kuwait Oil Company, a joint Anglo-American venture, opening the era of petroleum.

title: Discovery of the Burgan field
summary: Drilling revealed the giant Burgan oil field, one of the world's largest, though development was delayed by the Second World War.

title: First oil exports
summary: Kuwait began exporting crude oil in 1946, launching the rapid transformation of the pearling port into a wealthy oil state.

title: Independence from Britain
summary: Kuwait and Britain ended the 1899 protectorate agreement and Kuwait declared full sovereignty under Sheikh Abdullah Al-Salim Al-Sabah, despite an immediate Iraqi claim.

title: Constitution and National Assembly
summary: A constitution was promulgated and elections in 1963 created the National Assembly, the Gulf's first and longest-serving elected parliament.

title: Iraq invades and annexes Kuwait
summary: About one hundred thousand Iraqi troops overran Kuwait in hours; Saddam Hussein declared the country annexed, and the ruling family fled to Saudi Arabia.

title: The UN condemns and authorizes force
summary: The Security Council passed Resolution 660 demanding withdrawal and Resolution 678 authorizing all necessary means to expel Iraq if it did not leave by 15 January 1991.

title: Operation Desert Storm liberates Kuwait
summary: A U.S.-led coalition launched an air campaign in mid-January and a ground assault on 24 February, expelling Iraqi forces and liberating Kuwait by late February.

title: Retreating Iraqis torch the oil fields
summary: As they withdrew, Iraqi forces set fire to and damaged over 700 Kuwaiti oil wells, causing a vast environmental disaster that took until November to fully extinguish.

title: Rapid post-war reconstruction
summary: International teams capped the burning wells and Kuwait restored oil output to pre-war capacity within about a year, while the UN set up a commission for Iraqi reparations.

title: Sheikh Sabah Al-Ahmad becomes emir
summary: The veteran foreign minister Sheikh Sabah Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah acceded as emir, a reign noted for diplomacy and humanitarian engagement until his death in 2020.

title: Sheikh Mishal accedes as emir
summary: After the deaths of Sheikh Sabah in 2020 and Sheikh Nawaf in 2023, Sheikh Mishal Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah became ruler of Kuwait.

title: Parliament dissolved and constitution suspended
summary: Emir Mishal dissolved the National Assembly and suspended several constitutional articles for up to four years, pausing the Gulf's oldest elected legislature.

title: The sacred landscape of Vat Phou
summary: Around the Champasak plain in the south, a planned Hindu landscape develops around the Vat Phou temple, growing over a millennium largely under Khmer influence; it is now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

title: Tai-Lao settlement of the Mekong
summary: Tai-speaking peoples migrating southward settle the middle Mekong valley, organizing into numerous small principalities (muang) such as Muang Swa, the future Luang Prabang.

title: Fa Ngum founds Lan Xang
summary: Fa Ngum unifies the Lao principalities of the Mekong by conquest and proclaims the kingdom of Lan Xang, the "million elephants," with its capital at Muang Swa (Luang Prabang).

title: Theravada Buddhism established
summary: During Fa Ngum's reign Theravada Buddhism of the Sinhalese school is introduced into the Lao kingdom, likely from Cambodia, becoming the foundational religion of Laos.

title: Setthathirath moves the capital to Vientiane
summary: Facing Burmese pressure, King Setthathirath transfers his capital from Luang Prabang to Vientiane, brings the Emerald Buddha, and builds the great stupa of That Luang.

title: Lan Xang splits apart
summary: After a disputed succession, the kingdom of Lan Xang divides in 1707 into the separate kingdoms of Luang Prabang and Vientiane, ending its unity.

title: Champasak secedes
summary: The far south breaks away to form the kingdom of Champasak, completing the fragmentation of Lan Xang into three rival Lao kingdoms.

title: The Lao kingdoms become Siamese vassals
summary: Divided and weakened, the rulers of Luang Prabang, Vientiane, and Champasak each fall under a Siamese commissioner and must pay tribute to Bangkok.

title: Siam destroys Vientiane
summary: After King Anouvong's failed revolt against Bangkok, Siamese forces sack and raze Vientiane and deport its people, ending the kingdom of Vientiane.

title: French protectorate established
summary: Following the Franco-Siamese crisis, Siam cedes the territory east of the Mekong and France makes the Lao states a protectorate within French Indochina, administered from Vientiane.

title: Japanese occupation and the Lao Issara
summary: Japan ousts the French administration in March 1945; after Japan's surrender, the nationalist Lao Issara (Free Lao) forms a provisional government to resist the return of French rule.

title: Founding of the Pathet Lao
summary: Prince Souphanouvong breaks with the Lao Issara to ally with the Viet Minh and proclaims the communist-oriented Pathet Lao ("Land of the Lao"), the future ruling movement.

title: Full independence from France
summary: The Franco-Lao Treaty of Amity and Association transfers the last French powers to the Royal Lao Government, recognizing Laos as a fully independent and sovereign state.

title: Geneva agreement on Lao neutrality
summary: An international agreement declares Laos neutral and provides for a coalition government, but the country remains a contested corridor of the Vietnam War.

title: The Secret War bombing
summary: The United States drops more than two million tons of bombs on Laos to cut the Ho Chi Minh Trail, making it the most heavily bombed country per capita; vast unexploded ordnance remains a deadly legacy.

title: Paris accords and U.S. withdrawal
summary: The Paris Peace Accords end direct American military involvement in Indochina, leaving the Lao factions to settle the civil war among themselves.

title: Founding of the Lao PDR
summary: The Pathet Lao take power, abolish the 600-year-old monarchy, and proclaim the Lao People's Democratic Republic, with Souphanouvong as president and Kaysone Phomvihane as prime minister.

title: New Economic Mechanism reforms
summary: Facing the failure of central planning, the ruling party launches market-oriented reforms, legalizing private enterprise and inviting foreign investment, echoing Vietnam's Doi Moi.

title: Luang Prabang inscribed by UNESCO
summary: The former royal capital of Luang Prabang, a fusion of Lao and French colonial architecture at the meeting of the Mekong and Nam Khan, is added to the UNESCO World Heritage List.

title: Laos joins ASEAN
summary: The Lao PDR is admitted to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, cementing its integration into the region after decades of isolation.

title: Laos-China Railway opens
summary: The 1,000-km railway linking Vientiane to Kunming begins operating, aiming to turn landlocked Laos into a land-linked hub of regional trade while deepening its debt to China.

title: Byblos trades cedar with Egypt
summary: Byblos flourishes as a port exporting Lebanese cedar to Egypt, beginning a record of urban habitation that makes it one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.

title: The Phoenician alphabet at Byblos
summary: A twenty-two letter alphabetic script comes into use at Byblos; adopted by the Greeks, it becomes the ancestor of the Greek and Latin alphabets and the writing of much of the world.

title: Tyre founds Carthage
summary: Tyrian colonists are traditionally credited with founding Carthage, the most powerful of the Phoenician colonies in the western Mediterranean.

title: Alexander the Great takes Tyre
summary: After a long siege and the building of a causeway to the island city, Alexander captures Tyre, ending the independence of the Phoenician city-states.

title: Baalbek becomes Roman Heliopolis
summary: Refounded as a Roman colony, Baalbek is endowed over more than two centuries with colossal temples to Jupiter, Bacchus and Venus, becoming one of the most famous sanctuaries of the Roman world.

title: Saint Maron and the Maronite origins
summary: The Maronite community traces its origin to Saint Maron, a Syrian hermit whose ascetic following grows into a distinct church that later takes refuge in the mountains of Lebanon.

title: Arab Muslim conquest of the Levant
summary: Arab armies defeat Byzantium and bring the Levant under Muslim rule, while the Christian communities of Mount Lebanon retain their distinct character in the highlands.

title: Ottoman conquest of Syria
summary: The Ottomans defeat the Mamluks and take Syria and Lebanon, but leave Mount Lebanon largely to local emirs, allowing a semi-autonomous emirate to develop.

title: Fakhr al-Din II unites the mountain
summary: Fakhr al-Din II of the Druze Maan dynasty unites the Druze and Maronite districts of Mount Lebanon, expands his domains across the Levant and cultivates ties with Tuscany.

title: Execution of Fakhr al-Din II
summary: Defeated by Ottoman forces wary of his power, Fakhr al-Din is captured and executed in Constantinople, but the union of Druze and Maronite districts he created endures.

title: Fall of Bashir Shihab II
summary: After siding with Egypt's Ibrahim Pasha, the long-ruling emir Bashir Shihab II is deposed and exiled when Egyptian rule in Syria collapses, ending the autonomous emirate.

title: Sectarian conflict in Mount Lebanon
summary: Violence between Druze and Maronites spreads to Damascus and kills many thousands of Christians (figures are disputed estimates), prompting a French-led European intervention.

title: The Mount Lebanon Mutasarrifate
summary: Under European pressure the Ottomans grant Mount Lebanon autonomy as the Mutasarrifate, governed by a Christian official and a council of the religious communities.

title: Creation of Greater Lebanon
summary: French High Commissioner Henri Gouraud proclaims the State of Greater Lebanon, enlarging the old province with the coastal cities and the Bekaa under a French mandate.

title: The Lebanese Republic and constitution
summary: Greater Lebanon is reorganised as the Lebanese Republic with a written constitution, though France retains ultimate authority under the mandate.

title: The National Pact
summary: Bechara El Khoury and Riad al-Solh agree the unwritten National Pact distributing the presidency, premiership and parliamentary speakership among Maronites, Sunnis and Shi'a.

title: U.S. recognition of Lebanon
summary: The United States formally recognises Lebanon as an independent state, and establishes diplomatic relations later that year.

title: French withdrawal completed
summary: The last French troops leave Lebanon, completing the country's transition to full sovereignty.

title: Beirut, the Paris of the Middle East
summary: Lebanon's golden age makes Beirut the banking, commercial and cultural capital of the region, renowned for its cosmopolitan prosperity.

title: The Lebanese Civil War
summary: Fighting erupts in Beirut and escalates into a fifteen-year civil war that draws in Syria, Israel and many militias; deaths are estimated, very approximately, in the range of 120,000–150,000.

title: Israeli invasion and siege of Beirut
summary: Israel invades Lebanon and besieges Beirut, forcing out the PLO; the assassination of president-elect Bashir Gemayel is followed by the Sabra and Shatila massacre.

title: The Taif Agreement
summary: Brokered with Arab support, the Taif Agreement winds down the war and rebalances the confessional system, shifting authority from the Maronite president to the Sunni prime minister and cabinet.

title: Hariri assassination and the Cedar Revolution
summary: A car bomb kills former prime minister Rafic Hariri and others; mass protests known as the Cedar Revolution lead Syria to withdraw its forces after nearly thirty years.

title: Economic collapse and the Beirut port explosion
summary: From 2019 Lebanon suffers one of the world's worst economic crises; on 4 August 2020 an ammonium-nitrate explosion at the port of Beirut kills more than 200 people and devastates the capital.

title: Settlement by Mande, Kwa, and Mel peoples
summary: Over centuries the region was settled by Niger-Congo-speaking peoples — Mande groups such as the Vai and Kpelle, Kwa groups such as the Kru, Grebo, and Bassa, and Mel groups such as the Gola and Kisi, the last regarded as among the oldest inhabitants.

title: Europeans name the Grain Coast
summary: Portuguese and other European mariners charted the coast and called it the Grain or Pepper Coast after the melegueta pepper traded there; Kru and Grebo seafarers became known along the West African coast.

title: Invention of the Vai script
summary: Momolu Duwalu Bukele and fellow Vai elders are credited with devising the Vai syllabary, one of the few indigenous writing systems created in sub-Saharan Africa, which remains in use; some accounts place its origin earlier.

title: Founding of the American Colonization Society
summary: The American Colonization Society was established in the United States to resettle free-born and freed African Americans in West Africa, drawing together abolitionists and slaveholders with sharply differing motives.

title: Acquisition of Cape Mesurado
summary: Society agents, backed by a U.S. naval officer, secured Cape Mesurado from local rulers as the site for the colony, after an earlier attempt to settle at Sherbro Island had failed.

title: First settlers land and found the colony
summary: Free-born and freed African American settlers went ashore at Cape Mesurado and established the settlement of Christopolis, the nucleus of the colony of Liberia, with the agent Jehudi Ashmun organising its early administration.

title: Christopolis renamed Monrovia
summary: The settlement was renamed Monrovia after U.S. President James Monroe, a patron of the Colonization Society, and the colony was named Liberia, 'land of the free'.

title: The Republic of Liberia is proclaimed
summary: Delegates issued the Liberian Declaration of Independence and proclaimed the Republic of Liberia under a U.S.-modelled constitution, making it the first modern republic in Africa.

title: Joseph Jenkins Roberts inaugurated
summary: Joseph Jenkins Roberts, a free man of colour born in Virginia, was inaugurated as the first president of the Republic of Liberia.

title: United States recognises Liberia
summary: Having delayed during the era of slavery, the United States formally recognised the Republic of Liberia in 1862 and concluded a treaty of commerce and navigation with it.

title: True Whig Party dominance begins
summary: From 1878 the True Whig Party, the party of the Americo-Liberian elite, held power virtually without interruption for more than a century, marginalising the indigenous majority.

title: The Firestone rubber concession
summary: The government granted the Firestone Tire and Rubber Company a 99-year concession to lease up to a million acres, creating one of the world's largest rubber plantations and binding Liberia's economy to a single foreign company.

title: William Tubman becomes president
summary: William V. S. Tubman took office as president and would govern until 1971, launching the 'Open Door' policy of foreign investment and the 'National Unification' policy toward the indigenous interior.

title: Tolbert succeeds Tubman
summary: On Tubman's death his vice-president William R. Tolbert became president, promising reform but facing mounting discontent over inequality and Americo-Liberian privilege.

title: The rice riots
summary: Protests in Monrovia against a proposed increase in the price of rice turned deadly, exposing the fragility of the Tolbert government and the depth of popular grievance.

title: Samuel Doe's coup ends settler rule
summary: Master Sergeant Samuel K. Doe led soldiers who killed President Tolbert and seized power, ending 133 years of Americo-Liberian and True Whig dominance; thirteen officials were soon publicly executed.

title: Doe confirmed in a flawed election
summary: Samuel Doe was declared the winner of a widely criticised election, formalising his presidency; his increasingly repressive and ethnically partisan rule deepened tensions across Liberia.

title: First Liberian Civil War begins
summary: Charles Taylor's National Patriotic Front of Liberia invaded from Côte d'Ivoire, beginning a brutal civil war marked by ethnic massacres and the widespread use of child soldiers.

title: Samuel Doe captured and killed
summary: President Samuel Doe was captured, tortured, and killed by a rival rebel faction, and a West African ECOMOG force deployed in an attempt to contain the spreading conflict.

title: Charles Taylor elected president
summary: After a 1996 peace accord, Charles Taylor won the 1997 presidential election amid intimidation and war-weariness, ending the first civil war but not the underlying conflict.

title: Second Liberian Civil War begins
summary: The rebel group LURD launched a new insurgency against Taylor's government from the north, opening a second civil war that would eventually besiege Monrovia.

title: Taylor resigns; Accra peace agreement
summary: With rebels besieging Monrovia and an international indictment over Sierra Leone hanging over him, Charles Taylor resigned and went into exile; a comprehensive peace agreement in Accra ended the war and a UN mission, UNMIL, deployed.

title: Taylor convicted of war crimes
summary: The Special Court for Sierra Leone convicted Charles Taylor of aiding and abetting war crimes and crimes against humanity in Sierra Leone and sentenced him to 50 years — the first former head of state convicted by an international tribunal since Nuremberg.

title: Ellen Johnson Sirleaf elected
summary: Ellen Johnson Sirleaf won the presidential run-off against George Weah and was inaugurated in January 2006 as the first woman elected to lead an African nation.

title: Sirleaf shares the Nobel Peace Prize
summary: Ellen Johnson Sirleaf was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, jointly with two other women, for non-violent work on behalf of women's safety and participation in peacebuilding.

title: The Ebola epidemic
summary: Liberia was among the countries worst hit by the West African Ebola epidemic, the largest in history, which killed thousands and overwhelmed a health system already weakened by war before transmission was halted.

title: Peaceful transfer to George Weah
summary: Sirleaf handed power to George Weah, who won the 2017 election — Liberia's first peaceful democratic transfer of power between elected presidents in over seven decades.

title: Boakai defeats Weah
summary: Joseph Boakai defeated the incumbent George Weah in the 2023 election and took office in 2024, marking another orderly transfer of power in post-war Liberia.

title: Phoenicians found Leptis Magna
summary: Phoenician colonists establish Leptis Magna, which with Oea (Tripoli) and Sabratha forms the 'three cities' that give Tripolitania its name.

title: Greeks found Cyrene
summary: Settlers from Thera, led by Battus, found Cyrene in eastern Libya; it becomes the chief city of the Cyrenaican Pentapolis and a renowned centre of Greek culture.

title: Cyrenaica passes to Rome
summary: On the death of Ptolemy Apion, Cyrenaica is bequeathed to Rome; Tripolitania likewise comes under Roman authority, opening centuries of prosperity.

title: Leptis Magna's golden age under Septimius Severus
summary: The emperor Septimius Severus, born at Leptis Magna, lavishes monuments on his home city, making it one of the foremost ports of Roman Africa.

title: Garamantes flourish in the Fezzan
summary: From their capital at Garama, the Garamantes sustain a desert kingdom through foggara irrigation and command of trans-Saharan trade.

title: Arab conquest of Cyrenaica
summary: Arab forces under Amr ibn al-As take Cyrenaica and advance into Tripolitania, beginning Libya's transformation into a Muslim, Arabic-speaking land.

title: Arab expeditions reach the Fezzan
summary: Campaigns associated with Uqba ibn Nafi extend Arab-Muslim authority into the Saharan Fezzan, ending the autonomy of the Garamantes' heartland.

title: Banu Hilal migration
summary: The westward migration of Arab Bedouin tribes such as the Banu Hilal accelerates the Arabisation of Libya's interior.

title: Ottomans capture Tripoli
summary: Ottoman admirals Sinan Pasha and Turgut Reis take Tripoli, establishing the Regency of Tripoli within the Ottoman Empire.

title: Karamanli dynasty seizes power
summary: Ahmed Karamanli founds a hereditary dynasty that rules Tripoli in semi-independence for 124 years under nominal Ottoman suzerainty.

title: First Barbary War with the United States
summary: Yusuf Karamanli's tribute demands provoke war with the United States; the US Navy blockades Tripoli until a treaty ends the conflict in 1805.

title: Ottomans restore direct rule
summary: Sultan Mahmud II ends the Karamanli dynasty and reimposes direct Ottoman administration over Tripolitania.

title: Founding of the Senussi order
summary: Muhammad ibn Ali al-Senussi founds the Sanusi religious order, which from the 1840s becomes the leading power in Cyrenaica and the eastern Sahara.

title: Italo-Turkish War and the invasion of Libya
summary: Italy attacks Tripoli on 3 October 1911 and seizes the Ottoman provinces; the 1912 Treaty of Lausanne cedes the territory to Italy.

title: Pacification of Libya
summary: Italian forces wage a war of 'pacification', crushing resistance and deporting Cyrenaica's population into concentration camps where tens of thousands die.

title: Execution of Omar al-Mukhtar
summary: The resistance leader Omar al-Mukhtar, the 'Lion of the Desert', is captured and publicly hanged at Soluch, breaking organised resistance in Cyrenaica.

title: Creation of Italian Libya
summary: Governor Italo Balbo merges Tripolitania and Cyrenaica into a single colony, Italian Libya, reviving the classical name.

title: North African desert campaigns
summary: The Second World War's desert war sweeps across Libya; by 1943 Allied forces expel the Axis, ending Italian rule and beginning Anglo-French administration.

title: Independence of the United Kingdom of Libya
summary: Libya is proclaimed an independent federal monarchy under King Idris—the first state created through the United Nations.

title: Commercial oil discovered
summary: The discovery of oil in commercial quantities at the Zelten field transforms Libya's prospects; exports begin in 1961.

title: Abolition of the federal system
summary: A constitutional reform replaces Libya's three-province federation with a unitary kingdom.

title: Gaddafi's coup overthrows the monarchy
summary: The Free Officers under Muammar Gaddafi depose King Idris in a near-bloodless coup and proclaim a republic, beginning 42 years of Gaddafi's rule.

title: Proclamation of the Jamahiriya
summary: Gaddafi declares the 'state of the masses' (Jamahiriya), his idiosyncratic political system set out in the Green Book.

title: US bombing of Tripoli and Benghazi
summary: In Operation El Dorado Canyon, US aircraft strike Libyan targets in retaliation for a Berlin disco bombing, deepening Libya's confrontation with the West.

title: Uprising, NATO intervention and Gaddafi's fall
summary: An uprising from February 2011 and a NATO air campaign from 19 March topple Gaddafi, who is captured and killed at Sirte on 20 October 2011.

title: Division and civil war
summary: Disputed elections split Libya between rival governments in Tripoli and the east; Haftar's 2019–2020 assault on Tripoli fails, and a 2021 unity government cannot reunite the country.

title: The county of Vaduz takes shape
summary: A separate county of Vaduz emerged in the fourteenth century in the upper Rhine valley, alongside the smaller lordship of Schellenberg, both small and often impoverished holdings within the Holy Roman Empire.

title: The House of Liechtenstein raised to princely rank
summary: Karl von Liechtenstein received the hereditary dignity of an imperial prince in 1608, confirmed for his brothers soon after, raising the wealthy Austrian dynasty to the highest rank of the nobility.

title: Hohenems debts open the way
summary: The counts of Hohenems, who held Vaduz and Schellenberg, fell into heavy debt, leaving the small Rhine territories available for sale to a buyer rich enough to redeem them.

title: Purchase of the lordship of Schellenberg
summary: Prince Johann Adam Andreas I bought the lordship of Schellenberg from the indebted Hohenems, the first of the two acquisitions that would form the principality; the prince did not attend the homage ceremony in person.

title: Purchase of the county of Vaduz
summary: Johann Adam Andreas I acquired the county of Vaduz, and from this time Vaduz Castle entered the possession of the princes of Liechtenstein, completing the territory of the future principality.

title: Foundation of the Principality of Liechtenstein
summary: Emperor Charles VI united Schellenberg and Vaduz and raised them to an Imperial Principality named Liechtenstein, granting the family the immediate standing and Diet seat it had sought; the founding diploma survives in the Princely Collections.

title: A prince visits at last
summary: Prince Alois II became the first reigning prince to set foot in Liechtenstein, more than a century after its foundation, the dynasty having until then governed entirely from its Austrian and Bohemian seats.

title: Sovereignty through the Confederation of the Rhine
summary: On the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire, Liechtenstein was admitted to Napoleon's Confederation of the Rhine, gaining recognised sovereignty and surviving the Napoleonic reordering of Germany.

title: Membership of the German Confederation
summary: After Napoleon's defeat, Liechtenstein joined the German Confederation created at the Congress of Vienna, remaining within it until 1866 while keeping close dynastic ties to Austria.

title: First constitution and the Landtag
summary: A constitution granted in 1862 established a parliament, the Landtag, beginning the slow growth of constitutional and representative institutions alongside the prince.

title: Full independence
summary: When the German Confederation dissolved after the Austro-Prussian War, Liechtenstein became a fully sovereign and independent state, its links thereafter resting on treaty and choice rather than confederation.

title: Abolition of the army and neutrality
summary: Liechtenstein disbanded its small military force as too costly and committed itself to permanent neutrality, a policy it has maintained through every subsequent European conflict.

title: Liberal constitution of 1921
summary: Following the First World War, Liechtenstein adopted a new constitution that combined the prince with an elected Landtag and instruments of direct democracy, modernising the state as it reoriented toward Switzerland.

title: Customs union with Switzerland and the Swiss franc
summary: A customs treaty signed in 1923 and in force from 1 January 1924 joined Liechtenstein and Switzerland into a single customs and economic area; Liechtenstein adopted the Swiss franc, binding its economy to its western neighbour.

title: A prince moves to Vaduz
summary: Prince Franz Josef II became the first reigning prince to take up permanent residence in Liechtenstein, ending more than two centuries of rule from abroad on the eve of the Second World War.

title: Confiscation under the Beneš decrees
summary: Czechoslovakia confiscated the vast Bohemian and Moravian estates of the House of Liechtenstein under the Beneš decrees, treating the family as German; the seized land, around 1,600 square kilometres, far exceeded the area of the principality.

title: Women's suffrage introduced
summary: By a referendum of male voters carried by a narrow margin, Liechtenstein granted women the right to vote in national elections, becoming the last country in Europe to do so.

title: Admission to the United Nations
summary: Liechtenstein was admitted as the 160th member state of the United Nations, marking the small principality's full emergence as a recognised actor in international affairs.

title: Accession to the European Economic Area
summary: Liechtenstein joined the European Economic Area, integrating into the European single market as an EFTA state while remaining outside the European Union and preserving its Swiss customs union.

title: Constitutional referendum expands the prince's powers
summary: Voters approved Prince Hans-Adam II's constitutional revision, enlarging the reigning prince's powers including a veto over legislation and the right to dismiss the government, after he threatened to leave the country.

title: ICJ judgment in Liechtenstein v. Germany
summary: In Certain Property (Liechtenstein v. Germany), brought to the International Court of Justice in 2001 over a confiscated van Laer painting, the Court ruled on 10 February 2005 that it had no jurisdiction, locating the dispute's source in the 1945 Beneš-era confiscations.

title: Diplomatic relations with the Czech Republic
summary: After more than six decades without recognition arising from the 1945 confiscations, Liechtenstein and the Czech Republic established diplomatic relations in 2009 and created a joint commission of historians.

title: Sinhalese settlement and the founding of Anuradhapura
summary: By tradition Prince Vijaya's followers settle the island; the kingdom of Anuradhapura is founded under Pandukabhaya and grows into the strongest Sinhalese state, capital for over a thousand years.

title: Buddhism introduced under Devanampiya Tissa
summary: The missionary Mahinda, sent during the reign of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka, converts King Devanampiya Tissa near Mihintale, establishing Theravada Buddhism as the island's defining faith.

title: Hydraulic civilisation and South Indian invasions
summary: Anuradhapura's kings build vast reservoir-and-channel systems to irrigate the dry plain, while recurrent invasions from South India culminate in the Chola conquest and the abandonment of the capital around 1017.

title: Kassapa I builds Sigiriya
summary: A king who took the throne by killing his father moves the capital to the summit of a 180-metre granite peak, entered through a stair rising from the mouth of a brick lion.

title: Polonnaruwa becomes the capital
summary: Following the Chola conquest and the abandonment of Anuradhapura, Polonnaruwa is established as Sri Lanka's second great capital in the north-central dry zone.

title: Golden age under Parakramabahu I
summary: Parakramabahu I rebuilds the city and its irrigation, creating the immense Parakrama Samudra reservoir and a garden-capital that marks the high point of the Polonnaruwa period.

title: Decline and the drift southward
summary: Invasion, the breakdown of the dry-zone irrigation system and disease lead to the abandonment of the northern capitals and the migration of Sinhalese power toward the south-west and the Kandyan hills.

title: Arrival of the Portuguese
summary: A Portuguese fleet reaches Colombo, opening more than a century of Portuguese control over Ceylon's coasts and its profitable cinnamon trade.

title: Dutch supplant the Portuguese
summary: Allied with Kandy, the Dutch East India Company takes Galle (1640) and expels the Portuguese with the fall of Colombo (1656) and Jaffna (1658), ruling the maritime provinces for cinnamon.

title: Britain takes the Dutch coasts
summary: With the Netherlands under French control in Europe, Britain begins taking over the maritime provinces — the island changes hands as a consequence of a war fought elsewhere.

title: Kandyan Convention unifies the island under Britain
summary: The Kandyan chiefs cede the highland kingdom to the British crown, ending the last independent Sinhalese kingdom and placing the whole island under a single colonial administration.

title: Plantation economy and Tamil labour migration
summary: British coffee and later tea estates transform the highlands; indentured South Indian Tamil labourers are brought in to work them, forming the Indian Tamil community of the plantation districts.

title: One administration for the whole island
summary: Reform dissolves the separate systems of the maritime provinces and the highlands, governing Ceylon as a single colony for the first time.

title: Universal suffrage and reform
summary: Constitutional reforms grant universal adult suffrage in Ceylon, far ahead of most colonies, strengthening a moderate movement for self-government.

title: Independence of the Dominion of Ceylon
summary: Ceylon becomes an independent dominion within the Commonwealth as its 1947 constitution takes effect, with D. S. Senanayake as first prime minister.

title: Indian Tamil plantation workers disenfranchised
summary: The estate workforce brought from South India is stripped of the vote a year after independence — the opening move of a nationalism that alienated the Tamil minority.

title: Ceylon becomes the Republic of Sri Lanka
summary: A new republican constitution ends dominion status and changes the country's name from Ceylon to Sri Lanka, while it remains within the Commonwealth.

title: The Sinhala Only Act
summary: S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike is elected on a wave of Sinhalese nationalism and makes Sinhala the sole official language, alongside measures elevating Buddhism.

title: The JVP insurrection
summary: A Marxist rising is put down; its missing would still be uncounted in the state's own figures forty-five years later.

title: The LTTE is founded
summary: The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam form to fight for Tamil rights, seven years before the war that would define them.

title: Civil war between the state and the LTTE
summary: After the anti-Tamil violence of Black July in 1983, the LTTE fights for a separate Tamil state; the war ends with the group's military defeat in May 2009 after about twenty-six years.

title: The Indo-Lanka accords and the Indian peacekeepers
summary: Accords create new councils for the Tamil north and east and bring in an Indian peacekeeping force, which spends three years bogged down in the fighting it came to end.

title: Indian withdrawal and the expulsion of northern Muslims
summary: Indian troops leave and the war escalates; the LTTE expels thousands of Muslims from the northern districts.

title: Indian Ocean tsunami
summary: Waves from a magnitude-9.1 undersea earthquake off Sumatra devastate Sri Lanka's coasts, killing more than 30,000 people in the country's deadliest natural disaster.

title: Economic crisis and sovereign default
summary: A foreign-exchange crisis forces Sri Lanka's first sovereign default; shortages and protests topple President Gotabaya Rajapaksa, leading to an IMF bailout and, in 2024, the election of Anura Kumara Dissanayake.

title: The state counts its missing
summary: The government acknowledges for the first time that some 65,000 people are missing from the 26-year war and the 1971 insurrection.

title: The Easter Sunday bombings
summary: Jihadist suicide bombers attack churches and hotels, killing more than 350 people.

title: San rock art of the Maloti-Drakensberg
summary: San hunter-gatherers occupy the mountain rock shelters, leaving one of the world's richest bodies of rock art depicting eland, dance and trance.

title: Sotho-Tswana settlement
summary: Bantu-speaking Sotho-Tswana farmers and herders settle the region, bringing cattle, cultivation and iron-working alongside earlier San and Khoekhoe peoples.

title: Dispersed Sotho chiefdoms
summary: Numerous small, rivalrous Sotho-speaking chiefdoms occupy the highveld and mountains, with no single overarching authority.

title: Moshoeshoe occupies Thaba Bosiu
summary: Moshoeshoe I settles the defensible mountain of Thaba Bosiu, the stronghold from which he gathers difaqane refugees into the Basotho nation.

title: Paris missionaries arrive
summary: Moshoeshoe invites the Paris Evangelical Missionary Society into his kingdom; the missionaries help create a written Sesotho and advise him on dealings with Europeans.

title: Senekal's War with the Orange Free State
summary: Conflict erupts with the Boers of the Orange Free State over land in the western lowlands, the first of the Free State–Basotho Wars.

title: Seqiti War and loss of the lowlands
summary: A devastating war with the Orange Free State sees Boer commandos overrun much of the fertile western lowlands and besiege Thaba Bosiu.

title: Basutoland declared a British protectorate
summary: Britain takes Moshoeshoe's kingdom under its protection, halting Boer absorption and fixing the borders that broadly survive as modern Lesotho.

title: Convention of Aliwal North
summary: The boundary settlement with the Orange Free State confirms the loss of the fertile western lowlands, the "Conquered Territory", to the Boers.

title: Annexation to the Cape Colony
summary: Basutoland is annexed to the Cape Colony without Basotho consent, beginning a deeply unpopular period of colonial rule.

title: The Gun War
summary: The Basotho rebel against Cape disarmament and taxation; they retain their guns and effectively repudiate Cape authority.

title: Return to direct British rule
summary: Unable to control the territory, the Cape gives it up; Basutoland reverts to direct rule from Britain under a resident commissioner.

title: Kept out of the Union of South Africa
summary: On the formation of the Union, Basutoland is excluded as a British High Commission Territory rather than incorporated into South Africa.

title: Migrant labour to South Africa
summary: With little arable land, large numbers of Basotho men become migrant workers on South African farms and gold mines, and remittances become central to the economy.

title: Basotho National Party wins the pre-independence election
summary: Leabua Jonathan's BNP narrowly defeats the Basutoland Congress Party, positioning him to lead the territory to independence.

title: Independence as the Kingdom of Lesotho
summary: Basutoland becomes the independent Kingdom of Lesotho under King Moshoeshoe II and Prime Minister Leabua Jonathan, ending British rule.

title: Constitution suspended after lost election
summary: Having apparently lost the first post-independence election, Leabua Jonathan annuls the result, suspends the constitution and rules by decree.

title: Military coup and the water treaty
summary: A military coup overthrows Jonathan; in the same year the new government signs the treaty launching the Lesotho Highlands Water Project with South Africa.

title: Death of Moshoeshoe II
summary: After exile and a brief restoration, King Moshoeshoe II dies in a car accident; his son Letsie III returns to the throne.

title: Disputed election and SADC intervention
summary: A contested election sparks unrest and a South African-led SADC military intervention; much of Maseru is left in ruins.

title: Katse and Mohale dams completed
summary: The Katse Dam (Phase 1A) and then the Mohale Dam are completed, sending Lesotho's mountain water to South Africa's Vaal system in exchange for royalties.

title: Coronation of Mindaugas
summary: Having accepted baptism around 1251, Mindaugas was crowned King of Lithuania by authority of Pope Innocent IV, the only ruler ever crowned king of the country and the founder of the Lithuanian state.

title: Assassination of Mindaugas and pagan reversion
summary: Mindaugas was murdered amid noble rivalry; Lithuania abandoned the royal title and Christianity, returning to paganism and to rule by grand dukes for more than a century.

title: Vilnius founded by Gediminas
summary: The capital Vilnius is first recorded in Grand Duke Gediminas's letters of 1323, in which he invited merchants, craftsmen and clergy from across Europe to settle freely in his expanding realm.

title: Reign of Gediminas and the Gediminid dynasty
summary: Gediminas consolidated the grand duchy, founded the dynasty that bears his name and began the expansion that carried Lithuanian power deep into the lands of the former Kievan Rus.

title: Union of Krewo
summary: Grand Duke Jogaila agreed to marry Queen Jadwiga of Poland, convert to Christianity and unite the two realms; baptised as Wladyslaw II Jagiello, he founded the Jagiellonian dynasty.

title: Christianization of Lithuania
summary: A bishopric was founded at Vilnius and Lithuania, the last major pagan state in Europe, formally accepted Latin Christianity following the union with Poland.

title: Battle of Grunwald (Zalgiris)
summary: Polish and Lithuanian forces under Wladyslaw II Jagiello and Grand Duke Vytautas annihilated the army of the Teutonic Knights, ending the Order's expansion in the Baltic.

title: Reign of Vytautas the Great
summary: Vytautas consolidated the Grand Duchy and extended its borders to the Black Sea, making Lithuania one of the largest states in Europe at the height of its power.

title: Union of Lublin
summary: Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania united into the federal Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, ruled by an elected monarch and a common Sejm, with Lithuania keeping its own laws and institutions.

title: Final partition and annexation by Russia
summary: In the third partition of the Commonwealth, Russia, Prussia and Austria completed its dismemberment; the Grand Duchy of Lithuania was annexed almost wholly by the Russian Empire, ending Lithuanian statehood.

title: The Lithuanian press ban
summary: After the 1863 uprising the tsarist regime banned Lithuanian books in the Latin alphabet; the ban lasted forty years before being lifted in 1904.

title: The book smugglers (knygnesiai)
summary: Defying the press ban, a clandestine network of book carriers smuggled Latin-script Lithuanian books across the Prussian frontier, preserving the language and fuelling the national revival.

title: Act of Independence
summary: The Council of Lithuania in Vilnius proclaimed the restoration of an independent State of Lithuania on democratic principles, with Vilnius as its capital, severing all former ties to other states.

title: Zeligowski's Mutiny and the seizure of Vilnius
summary: Polish forces under General Zeligowski, secretly directed by Pilsudski, seized Vilnius and its region; a 'Republic of Central Lithuania' was created and annexed by Poland in 1922.

title: The Klaipeda Revolt
summary: Lithuania staged a revolt that seized the Allied-administered Klaipeda (Memel) Territory; the powers accepted the outcome and recognised Lithuanian sovereignty over the port and its region.

title: German ultimatum and loss of Klaipeda
summary: Nazi Germany demanded the Klaipeda region by ultimatum on 20 March 1939, threatening invasion; Lithuania capitulated and German troops occupied the territory on 23 March.

title: Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact
summary: The German-Soviet non-aggression pact and its secret protocol divided eastern Europe into spheres of influence; an adjustment that autumn assigned Lithuania, with the other Baltic states, to the Soviet sphere.

title: Soviet occupation and annexation
summary: The Soviet Union occupied Lithuania in June 1940 and annexed it in August as the Lithuanian SSR, an incorporation never recognised as lawful by the United States and most Western states.

title: Mass deportations to Siberia
summary: The Soviet regime deported well over one hundred thousand Lithuanians to camps and forced settlements, with the largest operations in 1948 and 1949, to crush resistance and impose collectivisation.

title: The Forest Brothers' partisan war
summary: Thousands of Lithuanians fought a guerrilla war against the returning Soviet forces; the partisan movement controlled much of the countryside before being crushed by the early 1950s.

title: The rise of Sajudis
summary: The reform movement Sajudis emerged as Soviet controls loosened, mobilising mass support for Lithuanian sovereignty and winning a majority in the 1990 elections to the republic's parliament.

title: Restoration of independence
summary: The Supreme Council adopted the Act on the Re-establishment of the State of Lithuania, making Lithuania the first Soviet republic to declare the restoration of its independence.

title: The January events in Vilnius
summary: Soviet forces stormed the Vilnius television tower and broadcasting centre, killing fourteen unarmed civilians; the defenders held parliament and the crackdown discredited Moscow.

title: Accession to NATO
summary: Lithuania formally joined NATO on 29 March 2004, anchoring its security in the Atlantic alliance a little over a decade after the withdrawal of Soviet forces.

title: Accession to the European Union
summary: Lithuania joined the European Union on 1 May 2004 and adopted the euro in 2015, completing its return to the institutions of the West.

title: Siegfried acquires Lucilinburhuc
summary: Count Siegfried of the Ardennes obtained the rocky promontory of Lucilinburhuc above the Alzette and built a castle on the Bock, the founding act of the city, the country and the nation.

title: The town is walled
summary: The settlement gathered beneath Siegfried's castle was enclosed with stone ramparts around the middle of the twelfth century, beginning its long evolution into a fortified city.

title: Henry of Luxembourg elected King of the Romans
summary: Count Henry, head of the House of Luxembourg, was elected King of the Romans, opening the dynasty's rise to the imperial throne of the Holy Roman Empire.

title: John the Blind becomes King of Bohemia
summary: John of Luxembourg, son of Henry VII, became king of Bohemia in 1310 and count of Luxembourg in 1313, a renowned warrior-prince later celebrated as a national hero of Luxembourg.

title: Death of John the Blind at Crecy
summary: Blind in his final years, John of Luxembourg insisted on joining the fighting and was killed at the Battle of Crecy on the side of France, becoming an emblematic figure of Luxembourg's chivalric past.

title: Luxembourg raised to a duchy
summary: Emperor Charles IV of the House of Luxembourg elevated the County of Luxembourg to the rank of a duchy, entrusting it to his half-brother Wenceslaus as its first duke.

title: Burgundy seizes Luxembourg
summary: Philip the Good, duke of Burgundy, took Luxembourg in 1443, ending the rule of the House of Luxembourg and absorbing the duchy into the Burgundian dominions.

title: Treaty of the Pyrenees: the First Partition
summary: The peace between France and Spain ceded a southern band of the duchy, including Thionville, Montmedy and Stenay, to Louis XIV's France, the first partition of Luxembourg's territory.

title: Louis XIV takes the fortress; Vauban rebuilds it
summary: French forces captured Luxembourg City in 1684, and the engineer Vauban remodelled its fortifications before the stronghold was later returned to Spanish rule.

title: Return to the Habsburgs
summary: Luxembourg reverted to Habsburg rule, passing in the eighteenth century from the Spanish to the Austrian branch of the dynasty while remaining a frontier fortress.

title: Revolutionary France captures the fortress
summary: After a long blockade, French Revolutionary forces took the fortress in 1795 and Luxembourg was annexed to the French Republic, ending the era of Habsburg rule.

title: Congress of Vienna creates the Grand Duchy
summary: Luxembourg was raised to a Grand Duchy under William I of the Netherlands in personal union, placed within the German Confederation with a Prussian garrison, and lost an eastern slice to Prussia in a second partition.

title: Treaty of London: the cession to Belgium
summary: The 1839 Treaty of London partitioned the Grand Duchy a third time, ceding its larger French-speaking western half to the new kingdom of Belgium while confirming the independence of the German-speaking remainder.

title: Entry into the Zollverein
summary: The reduced Grand Duchy joined the German customs union in 1842, binding its economy closely to the neighbouring German territories for the rest of the century.

title: Treaty of London: neutrality and the razing of the fortress
summary: After the Luxembourg Crisis between France and Prussia, the powers guaranteed the Grand Duchy's perpetual neutrality, withdrew the Prussian garrison and ordered the fortress dismantled, a demolition completed in 1883.

title: Separation of the crown from the Netherlands
summary: On the death of William III the personal union ended; the Dutch crown passed to Wilhelmina while Luxembourg, under male-line succession, passed to Adolphe of Nassau-Weilburg, founding a national dynasty.

title: German invasion in the First World War
summary: German forces occupied neutral Luxembourg on 2 August 1914 to control its railways for the advance on France, holding the country until November 1918 despite its formal protest.

title: Abdication of Marie-Adelaide
summary: Criticised for her conduct under the German occupation, Grand Duchess Marie-Adelaide abdicated in January 1919 in favour of her sister Charlotte, who reigned until 1964.

title: Second German invasion and annexation
summary: The Wehrmacht overran Luxembourg on 10 May 1940; the government and Grand Duchess fled into exile, and the territory was placed under a German civil administration aimed at its full integration into the Reich.

title: Conscription and the general strike
summary: When the occupier imposed German citizenship and Wehrmacht conscription in August 1942, a general strike spread from 31 August, the first in Nazi-occupied Europe; the Germans declared martial law and executed twenty-one strikers.

title: Liberation and the Battle of the Bulge
summary: Allied forces liberated Luxembourg in September 1944, but the German Ardennes offensive launched on 16 December 1944 overran the north of the country, which had to be liberated a second time before war's end.

title: The Benelux customs convention
summary: The exiled governments of Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg signed a customs union in London on 5 September 1944, launching the Benelux that entered into force in 1948 and was deepened by the 1958 Economic Union.

title: Founding member of NATO
summary: Having renounced its enforced neutrality, Luxembourg was one of the twelve states that signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington on 4 April 1949, founding the Atlantic alliance.

title: Founding member of the ECSC
summary: Following the Schuman Declaration of 9 May 1950, Luxembourg joined Belgium, France, Italy, the Netherlands and West Germany as a founding member of the European Coal and Steel Community, operating from 1952.

title: Founding member of the European Communities
summary: Under the Treaties of Rome, Luxembourg became a founding member of the European Economic Community, joining what is now the European Union from 1 January 1958 and later adopting the euro.

title: The Schengen Agreement
summary: On 14 June 1985 five states signed, at the village of Schengen on the Luxembourg Moselle, the agreement abolishing internal border controls that gave a Luxembourg name to Europe's borderless travel area.

title: Foundation of Riga by Bishop Albert
summary: Bishop Albert of Buxhoevden founded Riga at the mouth of the Daugava as the base for the German mission and conquest, the city that became the centre of crusader Livonia and a great Hanseatic port.

title: Order of the Brothers of the Sword founded
summary: With papal sanction Bishop Albert established the Order of the Brothers of the Sword to subjugate and convert the Baltic tribes, launching decades of crusading warfare in Livonia.

title: Absorption into the Teutonic Order
summary: After heavy defeats the Sword Brothers were merged into the Teutonic Order as the autonomous Livonian Order; by this time the Latvian and Livonian tribal lands had largely been conquered and bound into Terra Mariana.

title: Riga joins the Hanseatic League
summary: Riga entered the Hanseatic League, the powerful association of northern European merchant towns, cementing its prosperity as the chief trading city between Russia and western Europe.

title: Dissolution of Livonia and the Duchy of Courland
summary: The collapse of the Livonian Order during the Livonian War split the land: Livonia passed under Polish-Lithuanian rule, while Gotthard Kettler founded the vassal Duchy of Courland and Semigallia.

title: Swedish conquest of Riga
summary: Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden captured Riga and most of Livonia from Poland-Lithuania, opening the period of Swedish rule remembered by Latvians as the 'good Swedish times'.

title: Courland's overseas colonies
summary: Under Duke Jacob Kettler the Duchy of Courland founded short-lived colonies on the Gambia River and on Tobago, a striking commercial venture by a small Baltic state before its decline.

title: Russia takes Riga
summary: During the Great Northern War the forces of Peter the Great captured Riga from Sweden; the cession of Swedish Livonia was confirmed at the Peace of Nystad in 1721, bringing the region into the Russian Empire.

title: Courland annexed by Russia
summary: In the third partition of Poland-Lithuania the Duchy of Courland was incorporated into the Russian Empire, completing Russian rule over all the Latvian lands.

title: The First National Awakening
summary: The Young Latvians led a cultural revival that championed the Latvian language and folklore against Baltic German dominance, creating the basis for a modern Latvian nation.

title: Proclamation of the Republic of Latvia
summary: As the empires collapsed at the end of the First World War, the People's Council of Latvia proclaimed an independent, democratic Republic of Latvia in Riga.

title: Latvian-Soviet Treaty of Riga
summary: Concluding the War of Independence, Soviet Russia signed the Treaty of Riga, in which it voluntarily and irrevocably renounced all sovereign rights over the Latvian people and territory, recognising Latvia's independence.

title: Adoption of the Satversme
summary: Latvia adopted its democratic constitution, the Satversme, in 1922, establishing the institutions of the parliamentary first republic.

title: The Ulmanis coup
summary: Prime Minister Kārlis Ulmanis staged a self-coup, suspending the constitution, dissolving the Saeima and the parties, and establishing an authoritarian regime that lasted until 1940.

title: The Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact
summary: The Nazi-Soviet non-aggression pact and its secret protocol assigned Latvia and the other Baltic states to the Soviet sphere of influence, sealing the country's fate in the coming war.

title: Soviet occupation and annexation
summary: The Red Army occupied Latvia in June 1940; after a staged election a puppet parliament requested incorporation, and the Soviet Union annexed the country in August 1940.

title: The June 1941 deportations
summary: The Soviet regime deported some fifteen thousand people from Latvia to Siberia in a single operation, targeting the country's political, economic and intellectual elite; many never returned.

title: The Rumbula massacre
summary: Under the Nazi occupation, SS units led by Friedrich Jeckeln shot about twenty-five thousand Jews, chiefly from the Riga ghetto, in the Rumbula forest, among the largest single massacres of the Holocaust.

title: The March 1949 deportations
summary: In Operation Priboi the Soviet authorities deported tens of thousands of Latvians to Siberia, many of them farmers resisting collectivisation, in the largest single act of repression of the postwar years.

title: The Baltic Way
summary: On the fiftieth anniversary of the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, about two million people formed a human chain from Tallinn through Riga to Vilnius, demanding the restoration of Baltic independence.

title: Declaration on the Restoration of Independence
summary: The Supreme Council of Latvia adopted the declaration restoring independence, reaffirming the 1918 constitution and declaring the 1940 Soviet occupation illegal.

title: Full restoration of independence
summary: After the collapse of the Moscow coup, the Supreme Council adopted a constitutional law fully restoring the independence of the Republic of Latvia, soon recognised internationally.

title: Accession to NATO and the European Union
summary: Latvia became a member of NATO on 29 March 2004 and of the European Union on 1 May 2004, anchoring the restored state firmly within Western institutions.

title: Latvia-Russia border treaty
summary: The border treaty with Russia entered into force, fixing the frontier and renouncing Latvia's claim to the Abrene district transferred to the Russian SFSR in 1944, while the Constitutional Court reaffirmed state continuity.

title: Kingdom of Mauretania and Volubilis
summary: The Amazigh kingdom of Mauretania emerges in the western Maghreb; Volubilis, founded around the third century BCE, becomes one of its leading cities.

title: Roman annexation of Mauretania
summary: Rome annexes the kingdom of Mauretania and the emperor Claudius organises the western part as the province of Mauretania Tingitana, governed from Tingis (Tangier).

title: Volubilis flourishes as a Roman city
summary: Volubilis reaches its height as a thriving provincial city, adorned with a basilica, triumphal arch, temples and elaborate mosaics before Rome withdraws from the interior.

title: Idris I and the founding of the dynasty
summary: Idris ibn Abdallah, a sharif fleeing Abbasid persecution, wins the allegiance of the Awraba Berbers near Walila and founds the Idrisid dynasty, Morocco's first Muslim state.

title: Idris II founds Fez
summary: Idris II establishes Fez as his capital; it becomes a leading political and religious centre of the western Islamic world.

title: Foundation of the Qarawiyyin
summary: The mosque and centre of learning of al-Qarawiyyin is established in Fez, later regarded as one of the oldest continuously operating institutions of higher education in the world.

title: Almoravids found Marrakesh
summary: The Almoravids establish Marrakesh as the capital of an empire uniting Morocco and the western Sahara under a reformist Islamic banner.

title: Almoravids enter al-Andalus
summary: Yusuf ibn Tashfin leads the Almoravids into Spain, checking the Christian Reconquista and bringing Muslim al-Andalus under Moroccan rule.

title: Almohads capture Marrakesh
summary: The Almohads under Abd al-Mu'min take Marrakesh, supplanting the Almoravids and building an empire across the whole Maghreb and al-Andalus.

title: Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa
summary: A Christian coalition decisively defeats the Almohads in Spain, beginning the dynasty's decline and reopening al-Andalus to the Reconquista.

title: Fall of the Almohads
summary: The Marinids capture Marrakesh, ending Almohad rule and inaugurating a new Berber dynasty centred on Fez.

title: Marinids master Morocco from Fez
summary: Having taken Fez in 1248 and Marrakesh in 1269, the Marinids rule Morocco from Fez, endowing the city with famous madrasas.

title: Battle of the Three Kings
summary: The Saadian sultan Abd al-Malik annihilates the invading Portuguese army of King Sebastian near Ksar el-Kebir; three kings die, and Morocco's independence is preserved.

title: Saadian conquest of Songhai
summary: Ahmad al-Mansur sends an army across the Sahara that defeats the Songhai Empire at Tondibi, extending Saadian reach toward the gold of the Niger.

title: Alaouite dynasty unifies Morocco
summary: Moulay al-Rashid reunites Morocco and establishes the rule of the Alaouite dynasty, which continues to reign today; his successor Moulay Ismail builds a strong centralised state from Meknes.

title: Moroccan-American Treaty of Friendship
summary: Morocco and the United States conclude a treaty of peace and friendship, recognised in 1786, making Morocco one of America's earliest treaty partners.

title: Treaty of Fez establishes the protectorates
summary: Sultan Abd al-Hafid signs the Treaty of Fez, making Morocco a French protectorate; a Spanish zone in the north and south and an international zone at Tangier are settled the same year.

title: Battle of Annual and the Rif War
summary: Abd el-Krim's Riffian fighters destroy a Spanish army at Annual and proclaim a Republic of the Rif; a Franco-Spanish coalition suppresses the rebellion by 1926.

title: Exile of Mohammed V
summary: France deposes and exiles Sultan Mohammed V, an act that inflames the independence movement and unites Moroccans behind the monarchy.

title: Restoration of independence
summary: France ends its protectorate by agreement with Morocco; Spain relinquishes most of its northern zone in April, restoring Moroccan independence under Sultan Mohammed V.

title: Mohammed V becomes king
summary: Mohammed V adopts the title of king, formalising the modern Moroccan monarchy as the country builds its independent institutions.

title: The Green March
summary: King Hassan II leads the Green March, in which about 350,000 unarmed Moroccans enter the Western Sahara to assert Morocco's claim as Spain withdraws; the territory's status remains disputed.

title: Accession of Mohammed VI
summary: Mohammed VI succeeds Hassan II and undertakes gradual reforms, including a revised family law code and major development projects.

title: Constitutional reform
summary: Following Arab Spring protests, a new constitution approved by referendum expands the powers of parliament and the prime minister and recognises Tamazight, while the king retains ultimate authority.

title: Monoikos named by Hecataeus
summary: The Greek geographer Hecataeus of Miletus refers to Monoikos as a Ligurian town, the earliest known mention of the site that would become Monaco; later the Phocaeans of Massalia developed it as a port.

title: The harbour at its height
summary: The port of Monoikos, associated with the cult of Hercules, flourished as part of Mediterranean trade, as shown by coins and goods recovered from the harbour.

title: Portus Herculis Monoeci under Rome
summary: After Rome's conquest of the region the harbour became Portus Herculis Monoeci, a refuge on the route between Italy, Gaul and Hispania used by Roman expeditions.

title: Caesar uses the port
summary: Julius Caesar is recorded as having used the harbour of Monoeci around 50 BCE, a measure of its importance as a Roman anchorage on the Ligurian coast.

title: Genoa fortifies the Rock
summary: Genoese Ghibellines under Fulco del Cassello began building a fortress of four towers on the Rock of Monaco, offering land and tax exemptions to draw settlers to the new stronghold.

title: Grimaldi seizes the Rock
summary: François Grimaldi, called Malizia, took the fortress disguised as a Franciscan monk, beginning the Grimaldi presence in Monaco, an event commemorated by the armed monks of the princely coat of arms.

title: Purchase of Menton
summary: Charles I Grimaldi, regarded as the founder of the principality, enlarged the Grimaldi domain by purchasing the lordship of Menton, which remained Monégasque until 1861.

title: Purchase of Roquebrune
summary: The Grimaldi added the lordship of Roquebrune to their possessions, completing the territory that, with Monaco and Menton, would define the principality for five centuries.

title: Honoré II takes the title of Prince
summary: Honoré II became the first Grimaldi to call himself Prince and Lord of Monaco, marking the principality's emergence as a sovereign state out of the medieval lordship.

title: Treaty of Péronne
summary: Honoré II and Louis XIII signed the Treaty of Péronne, shifting Monaco from Spanish to French protection while recognising the principality's independence and the prince's sovereignty.

title: French titles for the Grimaldi
summary: Under the Péronne settlement the prince of Monaco received French titles and estates, including the duchy of Valentinois, binding the dynasty to the French crown.

title: The fortress becomes a palace
summary: Honoré I and Honoré II employed leading architects to transform the Genoese fortress into a princely residence, creating one of the most remarkable palaces of the seventeenth century.

title: Revolutionary France annexes Monaco
summary: Revolutionary France abolished the Grimaldi sovereignty and annexed the principality, expelling the dynasty and scattering the palace's art collections.

title: Menton and Roquebrune secede
summary: Amid the revolutions of 1848, Menton and Roquebrune declared themselves free towns, banished the prince and sought union with Sardinia, which then occupied them.

title: Cession of Menton and Roquebrune
summary: By the Franco-Monégasque Treaty, Prince Charles III ceded Menton and Roquebrune to France for four million francs; France recognised Monaco's sovereignty over its remaining territory.

title: Founding of the Société des Bains de Mer
summary: Charles III established the Société des Bains de Mer to develop a casino quarter, leasing the gambling monopoly to François Blanc, who had previously enriched the spa of Homburg.

title: Monte-Carlo named
summary: Prince Charles III decreed that the new casino district be called Monte-Carlo in his honour; its gambling revenues rebuilt Monaco's finances and let the principality abolish direct taxation in 1869.

title: Monaco's first constitution
summary: Prince Albert I granted Monaco a constitution on 5 January 1911, ending absolute princely rule and beginning the principality's evolution into a constitutional state.

title: Franco-Monégasque Treaty of 1918
summary: Signed amid a succession crisis, the treaty aligned Monaco's policy with French interests and provided that the principality would fall under French protection should the Grimaldi line end; it was noted in the 1919 Treaty of Versailles.

title: Rainier III marries Grace Kelly
summary: Prince Rainier III married the American actress Grace Kelly, who became Princess Grace; their union brought the principality international glamour and helped drive its post-war revival.

title: The 1962 constitution
summary: Rainier III promulgated a new constitution that reduced the sovereign's powers, abolished capital punishment and granted women the right to vote.

title: Monaco joins the United Nations
summary: Monaco was admitted as the 183rd member state of the United Nations, an unambiguous international recognition of its full sovereignty.

title: Treaty of 2002 guarantees independence
summary: A new Franco-Monégasque treaty, with the revised constitution and succession law, ended the clause returning Monaco to France if the Grimaldi line failed, guaranteeing the principality's continued independence.

title: Founding of the Principality of Moldavia
