summary: Vlach migrants from Maramures established a principality east of the Carpathians; its independence is traditionally attributed to the voivode Bogdan I, making Moldavia the second Romanian principality.

title: Reign of Stephen the Great
summary: Stephen IV ruled Moldavia for nearly half a century, winning European renown for resisting the Ottomans while defending the principality against Hungary and Poland and endowing many churches and monasteries.

title: Battle of Vaslui
summary: Stephen the Great destroyed a much larger Ottoman army at Vaslui, a victory celebrated across Christian Europe that briefly halted the Turkish advance into Moldavia.

title: Defeat at Valea Alba
summary: An Ottoman counter-offensive under Sultan Mehmed II defeated Stephen at Valea Alba; though he survived and recovered, the campaign exposed the mounting pressure on the small principality.

title: Moldavia becomes an Ottoman tributary
summary: Following the death of Stephen the Great, Moldavia was reduced to a tributary vassal of the Ottoman Empire, keeping its princes, church and laws but paying tribute and following the sultan's lead in foreign affairs.

title: Beginning of Phanariot rule
summary: After Prince Dimitrie Cantemir's failed alliance with Russia, the Porte ended native rule and began appointing Greek princes from the Phanar district of Constantinople, who governed until 1821.

title: Partition of Moldavia at the Treaty of Bucharest
summary: The Treaty of Bucharest ending the Russo-Turkish War allowed Russia to annex Bessarabia, the eastern half of the principality between the Prut and the Dniester, splitting Moldavia in two.

title: Annexation of Bessarabia
summary: By the Treaty of Bucharest, Russia annexed the land between the Prut and the Dniester from the Ottoman Empire, organizing it as the province of Bessarabia and severing it from the rest of Moldavia.

title: Curtailment of Bessarabian autonomy
summary: After an initial period of limited self-government, Russia integrated Bessarabia into the imperial administration, beginning a policy of Russification that made Russian the language of government and schooling.

title: Southern Bessarabia briefly returned
summary: The Treaty of Paris ending the Crimean War returned the southern strip of Bessarabia to Moldavia; Russia recovered it in 1878 at the Congress of Berlin, underlining the province's status as a contested borderland.

title: Kishinev pogrom
summary: A violent anti-Jewish pogrom in the provincial capital Kishinev (Chisinau) drew international condemnation and became a notorious symbol of the persecution of Jews in the late Russian Empire.

title: Moldavian Democratic Republic proclaimed
summary: After the Russian Revolution, the Sfatul Tarii (national council) in Chisinau proclaimed the Moldavian Democratic Republic, soon declaring full independence from Russia amid the turmoil of 1917-1918.

title: Union of Bessarabia with Romania
summary: The Sfatul Tarii voted to unite Bessarabia with Romania (27 March, Old Style; 9 April, New Style); the union, at first conditional on autonomy, was made unconditional in November 1918.

title: Creation of the Moldavian ASSR
summary: Refusing to recognize the loss of Bessarabia, the Soviet Union established the Moldavian Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic on the east bank of the Dniester within Soviet Ukraine, as a standing claim to the territory across the river.

title: International recognition of the union
summary: A treaty signed in Paris by Romania, Britain, France, Italy and Japan recognized the union of Bessarabia with Romania, though the Soviet Union never accepted it.

title: Soviet annexation of Bessarabia
summary: Acting on the secret protocol of the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, the Red Army occupied Bessarabia after an ultimatum to Romania, ending more than two decades of Romanian rule.

title: Creation of the Moldavian SSR
summary: The Soviet Union proclaimed the Moldavian Soviet Socialist Republic, joining most of annexed Bessarabia to the Moldavian ASSR east of the Dniester, with the new republic's borders deliberately reshaped.

title: The man-made famine
summary: A famine aggravated by harsh Soviet grain requisitioning swept Moldavia in 1946-1947, killing well over a hundred thousand people in one of the least-known episodes of Stalinist terror.

title: Operation South deportations
summary: On the night of 5-6 July 1949 Soviet authorities deported tens of thousands of Moldavians condemned as kulaks to Siberia and Kazakhstan, accelerating the forced collectivization of agriculture.

title: Declaration of Independence
summary: Moldova's parliament declared independence from the Soviet Union on 27 August 1991, in the wake of the failed Moscow coup, with Mircea Snegur as the new state's first president.

title: The Transnistria war and ceasefire
summary: War with the Russian-backed Transnistrian separatists peaked in the battle for Bender; the intervention of the Russian 14th Army proved decisive, and a ceasefire on 21 July 1992 froze the conflict, leaving Russian troops in place.

title: OSCE Mission to Moldova
summary: The OSCE established its Mission to Moldova to facilitate a comprehensive settlement consolidating Moldova's sovereignty and territorial integrity with a special status for Transnistria, later working through the 5+2 format.

title: Autonomy for Gagauzia
summary: A Moldovan law granted broad self-government to the Turkic-speaking Gagauz of the south, creating the autonomous territorial unit of Gagauzia and peacefully resolving their bid for separation.

title: UN resolution on foreign forces
summary: The UN General Assembly adopted resolution 72/282 by 64 votes to 15, urging Russia to complete the unconditional withdrawal of its Operational Group of Forces from Moldova, in line with the 1999 OSCE Istanbul commitments.

title: EU candidate status
summary: After applying for membership on 3 March 2022, Moldova was granted European Union candidate status by the European Council on 23 June 2022, opening accession negotiations in 2024.

title: Austronesian settlement of Madagascar
summary: Seafarers from the Borneo region cross the Indian Ocean and become the island's first lasting inhabitants.

title: Bantu African arrivals
summary: Migrants from the East African mainland mix with Austronesian settlers, forming the Malagasy people and language.

title: Swahili and Arab trade contacts
summary: Muslim Swahili traders (the Antalaotra) settle the northwest coast, linking Madagascar to Indian Ocean commerce.

title: Bantu and Tamil arrivals deepen the mix
summary: Bantu-speaking migrants from southeast Africa arrive in numbers alongside Tamil merchants from southern India, drawing the island's population from three continents.

title: Rise of the Sakalava kingdom
summary: The Maroseraña dynasty builds the island's largest realm on the west coast, later dividing into Menabe and Boina.

title: Île Sainte-Marie pirate haven
summary: The northeastern island becomes a major base on the pirate 'Round'; legend later names it the site of Libertalia.

title: Ratsimilaho unites the Betsimisaraka
summary: Ratsimilaho forges the eastern peoples into the Betsimisaraka confederation, becoming a dominant king by 1730.

title: Portuguese and French trading posts
summary: European powers establish coastal posts but never hold ground inland; the island's kingdoms keep the terms of trade.

title: Andrianampoinimerina unifies Imerina
summary: From Ambohimanga and Antananarivo, the king ends civil war and begins the conquest of much of the island.

title: Radama I, Britain and the missionaries
summary: Radama I is recognised King of Madagascar by Britain and admits the London Missionary Society, bringing literacy and Christianity.

title: The London Missionary Society arrives
summary: LMS missionaries open schools, render Malagasy in the Latin alphabet and translate the Bible — literacy arrives with a creed attached.

title: Ranavalona I bans Christianity
summary: Fearing foreign influence, the queen proscribes Christian practice; persecution and executions follow over decades.

title: Treaty of peace, friendship and commerce with the United States
summary: Following a commercial convention in 1867, Washington concludes a full treaty with the Kingdom of Madagascar — a sovereign state in the diplomatic record fifteen years before annexation.

title: First Franco-Hova War
summary: France invades and takes Antsiranana (Diego Suarez), the deep northern harbour it had wanted for a generation.

title: Britain accepts a French protectorate
summary: London concedes the imposition of a protectorate over the island; the government in Antananarivo, never consulted, refuses to accept it.

title: French capture Antananarivo
summary: Franco-Hova war ends with the fall of the capital; Madagascar is forced into a French protectorate.

title: Monarchy abolished, Ranavalona III exiled
summary: France ends the Merina monarchy and exiles the last queen, ultimately to Algiers, where she dies in 1917.

title: The 'pacification' campaign
summary: The formal declaration of a colony opens fifteen years of French military operations against a resistance that never conceded the point.

title: The Battle of Madagascar
summary: British forces invade the Vichy-administered island to deny its harbours to the Japanese navy; the colonial administration's prestige does not recover.

title: Madagascar becomes a French overseas territory
summary: Reorganisation gives Malagasy deputies representation in Paris; its failure to deliver independence sends nationalists to arms the following year.

title: The Malagasy Uprising
summary: A nationalist insurrection from March 1947 is suppressed with great loss of life; estimates range up to roughly 90,000 dead.

title: Independence from France
summary: Madagascar becomes a sovereign republic; Philibert Tsiranana is its first president.

title: The rotaka topples Tsiranana
summary: Economic stagnation triggers mass protests; the first president hands power to a military council, ending the First Republic.

title: Ratsiraka and the socialist republic
summary: Didier Ratsiraka takes power, founds the Democratic Republic and nationalises the economy under the 'Red Book'.

title: Ravalomanana and the 2002 crisis
summary: A disputed election triggers months of confrontation; Marc Ravalomanana takes power and Ratsiraka flees.

title: The 2009 coup
summary: Andry Rajoelina ousts Ravalomanana with military backing, in a transfer widely condemned as unconstitutional.

title: The Third Republic constitution
summary: Democratic reforms end the socialist republic and usher in a new constitution and multiparty politics.

title: Rainforests of the Atsinanana inscribed
summary: Six eastern national parks — home to species found nowhere else after 60 million years of isolation — join the World Heritage List.

title: The rainforests are listed in Danger
summary: Three years after inscription, illegal logging and lemur hunting put the Atsinanana on the List of World Heritage in Danger.

title: Drought and famine in the Grand Sud
summary: The worst drought in four decades leaves over 1.14 million people food insecure and some 14,000 in IPC Phase 5 — catastrophe — in the island's far south.

title: Rajoelina wins a third term
summary: An election boycotted by ten rivals, preceded by six weeks of protest, returns Rajoelina on the lowest turnout in the country's history.

title: Olmec civilisation flourishes
summary: The Olmec arise on the Gulf coast as the first complex society of Mesoamerica, carving colossal stone heads and shaping a cultural template inherited by later peoples.

title: Teotihuacan, city of the gods
summary: Teotihuacan grows into a metropolis of monumental pyramids and a planned ceremonial axis, dominating central Mexico before its decline around 550-650 CE.

title: Classic Maya civilisation
summary: Maya city-states reach their height, producing hieroglyphic writing, advanced calendars, and astronomy, before the southern lowland centres are abandoned by about 900 CE.

title: Founding of Tenochtitlan
summary: The Mexica establish their capital on an island in Lake Texcoco, the site of present-day Mexico City.

title: The Triple Alliance
summary: Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, and Tlacopan ally, inaugurating the tribute empire of the Aztecs across central Mexico.

title: Reign of Moctezuma II
summary: Moctezuma II ascends as huey tlatoani, ruling the empire at its territorial peak until the Spanish arrival.

title: Cortes lands in Mexico
summary: Hernan Cortes arrives on the Gulf coast and marches inland, allying with peoples opposed to Mexica rule.

title: Fall of Tenochtitlan
summary: After a siege of some three months, the city falls to Cortes and his indigenous allies, ending the Aztec empire.

title: Viceroyalty of New Spain established
summary: Spain formalises colonial government under a viceroy, with Mexico City as the capital of a vast realm.

title: Grito de Dolores
summary: Miguel Hidalgo calls for rebellion against Spanish rule, beginning the Mexican War of Independence.

title: Independence consummated
summary: The Army of the Three Guarantees enters Mexico City following the Treaty of Cordoba, ending Spanish rule.

title: First federal republic
summary: The Constitution of 1824 founds the United Mexican States as a federal republic, with Guadalupe Victoria as first president.

title: Mexican-American War
summary: Defeat by the United States costs Mexico roughly half its territory under the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo.

title: Constitution of the Reform
summary: The liberal Constitution of 1857 limits church and army privileges and establishes a bill of rights, deepening conflict between liberals and conservatives.

title: Fall of the Second Empire
summary: Mexican forces under Juarez defeat the French intervention; Emperor Maximilian is captured and executed, restoring the republic.

title: The Porfiriato
summary: Porfirio Diaz rules Mexico for over three decades, modernising the economy while entrenching authoritarian government and land inequality.

title: Mexican Revolution
summary: A decade of revolution and civil war overthrows Diaz, costs over a million lives, and produces the Constitution of 1917.

title: Oil nationalisation
summary: President Lazaro Cardenas nationalises the petroleum industry, creating Pemex and asserting economic sovereignty.

title: NAFTA and the Zapatista uprising
summary: The North American Free Trade Agreement takes effect as the Zapatistas rise in Chiapas; a peso crisis follows that December.

title: End of one-party rule
summary: Vicente Fox's election ends 71 years of uninterrupted PRI government, marking Mexico's democratic alternation of power.

title: Reign of Philip II of Macedon
summary: Philip II reformed the Macedonian army and won mastery over the Greek city-states at Chaeronea, laying the foundations for the empire his son Alexander the Great would build across Asia.

title: Conquests of Alexander the Great
summary: Alexander III led Macedonian and Greek forces in the conquest of the Persian empire, carrying Hellenistic civilization from Egypt to the Indus before his death at Babylon in 323 BCE.

title: Macedonia becomes a Roman province
summary: After Rome defeated the last Macedonian claimant near Pydna, Macedonia was organised as a Roman province, beginning centuries of Roman and later Byzantine rule over the region.

title: Destruction of Scupi
summary: A devastating earthquake destroyed the Roman city of Scupi near present-day Skopje, an event marking the late-antique decline of the region's classical urban life on the eve of Slavic settlement.

title: Slavic settlement of the region
summary: Slavic tribes migrated into the Macedonian interior from the sixth century, transforming the population of the region and laying the basis for its later Slavic-speaking identity.

title: The Ohrid literary school of Clement and Naum
summary: Saint Clement of Ohrid, with Saint Naum, founded a Slavonic literary school at Ohrid, spreading the Slavic script and Christian learning and making the city a cradle of medieval Slavic culture.

title: Tsar Samuel's state centred on Ohrid
summary: Samuel built a powerful western Bulgarian state with its capital and a patriarchate at Ohrid, resisting Byzantine expansion for decades until his defeat by the emperor Basil II.

title: Battle of Kleidion and the fall of Samuel
summary: The Byzantine emperor Basil II destroyed Samuel's army at Kleidion; the tsar died shortly afterwards, and by 1018 the region was fully reabsorbed into the Byzantine Empire.

title: The Archbishopric of Ohrid
summary: After the Byzantine reconquest an autocephalous archbishopric was established at Ohrid, sustaining the city's role as a centre of Orthodox church life and Slavonic learning.

title: Ottoman conquest of the region
summary: Ottoman forces conquered Macedonia in the late fourteenth century, beginning roughly five centuries of Ottoman rule during which the region's name lapsed as an administrative term.

title: Founding of IMRO
summary: The Internal Macedonian Revolutionary Organization was founded at Salonika to work for an autonomous Macedonia, its early leaders combining a Macedonian regional with a Bulgarian national identity.

title: The Ilinden Uprising
summary: On St Elijah's Day IMRO launched the Ilinden Uprising against Ottoman rule; though quickly crushed amid severe reprisals, it became a founding event of Macedonian national identity.

title: The Kruševo Republic
summary: During the uprising the insurgents proclaimed a short-lived republic in the town of Kruševo, which the Ottoman army overran after about ten days.

title: The Balkan Wars and the partition of Macedonia
summary: The Balkan Wars ended Ottoman rule and divided historic Macedonia among Greece, Serbia and Bulgaria; the northern Vardar region passed to Serbia, becoming the core of the future republic.

title: Vardar Macedonia within Yugoslavia
summary: After the First World War the Vardar region was incorporated into the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (later Yugoslavia), where it was administered as part of Serbia and its Slavic identity discouraged.

title: Proclamation of a Macedonian state (ASNOM)
summary: The Anti-Fascist Assembly for the National Liberation of Macedonia met on St Elijah's Day 1944 and proclaimed a Macedonian state within a future Yugoslav federation.

title: Socialist Republic of Macedonia and the codified language
summary: A People's (later Socialist) Republic of Macedonia was constituted as one of Yugoslavia's six republics, and a standard Macedonian literary language was codified for the first time.

title: The Skopje earthquake
summary: A powerful earthquake devastated Skopje, killing more than a thousand people; the city was rebuilt with international aid as the modern capital of the republic.

title: Independence referendum
summary: Citizens voted by some 96 percent for independence, and the republic seceded peacefully from Yugoslavia under President Kiro Gligorov, alone among the Yugoslav republics in avoiding war.

title: UN admission as 'FYROM'
summary: Owing to Greece's objection over the name, the country was admitted to the United Nations under the provisional designation 'the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia'.

title: The Interim Accord with Greece
summary: Greece and the country signed an Interim Accord under which Greece agreed not to object to its membership of international bodies referred to by the provisional name.

title: ICJ rules against Greece
summary: The International Court of Justice held that Greece had breached the Interim Accord by objecting to the country's admission to NATO at the 2008 Bucharest summit.

title: The Prespa Agreement
summary: Greece and the country signed the Prespa Agreement, renaming it the Republic of North Macedonia (used erga omnes), terminating the 1995 accord and distinguishing the modern Slavic state from ancient Macedon.

title: The Ohrid Framework Agreement
summary: The agreement ended the 2001 ethnic Albanian insurgency, rejecting territorial partition and granting the Albanian minority greater rights through decentralisation, equitable representation, language rights and double-majority voting.

title: EU candidate status
summary: Having applied for membership in 2004, the country was granted European Union candidate status in December 2005, opening a long road toward accession.

title: North Macedonia joins NATO
summary: After the Prespa Agreement lifted Greece's objection, North Macedonia deposited its instrument of accession and became NATO's thirtieth member on 27 March 2020.

title: Bulgaria blocks EU accession talks
summary: Bulgaria vetoed the opening of EU accession negotiations over disputes about history, language and identity, including claims that Macedonian derives from Bulgarian.

title: EU accession negotiations open
summary: Following a French-brokered compromise, North Macedonia formally opened European Union accession negotiations, though Bulgaria's conditions continued to complicate the process.

title: Ibn Hawqal records Ghana's wealth
summary: The Arab geographer Ibn Hawqal, visiting the western Sudan, describes Ghana's ruler as among the richest kings in the world on account of his gold.

title: Apogee of the gold-and-salt trade
summary: Ghana controls a broad swathe of the western Sahel, acting as the broker between southern goldfields and North African salt caravans.

title: Almoravids take Kumbi Saleh
summary: Berber Almoravids from present-day Mauritania capture Ghana's chief city, weakening the empire and the trade routes it controlled.

title: Battle of Kirina and the founding of Mali
summary: Sundiata Keita defeats Sumanguru Kanté of the Soso, unifying the Malinke and establishing the Mali Empire with its capital at Niani.

title: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca
summary: Mansa Musa journeys to Mecca with a vast retinue and quantities of gold so great his almsgiving is said to have disrupted Egypt's gold prices, spreading Mali's fame abroad.

title: Timbuktu and Djenné flourish
summary: Under Mali's mansas the Niger cities grow into major centres of trans-Saharan trade and Islamic scholarship, attracting merchants and scholars.

title: Sonni Ali takes Timbuktu
summary: Sonni Ali captures Timbuktu, and in 1473 Djenné, bringing the Niger trade cities under Songhai control and laying the foundation of the empire.

title: Askia Muhammad founds the Askiya dynasty
summary: A former general seizes power as Askia Muhammad, reorganising the empire and ushering in the golden age of Timbuktu's scholarship.

title: Battle of Tondibi ends the Songhai Empire
summary: Moroccan forces under Judar Pasha, armed with firearms, rout the Songhai army at Tondibi near Gao, collapsing the last of the great Niger empires.

title: Bitòn Coulibaly consolidates the Bambara kingdom of Segou
summary: Mamari (Bitòn) Coulibaly transforms a youth society into an army, founding the centralised Bambara state of Segou on the middle Niger.

title: Umar Tal's Tukulor empire conquers Segou
summary: Al-Hajj Umar Tal, leading the Tijaniyya jihad begun in the 1850s, overthrows the Bambara kingdom of Segou and extends the Tukulor empire across the upper Niger.

title: Death of Umar Tal
summary: The Tukulor leader dies in 1864 near Hamdallahi amid revolt; his successors face mounting French pressure.

title: Capture of Samori Touré
summary: French forces seize Samori Touré, founder of the Wassoulou Empire and Mali's last great armed resister, ending nearly two decades of war.

title: Colony of French Soudan
summary: The conquered upper Niger is administered as French Soudan within French West Africa, its economy reoriented toward the colonial metropole.

title: The Mali Federation with Senegal
summary: French Soudan and Senegal join in the short-lived Mali Federation, with Modibo Keïta as a leading figure; it dissolves in August 1960.

title: Independence of the Republic of Mali
summary: The former French Soudan becomes the independent Republic of Mali; Modibo Keïta becomes its first president the following day.

title: Military coup ousts Modibo Keïta
summary: Lieutenant Moussa Traoré leads a coup against the socialist one-party government, beginning 23 years of his rule.

title: Fall of Moussa Traoré and democratic transition
summary: After a deadly crackdown on protesters on 22 March, officers led by Amadou Toumani Touré oust Traoré; a transition leads to multiparty rule under Alpha Oumar Konaré in 1992.

title: Tuareg rebellion, coup and jihadist seizure of the north
summary: The MNLA's January rebellion and a 22 March coup precipitate collapse; AQIM, Ansar Dine and allied jihadists take Timbuktu, Gao and Kidal.

title: France launches Operation Serval
summary: As jihadist forces drive toward Bamako, France intervenes militarily, stopping the advance and recapturing the northern cities.

title: Coup ousts President Ibrahim Boubacar Keïta
summary: Amid mass protests and a worsening insurgency, military officers arrest President Keïta, who resigns; a transitional government is formed.

title: Second coup brings Assimi Goïta to power
summary: Colonel Assimi Goïta removes the transitional civilian president and prime minister and takes the presidency himself.

title: The temples of Ggantija raised on Gozo
summary: The two megalithic temples of Ggantija were built on Gozo, the South Temple around 3600 BCE, ranking among the oldest free-standing monumental buildings in the world.

title: The Maltese temple culture flourishes
summary: A Neolithic society raised the temples of Hagar Qim, Mnajdra, Tarxien, Skorba and Ta' Hagrat in successive phases, creating monumental architecture without the use of metal tools.

title: The Hal Saflieni Hypogeum
summary: A vast underground necropolis was cut on three levels into the limestone, holding the remains of about 7,000 people and the famous Sleeping Lady figurine.

title: The temple builders disappear
summary: Around 2500 BCE the temple-building culture came to an end for reasons still debated, and a new Bronze Age population succeeded the people who had raised the great monuments.

title: Carthaginian Malta
summary: Following earlier Phoenician use of the islands as a trading station, the Carthaginians were firmly established in Malta by the sixth century BCE, leaving coins, inscriptions and Punic rock tombs.

title: Malta becomes Roman
summary: During the Second Punic War Malta passed under Roman control and was attached to the praetorship of Sicily, beginning some seven centuries of Roman and then Byzantine rule.

title: The shipwreck of the Apostle Paul
summary: Christian tradition, drawing on the Acts of the Apostles, holds that Paul was shipwrecked on Malta around 60 CE, welcomed by the islanders and the leading man Publius, and stayed three months, beginning the islands' conversion.

title: Roman municipium
summary: Under Rome the Maltese were allowed to coin money, send delegations to Rome and manage their own affairs, and the islands were granted the status of a Roman municipium.

title: Arab conquest of Malta
summary: An Arab force seized Malta from the Byzantine Empire, beginning a period of more than two centuries that would shape the islands' language and culture.

title: Birth of the Maltese language
summary: The Arabic of the islands' settlers evolved into Maltese, a Semitic language that is unique in being written in the Latin alphabet and that survives as the national language today.

title: Norman conquest by Roger I
summary: Count Roger I of Sicily took Malta from the Arabs in 1091, attaching the islands to the Kingdom of Sicily and beginning their return to Latin Christendom.

title: Rule under Sicily and Aragon
summary: As part of the Kingdom of Sicily, Malta passed through Norman, Swabian, Angevin and Aragonese hands, governed by feudal lords and a local council, until 1530.

title: Charles V grants Malta to the Knights
summary: Eight years after losing Rhodes to the Ottomans, the Order of St John received Malta from the Emperor Charles V, who held Sicily, in return for a token annual tribute, and made the islands their new sovereign base.

title: The Great Siege of Malta
summary: An Ottoman army sent by Suleiman the Magnificent besieged the Knights and Maltese for nearly four months; under Grand Master Jean Parisot de la Valette the defenders held out until a Sicilian relief force compelled the Ottomans to withdraw.

title: Founding of Valletta
summary: In the year after the siege the Knights began building a new fortified capital on Mount Sciberras, named Valletta after the Grand Master and conceived as a planned Renaissance fortress-city; it became the capital in 1570.

title: Two and a half centuries of the Order
summary: From their new capital the Knights ruled Malta as a sovereign order-state, building auberges, hospitals and the conventual church of St John and shaping a baroque culture until their fall in 1798.

title: Napoleon seizes Malta
summary: On his way to Egypt, Napoleon Bonaparte captured Malta from the Knights of St John, whose rule collapsed almost without a fight, ending two and a half centuries of the Order's sovereignty.

title: Maltese uprising and French surrender
summary: French seizures of church property triggered a Maltese revolt; with British and Sicilian naval support the insurgents blockaded the French garrison in Valletta until it surrendered in 1800.

title: British rule confirmed by the Treaty of Paris
summary: Having acknowledged British sovereignty, the Maltese saw the islands' attachment to Britain confirmed by the Treaty of Paris in 1814, making Malta a Crown colony.

title: Malta as a naval fortress
summary: British development of the Grand Harbour dockyard made Malta one of the chief bases of the Royal Navy and the strategic centre of British power in the Mediterranean.

title: The siege of Malta
summary: From 1940 Malta, lying between Sicily and Axis North Africa, was subjected to relentless Italian and German bombing and a near-starvation blockade while its forces struck at Axis supply convoys.

title: Malta awarded the George Cross
summary: King George VI awarded the George Cross to the whole island of Malta to honour its heroism and endurance under siege, the only time the decoration has been given to an entire population.

title: Independence
summary: Malta became an independent sovereign state within the Commonwealth on 21 September 1964, ending more than a century and a half of British colonial rule.

title: Malta becomes a republic
summary: Constitutional amendments made Malta a republic on 13 December 1974, replacing the British monarch with a Maltese president as head of state.

title: Accession to the European Union
summary: Malta joined the European Union on 1 May 2004 in its largest enlargement and adopted the euro on 1 January 2008, completing its integration into Europe.

title: Rise of the Pyu city-states
summary: Tibeto-Burman Pyu peoples establish walled, moated cities such as Beikthano, Halin and Sri Ksetra in the Irrawaddy basin, founding the region's first urban civilization.

title: Buddhism takes root
summary: The Pyu cities provide the earliest evidence of Buddhism's introduction into Southeast Asia, embedding the religion in the region's culture and statecraft.

title: Decline of the Pyu
summary: Raids from the Nanzhao kingdom and the southward migration of the Burman people erode Pyu power, clearing the way for the rise of Bagan.

title: Founding of Bagan
summary: The city of Bagan is traditionally established on a bend of the Irrawaddy, later to become the seat of the first Burmese kingdom.

title: Reign of Anawrahta
summary: Anawrahta unifies the Burman north and the Mon south into the first Burmese kingdom and adopts Theravada Buddhism as the state religion.

title: Conquest of Thaton
summary: Anawrahta captures the Mon city of Thaton, by tradition bringing Buddhist scriptures, monks and artisans that enrich Pagan's culture.

title: Mongol invasion and collapse
summary: Armies of Kublai Khan's Mongol empire invade and shatter the kingdom; a further incursion in 1297 ends Bagan as a unifying power.

title: Reign of Bayinnaung
summary: Bayinnaung of the Toungoo dynasty reunifies Myanmar and conquers the Shan states and Siam, building the most powerful empire in mainland Southeast Asia.

title: Alaungpaya founds the Konbaung dynasty
summary: The village chief Alaungpaya leads a revolt against Mon overlords and establishes the Konbaung dynasty, the last royal house of Burma.

title: Reconquest of Lower Burma
summary: Alaungpaya's forces capture Pegu and subdue the Mon south, reuniting the country under Konbaung rule.

title: Annexation of Arakan
summary: Konbaung expansion absorbs the kingdom of Arakan on the western coast, bringing the Burmese frontier up against British-held Bengal.

title: First Anglo-Burmese War
summary: War over the Arakan and Assam frontiers ends with the Treaty of Yandabo (1826), forcing Burma to cede Arakan and Tenasserim to Britain.

title: Second Anglo-Burmese War
summary: British forces annex Lower Burma, including the Irrawaddy delta and the province renamed Pegu, tightening control of the coastline.

title: Third Anglo-Burmese War and the end of the monarchy
summary: Britain takes Mandalay, exiles King Thibaw, and annexes Upper Burma on 1 January 1886, abolishing the Burmese monarchy and completing the conquest.

title: Burma separated from British India
summary: Burma is made a distinct crown colony with limited self-government, administered separately from the Indian Empire.

title: Assassination of Aung San
summary: Aung San, who had negotiated independence with Britain, is assassinated with most of his cabinet months before the transfer of power.

title: Independence of the Union of Burma
summary: Burma becomes a fully independent republic outside the Commonwealth under Prime Minister U Nu, soon facing communist and ethnic insurgencies.

title: Ne Win's coup
summary: General Ne Win overthrows the elected government, imprisons U Nu, and inaugurates decades of military rule under the Burmese Way to Socialism.

title: The 8888 uprising
summary: A nationwide pro-democracy uprising is crushed by the military, which forms a new junta; Aung San Suu Kyi emerges as the democracy movement's leader.

title: Annulled NLD election victory
summary: Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy wins elections in a landslide, but the junta ignores the result and detains her for years.

title: The Saffron Revolution
summary: Buddhist monks lead mass protests against the regime that are violently suppressed, drawing renewed international condemnation.

title: Reforms under Thein Sein
summary: A quasi-civilian government begins political and economic liberalization, releasing prisoners, easing censorship, and restoring Aung San Suu Kyi's freedoms.

title: NLD wins free elections
summary: Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy wins Myanmar's first fairly contested elections; she becomes state counsellor in a government sharing power with the army.

title: Rohingya crisis in Rakhine State
summary: Military 'clearance operations' drive more than 700,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh; a UN fact-finding mission later finds evidence of genocidal violence.

title: Military coup
summary: The army seizes power, detains Aung San Suu Kyi and the elected leadership, and installs a junta under Min Aung Hlaing, triggering mass protests and civil war.

title: Duklja wins independence from Byzantium
summary: Stefan Vojislav led a revolt that freed the principality of Duklja from Byzantine control and established the Vojislavljevic dynasty, the first medieval state on the territory of Montenegro.

title: Mihailo crowned king of Duklja
summary: Mihailo of Duklja became the first ruler of the region to bear the royal title, the crown bestowed on him by Pope Gregory VII, marking Duklja's standing among Christian states.

title: Principality of Zeta under the Balsic
summary: After the fall of the Serbian Empire an independent Zeta emerged, ruled by the House of Balsic and then from 1431 by the House of Crnojevic, under whom the name Montenegro came into use.

title: The Oktoih and the Crnojevic printing press
summary: Djurdje Crnojevic founded the first South Slavic printing house at Cetinje, which produced the Oktoih, the first Cyrillic book printed in southeastern Europe, before closing around 1496 amid the Ottoman advance.

title: Rise of the theocratic Prince-Bishopric
summary: Authority over the free Montenegrin highlands passed to the Orthodox bishops of Cetinje, who combined spiritual and temporal power as vladikas in a theocratic state that renounced Ottoman overlordship.

title: Petrovic-Njegos dynasty established
summary: Metropolitan Danilo Petrovic-Njegos secured the right to name his successor, founding the hereditary Petrovic-Njegos line of prince-bishops that ruled Montenegro until 1918, the title passing from uncle to nephew.

title: Rule of Petar II Petrovic-Njegos
summary: The poet-prince Petar II strengthened the state, founded schools and reformed taxation, and wrote The Mountain Wreath, becoming Montenegro's most celebrated cultural figure.

title: Publication of The Mountain Wreath
summary: Njegos published Gorski vijenac (The Mountain Wreath), a dramatic epic in verse set in eighteenth-century Montenegro that became a defining work of the national literature.

title: Montenegro becomes a secular principality
summary: Danilo renounced the office of prince-bishop, married and proclaimed himself prince, ending the theocracy; his 1855 code gave the principality its first modern legal framework.

title: Independence recognised at the Congress of Berlin
summary: The Treaty of Berlin recognised Montenegro's independence under Article XXVI, ending Ottoman suzerainty, and under Article XXIX enlarged the state and granted it the port of Antivari (Bar).

title: First Montenegrin constitution
summary: Prince Nikola I granted Montenegro its first constitution, establishing an assembly and modern institutions as the principality consolidated its recognised statehood.

title: Montenegro proclaimed a kingdom
summary: On the fiftieth anniversary of his reign, Prince Nikola I proclaimed Montenegro a kingdom and assumed the title of king, the last monarchy created in the Balkans.

title: The Balkan Wars
summary: Montenegro joined Serbia, Bulgaria and Greece in the First Balkan War against the Ottoman Empire and besieged Scutari, but was forced by the Great Powers to give up the captured city.

title: Battle of Mojkovac and Austro-Hungarian occupation
summary: The Montenegrin army won the Battle of Mojkovac (7-8 January 1916) to cover the Serbian retreat, but the kingdom was overrun and occupied by Austria-Hungary, and King Nikola I fled into exile.

title: The Podgorica Assembly
summary: An assembly in Podgorica deposed King Nikola I and the Petrovic-Njegos dynasty and proclaimed the unconditional union of Montenegro with Serbia in the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.

title: The Christmas Uprising and the Greens-Whites split
summary: Pro-independence 'Greens' rose against the union proclaimed at Podgorica but were defeated by the unionist 'Whites', a schism over Montenegro's statehood that endured for generations.

title: Socialist Republic of Montenegro
summary: After wartime occupation and partisan resistance, Montenegro became one of the six federal republics of socialist Yugoslavia, with its capital at Titograd, today's Podgorica.

title: Federal Republic of Yugoslavia
summary: As the other republics broke away, Montenegro joined Serbia in forming the rump Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, remaining bound to Belgrade through the wars and sanctions of the 1990s.

title: Unilateral adoption of the euro
summary: Montenegro made the euro its sole legal tender from March 2002, a unilateral euroisation undertaken without European Central Bank agreement that distanced its economy from Serbia's.

title: State Union of Serbia and Montenegro
summary: European mediation transformed the federation into the loose State Union of Serbia and Montenegro, whose Constitutional Charter allowed either republic to hold an independence referendum after three years.

title: Independence referendum
summary: On a turnout above 86 percent, 55.5 percent of voters chose independence, narrowly passing the EU-set 55 percent threshold; the OSCE/ODIHR found the vote met international standards.

title: Restoration of independence
summary: The parliament in Podgorica formally declared Montenegro an independent sovereign state, recognised by Serbia, restoring the statehood lost at the Podgorica Assembly of 1918.

title: Application for EU membership
summary: Montenegro applied to join the European Union, beginning the accession process that would make it one of the leading candidates among the Western Balkan countries.

title: EU candidate status
summary: The European Union granted Montenegro candidate status, a milestone toward the accession negotiations the country has pursued while retaining the euro as its currency.

title: Kosovo border demarcation
summary: Montenegro and Kosovo signed a demarcation of their 79-kilometre border in 2015; fiercely contested in Kosovo, it was finally ratified by Pristina's parliament in March 2018.

title: Accession to NATO
summary: Montenegro became NATO's twenty-ninth member, depositing its instrument of accession in Washington, despite strong Russian opposition and a divided domestic public.

title: The Xiongnu confederation reaches its height
summary: At the close of the third century BCE the Xiongnu unite the eastern steppe under a supreme chanyu, forming a nomadic empire that rivals the Qin and Han dynasties of China for centuries.

title: Break-up of the Xiongnu empire
summary: After prolonged war with China and internal division, the Xiongnu confederation fractures; some tribes are absorbed into China while others scatter, ending the first great steppe empire centred on Mongolia.

title: Uyghur khaganate in the Orkhon valley
summary: Turkic Uyghurs establish a khaganate centred on the Orkhon River, building the city of Khar Balgas; the valley remains the political and ceremonial heart of the eastern steppe.

title: Temüjin proclaimed Chinggis Khan
summary: An assembly of steppe leaders by the River Onon proclaims Temüjin as Chinggis Khan, 'Universal Ruler,' uniting the Mongol tribes into one nation governed by the Yassa law code, the founding act of the Mongol state.

title: Conquest of the Khwarazmian empire
summary: Mongol armies invade and destroy the powerful Khwarazmian empire of Central Asia, opening the way to Persia and the Russian steppe and demonstrating the reach of the new Mongol military.

title: Death of Chinggis Khan
summary: Chinggis Khan dies in August 1227 during a campaign against the Tangut Xixia kingdom, leaving an empire reaching from northern China to the Caspian Sea and a realm divided among his four sons.

title: Karakorum becomes the imperial capital
summary: Great Khan Ögödei walls the city of Karakorum in the Orkhon valley and builds a palace there, establishing a fixed capital for the Mongol Empire on the Mongolian steppe.

title: Kublai Khan founds the Yuan dynasty
summary: Chinggis Khan's grandson Kublai proclaims the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and completes the conquest of China by 1279, ruling all of China from Khanbaliq (Beijing) as its first non-Chinese sovereign.

title: Fall of the Yuan and retreat to the steppe
summary: The Chinese rebel Zhu Yuanzhang overthrows the Yuan and founds the Ming dynasty; the last Mongol emperor flees north into the steppes, ending Mongol rule over China.

title: Zanabazar enthroned as first Javzandamba
summary: Zanabazar, recognized as a reincarnation in 1639, is enthroned with the title Javzandamba khutagt, becoming the first Bogd Gegeen and supreme head of Tibetan Buddhism in Mongolia.

title: Khalkha Mongols submit to the Qing
summary: The Khalkha Mongols of the north accept Manchu overlordship, bringing Mongolia under the Qing dynasty; the Manchus govern through the Mongol nobility and impose religious controls to secure their rule.

title: Independence declared under the Bogd Khan
summary: As the Qing collapses, Mongolia expels the Manchu official and proclaims the Javzandamba as Bogd Khan, head of an independent theocratic monarchy, though only autonomy under Chinese suzerainty is recognized abroad.

title: People's Revolution captures the capital
summary: Damdin Sükhbaatar's People's Army, with the Soviet Red Army, drives out the White Russian forces of Baron Ungern-Sternberg and takes Niislel Khüree in July 1921, installing a people's government.

title: Mongolian People's Republic proclaimed
summary: After the death of the Bogd Khan in May 1924, the monarchy lapses and the Mongolian People's Republic is proclaimed in November, the world's second socialist state and a satellite of the Soviet Union.

title: The Great Repression
summary: Under Choibalsan and Soviet NKVD advisers, the state carries out mass purges, killing tens of thousands of people, executing thousands of lamas, and destroying hundreds of Buddhist monasteries.

title: Mongolia admitted to the United Nations
summary: Mongolia is admitted to the United Nations in 1961, broadening international recognition of its independence after decades in which its sovereignty had been disputed between its powerful neighbours.

title: Peaceful democratic revolution
summary: Demonstrations and hunger strikes in the capital lead the ruling party's leadership to resign in March 1990, ending one-party communist rule and opening the way to multiparty elections held that year.

title: Democratic constitution adopted
summary: A new constitution transforms Mongolia from a people's republic into a multiparty parliamentary democracy with an elected president and the State Great Khural, and commits the country to a market economy.

title: Oyu Tolgoi and the mining boom
summary: Agreement to develop the giant Oyu Tolgoi copper and gold deposit anchors a mining boom that multiplies Mongolia's income, reorients its economy from herding, and accelerates migration to Ulaanbaatar.

title: Sofala recorded as a gold port
summary: The geographer al-Masʿudi describes Muslim trade in the Sofala region; Sofala becomes the chief outlet for gold carried down from the interior highlands.

title: Coastal trading towns flourish
summary: Settlements at Sofala, Angoche, the Island of Mozambique, the Querimba Islands and the Zambezi mouth grow into nodes of the Swahili Indian Ocean trade.

title: Kilwa controls the Sofala gold trade
summary: The sultanate of Kilwa dominates the export of interior gold through Sofala, drawing wealth from the Zimbabwe and Mutapa goldfields into the wider Islamic world.

title: Rise of the Mutapa state
summary: The Mutapa (Monomotapa) state emerges on the Zimbabwean plateau, its gold and ivory passing down the Zambezi and out through the Mozambican ports.

title: Vasco da Gama reaches the coast
summary: Bound for India, Vasco da Gama anchors off the Island of Mozambique, where Muslim merchants receive him with suspicion; he sails on, marking the first European contact with the coast.

title: Portuguese occupy Sofala
summary: The Portuguese seize Sofala and build a fort to capture the gold trade, but find the port in decline and shift their base to the Island of Mozambique.

title: Chapel of Nossa Senhora do Baluarte built
summary: On the Island of Mozambique the Portuguese raise the small chapel of Nossa Senhora do Baluarte, often called the oldest surviving European building in the southern hemisphere.

title: Fort São Sebastião is built
summary: Construction begins on Fort São Sebastião on the Island of Mozambique, the largest Portuguese fortress in East Africa and the oldest complete fort still standing in sub-Saharan Africa.

title: Omanis take Fort Jesus at Mombasa
summary: Omani Arabs capture Fort Jesus in Mombasa, rolling back Portuguese power on the northern Swahili coast and confining it largely to the territory of modern Mozambique.

title: Prazo estates along the Zambezi
summary: The crown leases great estates, the prazos da coroa, to settlers along the Zambezi; their holders rule as semi-feudal lords with armies of slave-soldiers and a heavy stake in the slave trade.

title: Soshangane founds the Gaza Empire
summary: Nguni warriors fleeing the upheavals of the Mfecane, led by Soshangane, conquer much of southern Mozambique and establish the Gaza Empire.

title: Berlin Conference and the scramble
summary: The Berlin Conference requires Portugal to occupy the territory it claims, spurring a drive to subdue the Mozambican interior.

title: Defeat and capture of Gungunhana
summary: Portuguese forces crush the Gaza army at Coolela and capture King Gungunhana at Chaimite, ending the Gaza Empire; he is exiled to the Azores, where he dies.

title: Mozambique Company chartered
summary: The Mozambique Company receives a vast concession with powers to tax, govern and recruit labour, one of several chartered companies to which Portugal subcontracts colonial rule.

title: Estado Novo and tightened control
summary: The authoritarian Estado Novo regime takes shape in Portugal, hardening colonial policy and entrenching forced labour and compulsory cultivation in Mozambique.

title: Forced cotton cultivation and chibalo
summary: Compulsory cotton-growing for Portuguese industry and the chibalo forced-labour system compel Mozambicans to grow cash crops and build infrastructure, reducing food production and worsening rural diets.

title: Colonies redesignated 'overseas provinces'
summary: Portugal renames its African colonies overseas provinces to resist decolonisation, while withholding citizenship and political rights from the African majority.

title: FRELIMO is founded
summary: Exiled nationalist groups unite in Dar es Salaam to form FRELIMO under Eduardo Mondlane, dedicated to ending Portuguese rule in Mozambique.

title: War of independence begins
summary: FRELIMO launches its first armed attacks in Cabo Delgado, opening a decade-long guerrilla war against Portuguese colonial forces.

title: Assassination of Eduardo Mondlane
summary: FRELIMO's founding president is killed by a parcel bomb in Dar es Salaam; after a leadership struggle, Samora Machel emerges at the head of the movement.

title: Carnation Revolution and the Lusaka Accord
summary: Lisbon's Carnation Revolution of April 1974 ends the dictatorship; in September Portugal and FRELIMO sign the Lusaka Accord, agreeing a transition to independence.

title: Independence of Mozambique
summary: The People's Republic of Mozambique is proclaimed with Samora Machel as first president; most of the colony's Portuguese settlers depart, taking skills and capital with them.

title: Civil war and the rise of RENAMO
summary: RENAMO, backed first by Rhodesia and then by apartheid South Africa, wages war on the FRELIMO government; the conflict devastates the countryside for fifteen years.

title: Death of Samora Machel
summary: President Machel dies when his aircraft crashes near the South African border; Joaquim Chissano succeeds him and begins to move FRELIMO toward reform and negotiation.

title: Rome General Peace Accords
summary: Mediated by the Community of Sant'Egidio, President Chissano and RENAMO leader Afonso Dhlakama sign a peace agreement in Rome, ending a war that killed about a million people.

title: First multiparty elections
summary: Under UN supervision Mozambique holds its first multiparty elections, won by FRELIMO; the following year the country joins the Commonwealth.

title: Offshore gas discovered in the Rovuma basin
summary: Major natural-gas finds in the deep waters of the Rovuma basin attract tens of billions of dollars in planned investment and reshape the country's economic prospects.

title: Cabo Delgado insurgency
summary: An Islamist insurgency erupts in Cabo Delgado; its 2021 assault on Palma halts the main gas project, and the violence kills thousands and displaces close to a million people.

title: Ghana Empire dominates the trade routes
summary: The Soninke kingdom of Ghana (Wagadou) controls the trans-Saharan gold-and-salt trade, with its influence reaching into the south of present-day Mauritania.

title: Koumbi Saleh as a Saharan emporium
summary: Koumbi Saleh, widely identified as Ghana's capital, grows into a major trading town with a Muslim merchants' quarter and, at its peak, tens of thousands of inhabitants.

title: Break-up of the Sanhaja confederation
summary: The confederation of veiled Sanhaja Berbers controlling the western Saharan trade routes fragments, producing warfare and unrest among the desert tribes.

title: Abdallah ibn Yasin founds the Almoravid movement
summary: The theologian Abdallah ibn Yasin begins preaching a reformed Islam among the Sanhaja, gathering the disciplined religious-military following known as the al-Murabitun (Almoravids).

title: Death of Ibn Yasin; Abu Bakr leads the desert wing
summary: After Ibn Yasin is killed in 1059, Abu Bakr ibn Umar takes command of the Almoravid forces in the Sahara, while Yusuf ibn Tashfin leads the northern conquests.

title: Almoravids said to take Koumbi Saleh
summary: Tradition records that Almoravid forces under Abu Bakr captured the Ghanaian capital of Koumbi Saleh around 1076, contributing to the decline of the Ghana Empire—though the campaign's scale is debated.

title: Fall of the Almoravid empire
summary: The Almoravid empire, which had stretched from the Senegal River to Spain, is overthrown by the Almohads, but Islam remains firmly rooted in the western Sahara.

title: Beni Hassan Arab migration
summary: Waves of Banu Maqil Arabs, including the Beni Hassan, migrate south into the western Sahara, spreading Hassaniya Arabic and gradually transforming the region's Berber society.

title: Foundation of the caravan ksour
summary: The fortified towns of Ouadane, Chinguetti, Tichitt and Oualata are founded to serve the trans-Saharan caravans, becoming trading and religious centres of Islamic culture.

title: The Char Bouba (Marabout) war
summary: Sanhaja Berber religious leaders fight the Arab Beni Hassan tribes; the war's outcome confirms Arab warrior dominance and the social hierarchy of Moorish society.

title: Rise of the Moorish emirates
summary: Moorish society consolidates into the emirates of Trarza, Brakna, Tagant and Adrar, each governed by an emir of the Hassan warrior elite.

title: Coppolani's pacification campaign begins
summary: Xavier Coppolani launches France's drive to extend control over Mauritania, combining alliances with marabout tribes and military pressure on the emirates.

title: Mauritania organised within French West Africa
summary: The territory is formally constituted as the civil territory of Mauritania within French West Africa.

title: Assassination of Coppolani
summary: Xavier Coppolani is killed at Tidjikja, a setback to the French advance, though the conquest of the interior continues afterward.

title: Completion of the conquest
summary: After decades of resistance by the desert emirates and nomadic tribes, French military control over the far north of Mauritania is finally consolidated in the 1930s.

title: Autonomous republic and Nouakchott
summary: Mauritania becomes an autonomous republic within the French Community, and the new capital of Nouakchott is established on the coast.

title: Independence of the Islamic Republic
summary: Mauritania gains full independence from France; Moktar Ould Daddah leads the new state and becomes its first president in 1961.

title: National currency and Arab orientation
summary: Mauritania leaves the franc zone and introduces the ouguiya, reflecting Ould Daddah's policy of national consolidation and a turn toward the Arab world.

title: Annexation of southern Western Sahara
summary: Following the 1975 Madrid Accords, Mauritania and Morocco partition Western Sahara; Mauritania annexes the southern third as Tiris al-Gharbiyya, drawing it into war with the Polisario Front.

title: Coup ends the Daddah era
summary: A military coup deposes President Moktar Ould Daddah after eighteen years in power, as the costly Western Sahara war destabilises the country.

title: Withdrawal from Western Sahara
summary: Mauritania renounces its claim to Tiris al-Gharbiyya and withdraws its forces, ending its part in the Western Sahara war; Morocco then absorbs the vacated territory.

title: Slavery formally abolished
summary: Mauritania abolishes slavery by decree—frequently cited as the last country in the world to do so—though no penalties were initially attached to the ban.

title: Ould Taya takes power
summary: Colonel Maaouya Ould Sid'Ahmed Taya seizes power in a coup and goes on to rule Mauritania for some twenty years.

title: Coup ends the Taya era
summary: A military council overthrows President Ould Taya, beginning a period of transition punctuated by a further coup in 2008.

title: Slavery criminalised
summary: A law makes slavery a criminal offence; the constitution later recognises it as a crime against humanity in 2012, although rights groups report that descent-based slavery has persisted in practice.

title: Known to Arab and Malay sailors
summary: Mariners crossing the Indian Ocean are thought to have known the uninhabited island, reputedly recorded on Arab maps as 'Dina Arobi'.

title: Portuguese chart the Mascarenes
summary: Portuguese navigators sight and map Mauritius and the neighbouring islands as a provisioning stop, but found no colony.

title: The Dutch name the island Mauritius
summary: Admiral Wybrand van Warwijck claims the island and names it for Maurice of Nassau, stadtholder of the Dutch Republic.

title: First permanent Dutch settlement
summary: The Dutch East India Company establishes a settlement, exploiting ebony forests and introducing sugar cane and livestock.

title: Extinction of the dodo
summary: Hunting, deforestation and introduced animals wipe out the flightless dodo within decades of human arrival; last accepted sightings fall in the 1660s.

title: The Dutch abandon Mauritius
summary: After unprofitable settlements plagued by storms, pests and disease, the Dutch East India Company leaves the island.

title: France claims the Isle de France
summary: France takes formal possession of the uninhabited island, renaming it Isle de France; colonisation begins under the French East India Company from 1721.

title: La Bourdonnais founds Port Louis
summary: Governor Mahé de La Bourdonnais develops Port Louis as a fortified naval base, dockyard and capital, anchoring French power in the Indian Ocean.

title: A slave-worked plantation economy
summary: Enslaved Africans, Malagasy and others are imported in large numbers to work sugar and other estates; they become the majority of the population.

title: Maroons of Le Morne Brabant
summary: Escaped slaves take refuge on the isolated cliffs of Le Morne, later inscribed by UNESCO as a symbol of the struggle for freedom.

title: British capture of the Isle de France
summary: After the French naval victory at Grand Port, a large British force lands and compels the surrender of the island in December 1810.

title: Treaty of Paris confirms British rule
summary: Britain retains the island and renames it Mauritius, while French settlers keep their language, laws and religion.

title: Abolition of slavery
summary: Slavery is formally ended in Mauritius, freeing tens of thousands of enslaved people, followed by a transitional 'apprenticeship'.

title: Indian indenture and the Aapravasi Ghat
summary: Around half a million indentured labourers from India arrive through the Port Louis depot, the 'Great Experiment', reshaping the island's population.

title: Founding of the Labour Party
summary: The Mauritius Labour Party is founded, channelling demands of workers and the indentured-descended majority for rights and representation.

title: Chagos detached as the BIOT
summary: Before independence, Britain separates the Chagos Archipelago to create the British Indian Ocean Territory, leasing Diego Garcia for a US base.

title: Independence from the United Kingdom
summary: Mauritius becomes an independent state within the Commonwealth, with Seewoosagur Ramgoolam as first prime minister.

title: Diversification beyond sugar
summary: An export-processing zone, tourism and financial services transform a one-crop colony into a diversified, growing economy.

title: Mauritius becomes a republic
summary: The island replaces the British monarch with a Mauritian president as head of state, retaining its parliamentary democracy.

title: ICJ advisory opinion on Chagos
summary: The International Court of Justice finds Britain's continued administration of the Chagos Archipelago unlawful; the UN General Assembly concurs.

title: UK–Mauritius Chagos agreement
summary: The two states sign a treaty recognising Mauritian sovereignty over the archipelago while leasing the Diego Garcia base to the UK for an initial 99 years.

title: Bantu-speaking farmers settle the plateau
summary: Bantu-speaking peoples moved into the Lake Malawi region during the early centuries of the Common Era, introducing ironworking and settled agriculture and absorbing or displacing earlier hunter-gatherer communities.

title: The Chewa rock-painting tradition at Chongoni
summary: Chewa farming communities, especially women, developed a distinctive rock-painting tradition on the granite hills of the central plateau, linked to initiation, funerals and rainmaking, building on far older paintings by BaTwa hunter-gatherers.

title: Founding of the Maravi Confederacy
summary: The Amaravi, ancestors of the Chewa, established a confederacy under the Kalonga on the southwestern shores of Lake Nyasa, ruling from Mankhamba — the state that gave Malawi its name.

title: Gaspar Bocarro crosses the region
summary: The Portuguese traveller Gaspar Bocarro journeyed through the territory, leaving what is generally regarded as the first European account of the land and peoples of the future Malawi.

title: The Maravi Empire at its peak
summary: In the seventeenth century the confederacy administered a broad domain reaching across parts of modern Malawi, Mozambique and Zambia, trading ivory and iron with Portuguese and Swahili merchants on the coast.

title: Decline of the confederacy
summary: Fighting among the sub-chiefs and the spreading slave trade eroded the Kalonga's authority, and the Maravi state fragmented into smaller Chewa chiefdoms.

title: Ngoni and Yao migrations reshape the region
summary: Ngoni warrior bands fleeing the Mfecane settled around Lake Nyasa, while the Yao migrated from northern Mozambique and the Tumbuka occupied the northern highlands, overlaying new peoples on the older Chewa chiefdoms.

title: The Jumbe and the slave trade at Nkhotakota
summary: The Swahili-Arab trader Salim bin Abdallah, the Jumbe, established himself at Nkhotakota, which became a major slaving entrepôt on the western lakeshore; the Yao became leading participants in the trade across the lake.

title: Livingstone reaches Lake Nyasa
summary: David Livingstone, on the Zambezi expedition, reached Lake Nyasa and reported it as a corridor of the slave caravans, calling for commerce and Christianity to end the trade.

title: Scottish missions founded at Livingstonia and Blantyre
summary: Inspired by Livingstone, the Free Church of Scotland established the Livingstonia mission in 1875 and the Church of Scotland the Blantyre mission in 1876; both campaigned against the slave trade and trained an African Christian elite.

title: British Central Africa Protectorate proclaimed
summary: Britain proclaimed a protectorate over the lake region and the Shire highlands, with Harry Johnston as first commissioner; he suppressed the slave trade by force and parcelled out land to European settlers through certificates of claim.

title: The protectorate renamed Nyasaland
summary: The British Central Africa Protectorate was renamed the Nyasaland Protectorate, the name by which the territory would be known until independence.

title: The Chilembwe rising
summary: Reverend John Chilembwe led an uprising against colonial rule, forced labour and wartime conscription; his followers attacked the A. L. Bruce estate at Magomero and killed William Jervis Livingstone before British forces swiftly suppressed the revolt.

title: Chilembwe killed
summary: John Chilembwe was shot dead as he fled toward Mozambique; though the rising failed, he became an enduring symbol of Malawian nationalism and is honoured as a national martyr.

title: Founding of the Nyasaland African Congress
summary: African political associations coalesced into the Nyasaland African Congress, the first territory-wide nationalist body, which would later spearhead opposition to federation.

title: Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland created
summary: Britain bound Nyasaland into a settler-dominated federation with Southern and Northern Rhodesia, provoking deep and sustained African opposition across Nyasaland.

title: State of emergency and Operation Sunrise
summary: Amid mounting agitation against federation, the governor declared a state of emergency and detained Banda and over a thousand Congress members; the Devlin Commission later condemned the use of force and likened Nyasaland to a police state.

title: Malawi Congress Party wins the elections
summary: Banda's Malawi Congress Party won the 1961 legislative elections decisively, securing African control of the colonial legislature and accelerating the path to self-government.

title: The Federation dissolved
summary: Faced with African opposition and irreconcilable tensions, the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland was dissolved at the end of 1963, clearing the way for the separate independence of Malawi, Zambia and Rhodesia.

title: Malawi independent
summary: Nyasaland became the independent state of Malawi within the Commonwealth, with Hastings Kamuzu Banda as prime minister; the United States recognised the new nation the same day.

title: Banda declared President for Life
summary: After Malawi became a republic in 1966 with the Malawi Congress Party as sole legal party, the National Assembly in 1971 proclaimed Banda President for Life, completing the one-party state.

title: Three decades of one-party rule
summary: Banda ruled as life-president through the Malawi Congress Party, detaining, exiling or killing opponents and maintaining a tightly controlled, conservative and pro-Western state.

title: Referendum ends the one-party state
summary: Malawians voted by roughly two to one to abandon single-party rule and adopt multiparty democracy, opening the way to free elections.

title: First multiparty elections; Banda defeated
summary: In the first multiparty general election since independence, Bakili Muluzi of the United Democratic Front defeated Hastings Banda, who peacefully gave up power after three decades.

title: Joyce Banda becomes head of state
summary: After the death in office of President Bingu wa Mutharika, Vice-President Joyce Banda succeeded him, becoming Malawi's first woman president.

title: Court-ordered election re-run
summary: After the Constitutional Court annulled the 2019 presidential election for irregularities, Lazarus Chakwera won the court-ordered re-run, a rare judicial reversal of a presidential result on the continent.

title: Peaceful alternation of power
summary: Peter Mutharika won the 2025 general election, defeating the incumbent Lazarus Chakwera, who conceded — marking another peaceful transfer of power in multiparty Malawi.

title: Rise of the Srivijaya thalassocracy
summary: Based at Palembang in Sumatra, the Buddhist kingdom of Srivijaya comes to control the Strait of Malacca and the maritime trade between India and China, becoming the dominant commercial power of the Malay world.

title: Chola naval raid weakens Srivijaya
summary: A naval expedition from the south Indian Chola dynasty strikes Srivijaya's ports, contributing to the long decline of its dominance over the strait.

title: Founding of Malacca by Paramesvara
summary: The Sumatran prince Paramesvara, having fled Palembang and Tumasik before Majapahit's forces, settles at Malacca and founds a city that becomes the leading port of the Malay world.

title: Malacca, Islam and ties with Ming China
summary: Through marriage to a Muslim princess and the adoption of the title Sultan, Malacca's court embraces Islam, while tributary relations with Ming China, marked by Zheng He's visits, secure its trade.

title: Malacca, the great entrepot of the strait
summary: Malacca grows into the most important trade centre in the region, where gold, spices, silk and tea pass between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea, and Malay court culture flourishes.

title: Portuguese capture of Malacca
summary: Afonso de Albuquerque storms Malacca after a siege, ending the independent sultanate and beginning sustained European control of the strait and its trade.

title: Dutch conquest of Malacca
summary: The Dutch East India Company, allied with the Sultanate of Johor, takes Malacca from the Portuguese, holding it as a lesser outpost while focusing power on Batavia.

title: Penang, Singapore and the Straits Settlements
summary: Britain founds Penang in 1786 and Singapore in 1819 and, with Malacca, combines them in 1826 as the Straits Settlements, the base for expanding British control over the peninsula.

title: James Brooke becomes Raja of Sarawak
summary: The Sultan of Brunei appoints the Englishman James Brooke raja of Sarawak, founding the 'White Raja' dynasty and beginning the absorption of the Borneo territories into the British sphere.

title: Japanese occupation and the fall of Singapore
summary: Japanese forces overrun Malaya and capture Singapore on 15 February 1942, beginning a three-and-a-half-year occupation that shatters British prestige and deepens communal divisions.

title: Malayan Union opposition and the founding of UMNO
summary: Malay opposition to the centralising Malayan Union proposal gives rise to the United Malays National Organisation, the country's first major political party, and the union is soon replaced by the Federation of Malaya.

title: The Malayan Emergency
summary: After the Malayan Communist Party launches a guerrilla insurgency, the government declares a state of emergency on 18 June 1948, beginning a counterinsurgency that lasts until 1960.

title: Merdeka: independence of Malaya
summary: The Federation of Malaya achieves independence under Tunku Abdul Rahman, who proclaims a sovereign, democratic state at Merdeka Stadium in Kuala Lumpur.

title: Formation of the Federation of Malaysia
summary: Malaya joins with Singapore, Sabah (North Borneo) and Sarawak under the Malaysia Agreement to form Malaysia, the founding act of the modern federation.

title: Indonesian Confrontation (Konfrontasi)
summary: Indonesia's President Sukarno opposes the new federation and wages an undeclared campaign of armed confrontation against Malaysia until 1966, drawing in Britain, Australia and the United States.

title: Singapore's separation from Malaysia
summary: Amid deepening communal and political friction, Singapore is separated from Malaysia by mutual agreement and becomes an independent state.

title: The 13 May communal riots
summary: Racial rioting between Malays and Chinese in Kuala Lumpur follows a divisive general election, leaving many dead and leading to a suspension of parliament that transforms Malaysian politics.

title: The New Economic Policy
summary: In the wake of the 1969 riots, the government launches a twenty-year programme of affirmative action to reduce poverty and raise the economic share of the Bumiputera majority, reshaping Malaysian society.

title: The Mahathir era and rapid modernisation
summary: Mahathir Mohamad serves as prime minister for twenty-two years, driving industrialisation and signature projects such as the Petronas Twin Towers while centralising political power.

title: Melaka and George Town inscribed by UNESCO
summary: UNESCO lists Melaka and George Town, Historic Cities of the Straits of Malacca, recognising more than five centuries of trade and multicultural exchange between East and West.

title: 1MDB scandal ends Barisan Nasional rule
summary: Amid the 1MDB corruption scandal, an opposition alliance led by Mahathir defeats Najib Razak, ending more than six decades of Barisan Nasional government; Najib is later convicted and jailed.

title: Anwar Ibrahim becomes prime minister
summary: After years of imprisonment and opposition and a period of post-2020 instability, Anwar Ibrahim is appointed Malaysia's tenth prime minister following an inconclusive general election.

title: San hunter-gatherers of the Namib
summary: The San, among the oldest human populations on Earth, ranged across the Namib and its margins for tens of thousands of years, hunting, gathering and recording their world in rock art.

title: The engravings of Twyfelfontein
summary: San artists pecked thousands of petroglyphs into the sandstone at Twyfelfontein over roughly two thousand years, depicting animals and tracks bound up with hunter-gatherer ritual; the site was inscribed by UNESCO in 2007.

title: Khoekhoe and Damara herders
summary: Khoekhoe pastoralists, including the Nama, and the Damara established themselves across central and southern Namibia, herding cattle and sheep and speaking Khoekhoe click languages.

title: Bantu-speaking peoples settle the north
summary: Over the past fifteen hundred years Bantu-speaking Ovambo, Kavango and Herero peoples migrated into the north and centre, bringing iron-working, agriculture and cattle pastoralism.

title: Diogo Cão reaches the coast
summary: The Portuguese navigator Diogo Cão landed on the Namib coast and raised a stone cross at Cape Cross; the waterless, harbourless shore — later the Skeleton Coast — long deterred European settlement.

title: Jonker Afrikaner and the Orlam
summary: Jonker Afrikaner led his Orlam followers north into the central highlands, founding a settlement at Windhoek around 1840 and building a mounted, gun-armed state that dominated the interior until 1861.

title: Britain annexes Walvis Bay
summary: Britain annexed Walvis Bay, the territory's only deep-water harbour, creating an enclave that would remain in South African hands long after the rest of the country, until 1994.

title: Germany declares a protectorate
summary: Following Adolf Lüderitz's purchase at Angra Pequena in 1883, Bismarck declared a German protectorate over the territory in 1884, founding the colony of German South West Africa.

title: The Herero uprising begins
summary: Herero forces under paramount chief Samuel Maharero rose against German colonial rule, killing more than a hundred settlers and triggering a brutal German military response.

title: Battle of Waterberg
summary: German forces under Lothar von Trotha defeated the main Herero force at Waterberg and drove the survivors into the Omaheke desert, where thousands, including women and children, died of thirst.

title: Von Trotha's extermination order
summary: Von Trotha issued the Vernichtungsbefehl, ordering that every Herero within the colony, armed or not, be shot; a second order against the Nama followed in April 1905, opening a war of extermination.

title: Shark Island and the concentration camps
summary: Herero and Nama survivors were imprisoned in concentration camps, most notoriously on Shark Island at Lüderitz, where up to 80 percent of prisoners died; by 1908 tens of thousands of Herero and Nama had perished in what is widely called the first genocide of the twentieth century.

title: South Africa conquers the colony
summary: South African forces invaded German South West Africa during the First World War and forced the German garrison to surrender, beginning seventy-five years of South African rule.

title: League of Nations mandate
summary: The League of Nations granted South Africa a mandate to administer the territory as a trust for its inhabitants; South Africa instead governed it as a near-province, settling white farmers and suppressing African political life.

title: South Africa refuses UN trusteeship
summary: After the founding of the United Nations, South Africa refused to place the territory under UN trusteeship and sought to annex it, beginning a long international dispute over its status.

title: The Old Location shootings
summary: Police killed about a dozen residents of Windhoek's Old Location protesting forced removal to Katutura township, an atrocity that helped galvanise the nationalist movement.

title: Founding of SWAPO
summary: The South West African People's Organisation was founded under Sam Nujoma as successor to the Ovamboland People's Organisation, becoming the leading movement for Namibian independence.

title: Armed struggle begins at Omugulugwombashe
summary: SWAPO's military wing, PLAN, fought South African forces at Omugulugwombashe, marking the start of the armed liberation war and of South Africa's long Border War.

title: UN revokes the mandate
summary: The UN General Assembly terminated South Africa's mandate over the territory, declaring its continued administration illegal, and later renamed the territory Namibia in 1968.

title: ICJ rules the occupation illegal
summary: The International Court of Justice held that South Africa's continued presence in Namibia was illegal and that it was obliged to withdraw its administration immediately.

title: Security Council Resolution 435
summary: The UN Security Council adopted Resolution 435, setting out a plan for a ceasefire and UN-supervised elections that would eventually frame Namibia's transition to independence.

title: UN-supervised elections
summary: With Resolution 435 in force from 1 April 1989 under the UN Transition Assistance Group (UNTAG), Namibians elected a Constituent Assembly that SWAPO won with about 57 percent of the vote; the assembly drafted a democratic constitution adopted in February 1990.

title: Independence and Nujoma's inauguration
summary: At midnight on 21 March 1990 the Namibian flag was raised in Windhoek, ending South African rule, and Sam Nujoma was sworn in as the first president of the independent Republic of Namibia.

title: Reincorporation of Walvis Bay
summary: South Africa transferred the port enclave of Walvis Bay and the offshore islands to Namibia, completing the country's territory and giving it sovereignty over its only deep-water harbour.

title: First peaceful transfer of power
summary: Sam Nujoma stepped down after fifteen years and was succeeded as president by Hifikepunye Pohamba, the first of several peaceful handovers within SWAPO governments.

title: Germany acknowledges the genocide
summary: Germany formally recognised the 1904–1908 killings of the Herero and Nama as genocide and pledged development funding, though many descendants rejected the terms as inadequate.

title: First woman president elected
summary: Namibians elected Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah, a veteran of the liberation struggle, as the country's first woman president, extending SWAPO's continuous tenure since independence.

title: Lapita settlement of New Caledonia
summary: Austronesian voyagers of the Lapita culture reached the archipelago, establishing the earliest human presence and leaving the dentate-stamped pottery first studied at the New Caledonian site that gives the culture its name.

title: Emergence of the Kanak
