summary: Successive waves of Melanesian migrants intermarried with the Lapita settlers, giving rise to the Kanak, the Melanesian people indigenous to New Caledonia, with a clan-based society organised around chiefs, yam cultivation and ancestral land.

title: Cook names New Caledonia
summary: The British explorer James Cook landed at Balade on the east coast and named the territory New Caledonia after the classical name for Scotland, marking the first recorded European contact.

title: Sandalwood traders and missionaries arrive
summary: From the 1840s sandalwood traders and Christian missionaries — Protestant and, from 1843, French Catholic Marists — established themselves among the Kanak, bringing trade goods, conversion, firearms and epidemic disease.

title: France annexes New Caledonia
summary: Rear Admiral Febvrier-Despointes took possession of the archipelago for France, beginning formal colonial rule and pre-empting British ambitions in the region.

title: Penal colony established
summary: France made New Caledonia a penal settlement, transporting tens of thousands of convicts — including Communards after 1871 — whose forced labour helped build the colonial economy until transportation ended in the 1890s.

title: The revolt of Ataï
summary: The high chief Ataï led a major Kanak insurrection against land dispossession; the rising killed about 200 colonists and gendarmes and was crushed at the cost of roughly a thousand Kanak lives, with Ataï killed and his head sent to Paris.

title: Nickel mining begins
summary: The Société Le Nickel began industrial exploitation of New Caledonia's nickel — among the largest deposits in the world — making mining the economic engine that drew settlers and accelerated Kanak dispossession.

title: FLNKS founded
summary: Pro-independence parties united in the Kanak and Socialist National Liberation Front (FLNKS) under Jean-Marie Tjibaou, demanding sovereignty for a country it called Kanaky and opening the most intense phase of the independence struggle.

title: Re-inscribed on the UN decolonisation list
summary: The UN General Assembly re-inscribed New Caledonia on its list of Non-Self-Governing Territories, formally recognising the Kanak people's right to self-determination and placing the territory back on the UN decolonisation agenda.

title: Ouvéa cave crisis
summary: FLNKS militants killed four gendarmes and seized hostages in a cave on Ouvéa; a French military assault on 5 May freed the hostages but left nineteen Kanak dead, a tragedy that became a turning point toward negotiation.

title: Matignon Accords
summary: The French state, FLNKS and RPCR signed the Matignon Accords, ending les Événements, dividing the territory into three provinces and scheduling a self-determination referendum for 1998.

title: Nouméa Accord signed
summary: The Nouméa Accord set out a gradual, declared-irreversible transfer of powers, recognition of Kanak identity and up to three referendums on full sovereignty, making New Caledonia a sui generis collectivity within the French Republic.

title: Accord ratified by referendum
summary: New Caledonian voters approved the Nouméa Accord by about 72%, and its provisions were written into the French Constitution (Articles 76–77).

title: The Tjibaou Cultural Centre opens
summary: Named for the assassinated Kanak leader and built at Nouméa by the Agence de developpement de la culture kanak, it opened the same month the Nouméa Accord was signed — the accord's cultural half made permanent in wood and steel.

title: The lagoons join the World Heritage List
summary: UNESCO inscribes the Lagoons of New Caledonia for reef diversity and intact ecosystems — the territory's other inheritance, held in common by both of its political camps.

title: First independence referendum
summary: In the first Nouméa Accord referendum, voters chose to remain part of France by about 56.7% to 43.3%, with the independence vote concentrated among the Kanak.

title: Second independence referendum
summary: Independence was again rejected, but by a narrower margin of about 53.3% to 46.7%, a closing gap that sharpened the political contest.

title: Third referendum and Kanak boycott
summary: The final referendum rejected independence by about 96% to 4%, but turnout was only ~44%: pro-independence parties and most Kanak voters boycotted after France declined to postpone the vote, and the two sides drew opposite conclusions about its legitimacy.

title: Deadly unrest over electoral reform
summary: A French move to widen the provincial electorate — feared to dilute the Kanak vote — triggered the worst violence in decades from 13 May: fourteen dead, some €2 billion in damage and a state of emergency.

title: Bougival agreement
summary: France and most local parties signed the Bougival agreement proposing a "State of New Caledonia" within the Republic with a Caledonian nationality; the pro-independence FLNKS rejected it and the ratifying referendum was delayed, leaving the territory's status unresolved into 2026.

title: The census counts a shrinking territory
summary: The first census since the unrest finds the population down by 6,811 since 2019 — a fall of about 4 per cent, roughly 1,200 people a year.

title: The Elysée-Oudinot agreement
summary: A further accord is signed in Paris in Macron's presence by the parties represented in the Congress, including the moderate pro-independence PALIKA and UPM who have split from the FLNKS; the FLNKS itself stayed away and rejected it.

title: The FLNKS loses its moderates
summary: PALIKA and then the UPM quit the coalition that had carried the independence cause since 1984, and five FLNKS members resign from the eleven-member executive.

title: Nickel, still the ground everyone stands on
summary: Through the unrest and its aftermath the territory mined 116,000 tonnes of nickel in 2024 and an estimated 140,000 in 2025 — one of the largest outputs on earth, and the revenue any future status has to be paid for out of.

title: Burials begin at Gobero
summary: Beside a lake in the present-day Ténéré, the Kiffian people began burying their dead at Gobero, creating what archaeologists identify as the oldest known cemetery in the Sahara.

title: The Tenerean herders
summary: After a dry interval, the more lightly built Tenerean people reoccupied Gobero, herding cattle as the lake shallowed; their graves include the famous burial of a woman with two children, hands interlinked.

title: Rock art of a green Sahara
summary: Across the Aïr and Ténéré, engraved and painted rock art recorded cattle, giraffes and elephants, documenting a watered landscape utterly unlike the desert that exists today.

title: The desert returns
summary: As the climate dried, the lakes retreated and the Sahara hardened into desert, pushing human settlement and trade southward toward the Sahel.

title: Founding of the Sultanate of Aïr
summary: Tuareg clans of the Aïr massif organised the Sultanate of Aïr, choosing a sultan to mediate their rivalries; its capital Agadez became a major trans-Saharan trading and religious centre. (Some accounts place the city's rise nearer 1449.)

title: Songhai pushes into Aïr
summary: The Songhai emperor Askia Muhammad campaigned into the Aïr mountains and established a Songhai presence at Agadez to control the northern caravan markets, the empire's eastern reach into present-day Niger.

title: The salt caravans of Bilma
summary: The azalai salt caravans carried Bilma and Fachi salt and dates southward to the Hausa markets, making Agadez and the eastern oases pillars of the trans-Saharan trade alongside the traffic in enslaved people.

title: Agadez inscribed by UNESCO
summary: The Historic Centre of Agadez — the mudbrick capital of the Sultanate of Aïr, with its tall earthen mosque minaret — was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, recognising its role in trans-Saharan trade and Islam.

title: Founding of the Sultanate of Damagaram
summary: Muslim aristocrats founded the Sultanate of Damagaram around Zinder; beginning as a vassal of the declining empire of Bornu, it would expand to dominate much of the southeast of present-day Niger.

title: Zinder, a trans-Saharan hub
summary: Damagaram's capital Zinder grew rich astride the desert route linking Tripoli to Kano, becoming a walled and well-armed trading state and one of the strongest powers in the region.

title: Sokoto jihad reshapes the Hausa lands
summary: The Sokoto Caliphate's rise to the south drove Hausa rivals such as Gobir and the Katsina rulers northward into present-day Niger, recasting the politics of the southern savanna.

title: Bornu's enduring influence
summary: The empire of Kanem-Bornu near Lake Chad continued to project Islamic culture and political weight over Niger's east, where many small states had begun as its tributaries.

title: The Voulet-Chanoine mission
summary: A French military column under Captains Voulet and Chanoine drove across the region with extreme brutality, massacring the people of Birni-N'Konni on 8 May 1899 before disintegrating into mutiny and the murder of Colonel Klobb.

title: The Kaocen revolt at Agadez
summary: During the First World War the Tuareg leader Kaocen led a major revolt against French rule, besieging the garrison at Agadez before the rising was crushed.

title: Niger becomes a French colony
summary: After the desert Tuareg were finally subdued in the early 1920s, Niger was constituted as a colony within French West Africa, administered through the federation's governor-general in Dakar.

title: Autonomous republic within the French Community
summary: In the 1958 referendum Niger voted to become a self-governing republic within the French Community, with Hamani Diori emerging at the head of its government on the road to independence.

title: Niger gains independence
summary: Niger became a sovereign republic on 3 August 1960 with Hamani Diori as its first president; the United States recognised it the same day. Diori established a one-party state closely tied to France.

title: The Great Sahel drought
summary: A catastrophic drought devastated Niger's crops and herds; the famine of this period and the 1980s killed many and left hundreds of thousands dependent on food aid, deepening the crisis of the Diori regime.

title: Uranium mining begins at Arlit
summary: After deposits were developed from 1968 through the company SOMAÏR, the open-pit mine at Arlit began commercial uranium production in 1971, founding the industry that became Niger's leading export.

title: Kountché's coup ousts Diori
summary: Amid famine, corruption allegations over relief supplies, and a dispute with France over uranium prices, Lieutenant-Colonel Seyni Kountché overthrew President Diori, beginning thirteen years of military rule.

title: Transition to multiparty democracy
summary: A 1991 national conference opened Niger's politics; elections in 1993 brought the first freely chosen government, beginning a turbulent experiment in multiparty rule.

title: First Tuareg rebellion
summary: Tuareg fighters in the north rebelled over marginalisation and the distribution of uranium wealth; the rising was ended by a 1995 peace accord promising decentralisation.

title: Second Tuareg rebellion
summary: The Niger Movement for Justice (MNJ) launched a new insurgency, attacking the army and the uranium-mining zone around Agadez and Arlit, before a settlement was reached in 2009.

title: Coup ousts President Tandja
summary: The army removed President Mamadou Tandja after he manoeuvred to extend his term, one of a series of military interventions that punctuated Niger's democratic experiment.

title: Coup against President Bazoum
summary: The presidential guard detained elected president Mohamed Bazoum and General Abdourahamane Tchiani proclaimed a military junta — Niger's fifth coup since independence — drawing condemnation from ECOWAS and the West.

title: Rise of the Nok culture
summary: On the central Nigerian plateau the Nok culture emerged, producing distinctive terracotta sculpture and, in its later phases, smelting iron — among the earliest such traditions in sub-Saharan Africa.

title: Nok terracottas first recognised
summary: Terracotta heads unearthed near the village of Nok during tin-mining drew scholarly attention, giving the ancient culture its name and revealing the antiquity of Nigerian art.

title: The bronzes of Igbo-Ukwu
summary: An Igbo community at Igbo-Ukwu produced sophisticated cast-bronze ritual objects and vast quantities of trade beads, evidence of advanced metalworking and long-distance trade in the southeastern forests.

title: Rise of the Kanem empire
summary: Around Lake Chad the empire of Kanem emerged under the Sayfawa dynasty, growing wealthy as the southern terminus of the trans-Saharan trade and gradually adopting Islam.

title: Shift from Kanem to Bornu
summary: After conflict with the Bulala forced the dynasty to abandon its eastern heartland, the state re-centred west of Lake Chad at Bornu, beginning the era of the Bornu Empire.

title: Peak of Bornu under Idris Alooma
summary: Mai Idris Alooma reformed Bornu's army and administration, extended its control over central Saharan trade routes, and deepened the role of Islamic law at its height of power.

title: Flourishing of Benin and Oyo
summary: The Edo kingdom of Benin and the Yoruba empire of Oyo rose as major forest powers, Benin renowned for its court art and Oyo for the cavalry empire of its Alaafin.

title: The Atlantic slave trade
summary: European demand drew the Bights of Benin and Biafra into the transatlantic slave trade; ports such as Bonny and Old Calabar became major export points, and vast numbers of people were deported in conditions of extreme violence.

title: Usman dan Fodio launches his jihad
summary: The Fulani scholar Usman dan Fodio began a jihad in the Hausa lands, rallying followers against the existing rulers and igniting a religious and political revolution across the north.

title: Founding of the Sokoto Caliphate
summary: Dan Fodio's victories consolidated into the Sokoto Caliphate, a vast confederation of emirates under Islamic law that became one of nineteenth-century Africa's largest states.

title: Britain abolishes its slave trade
summary: Britain outlawed its own transatlantic slave trade and began naval patrols of the West African coast, though illegal slaving from the region continued for decades.

title: Britain annexes Lagos
summary: After occupying Lagos in 1851, Britain annexed it as a crown colony in 1861, establishing a coastal foothold from which colonial power spread into the interior.

title: British sack of Benin City
summary: A British punitive expedition destroyed Benin City, exiled the Oba, and looted thousands of the Benin Bronzes, dispersing centuries of court art to foreign museums and collectors.

title: Fall of the Sokoto Caliphate
summary: Frederick Lugard's forces defeated the Sokoto army in March 1903; the last independent sultan, Attahiru I, was killed at Burmi in July, ending the caliphate's independence and bringing the north under British control.

title: Amalgamation of Nigeria
summary: Lord Lugard joined the Northern and Southern Protectorates into a single Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria, creating the territorial shape of the modern country under indirect rule.

title: Nigeria gains independence
summary: Nigeria became an independent state within the Commonwealth on 1 October 1960, with Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa as its first prime minister; it became a republic in 1963.

title: Military coups and unrest
summary: A January 1966 coup killed Prime Minister Balewa; a July counter-coup and ensuing violence against Igbo communities deepened the crisis that would lead to civil war.

title: Secession of Biafra
summary: Colonel Odumegwu Ojukwu declared the Eastern Region an independent Republic of Biafra, precipitating the Nigerian Civil War.

title: The Nigerian Civil War
summary: Federal forces under General Gowon fought to reunify the country and blockaded Biafra; the resulting famine and fighting killed an estimated one to two million people, mostly civilians, before Biafra surrendered in January 1970.

title: Abuja chosen as new capital
summary: Amid an oil-fuelled boom, the federal government decided to build a new, centrally located capital at Abuja to replace Lagos, a project realised over the following decades.

title: Annulled election and Abacha's rule
summary: The military annulled the 1993 presidential election, widely believed won by Moshood Abiola, ushering in the repressive regime of General Sani Abacha until his death in 1998.

title: Return to civilian rule and the Fourth Republic
summary: The military handed power to the elected president Olusegun Obasanjo, ending sixteen years of military government and inaugurating the Fourth Republic, Nigeria's longest period of continuous civilian rule.

title: Africa's largest economy
summary: After rebasing its GDP, Nigeria was confirmed as the largest economy in Africa, underscoring its weight as the continent's most populous nation and a major oil producer.

title: First opposition election victory
summary: Muhammadu Buhari defeated the sitting president Goodluck Jonathan, the first time an opposition candidate won Nigeria's presidency through the ballot box, marking a democratic milestone.

title: Nicarao and Chorotega settle the Pacific lowlands
summary: Nahua-speaking Nicarao and Oto-Manguean Chorotega establish chiefdoms in western Nicaragua, farming the volcanic lowlands around Lakes Managua and Nicaragua.

title: First Spanish contact
summary: The expedition of Gil González Dávila reaches the Pacific coast and encounters the Nicarao, opening the way to Spanish conquest.

title: Founding of León and Granada
summary: Francisco Hernández de Córdoba founds León and Granada, the rival cities whose Liberal and Conservative elites would shape Nicaraguan politics for generations.

title: León Viejo abandoned
summary: The original León, struck by the Momotombo eruption of 1578 and the earthquake of 1610, is abandoned; its buried ruins later become Nicaragua's first UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: British protectorate over the Mosquito Coast
summary: Great Britain allies with the Miskito kings and treats the Caribbean Mosquito Coast as a protectorate, leaving the region distinct from Hispanic Pacific Nicaragua.

title: Independence from Spain
summary: Nicaragua, with the other provinces of the Captaincy General of Guatemala, declares independence from Spain in the Act of Independence of Central America.

title: Separation from the Central American federation
summary: Amid regional rivalry, Nicaragua withdraws from the Federal Republic of Central America to become a fully sovereign state.

title: William Walker's filibuster
summary: Hired by León's Liberals, the American filibuster William Walker seizes Granada and makes himself president of Nicaragua in 1856 before a coalition of Central American states expels him.

title: Treaty of Managua
summary: Britain cedes its claims on the Caribbean coast to Nicaraguan sovereignty, creating a self-governing Mosquito Reserve.

title: Incorporation of the Mosquito Coast
summary: President José Santos Zelaya militarily incorporates the British-influenced Caribbean coast into the Nicaraguan state.

title: United States Marine occupation
summary: US Marines are stationed in Nicaragua to support Conservative governments and oversee its finances, with only a brief interruption, until 1933.

title: Sandino's resistance
summary: Augusto César Sandino wages guerrilla war against the Marines and National Guard, becoming a hemispheric symbol of resistance to US intervention.

title: Assassination of Sandino
summary: Sandino is lured to Managua and murdered by National Guard officers under Anastasio Somoza García, opening the way to the Somoza dictatorship.

title: Rise of the Somoza dynasty
summary: Anastasio Somoza García seizes the presidency, founding a family dictatorship that, directly or through proxies, rules Nicaragua until 1979.

title: Sandinista Revolution
summary: The FSLN overthrows Anastasio Somoza Debayle, ending the dynasty; the insurrection is estimated to have cost about 50,000 lives.

title: The Contra war
summary: The United States finances and arms the Contra insurgency against the Sandinista government; the war kills an estimated tens of thousands and devastates the economy. Casualty figures vary and are estimates.

title: Esquipulas II peace accord
summary: Central American presidents sign a regional peace plan committing to democratisation and an end to support for insurgencies.

title: Chamorro defeats Ortega
summary: Violeta Barrios de Chamorro wins the presidency for an opposition coalition; Ortega cedes power in a peaceful transfer that ends the war.

title: Ortega returns to power
summary: Having won the 2006 election, Daniel Ortega is inaugurated president again, beginning a long second period in office.

title: Re-election limits removed
summary: A 2009 court ruling and 2014 constitutional reform abolish term limits, enabling Ortega's continued re-election and the consolidation of FSLN control.

title: The 2018 crisis
summary: Protests against social-security cuts become a mass anti-government movement met with deadly force; the UN and IACHR document a death toll estimated upward of 300 (figures are estimates).

title: Contested re-election
summary: Ortega wins a further term after leading opposition candidates are detained, in an election widely criticised internationally.

title: Caesar campaigns in the Low Countries
summary: Julius Caesar's wars in Gaul bring Roman power to the peoples of the Rhine and Meuse delta, opening the region to Roman influence.

title: The Batavian Revolt
summary: Julius Civilis leads the Batavians and allied tribes in a revolt against Rome during the chaos after Nero's death; it is suppressed after roughly a year.

title: Christianisation of the Frisians
summary: Missionaries such as Willibrord begin converting the Frisians, tying the delta into the Christian, Frankish world of western Europe.

title: St. Lucia's flood
summary: A catastrophic North Sea storm surge drowns tens of thousands and reshapes the coastline, helping form the Zuiderzee and underlining the delta's perpetual struggle with water.

title: St. Elizabeth's flood
summary: A storm surge breaks the dikes of the Grote Hollandse Waard, drowning villages and thousands of people and creating the Biesbosch wetlands.

title: Habsburg inheritance
summary: Mary of Burgundy marries Maximilian of Habsburg, bringing the Low Countries under Habsburg rule after the death of Charles the Bold.

title: The Seventeen Provinces united
summary: Charles V's acquisition of Guelders completes the union of the Seventeen Provinces under a single Habsburg ruler.

title: Pragmatic Sanction
summary: Charles V decrees that the Seventeen Provinces shall be inherited together as an indivisible whole, treating the Low Countries as a single political entity.

title: Abdication of Charles V
summary: Charles V cedes the Low Countries to his son Philip II of Spain, whose centralising and anti-Protestant policies will ignite the Dutch Revolt.

title: The Beeldenstorm (Iconoclasm)
summary: Calvinist crowds destroy religious images in churches across the Low Countries, provoking a harsh Spanish crackdown and pushing the provinces toward revolt.

title: Eighty Years' War begins
summary: Open revolt against Spanish rule breaks out under William of Orange, beginning a struggle for independence that will last eighty years.

title: Union of Utrecht
summary: The northern provinces sign a defensive alliance that becomes the constitutional foundation of the Dutch Republic.

title: Act of Abjuration
summary: The States General formally renounce allegiance to Philip II of Spain, a de facto declaration of independence giving rise to the Republic of the Seven United Provinces.

title: Peace of Münster (Westphalia)
summary: Spain formally recognises Dutch independence in the Peace of Münster, part of the Peace of Westphalia, ending the Eighty Years' War.

title: Founding of the VOC
summary: The Dutch East India Company is chartered as the world's first publicly traded joint-stock company, with a monopoly on Dutch trade in Asia and powers to wage war and govern.

title: Founding of the Dutch West India Company
summary: The WIC is chartered for trade and conquest in the Americas and West Africa, becoming central to Dutch participation in the transatlantic slave trade.

title: Rembrandt paints The Night Watch
summary: Rembrandt completes his monumental militia portrait, an emblem of the artistic achievement of the Dutch Golden Age, now in the Rijksmuseum.

title: The Rampjaar (Disaster Year)
summary: France, England and allied bishops invade the Republic; the Dutch open the dikes to flood the land and halt the advance, and William III rises to power.

title: The Batavian Republic
summary: French Revolutionary forces and Dutch Patriots overthrow the stadtholderate and proclaim the Batavian Republic, ending the old Dutch Republic.

title: Kingdom of the Netherlands founded
summary: After Napoleon's defeat, the Congress of Vienna establishes the Kingdom of the Netherlands under William I, uniting the northern and southern Low Countries.

title: Belgian Revolution
summary: The southern provinces rebel and declare independence as Belgium, dividing the United Kingdom of the Netherlands; separation is recognised in 1839.

title: Liberal constitution of Thorbecke
summary: A new constitution drafted by Johan Rudolf Thorbecke establishes ministerial responsibility and parliamentary government, founding modern Dutch democracy.

title: Abolition of slavery
summary: The Netherlands abolishes slavery in Suriname and the Caribbean, freeing enslaved people, though most are forced into ten more years of supervised plantation labour.

title: German invasion and occupation
summary: Nazi Germany invades the neutral Netherlands; after the bombing of Rotterdam the country surrenders, beginning five years of occupation.

title: The Holocaust in the Netherlands
summary: From July 1942 the occupiers and Dutch collaborators deport some 107,000 Jews, mostly to Auschwitz and Sobibor; about 104,000 Dutch Jews are murdered, the highest proportion in Western Europe.

title: Indonesian independence
summary: After a violent four-year war, the Netherlands transfers sovereignty over the Dutch East Indies to the Republic of Indonesia.

title: North Sea flood and the Delta Works
summary: A storm surge floods the southwest, killing more than 1,800 people in the Netherlands and prompting the construction of the Delta Works flood defences.

title: Suriname becomes independent
summary: Suriname leaves the Kingdom of the Netherlands to become a sovereign state, while several Caribbean islands remain within the Kingdom. In 2022–2023 the Dutch government and King Willem-Alexander formally apologised for the Netherlands' role in slavery.

title: Battle of Hafrsfjord
summary: Harald Fairhair defeated a coalition of petty kings from the south-west at Hafrsfjord, the decisive victory by which tradition holds he became the first king over all of Norway.

title: Control of the coastal trade routes
summary: From his base at Avaldsnes on Karmøy, Harald Fairhair dominated the coastal sailing route that linked northern Norway with the markets of Kaupang and Hedeby, anchoring royal power in trade.

title: Death of Harald Fairhair and fragmentation
summary: On Harald's death his realm broke apart among his sons, beginning decades of dynastic conflict, though the idea of a single Norwegian kingship endured.

title: Conventional close of the Viking Age
summary: The era of large-scale Scandinavian raiding is conventionally closed in 1066, by which time Norway was a Christianising kingdom rather than a society of independent sea-kings.

title: Moster assembly and Christian law
summary: Olaf II established a nationwide church organisation and Christian law at Moster, banning non-Christian worship and making Christianity the kingdom's only permitted religion.

title: Battle of Stiklestad and the death of St Olaf
summary: King Olaf II was killed at Stiklestad. Declared holy within a year and enshrined at Nidaros, he became Norway's patron saint and eternal king, accelerating the Christianisation of the realm.

title: The national law of Magnus the Lawmender
summary: King Magnus VI codified a national law for the whole kingdom, one of the most advanced legal codes in medieval Europe and a mark of the consolidated Christian monarchy.

title: The Hanseatic Kontor at Bryggen
summary: German merchants of the Hanseatic League established their trading office at Bryggen in Bergen, which became Norway's foremost town and a hub of northern commerce for some four centuries, until 1754.

title: The Black Death reaches Norway
summary: Plague arrived by ship at Bergen and spread through the country, killing about half the population and devastating the native aristocracy and clergy, a turning point in Norwegian history.

title: The Kalmar Union
summary: Under Queen Margaret I of Denmark, Denmark, Norway and Sweden were united in the Kalmar Union, with Erik of Pomerania crowned common king; Norway became the weakest of the three partners.

title: Norway reduced to a Danish province
summary: After Sweden left the union, Norway remained tied to Denmark and was governed from Copenhagen, becoming in effect a Danish province while keeping its own laws and church.

title: The Treaty of Kiel
summary: Defeated in the Napoleonic Wars, Denmark-Norway was forced to cede Norway: by the Treaty of Kiel the Danish king renounced all claims to Norway in favour of the king of Sweden.

title: The Constitution of Eidsvoll
summary: A constituent assembly at Eidsvoll signed Norway's constitution on 17 May 1814, declaring the country a free kingdom with an elected Storting; the date became the national day.

title: Union with Sweden
summary: After a short war, Sweden accepted the Eidsvoll constitution and the Storting voted to enter a personal union with Sweden under a shared king, with Norway keeping its parliament and laws.

title: Romantic nationalism and a national culture
summary: A movement of romantic nationalism drew on Norwegian history, landscape and folk tradition; Ibsen, Grieg and Munch gave the nation a place in world culture and reinforced a separate identity.

title: Parliamentarism and the consular dispute
summary: The introduction of parliamentary government strengthened the Storting, while the conflict with Sweden over Norway's right to its own consular service drove the two countries apart.

title: Dissolution of the union with Sweden
summary: The Storting declared the union with Sweden dissolved; confirmed by referendum and settled peacefully at Karlstad, it made Norway a fully sovereign state for the first time in centuries.

title: Election of King Haakon VII
summary: After a plebiscite to retain a monarchy, the Storting elected Prince Carl of Denmark as king; he took the name Haakon VII, founding the modern Norwegian royal house.

title: The Svalbard (Spitsbergen) Treaty
summary: Signed in Paris, the treaty recognised Norwegian sovereignty over Svalbard while granting all signatories equal rights to economic activity and barring warlike use; Norway took over administration in 1925.

title: Eastern Greenland case
summary: The Permanent Court of International Justice ruled against Norway's claim to part of eastern Greenland, upholding Danish sovereignty over the whole island; Norway abandoned its claim.

title: German invasion and the Quisling regime
summary: Germany invaded on 9 April 1940; the king and government went into exile while Vidkun Quisling proclaimed a government, beginning five years of occupation and collaboration.

title: Norway joins NATO
summary: Abandoning prewar neutrality, Norway became a founding member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, anchoring its security in the Western alliance.

title: Oil discovered at Ekofisk
summary: Phillips Petroleum struck oil at the Ekofisk field in the North Sea, confirmed on Christmas Eve 1969; the discovery transformed Norway into a wealthy petroleum state with a vast sovereign wealth fund.

title: First referendum rejects the European Community
summary: A majority of 53.5 per cent of Norwegians voted against joining the European Community, keeping the country outside the integration process.

title: Second referendum rejects the European Union
summary: A majority of 52.2 per cent again rejected membership, this time of the European Union; Norway remained outside the EU while joining its single market through the EEA.

title: Barents Sea delimitation treaty with Russia
summary: Norway and Russia signed a treaty dividing the disputed 175,000 sq km of the Barents Sea and Arctic Ocean, ending a roughly forty-year dispute; in force from 2011, it replaced the Grey Zone arrangement.

title: Rise of the Licchavi dynasty
summary: The Licchavis establish the first well-documented dynasty of the Kathmandu Valley, using Sanskrit, minting coins and linking India and Tibet by trade.

title: Licchavi stone inscriptions
summary: Dense Licchavi-era inscriptions and chronicles make the valley one of the best-documented early states of the Himalayas, recording Hindu and Buddhist patronage alike.

title: Traditional founding of Kathmandu
summary: Tradition credits Raja Gunakamadeva with founding the town of Kathmandu during the Licchavi period; it would later give its name to the valley and the nation's capital.

title: Birth of the Buddha at Lumbini
summary: Siddhartha Gautama, of the Shakya clan, is born at Lumbini to Queen Mayadevi and King Suddhodana of Kapilavastu; he later founds Buddhism.

title: Ashoka's pillar at Lumbini
summary: The Mauryan emperor Ashoka visits Lumbini and erects an inscribed sandstone pillar, the earliest material evidence identifying the Buddha's birthplace.

title: Lumbini inscribed as World Heritage
summary: UNESCO inscribes Lumbini on the World Heritage List, recognising it as the birthplace of the Buddha and a centre of Buddhist pilgrimage since the 3rd century BCE.

title: Malla dynasty rules the valley
summary: The Mallas govern the Kathmandu Valley, codifying Hindu-influenced law and patronising the Newar temple architecture for which the valley becomes famous.

title: Valley divided into three kingdoms
summary: Yaksha Malla partitions the valley among his sons, founding the rival city-states of Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur, which compete over Tibet–India trade.

title: The Durbar squares and Newar art
summary: Malla patronage produces the palace squares, pagoda temples and stupas later recognised as the seven monument zones of the Kathmandu Valley World Heritage Site.

title: Conquest of the Kathmandu Valley
summary: Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha captures Kathmandu in 1768 and the Malla kingdoms by 1769, unifying the hill states into the kingdom of Nepal.

title: Anglo-Nepalese War
summary: A border dispute with British India erupts into the Gurkha War; Nepali resistance is fierce but the East India Company prevails.

title: Treaty of Sugauli
summary: Nepal cedes the Tarai and western conquests and admits a British resident, but keeps its independence and monarchy — never becoming a colony.

title: Jung Bahadur founds Rana rule
summary: After a violent seizure of power, Jung Bahadur becomes prime minister for life with the hereditary title of Rana, sidelining the Shah kings for a century.

title: Revolution restores the monarchy
summary: A palace revolt and popular movement end Rana dominance and restore the sovereignty of the Shah crown under King Tribhuvan.

title: Panchayat autocracy
summary: King Mahendra dissolves parliament in 1960 and bans parties; the 1962 constitution installs the partyless panchayat system under royal control.

title: People's Movement restores democracy
summary: Nationwide protests force King Birendra to legalise political parties and accept a multiparty parliamentary system, ending the panchayat era.

title: Maoist insurgency
summary: The Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist) wages a decade-long armed insurgency that kills more than 12,000 people before a 2006 UN-mediated peace accord.

title: Monarchy abolished, republic declared
summary: A newly elected constituent assembly ends more than two centuries of Shah rule and declares Nepal a federal democratic republic.

title: Gorkha earthquake
summary: A magnitude-7.8 quake near Gorkha kills about 9,000 people and devastates Kathmandu Valley heritage, including Durbar squares and the Dharahara tower.

title: Federal constitution promulgated
summary: Nepal adopts a permanent constitution establishing a secular federal republic of seven provinces with a bicameral Federal Parliament.

title: Polynesian voyagers settle Aotearoa
summary: The ancestors of the Māori reached New Zealand from East Polynesia in great voyaging canoes around 1300 CE, making it one of the last large landmasses on Earth to be permanently settled.

title: The Māori world takes shape
summary: Settlers adapted to a temperate land and developed the distinct Māori culture of iwi and hapū, organised by whakapapa and rangatira and expressed through carving, weaving, and the working of pounamu.

title: Settlement of the Chatham Islands
summary: Māori reached the remote Chatham Islands (Rēkohu) over 750 km east of the mainland, where the settlers became the distinct Moriori people with their own traditions.

title: Abel Tasman sights New Zealand
summary: The Dutch navigator Abel Tasman became the first European to sight New Zealand, charting a fragment of the west coast but leaving without landing after a deadly clash with Māori in Golden Bay.

title: James Cook charts the islands
summary: James Cook sighted New Zealand and over 175 days circumnavigated and accurately charted both main islands aboard HMB Endeavour, fixing the country's outline for European maps.

title: First Christian mission
summary: Samuel Marsden conducted New Zealand's first Christian service at Rangihoua in the Bay of Islands, beginning the missionary presence that spread Christianity, literacy, and new ideas among Māori.

title: The musket wars
summary: The spread of firearms unleashed a generation of devastating inter-tribal warfare, with leaders such as Te Rauparaha driving migrations and conquests that killed tens of thousands and reshaped the tribal map.

title: Treaty of Waitangi signed
summary: The Crown and Māori rangatira signed the Treaty of Waitangi, founding British New Zealand; its differing English and Māori texts — over sovereignty versus governorship — left a meaning contested to this day.

title: The New Zealand Wars
summary: Disputes over land and sovereignty erupted into war in Taranaki in 1860 and spread across the North Island, pitting imperial and colonial forces against iwi defending their land and autonomy until about 1872.

title: Land confiscation legalised (raupatu)
summary: The New Zealand Settlements Act 1863 gave a legal cloak to the confiscation of about 1.2 million hectares of Māori land, chiefly in the Waikato and Taranaki, often taking land from iwi who had not fought the Crown.

title: First refrigerated meat shipment
summary: The first cargo of frozen meat sailed from New Zealand to Britain, launching the refrigerated export trade in meat and dairy that would underpin the country's economy for a century.

title: Women win the vote
summary: New Zealand became the first self-governing nation in the world to grant women the parliamentary vote, the culmination of a petition campaign led by Kate Sheppard and the temperance movement.

title: New Zealand becomes a Dominion
summary: New Zealand's status was raised from colony to Dominion within the British Empire, a symbolic advance toward nationhood that left its close ties to Britain largely intact.

title: Gallipoli and the Anzac legend
summary: New Zealand and Australian troops landed at Gallipoli, a costly campaign that, despite ending in withdrawal, became a foundational national story commemorated each year on Anzac Day.

title: The welfare state
summary: The first Labour government's Social Security Act 1938 created a comprehensive system of pensions, benefits, and public health, building a 'cradle to grave' welfare state admired around the world.

title: Statute of Westminster adopted
summary: New Zealand adopted the Statute of Westminster, ending the British Parliament's power to legislate for it and confirming the country's full legal independence — the last Dominion to do so.

title: Waitangi Tribunal established
summary: The Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975 created the Waitangi Tribunal to investigate Crown breaches of the Treaty's principles; in 1985 its mandate was extended back to 1840, enabling redress for historic wrongs.

title: Te reo Māori made official
summary: The Māori Language Act 1987 recognised te reo Māori as an official language and created a commission to promote it, a landmark in the post-1970s Māori cultural renaissance.

title: Waikato-Tainui settlement and Crown apology
summary: The Crown signed a Deed of Settlement with Waikato-Tainui including a formal royal apology for the wars and confiscations of the 1860s, a model for later Treaty settlements such as Ngāi Tahu in 1998.

title: UNESCO World Heritage recognition
summary: Tongariro National Park — inscribed for its dual natural and Māori cultural significance — and Te Wahipounamu in the south were recognised by UNESCO, honouring both landscape and Māori heritage.

title: Magan supplies copper to Mesopotamia
summary: Sumerian texts record a land called Magan, identified with Oman, as a source of copper and diorite carried by sea to the city-states of Mesopotamia.

title: Beehive tombs and towers at Bat
summary: The Bronze Age communities of Bat, Al-Khutm and Al-Ayn raised monumental stone towers and dry-stone beehive tombs, later inscribed by UNESCO in 1988 as the most complete such collection in the world.

title: The frankincense trade flourishes in Dhofar
summary: The resin of the Boswellia sacra tree, harvested in Dhofar, became one of antiquity's great luxury goods, carried by caravan and ship from southern Arabia to the Mediterranean.

title: Khor Rori and the incense ports
summary: The port of Khor Rori (Sumhuram) and later Al-Baleed served as gateways for the export of frankincense and goods across the Indian Ocean, anchoring the Land of Frankincense.

title: Oman accepts Islam
summary: According to tradition, the inhabitants of Oman embraced Islam during the lifetime of the Prophet Muhammad, beginning the country's long Islamic history.

title: The first Ibadi imamate
summary: Around 750 CE the Ibadis established their first imamate in Oman under al-Julanda ibn Masud, an elected imam uniting temporal and religious authority and giving Oman a distinctive political identity.

title: Ibadism becomes Oman's defining school
summary: The Ibadi school of Islam took root across the Omani interior, making Oman its principal home and shaping a tradition of imams chosen for learning and piety rather than heredity.

title: Albuquerque captures Muscat
summary: The Portuguese under Afonso de Albuquerque stormed Muscat and other Omani coastal towns, beginning more than a century of Portuguese dominance over the coast.

title: Rise of the Yarubid imamate
summary: A member of the Yarub tribe was elected imam, founding the Yarubid dynasty that would unite Oman and lead the campaign to expel the Portuguese.

title: Expulsion of the Portuguese from Muscat
summary: The Yarubid imams recaptured Muscat in 1650, ending Portuguese occupation of the Omani coast and launching Oman as an Indian Ocean naval power.

title: Persian invasion amid Yarubid civil war
summary: A succession dispute fractured the Yarubid state, and the Persian ruler Nadir Shah's forces invaded and occupied parts of Oman, plunging the country into crisis.

title: Ahmad bin Said founds the Al Bu Said dynasty
summary: Ahmad bin Said, governor of Suhar, expelled the Persian invaders and was elected imam, founding the Al Bu Said dynasty that still rules Oman.

title: Treaty of Amity and Commerce with the United States
summary: Said bin Sultan's government concluded a Treaty of Amity and Commerce with the United States, the first bilateral treaty between Washington and an Arab Gulf state.

title: Said bin Sultan moves the capital to Zanzibar
summary: Said bin Sultan transferred his capital from Muscat to Zanzibar, making the island the commercial heart of his Indian Ocean empire and the chief power in East Africa.

title: Death of Said and the split of the empire
summary: On Said bin Sultan's death his realm was divided between his sons, one taking Muscat and Oman and the other Zanzibar, severing the African empire from Arabia.

title: Zanzibar separated from Oman
summary: Following an arbitration award, Zanzibar was formally separated from Muscat and Oman as an independent sultanate, severing the African empire and its revenues for good.

title: Accession of Sultan Said bin Taimur
summary: Said bin Taimur came to the throne and ruled an increasingly isolated and undeveloped Oman, leaning on British support to hold the country together.

title: Outbreak of the Dhofar rebellion
summary: An uprising began in the neglected southern province of Dhofar against Said bin Taimur's rule, growing into a Marxist-led insurgency that would dominate Omani affairs for a decade.

title: Oil exports begin
summary: Oman began exporting oil in commercial quantities, the start of the revenue that would later finance the country's modern transformation.

title: Qaboos accedes in a palace coup
summary: Qaboos bin Said deposed his father Said bin Taimur and became sultan, ending Oman's isolation and beginning the modernization drive known as the Renaissance.

title: Defeat of the Dhofar rebellion
summary: With British and Iranian support and a policy of amnesty and development, Qaboos's forces overcame the Dhofar insurgency, securing the unity of the country.

title: Promulgation of the Basic Law
summary: Sultan Qaboos issued the Basic Law, Oman's first written constitution, defining the organs and guiding principles of the state.

title: Death of Qaboos and accession of Haitham
summary: Sultan Qaboos died after nearly fifty years on the throne, and his cousin Haitham bin Tariq was sworn in as sultan the following day in a smooth succession.

title: New Basic Statute and Vision 2040
summary: Sultan Haitham issued a new Basic Statute establishing a formal crown prince and primogeniture succession, advancing Oman Vision 2040 and economic diversification.

title: Mature phase of the Indus cities
summary: Mohenjo-daro, Harappa and hundreds of other settlements reach their peak, with grid-planned streets, advanced drainage and standardised weights across a vast trading network.

title: Mohenjo-daro flourishes
summary: On the right bank of the Indus in Sindh, Mohenjo-daro becomes one of the civilisation's largest cities, renowned for its citadel and Great Bath; it is today a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: Decline of the Harappan cities
summary: The major cities are gradually abandoned as weakening monsoons and shifting rivers undermine the agricultural base, ending the civilisation's urban phase.

title: Achaemenid Persia annexes the Indus lands
summary: The Persian empire incorporates the Indus region as among its wealthiest provinces, bringing centralised administration and Aramaic writing to the area.

title: Alexander defeats Porus at the Hydaspes
summary: Alexander the Great crosses the Indus passes and defeats King Porus on the Jhelum, marking the easternmost reach of his empire before his army turns homeward.

title: Kanishka and the Gandhara golden age
summary: Under the Kushan emperor Kanishka, ruling from Peshawar, Mahayana Buddhism and the Greco-Buddhist Gandhara school of art flourish, depicting the Buddha in human form.

title: Muhammad ibn Qasim conquers Sindh
summary: An Umayyad army under Muhammad ibn Qasim conquers Sindh and southern Punjab, bringing Islam to the Indus lands for the first time.

title: Rise of the Delhi Sultanate
summary: Muslim dynasties ruling from Delhi extend their dominion over the Indus plains, deepening the region's Islamic culture over three centuries.

title: Babur founds the Mughal Empire
summary: Babur's victory ends the Delhi Sultanate and establishes the Mughal Empire, which makes Lahore one of its great capitals.

title: Badshahi Mosque built at Lahore
summary: Emperor Aurangzeb commissions the monumental Badshahi Mosque opposite the Lahore Fort, for centuries the largest mosque in the world and a landmark of Mughal Lahore.

title: Britain annexes the Punjab
summary: After defeating the Sikh kingdom, the British annex Punjab, completing colonial control over the lands that would become Pakistan.

title: Founding of the All-India Muslim League
summary: The All-India Muslim League is founded to represent the political interests of India's Muslims; it would become the engine of the Pakistan Movement.

title: The Lahore Resolution
summary: Meeting in Lahore, the Muslim League under Jinnah adopts the resolution demanding independent states for Muslims, the foundational charter of the Pakistan Movement.

title: Indian Independence Act passed
summary: The British Parliament passes the Indian Independence Act, partitioning British India and providing for the creation of the dominions of India and Pakistan.

title: Independence of Pakistan
summary: Pakistan becomes independent under the Indian Independence Act, with Jinnah as Governor-General and Liaquat Ali Khan as prime minister, comprising West and East Pakistan.

title: Partition migration and violence
summary: The Radcliffe Line divides Punjab and Bengal, and millions are uprooted across the new borders amid massacres and mass migration, with deaths estimated from the hundreds of thousands into the millions.

title: Assassination of Liaquat Ali Khan
summary: Pakistan's first prime minister is assassinated at a rally in Rawalpindi, deepening the political instability of the new state's early years.

title: Ayub Khan's military coup
summary: General Ayub Khan seizes power in Pakistan's first military takeover, beginning a decade of presidential rule and a recurring pattern of army intervention in politics.

title: Loss of East Pakistan and birth of Bangladesh
summary: After a brutal war and Indian intervention, Pakistani forces surrender at Dhaka and East Pakistan becomes the independent state of Bangladesh, dismembering the country.

title: Execution of Zulfikar Ali Bhutto
summary: Deposed in General Zia-ul-Haq's 1977 coup, former prime minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto is tried and hanged, ushering in a decade of military rule and Islamisation.

title: Pakistan conducts nuclear tests
summary: Following India's tests, Pakistan detonates nuclear devices in Balochistan, openly joining the ranks of nuclear-armed states.

title: Assassination of Benazir Bhutto
summary: Former prime minister Benazir Bhutto is assassinated at a rally weeks before national elections, after which civilian democratic rule is restored in 2008.

title: Spanish reach the isthmus
summary: Rodrigo de Bastidas and then Christopher Columbus explore the Caribbean coast of the isthmus, opening the region to Spanish colonisation.

title: Balboa sights the Pacific
summary: Vasco Nunez de Balboa crosses the isthmus and becomes the first European to see the Pacific Ocean from the Americas, claiming it for Castile.

title: Balboa executed
summary: Accused of treason by the governor Pedrarias Davila, Balboa is beheaded, the same year a new Pacific-coast city is founded.

title: Founding of Panama Viejo
summary: Pedrarias Davila founds Panama on the Pacific coast, the oldest European city on the Pacific shore of the Americas and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: Trade shifts to Portobelo
summary: Spain moves its Caribbean treasure port to Portobelo, whose fairs and fortifications anchor the trans-isthmus gold and silver route.

title: Henry Morgan sacks Panama
summary: The buccaneer Henry Morgan crosses the isthmus and takes Panama Viejo, which burns to the ground; the city is refounded on a new site in 1673.

title: Independence from Spain and union
summary: Panama declares independence from Spain and voluntarily joins Gran Colombia, remaining tied to Colombia after Gran Colombia dissolves.

title: Panama Railroad completed
summary: Spurred by the California Gold Rush, a U.S. company completes the trans-isthmus railroad, the shortest route between the oceans.

title: French canal attempt fails
summary: Ferdinand de Lesseps's company begins a sea-level canal but is defeated by disease and cost, collapsing in financial scandal.

title: Separation from Colombia
summary: With U.S. backing, Panama declares independence from Colombia and is swiftly recognised by the United States.

title: Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty
summary: The treaty grants the United States a Canal Zone across the isthmus in perpetuity and guarantees Panama's independence.

title: Panama Canal opens
summary: After a decade of U.S. construction, the lock canal opens to traffic, joining the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.

title: The Flag Riots
summary: Clashes over flying the Panamanian flag in the Canal Zone leave roughly two dozen Panamanians and several Americans dead, hardening demands to revise the 1903 treaty.

title: Torrijos takes power
summary: A military coup brings General Omar Torrijos to power; his government makes recovery of the canal its central aim.

title: Torrijos-Carter Treaties
summary: Torrijos and President Carter sign treaties abolishing the Canal Zone and committing to transfer the canal to Panama by the end of 1999.

title: U.S. invasion ousts Noriega
summary: Operation Just Cause removes General Manuel Noriega; casualty estimates vary, and Panamanian deaths are reported from several hundred to around a thousand.

title: Canal transferred to Panama
summary: At noon, the United States hands the Panama Canal to Panama, ending nearly a century of foreign control.

title: Panama administers the canal
summary: The Panama Canal Authority assumes full management of the waterway, anchoring a service and logistics economy.

title: Expanded canal opens
summary: New Agua Clara and Cocoli locks open, roughly doubling capacity and admitting larger Neopanamax vessels.

title: The Sacred City of Caral-Supe
summary: On the central coast the monumental city of Caral rises, with pyramids and sunken plazas, among the oldest urban centres of the Americas and the heart of the Norte Chico tradition.

title: Rise of Chavin de Huantar
summary: The highland temple of Chavin de Huantar becomes a centre of pilgrimage and oracle, spreading a powerful religious art and ideology across the central Andes.

title: Moche and Nazca cultures
summary: The Moche of the north coast create realistic pottery and adobe pyramids, while the Nazca of the southern deserts inscribe their giant lines and geoglyphs.

title: The Wari state
summary: From the Ayacucho region the Wari build an expansive state with roads and planned centres, prefiguring the imperial methods later used by the Inca.

title: Pachacuti transforms the Inca state
summary: After defending Cusco against the Chanca, Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui takes power and begins the swift expansion that turns the kingdom of Cusco into the empire of Tawantinsuyu.

title: Building of Machu Picchu
summary: The Inca raise the mountain sanctuary of Machu Picchu above the Urubamba, a masterpiece of stonework later recognised as a World Heritage site.

title: Empire at its height
summary: Under Pachacuti's successors the Inca extend Tawantinsuyu from present-day Colombia to Chile and Argentina, bound by roads, storehouses and the mita labour system.

title: Inca civil war
summary: A ruinous war of succession between the half-brothers Atahualpa and Huascar divides the empire just as the Spanish appear on its coasts.

title: Capture of Atahualpa at Cajamarca
summary: Francisco Pizarro's small force seizes the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca after massacring his escort, a decisive stroke in the conquest of Peru.

title: Execution of Atahualpa
summary: After paying a vast ransom in gold and silver, Atahualpa is executed by the Spanish; with the emperor dead, Pizarro advances on Cusco, taken later that year.

title: Founding of Lima
summary: Pizarro founds Lima, the City of Kings, on the coast; it becomes the capital of the future Viceroyalty of Peru, chosen over Cusco for its links to Spain.

title: Viceroyalty of Peru established
summary: Spain creates the Viceroyalty of Peru, second of its American viceroyalties, governing most of Spanish South America from Lima for nearly three centuries.

title: The silver of Potosi
summary: The opening of the great silver mountain of Potosi makes Peru the crown's richest American realm, worked through the forced-labour mita that consumes Indigenous lives.

title: Revolt of Tupac Amaru II
summary: Jose Gabriel Condorcanqui, taking the name Tupac Amaru II, leads a vast Indigenous uprising against Spanish rule across the southern Andes.

title: Execution of Tupac Amaru II
summary: Captured by the Spanish, Tupac Amaru II is forced to witness the deaths of his family and is then executed at Cusco; the rebellion is suppressed but remembered.

title: Independence proclaimed by San Martin
summary: Having entered Lima, Jose de San Martin proclaims the independence of Peru and becomes its Protector, though Spanish armies still hold the highlands.

title: Battle of Junin
summary: Bolivar's forces win a cavalry battle at Junin, opening the way to the final campaign against the royalists in the Peruvian sierra.

title: Battle of Ayacucho
summary: Antonio Jose de Sucre defeats the main royalist army and captures the viceroy at Ayacucho, sealing the independence of Peru and the new South American republics.

title: The guano boom
summary: Exports of coastal guano as fertiliser bring the Peruvian state a vast but poorly managed windfall, funding reforms including the abolition of slavery in 1854.

title: War of the Pacific
summary: Allied with Bolivia, Peru fights Chile over the nitrate-rich Atacama; Chilean forces occupy Lima in 1881 and Peru is defeated.

title: Treaty of Ancon
summary: Peru cedes Tarapaca to Chile and loses control of Tacna and Arica, a humiliating settlement whose final terms were not fixed until 1929.

title: The Leguia era
summary: Augusto Leguia governs Peru for eleven increasingly authoritarian years, promoting public works and a new constitution before falling in the Depression.

title: Founding of the Aprista movement
summary: Victor Raul Haya de la Torre founds the American Popular Revolutionary Alliance (APRA), a mass movement for social reform that shapes Peruvian politics for decades.

title: Velasco and the military reforms
summary: General Juan Velasco Alvarado leads a leftist military government that enacts sweeping agrarian reform and nationalisations before being eased from power.

title: Shining Path launches its insurgency
summary: As civilian democracy is restored, the Maoist Shining Path under Abimael Guzman begins an armed insurrection in the Ayacucho highlands, opening two decades of internal conflict.

title: Capture of Abimael Guzman
summary: Police capture the Shining Path leader Abimael Guzman in Lima; he is sentenced to life imprisonment and the insurgency is broken.

title: Truth and Reconciliation Commission report
summary: The Commission estimates that some 69,000 people died or disappeared in the 1980-2000 conflict, attributing most deaths to the Shining Path while also documenting state abuses.

title: Impeachment of Pedro Castillo
summary: President Pedro Castillo is impeached and detained after attempting to dissolve Congress; Vice President Dina Boluarte succeeds him amid deadly protests.

title: The Laguna Copperplate Inscription
summary: Dated to 900 CE, the earliest known Philippine document records a debt remission and reveals an organised society of datus and nobles already linked to the wider Malay and Javanese world.

title: Founding of the Sultanate of Sulu
summary: Islam takes political form as the Sultanate of Sulu rises around Jolo, becoming a powerful maritime state controlling trade across the Sulu Sea and toward Borneo.

title: Islam consolidates in Maguindanao
summary: The conversion of ruling families on Mindanao, associated with the missionary Sharif Muhammad Kabungsuwan, founds the Sultanate of Maguindanao, which expands through the 16th and 17th centuries.

title: Legazpi founds the first Spanish settlement at Cebu
summary: Miguel Lopez de Legazpi establishes Spain's first permanent settlement in the islands at Cebu, beginning more than three centuries of Spanish colonial rule.

title: Founding of Manila
summary: Legazpi establishes Manila as the capital of the Spanish colony; by the century's end most lowland Luzon and the Visayas are under Spanish control.

title: The Manila-Acapulco galleon trade
summary: For 250 years Spanish galleons exchange Chinese silks for Mexican silver across the Pacific, making Manila a hub of global commerce and an economic lifeline for the colony.

title: Founding of the Katipunan
summary: Andres Bonifacio establishes the secret revolutionary society the Katipunan, dedicated to winning Philippine independence from Spain by armed force.

title: Outbreak of the Philippine Revolution
summary: The discovery of the Katipunan sparks open revolt; Katipuneros proclaim the 'Cry' of defiance, beginning the armed revolution against Spanish rule.

title: Execution of Jose Rizal
summary: Spain executes the reformist writer Jose Rizal by firing squad in Manila; his martyrdom galvanises Filipinos and makes Spanish retention of the colony untenable.

title: Declaration of Philippine independence
summary: Emilio Aguinaldo proclaims independence from Spain at Kawit, Cavite, founding a provisional republic; this date later becomes the national Independence Day.

title: Treaty of Paris: Spain cedes the Philippines to the U.S.
summary: By the Treaty of Paris ending the Spanish-American War, Spain cedes the Philippines to the United States without consulting Filipinos, who had already declared independence.

title: The Philippine-American War
summary: Filipino nationalists under Aguinaldo fight the United States for independence; the war kills thousands of combatants and as many as 200,000 civilians before ending in 1902.

title: Establishment of the Commonwealth
summary: The Philippines becomes a self-governing Commonwealth under U.S. sovereignty, with Manuel L. Quezon as first president and a ten-year transition toward full independence.

title: Japanese occupation
summary: Japan occupies the Philippines during the Second World War; guerrilla resistance and the campaign to retake the islands leave over a million Filipinos dead and Manila in ruins.

title: Independence of the Republic of the Philippines
summary: The United States relinquishes sovereignty and recognises Philippine independence under the Treaty of Manila; Manuel Roxas becomes first president of the republic.

title: Marcos declares martial law
summary: Ferdinand Marcos imposes martial law under Proclamation No. 1081, arresting opponents and seizing one-man rule in a dictatorship that lasts until 1986.

title: People Power Revolution
summary: A peaceful uprising on EDSA, backed by defecting troops and the Catholic Church, drives Ferdinand Marcos into exile and installs Corazon Aquino as president, restoring democracy.

title: New democratic constitution
summary: Under President Corazon Aquino a new constitution is ratified, re-establishing democratic institutions, presidential term limits and a bill of rights after the Marcos dictatorship.

title: Return of the Marcos name to power
summary: Ferdinand 'Bongbong' Marcos Jr., son of the late dictator, wins the presidency, returning his family to the highest office 36 years after People Power.

title: First settlement of New Guinea
summary: People crossed from Southeast Asia to the joined landmass of Sahul, settling New Guinea in some of the earliest sea voyages and beginning one of the longest continuous human occupations on Earth.

title: Independent invention of agriculture at Kuk
summary: In the highland swamp of Kuk, communities drained wetlands to cultivate taro and bananas, one of only a few places on Earth where farming arose independently — recognised by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site.

title: Austronesian speakers reach the coasts
summary: A major migration of Austronesian-speaking peoples settles the coastal regions, layering a seafaring, trading world over the far older interior one.

title: More than 800 languages emerge
summary: Rugged terrain and long isolation gave rise to over 800 distinct languages and more than a thousand ethnic groups, making New Guinea the most linguistically diverse region in the world.

title: The first European visitor
summary: The Portuguese sailor Jorge de Meneses reaches the islands and calls them the ilhas dos Papuas; twenty years later a Spaniard names the main island New Guinea for its resemblance to the African coast.

title: The Kula ring and the trading seas
summary: Substantial exchange networks operate across New Guinea, the most extensive of them the Kula ring — a ceremonial circuit of shell valuables spanning hundreds of kilometres of open water.

title: Traders, missionaries, and labour recruiters arrive
summary: Whalers, plume hunters, and beche-de-mer traders worked the coasts, missionaries founded stations, and labour recruiters — including coercive 'blackbirders' — drew Melanesian workers to plantations in Queensland and Fiji.

title: The island is partitioned
summary: Germany proclaimed a protectorate over the north-east (German New Guinea) and Britain over the southern coast (British New Guinea) within days of each other, splitting eastern New Guinea between two empires.

title: Gold on the Mambare
summary: A strike on the Mambare River brings a gold rush and with it hostilities between miners and the people whose land they worked.

title: Australia takes over Papua
summary: Following the Papua Act of 1905, British New Guinea became the Australian Territory of Papua, and formal Australian administration began in 1906.

title: Australia occupies German New Guinea
summary: At the outbreak of the First World War, Australian forces seized German New Guinea, ending German colonial rule in the region.

title: League of Nations mandate over New Guinea
summary: Australia received a Class C League of Nations mandate to administer the former German territory as the Territory of New Guinea, governed from Rabaul and kept separate from Papua.

title: The Bulolo gold rush
summary: A major find along the Bulolo river draws a second rush, pulling outsiders and aircraft into country that had barely been mapped.

title: First contact in the highlands
summary: Australian prospectors and patrol officers walked into the central highlands and found densely populated farming valleys — perhaps a million people — entirely unknown to the outside world until then.

title: The Kokoda Track campaign
summary: Australian and Papuan troops halted the Japanese advance over the Owen Stanley Range toward Port Moresby and drove them back; over 600 Australians were killed in arguably Australia's most significant campaign of the war.

title: Papuan carriers and soldiers
summary: Papuan carriers moved supplies and the wounded across the mountains, and soldiers of the Papuan Infantry Battalion fought alongside Australian forces throughout the New Guinea campaigns.

title: The Bougainville campaign
summary: More than 30,000 Australians fought a long campaign of patrols and small actions on Bougainville, with over 500 killed, until the Japanese garrison surrendered in August 1945.

title: Papua and New Guinea united
summary: Australia combined its administration of Papua and the former German mandate into a single Territory of Papua and New Guinea, with the north held as a United Nations trust territory.

title: The first elections with indigenous voters
summary: Papuans and New Guineans vote for the first time, sixteen years after the two territories were joined under one administration.

title: West New Guinea transferred to Indonesia
summary: The United Nations hands control of the island's western half to Indonesia; the two governments agree the position of their shared border ten years later.

title: An elected indigenous majority
summary: A 64-member House of Assembly replaces the Legislative Council, and for the first time indigenous representatives hold most of the seats.

title: The country is named Papua New Guinea
summary: The two territories that two empires had drawn take a single name, four years before they take a flag.

title: Internal self-government
summary: Papua New Guinea achieved internal self-government with Michael Somare as chief minister, a peaceful step toward full independence from Australia.

title: Independence
summary: Papua New Guinea became an independent nation under Prime Minister Michael Somare; Australia transferred sovereignty and the United States recognised the new state the same day.

title: The Bougainville conflict
summary: A secessionist war over the Panguna mine, land, and environmental damage pitted Bougainvillean rebels against the PNG Defence Force; death-toll estimates range widely, commonly cited at roughly 10,000–20,000 and treated as estimates.

title: Sandline, the mutiny and the Burnham Truce
summary: The government hires mercenaries to reinforce its troops on Bougainville, provoking a mutiny in its own army; the Burnham Truce later that year ends the decade of armed struggle.

title: Bougainville Peace Agreement
summary: Following a 1998 ceasefire, a peace agreement created the Autonomous Region of Bougainville and promised a future referendum on the island's political status.

title: Bougainville independence referendum
summary: Bougainvilleans voted about 98 per cent for independence over greater autonomy; the non-binding result must be negotiated with PNG and ratified by its parliament.

title: The Baptism of Poland
summary: Duke Mieszko I accepted Christianity in the Latin rite, conventionally dated to 14 April 966, bringing his realm into Western Christendom and marking the traditional birth of the Polish state.

title: Congress of Gniezno
summary: Emperor Otto III made pilgrimage to Gniezno and an independent Polish church province was established, recognising the young state's standing within Christian Europe.

title: Coronation of Boleslaw I the Brave
summary: Boleslaw I was crowned king at Gniezno, the first ruler to bear the royal title of Poland and to win recognition of the realm as a kingdom rather than a duchy.

title: Testament of Boleslaw III and fragmentation
summary: The dying Boleslaw III Wrymouth divided Poland among his sons, beginning nearly two centuries of fragmentation into rival duchies that weakened the state against its neighbours.

title: Reign of Casimir III the Great
summary: The last Piast king reformed the law, founded the University of Krakow in 1364, expanded the kingdom and welcomed Jewish settlers, leaving Poland prosperous and consolidated.

title: Union of Krewo and the Jagiellonian dynasty
summary: The agreement at Krewo arranged the marriage of Queen Jadwiga to Jogaila of Lithuania, who was baptised as Wladyslaw II Jagiello, joining Poland and Lithuania under a new dynasty.

title: Battle of Grunwald
summary: Polish and Lithuanian forces under Wladyslaw II Jagiello destroyed the army of the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald, halting the Order's eastward expansion in the Baltic.

title: Copernicus publishes 'On the Revolutions'
summary: The Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus published his heliocentric theory, placing the Sun rather than the Earth at the centre of the cosmos and helping to launch modern astronomy.

title: Union of Lublin
summary: Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania united into a single federal state, the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, ruled by an elected monarch and a common Sejm, one of Europe's largest powers.

title: Relief of Vienna
summary: King John III Sobieski led the allied cavalry charge that broke the Ottoman siege of Vienna, marking the high point of the Commonwealth's military reputation in Europe.

title: The Deluge
summary: A devastating Swedish invasion during the Second Northern War ravaged the Commonwealth, causing enormous loss of life and population and accelerating the state's long decline.

title: The Partitions of Poland
summary: In three stages (1772, 1793, 1795) Russia, Prussia and Austria divided the Commonwealth among themselves, despite the reforming Constitution of 3 May 1791, ending Polish statehood for 123 years.

title: Congress of Vienna and the 'Congress Kingdom'
summary: The post-Napoleonic settlement re-divided the Polish lands and created a nominally autonomous Kingdom of Poland under the Russian tsar, entrenching foreign rule.

title: The November Uprising
summary: Poles in the Russian partition rose against the tsar; after initial successes the rising was crushed, bringing reprisals, the end of the Kingdom's autonomy and a wave of political exile.

title: The January Uprising
summary: A protracted guerrilla insurrection against Russian rule ended in defeat and severe repression, including executions, deportations to Siberia and intensified Russification.

title: Restoration of independence
summary: As the partitioning empires collapsed at the end of the First World War, an independent Polish state was proclaimed under Jozef Pilsudski, ending 123 years without statehood.

title: Battle of Warsaw
summary: Polish forces under Pilsudski halted the advance of the Soviet Red Army outside Warsaw, securing the independence of the young republic in the Polish-Soviet War.

title: German and Soviet invasion of Poland
summary: Nazi Germany invaded on 1 September, starting the Second World War in Europe; the Soviet Union invaded from the east on 17 September, and the two powers again partitioned Poland.

title: Auschwitz-Birkenau and the Holocaust on Polish soil
summary: Germany operated its largest concentration and extermination camp at Auschwitz-Birkenau, where some 1.1 million people, overwhelmingly Jews, were murdered as part of the genocide carried out across occupied Poland.

title: The Warsaw Uprising
summary: The Polish Home Army rose against the German occupiers in Warsaw; after 63 days the rising was crushed, much of the city was destroyed and tens of thousands of civilians were killed.

title: Establishment of communist rule
summary: Backed by the Soviet Union and rigged elections, a communist government consolidated power, founding the Polish People's Republic within the Soviet bloc.

title: Birth of Solidarity
summary: Strikes at the Gdansk shipyard led by Lech Walesa produced Solidarity, the first independent trade union in the Soviet bloc, which rapidly grew to about ten million members.

title: Martial law
summary: The communist authorities imposed martial law, banned Solidarity and interned its leaders, including Walesa, driving the movement underground for the rest of the decade.

title: Semi-free elections and the fall of communism
summary: Round Table talks produced partly free elections that Solidarity won overwhelmingly, ending communist rule in Poland and helping trigger the collapse of the Soviet bloc.

title: Accession to the European Union
summary: Poland joined the European Union, completing its return to the West after the fall of communism and accelerating its economic and political integration into Europe.

title: Taíno settle Borikén
summary: Arawak-speaking peoples develop the Taíno culture on the island they call Borikén, living in cacique-led villages and farming cassava and other tropical crops.

title: Columbus claims the island
summary: On his second voyage, Christopher Columbus reaches the island and claims it for Spain, naming it San Juan Bautista.

title: Ponce de León founds Caparra
summary: Juan Ponce de León establishes the island's first Spanish settlement and becomes its first governor; the colony is soon moved to the islet of San Juan.

title: El Morro and the fortification of San Juan
summary: Spain begins the great harbour castle of El Morro; with La Fortaleza and a city wall completed by 1678, San Juan becomes a key Caribbean stronghold.

title: El Morro repels Francis Drake
summary: The new fortifications withstand an attack by the English privateer Sir Francis Drake, proving San Juan's defences.

title: Grito de Lares
summary: Rebels seize Lares and proclaim a Republic of Puerto Rico; though crushed, the uprising becomes the foundational moment of the island's independence movement.

title: Abolition of slavery
summary: Spain abolishes slavery in Puerto Rico, a reform widely linked to the pressure generated by the Lares revolt.

title: Charter of Autonomy
summary: Spain grants Puerto Rico an Autonomous Charter conceding limited self-government, only months before the Spanish-American War.

title: Treaty of Paris cedes Puerto Rico
summary: After the Spanish-American War, Spain cedes Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines to the United States, ending Spanish rule on the island.

title: U.S. takes control of Puerto Rico
summary: American military rule begins; the island passes from Spain to the United States as a new colonial relationship is established.

title: Jones-Shafroth Act grants citizenship
summary: Congress collectively confers U.S. citizenship on Puerto Ricans and restructures the island's government, but without the federal vote.

title: Albizu Campos leads the Nationalists
summary: Pedro Albizu Campos becomes president of the Nationalist Party, intensifying the campaign for outright independence.

title: First elected governor
summary: Luis Muñoz Marín is elected the island's first governor; his administration launches Operation Bootstrap to industrialise the economy.

title: Commonwealth established
summary: Muñoz Marín proclaims the Constitution of the Commonwealth (Estado Libre Asociado), giving Puerto Rico self-government within U.S. sovereignty.

title: Status plebiscites
summary: Non-binding votes in 1967, 1993, and 1998 ask Puerto Ricans to choose among commonwealth, statehood, and independence, producing no binding resolution.

title: U.S. Navy leaves Vieques
summary: After years of civil disobedience following a 1999 death, the Navy ends weapons testing and withdraws from Vieques.

title: Debt crisis and PROMESA
summary: With debt declared unpayable in 2015, Congress passes PROMESA in 2016, installing a federal oversight board over the island's finances.

title: Hurricane Maria
summary: A devastating hurricane wrecks Puerto Rico's power grid and infrastructure, with an official death toll later estimated near 2,975.

title: Statehood plebiscites
summary: Votes in 2012, 2017, and 2020 favour statehood, but the 2017 ballot was boycotted and drew only about 23% turnout, and Congress has not acted.

title: Legendary founding of Gojoseon
summary: According to the Samguk yusa, the mythical Dangun establishes Gojoseon, traditionally regarded as the first Korean kingdom and a shared origin point for both Koreas.

title: Silla unifies the peninsula
summary: Allied with Tang China, Silla conquers Baekje in 660 and Goguryeo in 668, then expels the Tang, achieving the first unification of Korea under native rule.

title: Goryeo dynasty founded
summary: Wang Geon establishes the Goryeo dynasty, which reunifies the peninsula and gives rise to the Western name Korea.

title: Joseon dynasty founded
