summary: Nayib Bukele, a former mayor of San Salvador, wins the presidency outside the FMLN and ARENA, ending decades of two-party dominance.

title: Bitcoin made legal tender
summary: El Salvador becomes the first country in the world to adopt Bitcoin as legal tender alongside the US dollar.

title: State of exception and gang crackdown
summary: After a surge of gang killings, the government imposes a state of exception suspending constitutional protections and launches mass arrests; homicides fall sharply amid human-rights concerns over tens of thousands detained.

title: Bukele re-elected
summary: Despite a constitutional ban on consecutive terms, cleared by a loyal court, Bukele is re-elected by a landslide of about 85 percent of the vote.

title: Foundation by Saint Marinus
summary: By tradition the stonemason Marinus, fleeing Diocletian's persecution of Christians, founded a free community on Mount Titano on 3 September 301, the act from which San Marino dates its existence.

title: 'I leave you free from both men'
summary: Marinus is said to have left his followers the words 'Relinquo vos liberos ab utroque homine', freedom from both emperor and pope, enshrined as the founding ideal of Sammarinese liberty.

title: The Placito Feretrano
summary: The earliest surviving document to name the community of San Marino records a legal dispute over its liberties, the first firm attestation that a self-governing community existed on Mount Titano.

title: Refuge on a fortified mountain
summary: Set atop the steep limestone massif of Mount Titano and of little strategic value to its powerful neighbours, the community could govern itself in isolation, a continuity of free republican life that UNESCO would later recognise as stretching from the Middle Ages to today.

title: First Captains Regent
summary: The republic adopted its signature institution, two Captains Regent serving jointly for six-month terms; since the late-thirteenth-century statute their office has alternated every six months without interruption.

title: The earliest Statutes
summary: San Marino set down its first written statutes, with a fuller body of state law following by 1295, formalising the self-government of the mountain commune.

title: Self-government affirmed within papal Romagna
summary: As the Papal States consolidated their hold over the surrounding Romagna, San Marino preserved its autonomy by diplomacy and the recognition of its rights, the strategy of survival that kept the commune free among far greater powers.

title: Promulgation of the Leges Statutae
summary: The republic enacted the Leges Statutae Republicae Sancti Marini, a six-book written constitution governing the Council, the Regents and the courts; it remains in force as the foundation of San Marino's law.

title: An island within the Papal States
summary: By the seventeenth century the lands of the Church surrounded San Marino on every side; the republic guarded its autonomy and secured papal acknowledgements of its rights, but its independence rested on the goodwill of a far greater neighbour.

title: The Alberoni occupation
summary: Cardinal Giulio Alberoni, papal legate of Ravenna, occupied San Marino with troops, suspended its constitution and sought to annex it to the Papal States, abolishing the Captains Regent.

title: Civil resistance
summary: Rather than fight, the Sammarinese practised civil disobedience and sent clandestine appeals to Rome documenting the legate's abuses, refusing to accept the imposed government.

title: Independence restored by Clement XII
summary: Pope Clement XII condemned the occupation and on 5 February 1740 recognised San Marino's rights and restored its independence, an event still celebrated each year on the feast of Saint Agatha.

title: Napoleon's offer declined
summary: Napoleon offered San Marino friendship, artillery and an extension of territory to the sea; the republic accepted the gifts but declined the land, satisfied with its existing borders, and was recognised by the Treaty of Tolentino.

title: Recognition at the Congress of Vienna
summary: The post-Napoleonic Congress of Vienna confirmed San Marino's independence, leaving the ancient republic untouched as Europe's monarchies were restored around it.

title: Garibaldi given refuge
summary: Fleeing the collapse of the Roman Republic and pursued by four armies, Giuseppe Garibaldi crossed into San Marino with his followers and was granted asylum by the Captain Regent before escaping by night toward the Adriatic.

title: Lincoln made an honorary citizen
summary: Abraham Lincoln accepted honorary citizenship of San Marino, writing that 'although your dominion is small, your State is nevertheless one of the most honored, in all history' - the beginning of US recognition of the republic.

title: First treaty of friendship with Italy
summary: After Italian unification, San Marino and the new Kingdom of Italy concluded a treaty of friendship in 1862 confirming the republic's independence, the first of the agreements that secure its sovereignty as an enclave.

title: The Arengo and the end of oligarchy
summary: Summoned for the first time in three centuries, the Arengo of household heads voted on 25 March 1906 to abolish lifelong co-option of councillors, opening the way to democracy.

title: First modern democratic elections
summary: Following the Arengo vote, San Marino held its first modern democratic elections on 10 June 1906, ending centuries of oligarchic rule by co-opted councillors.

title: Fascist seizure of power
summary: Amid postwar economic distress the Sammarinese Fascist Party took control in 1923 and dissolved the Grand and General Council, ruling the republic for two decades in step with Mussolini's Italy.

title: The bombing of San Marino
summary: Despite the republic's neutrality, a British air raid on 26 June 1944, based on faulty intelligence later admitted, killed about sixty people in the small state.

title: Refuge for 100,000 and liberation
summary: Neutral San Marino, with a population under 15,000, sheltered more than 100,000 wartime refugees, including Jews; after fighting crossed its soil in September 1944 it was liberated and its neutrality restored.

title: Admission to the United Nations
summary: On the recommendation of Security Council Resolution 744 (25 February 1992), San Marino was admitted to the United Nations on 2 March 1992 as a full member state.

title: Treaties of friendship with Italy
summary: San Marino's sovereignty as an enclave is secured by treaties of friendship and good-neighbourliness with Italy first concluded in 1862 and renewed in 1939 and later, regulating relations while guaranteeing independence.

title: Member of the Council of Europe
summary: San Marino joined the Council of Europe, one of the steps by which the ancient republic took its place among the institutions of postwar Europe while keeping its full sovereignty.

title: Euro monetary agreement
summary: Under a monetary agreement with the European Union, in force since 2012 in place of an earlier 2000 accord, San Marino uses the euro as official currency and mints its own euro coins with national designs.

title: Islam takes root on the Gulf of Aden coast
summary: Merchants and seafarers crossing the narrow Gulf of Aden carried Islam to the northern Somali shore very early, making it one of the oldest centres of Muslim life in Africa, with Zeila among its earliest mosque towns.

title: Zeila flourishes as a trading emporium
summary: The port of Zeila became a major centre of medieval Islamic commerce, exporting goods of the interior and importing wares from across the Red Sea, and an early seat of Muslim political power on the coast.

title: Rise of the Adal Sultanate
summary: The Adal Sultanate emerged as a major Muslim power of the Horn of Africa, its trade reaching the sea through Zeila and other coastal towns — a heritage shared across the region.

title: Britain establishes the Somaliland Protectorate
summary: Through protection treaties signed with northern Somali clans from the 1880s, Britain established a protectorate over the coast to safeguard the sea route to India, administered separately from Italian Somaliland to the south.

title: The Dervish resistance of Sayyid Muhammad Abdullah Hassan
summary: A two-decade religious-led resistance to colonial rule, headed by Sayyid Muhammad Abdullah Hassan, tied down British forces until it was broken around 1920 in a campaign that included aerial bombing.

title: Italian occupation and British reconquest
summary: Italy overran the protectorate in 1940; British forces retook it in 1941 and went on to capture Italian Somaliland, placing the region under British administration for a period.

title: Independence of the State of Somaliland
summary: The British Somaliland Protectorate became the independent State of Somaliland on 26 June 1960, briefly receiving diplomatic recognition from a number of governments before its planned union with the south.

title: Union with the south forms the Somali Republic
summary: Five days after its own independence, the State of Somaliland united on 1 July 1960 with the newly independent former Italian Somaliland to create the Somali Republic, fulfilling the pan-Somali ideal of a single state.

title: Early northern discontent with the union
summary: Power, the capital and government institutions concentrated in Mogadishu, and a 1961 constitutional referendum drew weak support in the north, planting early grievances about an unequal union.

title: Siad Barre seizes power in Somalia
summary: A military coup brought Mohamed Siad Barre to power, ushering in an increasingly centralised and authoritarian regime under which northern Isaaq communities came to feel marginalised.

title: Founding of the Somali National Movement
summary: Isaaq émigrés established the Somali National Movement (SNM), an armed opposition movement that waged a guerrilla campaign against Siad Barre's government through the 1980s.

title: Bombardment of Hargeisa and Burao
summary: After an SNM offensive took much of Burao and Hargeisa, government forces subjected both cities to indiscriminate artillery and aerial bombardment, destroying the bulk of each and displacing hundreds of thousands.

title: Mass killing of Isaaq civilians (Isaaq genocide)
summary: Human-rights investigators documented the systematic killing of Isaaq civilians; a 2001 UN inquiry found the crime of genocide had been perpetrated by the government between 1987 and 1989. Death-toll estimates vary widely and are cited with caution.

title: Declaration restoring Somaliland's independence
summary: Meeting at Burao as Somalia collapsed, clan elders and the SNM declared the north's withdrawal from the 1960 union and the restoration of its independence — a declaration that won no international recognition.

title: Borama conference and the Guurti
summary: A months-long clan reconciliation conference at Borama produced a national charter, institutionalised the House of Elders (Guurti), and elected Mohamed Haji Ibrahim Egal president, anchoring the new polity in indigenous institutions.

title: Constitution approved by referendum
summary: A national referendum approved Somaliland's constitution by an overwhelming margin, a vote widely interpreted as also confirming popular support for independence.

title: Peaceful transfer of power by election
summary: In the 2010 presidential election an opposition candidate won and power passed peacefully between rivals, a rare democratic transition in the Horn of Africa that bolstered Somaliland's standing as a functioning self-governing polity.

title: Dispute over Sool and Sanaag
summary: Somaliland's claim to its eastern regions, contested with Puntland on clan grounds, produced fighting over Las Anod in 2007 and again in 2023, when local forces expelled Somaliland's troops and the area's control fell into question.

title: Memorandum of understanding with Ethiopia
summary: Somaliland and Ethiopia announced an MoU giving landlocked Ethiopia coastal access, reportedly in exchange for moves toward recognition; Somalia condemned it as a violation of its sovereignty, heightening tensions in the Horn of Africa.

title: Israel recognises Somaliland
summary: Israel announced formal recognition of Somaliland — the first UN member state to do so. Somalia condemned the step as unlawful, and a broad range of states at the UN reaffirmed that they regard Somaliland as part of Somalia.

title: Status still disputed and unresolved
summary: Somaliland continues to govern itself de facto and claims sovereignty, yet it is recognised by only one UN member state; the African Union and the great majority of governments still regard it as part of Somalia, leaving its status unsettled.

title: Hatshepsut's expedition to Punt
summary: Reliefs at Queen Hatshepsut's temple at Deir el-Bahri record a major Egyptian trading voyage to the Land of Punt, returning with myrrh trees, incense, gold and ivory—the most celebrated ancient evidence of the trade.

title: Egyptian trade with Punt begins
summary: Egyptian records attest trading contact with Punt from the Old Kingdom onward, drawing the Horn of Africa into pharaonic commerce in aromatic resins and luxury goods.

title: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea
summary: A Greek mariner's handbook describes ports along the Horn coast trading frankincense, myrrh, ivory and tortoiseshell with Egypt, Arabia and India, documenting the region's role in Indian Ocean commerce.

title: Cushitic pastoralists spread across the Horn
summary: Cushitic-speaking herding peoples, ancestral to the Somalis, expand across the arid interior of the Horn of Africa, establishing the pastoral, clan-based society that would endure into modern times.

title: Islam established on the Somali coast
summary: Trade and migration across the Gulf of Aden carry Islam to the Horn, and Muslim merchant communities take root in the coastal towns that become Somalia's medieval city-states.

title: Zeila, Berbera and Mogadishu flourish
summary: The ports of Zeila, Berbera and Mogadishu grow wealthy on Indian Ocean trade with Arabia, Persia and India; Mogadishu mints its own coinage and becomes a leading commercial centre.

title: Ibn Battuta visits Mogadishu
summary: The traveller Ibn Battuta describes Mogadishu as a large, prosperous Muslim trading city, attesting to the wealth of the Benadir coast in the medieval Indian Ocean world.

title: Wars of Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi
summary: From the Adal Sultanate, Imam Ahmad 'Gurey' launches the Futuh al-Habasha campaigns against Christian Ethiopia, conquering much of the highlands before his defeat and death in 1543 with Portuguese intervention.

title: Death of Ahmad and decline of Adal
summary: Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi is killed in battle against an Ethiopian–Portuguese force, halting the Muslim conquest of the highlands and beginning the decline of the Adal Sultanate.

title: The Ajuran Sultanate
summary: The Ajuran empire dominates southern Somalia and the Horn, controlling the Shabelle and Jubba river systems, building wells and fortifications and resisting Oromo and Portuguese incursions before fragmenting in the late 17th century.

title: Rise of the Geledi Sultanate
summary: The Sultanate of the Geledi emerges from the breakup of the Ajuran state, with its capital at Afgooye, and under the Gobroon dynasty comes to dominate the trade of southern Somalia.

title: Majeerteen and Hobyo sultanates
summary: In north-eastern Somalia the Majeerteen Sultanate (Migiurtinia) and the Sultanate of Hobyo control the coast and its maritime trade, maintaining centralised authority and treaty relations with outside powers.

title: Geledi at the height of its power
summary: Under Sultan Yusuf Mahamud Ibrahim the Geledi Sultanate reaches its peak, commanding tribute across southern Somalia, before the sultan's death in battle in 1848 begins a gradual decline.

title: British Somaliland protectorate
summary: Britain signs treaties with northern Somali clans and establishes a protectorate over the northern coast to safeguard supplies for Aden, creating British Somaliland.

title: Italy's protectorates and Italian Somaliland
summary: Italy signs protectorate treaties with the Hobyo and Majeerteen sultanates and occupies the Benadir coast, building up Italian Somaliland in the south; the Benadir colony is formally established in 1905.

title: The Dervish resistance
summary: Sayyid Mohammed Abdullah Hassan leads the Dervish movement in a twenty-year armed struggle against British, Italian and Ethiopian forces, defeating several colonial expeditions from fortified bases in the interior.

title: RAF bombing ends the Dervish state
summary: Britain uses the Royal Air Force to bomb the Dervish forts, including Taleh; the movement collapses and Sayyid Mohammed Abdullah Hassan dies of illness later that year.

title: Italian Somaliland joins Italian East Africa
summary: After Fascist Italy's conquest of Ethiopia, Italian Somaliland is merged into the new colony of Italian East Africa; Britain takes control of the region during the Second World War, holding both Somalilands by 1941.

title: Birth of the Somali Republic
summary: British Somaliland (independent 26 June) and the former Italian Somaliland unite on 1 July 1960 to form the independent Somali Republic, with Aden Abdullah Osman Daar as first president.

title: Siad Barre seizes power
summary: Following the assassination of President Shermarke, the army stages a coup and General Mohamed Siad Barre takes control, suspending the constitution and establishing a one-party socialist dictatorship.

title: Somali written in Latin script
summary: Barre's government adopts a Latin-based orthography for the Somali language and launches mass literacy campaigns, a lasting cultural achievement of the early socialist period.

title: The Ogaden War
summary: Somalia invades Ethiopia to annex the Somali-inhabited Ogaden; initial gains are reversed in 1978 when the Soviet Union and Cuba back Ethiopia, inflicting a costly defeat on Somalia.

title: War in the north
summary: Government forces wage a brutal counter-insurgency against the Somali National Movement in the north, bombarding Hargeisa and killing many thousands of civilians as armed opposition spreads.

title: Fall of Siad Barre
summary: Rebel forces drive Siad Barre from Mogadishu, ending his 21-year dictatorship; with no agreement on a successor, central authority collapses and the country descends into civil war.

title: State collapse and Somaliland's declaration
summary: Central government disappears as faction leaders fight for control; the former British Somaliland declares independence as the Republic of Somaliland, which remains internationally unrecognised but largely self-governing.

title: Famine and Operation Restore Hope
summary: Drought and civil war cause a famine that kills several hundred thousand people; the UN sets up UNOSOM and a US-led force launches Operation Restore Hope in December to safeguard relief.

title: Battle of Mogadishu ('Black Hawk Down')
summary: A US raid against a faction leader turns into a fierce urban battle that kills 18 American and many Somali fighters and civilians, hastening the withdrawal of foreign forces by 1995.

title: Islamic Courts Union and the rise of Al-Shabaab
summary: The Islamic Courts Union briefly controls much of the south before an Ethiopian intervention ousts it; from its militant wing emerges Al-Shabaab, which launches a prolonged jihadist insurgency.

title: Federal Government of Somalia established
summary: A new permanent Federal Government is formed under a provisional constitution—the first central government since 1991—as African Union forces push Al-Shabaab back from major cities.

title: Drought, famine risk and renewed offensive
summary: A severe multi-season drought pushes parts of Somalia toward famine while the Federal Government, backed by local clan militias and international forces, mounts a renewed offensive against Al-Shabaab.

title: Stefan Nemanja founds the Nemanjić state
summary: As grand chieftain of Raška, Stefan Nemanja united the Serb principalities and founded the Nemanjić dynasty, which would develop Serbia into a major medieval Balkan power.

title: Foundation of Studenica Monastery
summary: Stefan Nemanja founded the marble monastery of Studenica, retiring there around 1196; its churches became a masterpiece of the Raška school and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: Stefan the First-Crowned becomes king
summary: Stefan Nemanjić obtained recognition as king, raising the grand principality of Raška to the rank of a kingdom and earning the name Prvovenčani, the 'First-Crowned'.

title: Autocephaly of the Serbian Orthodox Church
summary: Saint Sava obtained from the patriarch at Nicaea the status of autocephalous archbishop, founding an independent Serbian church that bound religious and royal authority together.

title: Imperial coronation of Stefan Dušan
summary: Having expanded the realm across the southern Balkans, Stefan Dušan was crowned 'Emperor of the Serbs and Greeks' and raised the church of Peć to a patriarchate, the high point of medieval Serbia.

title: Death of Dušan and the empire's collapse
summary: The death of Stefan Dušan in 1355 led to the rapid disintegration of the Serbian Empire into rival principalities, leaving the Balkans divided as the Ottomans advanced.

title: The Battle of Kosovo
summary: On the Field of Blackbirds the army of Prince Lazar fought the Ottoman sultan Murad I; both leaders were killed and Serbian resistance was broken, making Kosovo the central event of national memory.

title: The Serbian Despotate
summary: A reduced Serbian state survived as the Despotate, ruled latterly from Smederevo and balancing between the Ottomans and Hungary, prolonging Serb statehood for another half-century.

title: Ottoman conquest of Serbia
summary: The Ottomans captured the fortress of Smederevo and extinguished the Despotate, absorbing the Serb lands into the empire and beginning nearly four centuries of Ottoman rule.

title: Patriarchate of Peć
summary: Elevated under Dušan, the patriarchate of Peć became the spiritual heart of the Serbs; its medieval churches in Kosovo survive as UNESCO World Heritage monuments of the Serbian Orthodox tradition.

title: First Serbian Uprising
summary: Led by Karađorđe, Serbs rose against Ottoman rule and for nearly a decade governed a self-proclaimed state, the opening act of the Serbian Revolution before its suppression in 1813.

title: Second Uprising and autonomy under Miloš Obrenović
summary: Miloš Obrenović led the Second Uprising; by 1830 the Ottomans granted the principality full autonomy under him as hereditary prince, establishing self-governing Serbia.

title: Independence recognised at the Congress of Berlin
summary: The Treaty of Berlin confirmed Serbia's full independence in international law and enlarged the principality, which became the Kingdom of Serbia in 1882.

title: The Balkan Wars
summary: Serbia drove the Ottomans from most of their European lands and, after the Second Balkan War, gained Kosovo, Metohija and much of Macedonia, nearly doubling its territory and alarming Austria-Hungary.

title: Assassination at Sarajevo
summary: The Bosnian Serb Gavrilo Princip assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo; Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia, and its declaration of war triggered the First World War.

title: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes proclaimed
summary: Prince Regent Alexander proclaimed the South Slav kingdom in Belgrade, uniting Serbia and Montenegro with former Habsburg lands under the Serbian crown; it was renamed Yugoslavia in 1929.

title: Royal dictatorship and renaming as Yugoslavia
summary: Amid party deadlock King Alexander suspended the constitution, imposed a royal dictatorship and renamed the state the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, deepening tensions among its nations.

title: Axis invasion and occupation
summary: Germany and its allies invaded and dismembered Yugoslavia in April 1941, placing Serbia under occupation and unleashing a multi-sided war of resistance and civil conflict.

title: Socialist Yugoslavia under Tito
summary: Tito's Partisans triumphed and built a socialist federation of six republics; after breaking with Stalin in 1948, Yugoslavia pursued non-alignment, with Serbia its largest republic.

title: Autonomy for Vojvodina and Kosovo
summary: The federal constitution of 1974 granted wide autonomy to the Serbian provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo, a settlement resented by many Serbs that would ignite conflict after Tito's death.

title: Milošević curtails Kosovo's autonomy
summary: Riding a wave of Serbian nationalism, Slobodan Milošević revoked the autonomy of Kosovo and Vojvodina, deepening the crisis that would break Yugoslavia apart.

title: Wars in Croatia and Bosnia
summary: As Yugoslavia disintegrated, war engulfed Croatia and Bosnia amid ethnic cleansing and atrocity, with Belgrade backing Serb forces and the federation collapsing into a rump Yugoslavia.

title: Kosovo War and NATO bombing
summary: After fighting between Yugoslav forces and the Kosovo Liberation Army and the displacement of Albanian civilians, NATO bombed Yugoslavia for some eleven weeks until Milošević agreed to withdraw from Kosovo.

title: UN Security Council Resolution 1244
summary: The Security Council placed Kosovo under an international civil (UNMIK) and security presence, granting substantial autonomy while reaffirming the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yugoslavia.

title: Fall of Milošević
summary: After disputed elections, mass protests in Belgrade forced Milošević from power; he was later tried at the ICTY in The Hague but died in 2006 before a verdict was reached.

title: Montenegro's independence and the end of the State Union
summary: Following a referendum on 21 May 2006, Montenegro declared independence; Serbia accepted the result and declared itself the successor state, dissolving the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro.

title: Kosovo declares independence
summary: Kosovo's assembly declared independence from Serbia, a step recognised by many Western states but rejected by Serbia, which continues to regard Kosovo as its autonomous province.

title: ICJ advisory opinion on Kosovo
summary: The International Court of Justice found that Kosovo's 2008 declaration of independence did not violate international law; Serbia continued nonetheless to withhold recognition.

title: Brussels Agreement
summary: In the EU-facilitated dialogue, Belgrade and Pristina reached the First Agreement of Principles, integrating Serb-majority northern Kosovo into Kosovo's institutions without constituting Serbian recognition.

title: Agreement on the Path to Normalisation (Ohrid)
summary: Serbia and Kosovo agreed to develop normal relations and recognise each other's documents and symbols, with an implementation annex agreed at Ohrid, while leaving the question of status unresolved.

title: Portuguese reach the uninhabited islands
summary: Portuguese navigators, by tradition João de Santarém and Pero Escobar, reached São Tomé and Príncipe, finding the equatorial islands entirely uninhabited and suited to bases for mainland trade.

title: São Tomé settled by Álvaro Caminha
summary: The first successful settlement of São Tomé was established under a crown grant to Álvaro Caminha, beginning the islands' colonisation.

title: Deportation of Jewish children and convicts
summary: The early colonists included Portuguese degredados and some two thousand children taken from expelled Jewish families and deported to be raised as Christians, most of whom died — part of the forced human mixture that founded Creole society.

title: Settlement of Príncipe
summary: The smaller island of Príncipe was settled under a similar crown arrangement, extending Portuguese control over the archipelago.

title: The first sugar-slavery plantations
summary: Settlers planted sugar cane worked by enslaved Africans, creating one of the earliest Atlantic plantation economies — a model later exported to Brazil and the Caribbean.

title: São Tomé a leading sugar producer
summary: The number of sugar mills grew to around sixty, making São Tomé Africa's foremost sugar exporter and for a time one of the world's largest producers.

title: The Angolar maroon community
summary: Escaped slaves formed independent communities in the forested interior; the Angolares, of disputed origin, settled the rugged south and lived by fishing, rejecting plantation labour.

title: The revolt of Rei Amador
summary: Rei Amador united maroons and plantation slaves in a great revolt that overran much of São Tomé, one of the largest slave uprisings of the Atlantic world.

title: Capture and execution of Rei Amador
summary: After his forces had held much of the island, Amador was captured and executed by the Portuguese; he endured as a hero of resistance and is now honoured as a national figure.

title: Dutch sack of São Tomé
summary: Dutch forces captured and occupied São Tomé for several years, razing sugar mills and accelerating the long decline of the island's plantation economy.

title: Coffee and cocoa introduced
summary: Coffee and then cocoa, brought from Brazil around the 1820s, were planted on the islands, reviving the plantation economy after the long decline of sugar.

title: Portugal decrees abolition of slavery
summary: Portugal began abolishing slavery in its empire, with an 1869 decree and full emancipation completed in the 1870s — though forced contract labour soon took its place.

title: World's largest cocoa producer
summary: Worked by the roças and their contract labourers, São Tomé became for a time the world's leading producer of cocoa.

title: Nevinson exposes 'A Modern Slavery'
summary: The journalist Henry Nevinson published A Modern Slavery, exposing the serviçal contract-labour system as forced labour, with around one in five workers dying each year.

title: Cadbury and the cocoa boycott
summary: After Joseph Burtt's report confirmed the abuses, the chocolate firms Cadbury, Fry and Rowntree announced a boycott of São Tomé cocoa, an international scandal that shamed Portugal but left coerced labour largely intact.

title: The Batepá massacre
summary: Under Governor Carlos Gorgulho, colonial police and settlers killed many Forro islanders who resisted forced labour — a massacre, with the toll uncertain, that became the founding memory of São Toméan nationalism.

title: Founding of the MLSTP
summary: São Toméan exiles organised the liberation movement that became the MLSTP, based for a time in Gabon, drawing strength from the memory of Batepá.

title: Carnation Revolution in Portugal
summary: A military coup overthrew the Lisbon dictatorship, and the new government moved to decolonise, opening the path to São Toméan independence.

title: Transfer of power negotiated
summary: Portuguese and MLSTP representatives met to arrange the handover, recognising the MLSTP as the islands' representative and establishing a transitional government.

title: Independence proclaimed
summary: São Tomé and Príncipe became an independent state, with the MLSTP's Manuel Pinto da Costa as its first president.

title: One-party socialist state
summary: A new constitution made the MLSTP the sole legal party; Pinto da Costa built a one-party Marxist state aligned with the Eastern bloc and nationalised the cocoa plantations.

title: Multiparty constitution adopted
summary: Amid economic crisis, a referendum approved a new constitution introducing multiparty democracy and presidential term limits, making São Tomé an early African democratiser.

title: First free elections
summary: Free multiparty elections brought Miguel Trovoada, a former prime minister returning from exile, to the presidency as an independent candidate.

title: Short-lived military coup
summary: Soldiers briefly seized power over corruption and oil-revenue grievances; President Fradique de Menezes was restored within days through negotiation.

title: Carlos Vila Nova elected president
summary: Carlos Vila Nova won the presidency, continuing a record of peaceful, contested elections that has made São Tomé and Príncipe one of the region's more stable democracies.

title: Indigenous settlement
summary: Arawak, Carib, and other Indigenous peoples occupy the coast and interior of present-day Suriname over many centuries.

title: European voyages sight the coast
summary: Columbus sights the Guiana coast in 1498 and Spanish expeditions sail along it soon after, but no lasting settlement follows.

title: English settlement under Willoughby
summary: Lord Francis Willoughby of Barbados plants an English sugar colony on the Suriname River, with the first enslaved Africans set to work.

title: Dutch capture of the colony
summary: A Dutch force from Zeeland seizes the English colony during the Second Anglo-Dutch War.

title: Treaty of Breda
summary: The peace confirms Suriname to the Dutch while England keeps New Netherland and New Amsterdam, the future New York.

title: The sugar-slavery economy
summary: Dutch Suriname becomes a plantation colony worked by enslaved Africans under exceptionally harsh conditions, with Paramaribo as its capital and port.

title: Maroon peace treaties
summary: Unable to defeat the Maroons, the Dutch sign treaties from the 1760s recognising the freedom of the Ndyuka, Saramaka, and Matawai and their lands in the interior.

title: Death of the Maroon leader Boni
summary: Boni, leader of the Aluku, is killed after years of guerrilla war against colonial forces, becoming an enduring symbol of resistance.

title: Abolition of slavery
summary: The Netherlands abolishes slavery in Suriname, though the freed are bound to a further decade of supervised apprenticeship until 1873.

title: Hindustani indentured labour
summary: Contract labourers from British India, the Hindustanis, are recruited to the plantations; roughly thirty-four thousand arrive over the period.

title: Javanese indentured labour
summary: Indentured workers from Java join the plantation workforce, numbering some thirty-three thousand and forming a community unique in the Caribbean.

title: Independence from the Netherlands
summary: Suriname becomes a sovereign state; Johan Ferrier is the first president and the United States recognises the nation the same day.

title: Military coup
summary: Non-commissioned officers overthrow the elected government; Desi Bouterse emerges as the regime's strongman, ruling by decree.

title: The December murders
summary: Fifteen leading opponents of military rule are seized and killed at Fort Zeelandia in Paramaribo, drawing international condemnation.

title: The Interior War
summary: The mainly Maroon Jungle Commando under Ronnie Brunswijk fights the army in the east until a ceasefire in 1989 and a peace accord in 1992.

title: Paramaribo named World Heritage
summary: UNESCO inscribes the Historic Inner City of Paramaribo, a Dutch colonial town blending European and local building traditions.

title: Bouterse conviction upheld
summary: A Surinamese court upholds a twenty-year sentence against former president Desi Bouterse for the 1982 December murders.

title: GranMorgu oil decision
summary: TotalEnergies and APA take a final investment decision to develop the offshore GranMorgu field on Block 58, with first oil expected toward 2028.

title: First woman president
summary: The National Assembly elects Jennifer Geerlings-Simons as Suriname's first woman president amid an economic crisis and the promise of oil.

title: Founding of Great Moravia
summary: Prince Mojmír I expelled Pribina of Nitra and united the principalities of Moravia and Nitra into Great Moravia, the first powerful Slavic state of central Europe, with the Slovak lands at its core.

title: Mission of Cyril and Methodius
summary: At Prince Rostislav's request the Byzantine brothers Cyril and Methodius arrived in Great Moravia, devised the Glagolitic script and translated the liturgy into Old Church Slavonic, founding a written Slavic culture.

title: Reign of Svatopluk I
summary: Under Svatopluk I Great Moravia reached its greatest extent and won recognition from the papacy, becoming the dominant power of the middle Danube before the state fragmented after his death.

title: Fall of Great Moravia to the Magyars
summary: Weakened by internal strife and Frankish wars, Great Moravia collapsed as the Magyars occupied the Carpathian Basin; a Magyar victory in 906–907 is taken to mark the end of the state.

title: Incorporation into the Kingdom of Hungary
summary: The Slovak lands were absorbed into the Kingdom of Hungary founded by Stephen I, beginning roughly a thousand years under the Hungarian crown as the region known as 'Upper Hungary'.

title: Universitas Istropolitana at Pressburg
summary: Slovakia's first university, the Universitas Istropolitana, was founded at Pressburg, an early sign of the towns' wealth and learning within the Hungarian kingdom.

title: Pressburg made capital of Hungary
summary: As the Ottomans overran central Hungary, the parliament promoted Pressburg (now Bratislava) to capital of the Kingdom of Hungary, a secure stronghold close to Habsburg Vienna.

title: Pressburg the coronation city
summary: Between 1563 and 1830, eleven Hungarian kings and eight royal consorts were crowned at St Martin's Cathedral in Pressburg, including Maria Theresa in 1741, making the city the ceremonial heart of the kingdom.

title: Bernolák's first written Slovak
summary: The Catholic priest Anton Bernolák codified an early written Slovak based on western dialects, an opening move in the national awakening that the next generation would supersede.

title: Štúr codifies literary Slovak
summary: Ľudovít Štúr and his associates resolved to base a unified Slovak literary language on the central Slovak dialects; his standard, refined by later grammarians, became modern literary Slovak.

title: Magyarization under the Compromise
summary: After the Austro-Hungarian Compromise the Hungarian government intensified Magyarization, pressing the Magyar language on Slovak schools and public life and denying the Slovaks recognition as a nation.

title: Slovaks in the revolutions of 1848
summary: During the revolutions of 1848 Slovak leaders, Štúr among them, set out national demands and raised volunteers, asserting the Slovaks as a distinct people within the Hungarian kingdom.

title: Czechoslovakia and the Martin Declaration
summary: Czechoslovakia was declared in Prague on 28 October 1918; on 30 October the Slovak National Council endorsed the union in the Martin Declaration, giving the Slovaks their first modern statehood alongside the Czechs.

title: Proclamation of the Slovak State
summary: As Germany dismembered Czechoslovakia, a separate Slovak State was proclaimed under the priest Jozef Tiso, a clerical-authoritarian regime that became a client and ally of Nazi Germany.

title: Deportation of Slovak Jews
summary: Slovakia became the first Axis partner to consent to the deportation of its Jews; between March and October 1942 some 57,000 Slovak Jews were deported to German-occupied Poland, with more than 60,000 of Slovakia's Jews murdered overall.

title: Slovak National Uprising
summary: The Slovak National Uprising broke out at Banská Bystrica against the Tiso regime and German occupation; after two months of fighting the rising was crushed on 27 October 1944 amid brutal reprisals.

title: Communist takeover
summary: The Communist Party seized full power in Czechoslovakia, establishing a one-party state under Soviet domination that would last for four decades.

title: Federalization of Czechoslovakia
summary: After the Prague Spring was crushed, the Constitutional Law of Federation of 28 October 1968 created, from 1 January 1969, a Slovak Socialist Republic within a federal Czechoslovakia, the Slovaks' first republic in name.

title: The Velvet Revolution
summary: Beginning with a student march in Bratislava on 16 November and protests in Prague the next day, six weeks of demonstrations led the Communist Party to give up its monopoly, ending one-party rule peacefully.

title: The Velvet Divorce
summary: Czechoslovakia split peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia on 1 January 1993, creating, after more than a thousand years, the first fully independent Slovak state.

title: ICJ judgment on Gabčíkovo–Nagymaros
summary: The International Court of Justice ruled in the Gabčíkovo–Nagymaros Project case (Hungary/Slovakia) that both states had breached their obligations over the Danube dam treaty of 1977, ordering them to negotiate in good faith.

title: Slovakia joins NATO
summary: Slovakia officially became a member of NATO on 29 March 2004, part of the largest single enlargement in the Alliance's history, anchoring the young republic in the Western security community.

title: Accession to the European Union
summary: Slovakia joined the European Union on 1 May 2004, completing its integration into Western Europe little more than a decade after independence.

title: Slovakia adopts the euro
summary: Slovakia adopted the euro on 1 January 2009, becoming the sixteenth member of the euro area and the first of the Visegrád states to do so.

title: Slavic settlement of the eastern Alps
summary: Slavic peoples migrated into the eastern Alpine valleys after the fall of Roman authority, becoming the ancestors of the Slovenes and establishing the linguistic foundation of the later nation.

title: Founding of Carantania
summary: The Slavic principality of Carantania took shape in the eastern Alps, centred north of present-day Slovenia, and is remembered for the enthronement of its dukes in the Slovene language at the Prince's Stone.

title: Carantania under Frankish overlordship
summary: Allied with Bavaria against the Avars, Carantania was drawn into the Frankish realm and gradually Christianised, ending its independence and binding the region to the Holy Roman Empire.

title: Carniola first attested
summary: The march of Carniola, in the central part of present-day Slovenia, appears in the records as a frontier zone of the empire, the nucleus of the duchy that would later define the Slovene lands.

title: Habsburgs acquire Carniola and Carinthia
summary: Carinthia and Carniola passed to the Habsburg dynasty, which already held Styria, bringing nearly all the Slovene lands under the rule that would last about six centuries.

title: Carniola raised to a duchy
summary: Carniola was elevated to the status of a duchy, consolidating the core territorial unit of the Slovene lands, with Ljubljana as its principal city.

title: First books printed in Slovene
summary: Primoz Trubar published the Catechismus and Abecedarium, the first printed books in the Slovene language, founding the literary language as a product of the Protestant Reformation.

title: Dalmatin's Bible and Bohoric's grammar
summary: Jurij Dalmatin published a complete Slovene translation of the Bible and Adam Bohoric the first Slovene grammar, proving the new written language fit for the most demanding texts.

title: Mercury found at Idrija
summary: Mercury was first discovered at Idrija, which grew into one of the world's two largest mercury mines; the site is today recognised by UNESCO as part of the Heritage of Mercury.

title: The Illyrian Provinces
summary: Napoleon organised the southern Slovene lands as the Illyrian Provinces of the French Empire, with Ljubljana as their capital, introducing reforms and giving the Slovene language a place in public life.

title: Austria regains the Slovene lands
summary: After Napoleon's defeat the Congress of Vienna restored Habsburg rule over the Illyrian territories, returning the Slovene lands to the Austrian Empire.

title: Preseren writes Zdravljica
summary: The poet France Preseren composed Zdravljica, a toast to liberty and the brotherhood of nations whose seventh stanza became the lyric of the Slovene national anthem after independence.

title: The United Slovenia programme
summary: During the Spring of Nations, Slovene activists demanded a single autonomous unit joining all Slovene districts of the monarchy with the Slovene language in public use, marking the birth of modern Slovene politics.

title: Birth of the Yugoslav kingdom
summary: After the brief State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs, the Slovene lands joined the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, proclaimed on 1 December 1918 and renamed the Kingdom of Yugoslavia in 1929.

title: The Carinthian Plebiscite
summary: In the disputed southern Carinthian basin, a majority of about 59 per cent voted to remain with Austria rather than join Yugoslavia, leaving a Slovene minority on the Austrian side of the border.

title: Treaty of Rapallo and the Italian border
summary: Under the Treaty of Rapallo, Italy gained the Slovene Littoral, the Karst and parts of Inner Carniola, subjecting a large Slovene population to Italian and later Fascist rule.

title: Axis partition of Slovenia
summary: Following the invasion of Yugoslavia, the Axis powers carved up the Slovene lands among Germany, Italy and Hungary, while a Liberation Front founded in Ljubljana launched armed resistance.

title: Slovenia within socialist Yugoslavia
summary: Slovenia became one of the six republics of Tito's Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, developing into its most prosperous and industrialised member.

title: London Memorandum on Trieste
summary: The United States, United Kingdom, Italy and Yugoslavia agreed to divide the Free Territory of Trieste, placing Zone A under Italian and Zone B under Yugoslav administration.

title: Treaty of Osimo
summary: Italy and Yugoslavia signed the Treaty of Osimo, making the partition of the former Free Territory of Trieste definitive and settling the long-disputed western border.

title: Plebiscite on independence
summary: In a plebiscite with 93.2 per cent turnout, some 88.5 per cent of all eligible Slovene voters chose independence from Yugoslavia, providing the mandate for statehood.

title: Independence and the Ten-Day War
summary: Slovenia declared independence on 25 June 1991; the Yugoslav army's intervention sparked the Ten-Day War, which the Slovenes won, leading to the Brioni Declaration of 7 July and the withdrawal of federal forces.

title: Slovenia joins NATO
summary: After a 2003 referendum approved by some two-thirds of voters, Slovenia became a member of NATO on 29 March 2004, anchoring its security in the Western alliance.

title: Accession to the European Union
summary: Slovenia joined the European Union on 1 May 2004 in the bloc's largest enlargement, the only former Yugoslav republic to accede in that wave.

title: Adoption of the euro
summary: Slovenia became the first of the 2004 entrants to adopt the euro, replacing the tolar on 1 January 2007 and completing its integration into the core of the European Union.

title: Arbitration Agreement with Croatia
summary: Slovenia and Croatia signed an Arbitration Agreement submitting their land and maritime border dispute, including Piran Bay, to the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague.

title: PCA award on the Piran Bay border
summary: The Permanent Court of Arbitration rendered its Final Award, fixing the land and maritime boundary through Piran Bay and granting Slovenia a junction to the high seas; Slovenia accepted the award, Croatia rejected it.

title: The trading town of Birka
summary: Birka on the island of Björkö in Lake Mälaren flourished as a key Baltic trading settlement, connecting Scandinavia by river route to the Byzantine Empire and the Islamic world, before its abandonment in the late tenth century.

title: Ansgar's mission and the first Christian congregation
summary: The Frankish missionary Ansgar founded at Birka the earliest known Christian congregation in Sweden, the first organised Christian presence among a still largely pagan people.

title: The Rus and the eastern river routes
summary: Swedish Norsemen, called Varangians or Rus, opened and dominated the river trade routes east through Ladoga and Novgorod toward Constantinople and Baghdad, exchanging furs, silver and slaves.

title: Christianization advances under royal patronage
summary: The conversion of the Swedes proceeded through the eleventh century by way of baptised kings and the founding of churches, even as paganism endured at the temple of Uppsala until the faith finally prevailed.

title: Formation of the Kalmar Union
summary: Queen Margaret united Denmark, Norway and Sweden under one monarch, her grandnephew Erik of Pomerania, creating a Scandinavian union intended to resist German power but soon dominated by Denmark.

title: Swedish revolts and the Sture regents
summary: Resentment of Danish dominance and of taxes and offices given to royal favourites fuelled recurring Swedish risings, with regents of the Sture family ruling Sweden in defiance of the union crown.

title: The Stockholm Bloodbath
summary: After capturing Stockholm and breaking his promise of amnesty, King Christian II of Denmark had some eighty-two Swedish nobles, clergy and citizens condemned as heretics and executed, including Gustav Vasa's father.

title: The Swedish War of Liberation
summary: Gustav Vasa raised Dalarna in revolt against Christian II, leading a peasant army that expelled the Danes and was declared regent of Sweden, ending Danish control of the realm.

title: Gustav Vasa elected king
summary: The Estates meeting at Strängnäs elected Gustav Vasa king of Sweden, dissolving the Kalmar Union and founding the hereditary Vasa monarchy that is regarded as the start of the modern Swedish state.

title: Reign of Gustav I Vasa
summary: Gustav Vasa built a centralised national monarchy, restored royal finances, suppressed revolts and founded the Vasa dynasty, ruling for nearly four decades as the architect of the modern Swedish kingdom.

title: The Reformation at Västerås
summary: At the Riksdag of Västerås, Gustav Vasa broke with Rome, transferred the Catholic Church's property to the crown and took control of church administration, beginning Sweden's transformation into a Lutheran state.

title: The complete Swedish Bible
summary: The first full Bible in Swedish, the work of the reformers Olaus and Laurentius Petri, was printed, advancing the Lutheran cause and shaping the Swedish written language and popular literacy.

title: The crown made hereditary
summary: The Estates declared the Swedish crown hereditary in the Vasa line, ending the older elective principle and entrenching the dynasty's hold on the throne.

title: Sweden enters the Thirty Years' War
summary: Gustavus Adolphus landed in Pomerania and intervened on the Protestant side, turning the tide of the Thirty Years' War with a series of victories before his death at Lützen in 1632.

title: Peace of Westphalia
summary: The settlement ending the Thirty Years' War granted Sweden Western Pomerania, Bremen and Verden and a vote in the imperial diet, confirming it as a dominant power on the Baltic and in northern Germany.

title: Treaty of Roskilde
summary: After Charles X Gustav's invasion of Denmark, the Treaty of Roskilde forced Denmark to cede Scania, Blekinge, Halland and Bohuslän to Sweden, fixing its southern border and marking the empire's territorial peak.

title: Battle of Poltava
summary: Peter the Great of Russia routed Charles XII's invading army at Poltava in Ukraine, a decisive defeat that broke Swedish military power and began Russian supremacy in eastern Europe.

title: Treaty of Nystad ends the empire
summary: The peace ending the Great Northern War ceded Sweden's Baltic provinces — Estonia, Livonia, Ingria and part of Karelia — to Russia, ending the age of greatness, though Finland was restored to Sweden.

title: Treaty of Fredrikshamn: the loss of Finland
summary: Ending the Finnish War, the Treaty of Fredrikshamn (Hamina) ceded the whole of Finland and the Åland Islands to Russia, stripping Sweden of about a third of its territory and people.

title: Bernadotte chosen as heir
summary: The French marshal Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte was elected Swedish crown prince, founding the Bernadotte dynasty; he ruled from 1818 as Charles XIV John, king of Sweden and Norway.

title: Treaty of Kiel and the union with Norway
summary: Denmark ceded Norway to Sweden by the Treaty of Kiel; Norwegian resistance produced not annexation but a personal union of the two kingdoms under one crown, lasting until 1905.

title: The great emigration to America
summary: Driven by rural poverty and population growth, roughly 1.3 million Swedes emigrated, chiefly to the United States, in one of the largest population movements of the age, reshaping Swedish society at home.

title: Peaceful dissolution of the union with Norway
summary: After Norway's parliament declared the union dissolved, Sweden agreed at Karlstad to a peaceful separation, recognising Norwegian independence without war in a settlement held up as a diplomatic model.

title: Universal suffrage and democracy
summary: Sweden completed its democratic transformation, introducing universal and equal suffrage for men and women, as the Riksdag rather than the crown became the centre of political power.

title: The 'people's home' (folkhemmet)
summary: Per Albin Hansson set out the vision of Sweden as a folkhemmet, a good home built on equality and mutual care, which the Social Democrats made the foundation of the modern welfare state.

title: Neutrality in the Second World War
summary: Sweden preserved its neutrality through the Second World War, remaining unoccupied while continuing controversial trade with Germany and offering refuge to those fleeing Nazi persecution.

title: Accession to the European Union
summary: After the end of the Cold War made strict neutrality obsolete, Sweden joined the European Union, while choosing to keep its own currency rather than adopt the euro.

title: Sweden joins NATO
summary: Prompted by Russia's invasion of Ukraine, Sweden abandoned over two centuries of non-alignment and became NATO's 32nd member on 7 March 2024, gaining the protection of Article 5.

title: Nguni peoples move south
summary: Bantu-speaking Nguni groups, among them the ancestors of the Dlamini, migrate southward into south-eastern Africa over the following centuries.

title: Reign of Ngwane III
summary: Ngwane III, traditionally regarded as the first king of the modern Swazi, leads his followers across the Pongola and is remembered for founding the kingdom, with a capital at Shiselweni.

title: Accession of Sobhuza I
summary: On the death of Ndvungunye, Somhlolo becomes king as Sobhuza I and soon faces the pressures of the mfecane and the Ndwandwe under Zwide.

title: Migration into central Eswatini
summary: Attacked by the Ndwandwe, Sobhuza I moves his people north and establishes a kingdom centred on the Ezulwini valley, the heartland of the Swazi nation.

title: Reign of Mswati II begins
summary: Mswati II succeeds Sobhuza I; he reorganises the army into age-regiments and expands the kingdom to its greatest extent. The Swazi take their name from him.

title: Death of Mswati II
summary: The death of Mswati II ends the era of Swazi conquest and expansion, leaving a unified nation at its widest territorial reach.

title: Mbandzeni becomes king
summary: Mbandzeni (Dlamini IV) ascends the throne; his reign coincides with an influx of European concession-seekers into the kingdom.

title: The concessions era
summary: Mbandzeni grants extensive land, grazing and mineral concessions to Boer and British fortune-seekers, ceding control over most of the kingdom's land and resources.

title: Protectorate of the South African Republic
summary: By convention the Transvaal (South African Republic) takes over the administration of Swaziland as a protectorate, while the kingdom keeps nominal autonomy.

title: A High Commission Territory
summary: After the Second Boer War, control of Swaziland passes from the Transvaal governor to the High Commissioner for South Africa, making it a High Commission Territory under direct British oversight.

title: Kept out of the Union of South Africa
summary: When the Union of South Africa is formed, Swaziland remains under direct British control; despite later South African requests, the territory is never transferred.

title: Sobhuza II becomes Ngwenyama
summary: Sobhuza II assumes the kingship and makes the recovery of Swazi land lost in the concessions a defining cause of his long reign.

title: Self-government and elections
summary: Under a revised constitution Swaziland gains internal self-government; the king's Imbokodvo National Movement wins the elections, setting the stage for independence.

title: Independence of Swaziland
summary: Swaziland becomes an independent kingdom, free of British rule, with Sobhuza II as head of state under a Westminster-style constitution.

title: Sobhuza II repeals the constitution
summary: King Sobhuza II repeals the independence constitution, dissolves parliament and bans political parties, ruling thereafter by decree as an absolute monarch.

title: Death of Sobhuza II
summary: Sobhuza II dies after a reign of some sixty years, among the longest in recorded history, leaving the throne to a regency.

title: Coronation of Mswati III
summary: Aged eighteen, Mswati III is crowned king, continuing the absolute monarchy with his mother Ntfombi as Ndlovukati.

title: Swaziland becomes Eswatini
summary: On the fiftieth anniversary of independence, Mswati III renames the country the Kingdom of Eswatini, reviving its siSwati name.

title: Pro-democracy protests
summary: Pro-democracy protests sweep Eswatini and are met by a deadly crackdown, the most serious challenge yet to one of the world's last absolute monarchies.

title: Portuguese navigators sight the islands
summary: Vasco da Gama's second voyage to India recorded the Amirantes group; further Portuguese sightings followed in the early 1500s, giving Europe its first knowledge of the archipelago.

title: First recorded landing by the Ascension
summary: Crew of the English East India Company ship Ascension landed and found the islands fertile and uninhabited, but the Company chose not to settle.

title: A haunt of pirates
summary: For a century and a half the empty islands were used by pirates as a hideout and watering place while they preyed on Indian Ocean shipping.

title: France claims and names the islands
summary: Corneille Nicholas Morphey laid a stone of possession and named the archipelago after finance minister Jean Moreau de Séchelles; the main island was named Mahé.

title: First permanent settlement
summary: Colonists, enslaved Africans and Indians established the first lasting settlement near Mahé to begin spice cultivation.

title: Spice and plantation economy
summary: Pierre Poivre promoted spice gardens to challenge the Dutch monopoly; cotton, coconut, maize and cinnamon followed, all worked by enslaved Africans.

title: Capitulations during the Napoleonic Wars
summary: Administrator Quéau de Quincy surrendered the islands to British squadrons several times, restoring French rule whenever they left.

title: Cession to Britain by the Treaty of Paris
summary: Seychelles was formally ceded to Britain with Mauritius and governed thereafter as a dependency of Mauritius.

title: Abolition of slavery
summary: Emancipation freed the several thousand enslaved Africans who formed the majority of the colony's population.

title: Liberated Africans resettled
summary: The Royal Navy landed thousands of Africans rescued from intercepted slave dhows, deepening the islands' Creole society.

title: Separate Crown Colony
summary: Seychelles was detached from Mauritius and constituted as a British Crown Colony in its own right.

title: Aldabra Atoll inscribed by UNESCO
summary: The raised coral atoll, home to the world's largest giant-tortoise population, was added to the World Heritage List for its outstanding natural value.

title: Vallée de Mai inscribed by UNESCO
summary: Praslin's palm forest, where the coco de mer grows wild, was recognised as a World Heritage Site for its unique flora.

title: Independence from the United Kingdom
summary: Seychelles became an independent republic within the Commonwealth, with James Mancham as first president and France-Albert René as prime minister.

title: Coup brings René to power
summary: Supporters of France-Albert René overthrew Mancham in an almost bloodless coup while he was abroad; René took the presidency.

title: One-party socialist state
summary: A new constitution made the Seychelles People's Progressive Front the sole legal party, with nationalisations and restrictions on the press.

title: Mike Hoare's mercenary raid fails
summary: Mercenaries disguised as a beer-drinkers' club and backed from South Africa tried to seize power; the plot collapsed and they hijacked an airliner to flee.

title: Return to multiparty democracy
summary: A new constitution restored multiparty politics; the first competitive presidential elections were held, won by René.

title: High-income tourism and tuna economy
summary: Tourism became the dominant sector and tuna fishing a leading export, lifting Seychelles to high-income status.

title: The kingdom of Ebla
summary: Ebla dominates northern Syria, trading and corresponding with Egypt, Sumer and Mesopotamia; its cuneiform royal archives, rediscovered in the 20th century, reveal a literate Bronze Age state.

title: Mari and the palace of Zimri-Lim
summary: The Euphrates city of Mari flourishes as a planned trading capital, its palace archives preserving thousands of diplomatic letters, until Hammurabi of Babylon destroys it in the 18th century BCE.

title: The Ugaritic alphabet
summary: At the coastal city of Ugarit, scribes devise a cuneiform alphabet of about 30 signs — one of the earliest alphabetic writing systems in history, ancestral in spirit to later Semitic and Mediterranean alphabets.

title: The Aramaeans and Aram-Damascus
summary: Aramaean tribes settle Syria and make Damascus the capital of a powerful kingdom; their Aramaic language becomes the lingua franca of the Near East for over a millennium.

title: Pompey annexes Syria to Rome
summary: The Roman general Pompey ends Seleucid rule and makes Syria a Roman province; its cities prosper and Syria becomes an early heartland of Christianity, with Paul converted on the road to Damascus.

title: Zenobia, Palmyra and the war with Rome
summary: Queen Zenobia of Palmyra breaks from Rome and conquers Egypt and Asia Minor, before the emperor Aurelian defeats her armies and captures the city; Palmyra's ruins are today a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: The Muslim conquest of Syria
summary: Arab Muslim armies defeat the Byzantines and take Damascus and Aleppo within a few years; over time Arabic and Islam spread, though Christian and other communities remain.

title: Damascus, capital of the Umayyad Caliphate
summary: Muawiya founds the Umayyad dynasty and makes Damascus the capital of the first great Islamic empire, ruling from Spain to Central Asia until the Abbasid revolution of 750.

title: The Great Mosque of Damascus
summary: Under Caliph al-Walid the Umayyads build the Great (Umayyad) Mosque of Damascus, one of the oldest and grandest mosques in the world, on a site holy to Roman, Christian and Muslim worship.

title: The First Crusade reaches Syria
summary: Crusader armies seize cities along the Levantine coast and capture Jerusalem in 1099, founding Crusader states and beginning two centuries of intermittent warfare across Syria.

title: Saladin recaptures Jerusalem
summary: Saladin, founder of the Ayyubid dynasty that united Egypt and Syria, defeats the Crusaders and retakes Jerusalem, ending nearly nine decades of Frankish rule and becoming a legendary figure of the age.

title: Mamluk rule over Syria
summary: The Mamluks supplant the Ayyubids and govern Syria from Egypt for over two centuries, halting the Mongols and presiding over a flourishing of trade and architecture in Damascus and Aleppo.

title: Ottoman conquest of Syria
summary: Sultan Selim I defeats the Mamluks and incorporates Syria into the Ottoman Empire, beginning four centuries of Ottoman rule over Damascus, Aleppo and the Syrian lands.

title: End of Ottoman rule
summary: During the First World War the Arab Revolt and Allied forces drive the Ottomans from Syria, ending four hundred years of Ottoman dominion and opening the way to French and British arrangements for the region.

title: Arab Kingdom of Syria and the French Mandate
summary: An independent Arab Kingdom of Syria under Faisal is proclaimed in Damascus, but French forces defeat it at Maysalun in July 1920, and the League of Nations assigns Syria to France as a mandate.

title: Independence — evacuation of French troops
summary: After international recognition in 1944, the last French soldiers leave Syria on 17 April 1946, marking full independence — still commemorated as Evacuation Day.

title: Union with Egypt — the United Arab Republic
summary: Syria merges with Nasser's Egypt to form the United Arab Republic in 1958, but resentment of Egyptian dominance dissolves the union in a 1961 coup.

title: Hafez al-Assad seizes power
summary: After the Ba'ath Party's 1963 coup and years of factional struggle, defence minister Hafez al-Assad takes control in November 1970, founding a family rule that would endure for over half a century.

title: Bashar al-Assad succeeds his father
summary: On Hafez al-Assad's death, his son Bashar becomes president; early hopes of reform give way to a continuation of the authoritarian, single-party system.

title: Uprising and the start of the civil war
summary: Arab Spring protests across Syria meet a violent state response; armed opposition emerges and the country descends into a civil war drawing in regional and global powers.

title: Human cost of the war
summary: The UN human rights office estimates about 306,887 civilians killed over the war's first decade, while the UN refugee agency reports more than 13 million people displaced — figures cited as estimates from authoritative bodies.

title: The Assad government falls
summary: A rebel offensive led by Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham takes Damascus on 8 December 2024; Bashar al-Assad flees the country, ending over five decades of Assad family rule, and an interim government is formed.

title: Discovery of Toumaï
summary: A team led by Michel Brunet recovered the cranium of Sahelanthropus tchadensis at the Toros-Menalla (TM 266) site in the Djurab desert; the species was announced in 2002 and dated to about seven million years.

title: Rise of the Sao culture
summary: The Sao settled the lower Chari and southern Lake Chad, producing celebrated terracotta and bronze figures across more than 350 known sites before being absorbed by later states.

title: Hummay founds the Sayfawa dynasty
summary: Mai Hummay, the first Muslim ruler of Kanem, displaced the Duguwa and founded the Sayfawa (Sefuwa) dynasty, which would rule the empire for some seven centuries.

title: Zenith under Dunama Dibalemi
summary: Mai Dunama Dibalemi brought Kanem to its peak, projecting power from the Fezzan to the southern savanna and deepening trade and diplomatic ties with North Africa and Egypt.

title: Sayfawa flee Kanem for Bornu
summary: Pressed by the Bulala, the Sayfawa abandoned Njimi and re-established the state in Bornu, west of Lake Chad, later founding the capital Ngazargamu.

title: Golden age under Idris Alooma
summary: Mai Idris Alooma modernised the army with Ottoman firearms and advisers and promoted Islamic law, leading Kanem-Bornu to its second peak.

title: End of the Sayfawa line
summary: The traditional office of mai was abolished in 1846 after the al-Kanemi shehus, who had risen during the Fulani jihad, took full control of Bornu.

title: Founding of the Wadai Sultanate
summary: Abd al-Karim led an Islamic revolt that overthrew the Tunjur and established the Wadai (Ouaddaï) sultanate east of Lake Chad, ruled from Abéché.

title: Wadai's commercial expansion
summary: Under Muhammad Sabun, Wadai expanded and prospered by controlling caravan routes from Abéché north to Benghazi and the east-west trade between Darfur and Bornu.

title: Baguirmi and the slave trade
summary: The sultanate of Baguirmi, Islamic from the sixteenth century, supplied large numbers of captives to the trans-Saharan slave trade alongside skins, ivory and cotton.

title: Rabih conquers Bornu
summary: Rabih az-Zubayr overran the Kanem-Bornu lands with one of the best-equipped armies in sub-Saharan Africa, ruling the basin as a military dictatorship.

title: Battle of Kousséri
summary: Converging French columns defeated and killed Rabih near the Chari River; the French commander Major Lamy also fell, ending Rabih's empire and opening the basin to France.

title: Chad joins French Equatorial Africa
summary: France organised the conquered territory and incorporated Chad into the federation of French Equatorial Africa, governing the south far more closely than the Muslim north.

title: Autonomous republic proclaimed
summary: Chad became an autonomous republic within the French Community, a step toward the full independence achieved in 1960.

title: Independence under Tombalbaye
summary: Chad gained full independence from France, with François Tombalbaye as first president; his southern-centred, authoritarian rule soon stoked northern grievances.

title: FROLINAT and the civil war
summary: The National Liberation Front of Chad (FROLINAT) launched an insurgency rooted in northern and Muslim discontent, beginning decades of civil war.

title: Coup kills Tombalbaye
summary: Tombalbaye was assassinated in a military coup; General Félix Malloum took power but could not end the conflict with FROLINAT's factions.

title: Habré seizes power
summary: Hissène Habré captured N'Djamena and made himself president, establishing a repressive regime amid continuing war and Libyan intervention.

title: The Toyota War with Libya
summary: Chadian forces under Hassan Djamous won a string of victories at Fada, Bir Kora and Ouadi Doum, driving the Libyan army back toward the disputed Aouzou Strip.

title: Idriss Déby seizes power
summary: Leading the Patriotic Salvation Movement (MPS) from Sudan, Déby overthrew Habré and installed himself as president, beginning a thirty-year rule.

title: ICJ awards Aouzou Strip to Chad
summary: The International Court of Justice ruled that the disputed Aouzou Strip belonged to Chad; Libyan forces withdrew by the end of May 1994.

title: Habré convicted of crimes against humanity
summary: The Extraordinary African Chambers in Senegal sentenced Hissène Habré to life for crimes against humanity, war crimes and torture, a landmark of universal jurisdiction; the verdict was upheld on appeal in 2017.

title: Death of Idriss Déby; son takes power
summary: Déby died of wounds from fighting on the front line; a military council named his son, General Mahamat Idriss Déby, transitional president, widely seen as an unconstitutional succession.

title: Ewe ancestors present in the region
summary: By oral tradition and scholarly reconstruction, the ancestors of the Ewe had moved into the Togo–Ghana region from the east, settling around Tado and later the town of Notsé before their dispersal.

title: The Ewe exodus from Notsé
summary: Ewe tradition tells of escape from the walled town of Notsé and the tyranny of King Agokoli, after which the people dispersed westward and southward — a foundational narrative of Ewe identity across Ghana, Togo and Benin.

title: Northern peoples and the Batammariba
summary: The Kabye, Tem, Bassar and other groups settled the northern hills, while the Batammariba built the takienta mud tower-houses of the Koutammakou, living in largely decentralised, clan-based communities.

title: Founding of Aného (Petit-Popo)
summary: Ane settlers fleeing conflict around Elmina in present-day Ghana founded Aného on the Togolese coast; it grew into the region's chief commercial and slaving port and would later briefly serve as a colonial capital.

title: The Slave Coast and the Atlantic trade
summary: The Togolese shore formed part of the 'Slave Coast', through whose ports including Aného enslaved Africans were trafficked to the Americas — a sustained system of violence and dispossession that reshaped coastal and interior societies.

title: From slaving to 'legitimate' trade
summary: As the slave trade was suppressed, commerce on the coast turned to palm oil and other goods, and German and other European merchant houses established themselves at Aného and along the shore.

title: Nachtigal proclaims a protectorate
summary: Gustav Nachtigal signed a protectorate treaty on the coast, associated with a ruler styled Mlapa, declaring German authority over the shore — the founding act of the colony of Togoland.

title: The Berlin Conference recognises Togoland
summary: At the Berlin Conference the European powers laid down rules for partitioning Africa and recognised the German protectorate that became the colony of Togoland.

title: Lomé becomes the colonial capital
summary: The seat of German administration moved to Lomé, which grew into the colony's main port and commercial centre, served by railways and roads built across Togoland.

title: A 'model colony' built on forced labour
summary: Germany promoted Togoland as a profitable Musterkolonie, but its plantations, railways and balanced budget depended on heavy taxation and the coercion of forced African labour.

title: Anglo-French conquest of Togoland
summary: At the start of the First World War, British and French forces invaded German Togoland; after destroying the Kamina wireless station, the German garrison surrendered on 26 August 1914.

title: Partition into British and French mandates
summary: Togoland was divided between Britain and France and formalised by the League of Nations as two mandates — British Togoland in the west and French Togoland in the east — splitting the Ewe and other peoples.

title: British Togoland votes to join Ghana
summary: In a UN-supervised plebiscite, about 58 per cent of British Togoland's voters chose union with the Gold Coast; the territory was integrated into Ghana, which became independent in 1957.

title: Olympio's CUT wins the elections
summary: Sylvanus Olympio's nationalist CUT defeated the pro-French parties in the 1958 elections, and Olympio became head of government of the Trust Territory of French Togoland.

title: Independence of the Republic of Togo
summary: French Togoland became the fully independent Republic of Togo, ending UN trusteeship; the United States recognised the new state the same day, and Olympio was elected its first president in 1961.

title: Assassination of Sylvanus Olympio
summary: Demobilised soldiers, among them Étienne Gnassingbé Eyadéma, killed President Olympio in Lomé — widely cited as the first military coup against an elected leader in independent sub-Saharan Africa.

title: Grunitzky installed as president
summary: After the coup, Nicolas Grunitzky, Olympio's brother-in-law and political rival, headed a civilian government, but his weak administration left the military as the country's decisive power.

title: Eyadéma seizes power
summary: Étienne Gnassingbé Eyadéma overthrew President Grunitzky in a bloodless coup and took the presidency, beginning a rule that would last nearly four decades.

title: Founding of the RPT one-party state
summary: Eyadéma created the Rassemblement du Peuple Togolais as Togo's sole legal party, the institutional core of his personal autocracy and cult of personality.

title: Pro-democracy pressure and a new constitution
summary: A wave of unrest forced Eyadéma to accept a multiparty constitution in 1992, but he retained power through disputed elections and the loyalty of the army.

title: Death of Eyadéma and dynastic succession
summary: Eyadéma died after nearly 38 years in power, then Africa's longest-serving ruler; the army installed his son Faure Gnassingbé, prompting an international outcry over the unconstitutional handover.

title: Faure Gnassingbé elected amid violence
summary: After ECOWAS pressure forced him to step down, Faure Gnassingbé won a disputed election; the contested result was followed by violence that UN estimates put at hundreds of deaths.

title: Founding of the Sukhothai kingdom
summary: Tai chiefs cast off Khmer rule and establish Sukhothai in the upper Chao Phraya valley, traditionally counted as the first independent Thai kingdom.

title: Creation of the Thai script
summary: King Ramkhamhaeng is traditionally credited with devising the Thai alphabet, recorded on a stone inscription dated 1292, the earliest known text in the Thai language.

title: Reign of Ramkhamhaeng the Great
summary: Sukhothai reaches its zenith under Ramkhamhaeng, who expands its reach, opens relations with China, and champions Theravada Buddhism.

title: Sukhothai absorbed by Ayutthaya
summary: After a century of decline, Sukhothai is reduced to a vassal and finally incorporated into the expanding kingdom of Ayutthaya.

title: Foundation of Ayutthaya
summary: King Ramathibodi I founds Ayutthaya at the meeting of three rivers, beginning a kingdom that would dominate the Chao Phraya basin for over four centuries.

title: First Burmese conquest of Ayutthaya
summary: Burmese forces capture Ayutthaya and reduce it to vassalage; the kingdom later recovers its full independence under King Naresuan.

title: Reign of King Narai and the French embassies
summary: Under Narai, Ayutthaya reaches a height of international contact, exchanging embassies with Louis XIV's France and welcoming traders from across Eurasia.

title: Sack of Ayutthaya by Burma
summary: A Burmese army storms and burns Ayutthaya after a prolonged siege, ending the kingdom and leaving the celebrated city in ruins.

title: Taksin establishes Thonburi
summary: Taksin rallies resistance after the fall of Ayutthaya, drives out the Burmese, and founds a new capital at Thonburi, where he is crowned king.

title: Founding of the Chakri dynasty and Bangkok
summary: After Taksin's fall, the general Chao Phraya Chakri takes the throne as Rama I, founds the Chakri dynasty, and establishes the new capital of Bangkok.

title: Reign of Rama I
summary: Rama I rebuilds the Siamese state, revising its laws and Buddhist scriptures and restoring its power over neighbouring vassal states.

title: The Bowring Treaty
summary: King Mongkut signs the Bowring Treaty with Britain, opening Siam to Western trade and granting extraterritoriality; comparable treaties with other powers follow.

title: Reforms of Chulalongkorn (Rama V)
summary: Chulalongkorn abolishes slavery, reorganises the administration, and modernises law, finance, education, and infrastructure, building a centralised modern state.

title: Franco-Siamese crisis and loss of Laos
summary: After French gunboats threaten Bangkok, Siam cedes the Lao territories east of the Mekong to French Indochina, the heaviest of its frontier concessions.

title: Anglo-French guarantee of Siam's independence
summary: Britain and France declare their mutual respect for the independence of Siam's core territory, fixing the kingdom as a buffer state between their empires.

title: Constitutional revolution
summary: The People's Party stages a bloodless coup forcing King Prajadhipok to accept a constitution, ending the absolute monarchy and creating a constitutional one.

title: Siam renamed Thailand
summary: The nationalist government of Phibun changes the country's name from Siam to Thailand, asserting a Tai national identity.

title: Alliance with Japan in World War II
