summary: Phibun's government allies Thailand with Japan and declares war on Britain and the United States, while the Free Thai movement under Pridi resists covertly.

title: Death of King Ananda and accession of Bhumibol
summary: King Ananda Mahidol (Rama VIII) dies of a gunshot in unexplained circumstances and is succeeded by his brother Bhumibol Adulyadej (Rama IX).

title: Student uprising ends military rule
summary: A mass student-led uprising, with royal intervention by King Bhumibol, forces the ruling generals from power and briefly opens a democratic interlude.

title: Coup against Thaksin Shinawatra
summary: The military ousts populist Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra while he is abroad, opening nearly two decades of conflict between his movement and the establishment.

title: Coup against Yingluck Shinawatra
summary: The army overthrows the government of Yingluck Shinawatra, ruling directly and later entrenching its role in a new constitution adopted in 2017.

title: Death of Bhumibol; accession of Vajiralongkorn
summary: King Bhumibol Adulyadej dies after a 70-year reign and is succeeded by his son Maha Vajiralongkorn (Rama X), who formally accepts the throne in December 2016.

title: The proto-urban settlement of Sarazm
summary: In the Zeravshan valley near Penjikent, Sarazm grows into one of the oldest proto-urban settlements in Central Asia, a centre of metallurgy and long-distance trade, later inscribed as Tajikistan's first UNESCO World Heritage Site (2010).

title: Alexander the Great in Sogdiana and Bactria
summary: After overthrowing the Achaemenid Persians, Alexander the Great campaigns through Sogdiana and Bactria, the Iranian lands of Transoxania that later peoples would regard as the Tajik homeland.

title: Sogdian merchants dominate the Silk Road
summary: Sogdian traders from Samarkand and Penjikent become the principal caravan merchants of the Silk Road, and the Sogdian language serves as the commercial lingua franca of Central Asia.

title: The Samanid Empire centred on Bukhara
summary: The Persian Samanid dynasty rules eastern Iran and Central Asia from Bukhara, making the city a focal point of Islamic civilisation and a hub of Persianate culture.

title: The reign of Ismail Samani
summary: Ismail I ibn Ahmad unifies the Samanid realm and rules from Bukhara as one of the dynasty's most famous sovereigns; he is revered today as a founding symbol of the Tajik nation.

title: Rudaki and the rebirth of Persian poetry
summary: At the Samanid court in Bukhara, the poet Rudaki composes in New Persian and is honoured as the father of Persian poetry, anchoring the literary heritage Tajiks claim as their own.

title: Karakhanid conquest of Bukhara
summary: The Turkic Karakhanids capture Bukhara, ending Samanid rule in Transoxania and opening centuries of Turkic and Mongol domination over the region.

title: The Mongol conquest of Transoxania
summary: Genghis Khan's armies sweep through Central Asia, sacking Bukhara and Samarkand, ushering in centuries of Mongol and Turko-Mongol rule over the Persian-speaking population.

title: Timur makes Samarkand his capital
summary: The conqueror Timur (Tamerlane) builds a Timurid empire centred on Samarkand, whose courts become renowned centres of Persianate art, science and architecture.

title: Division between Bukhara and Kokand
summary: The territory of present-day Tajikistan is split mainly between the Emirate of Bukhara, which holds the south, and the Khanate of Kokand, which controls the northern Ferghana fringe.

title: Bukhara becomes a Russian protectorate
summary: Defeated by Russian forces, the Emir of Bukhara accepts Russian terms in 1868; the emirate becomes a protectorate and the northern Tajik lands are absorbed into Russian Turkestan.

title: Creation of the Tajik ASSR
summary: In the Soviet national delimitation of Central Asia, a Tajik Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic is established within the Uzbek SSR, with Dushanbe as its capital.

title: The Tajik SSR and the loss of Bukhara and Samarkand
summary: The Tajik ASSR is detached from Uzbekistan and elevated to a full union republic, but the historic Persian-speaking cities of Bukhara and Samarkand are left within the Uzbek SSR.

title: Declaration of independence
summary: As the Soviet Union disintegrates, the Supreme Soviet of the Tajik SSR declares the state independence of the Republic of Tajikistan — the country's founding moment and national day.

title: The Tajik civil war
summary: Civil war erupts between the post-communist government and an Islamic-democratic opposition alliance; it causes massive displacement and a death toll that remains contested and is best treated as an estimate.

title: Emomali Rahmon elected president; UNMOT established
summary: Emomali Rahmon, leader of the government side since 1992, is elected president; the UN establishes the Mission of Observers in Tajikistan (UNMOT) to monitor the ceasefire.

title: UN-brokered General Peace Agreement
summary: President Rahmon and United Tajik Opposition leader Said Abdullo Nuri sign the General Agreement on the Establishment of Peace and National Accord in Moscow, ending the civil war under UN auspices.

title: Tajik National Park inscribed by UNESCO
summary: The Tajik National Park (Mountains of the Pamirs), covering roughly 18 per cent of the country, becomes Tajikistan's first natural World Heritage Site, protecting the 'Roof of the World'.

title: Rahmon named 'Leader of the Nation'
summary: Parliament grants Emomali Rahmon the title 'Founder of Peace and National Unity — Leader of the Nation', extending his authority as his long rule continues.

title: A remittance-dependent economy
summary: Remittances from Tajik labour migrants, mostly working in Russia, reach close to half of GDP — among the highest shares in the world — leaving the economy heavily exposed to external shocks.

title: The Margiana oasis civilisation (BMAC)
summary: The Bronze Age Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex flourished in the southern Karakum oases, its Margiana centre at Gonur Depe — monumental architecture, irrigation farming and fine metalwork later excavated by Viktor Sarianidi.

title: Rise of the Parthian Empire
summary: The nomadic Parni founded the Parthian state, which grew into an empire ruling Iran and Central Asia for nearly five centuries and rivalling Rome, with Nisa among its early royal centres.

title: Royal city of Nisa
summary: Old and New Nisa, near modern Ashgabat, served as an early capital and royal residence of the Parthian Empire, with palaces, temples and treasuries that fused Hellenistic and Iranian art.

title: Nisa inscribed by UNESCO
summary: The Parthian Fortresses of Nisa were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2007 as an exceptional record of the Parthian civilisation at one of its earliest and most important cities.

title: Merv under the Arab caliphate
summary: After the fall of Sasanian Persia, Merv became a key garrison and administrative centre of the Arab caliphate in Khorasan, a base for the spread of Islam and for campaigns further into Central Asia.

title: Merv as Seljuk capital under Sultan Sanjar
summary: The Great Seljuk sultan Sanjar made Merv a capital; the city's population swelled and it became one of the largest and most cultured cities in the world, a hub of Silk Road science and faith.

title: Mausoleum of Sultan Sanjar
summary: Built at the death of Sultan Sanjar, the great domed mausoleum at the centre of Sultan Kala stands as the finest surviving monument of Seljuk Merv.

title: Mongol destruction of Merv
summary: A Mongol army under Tolui, son of Genghis Khan, besieged Merv during the conquest of the Khwarazmian Empire and massacred its population, ending the city's age as a great metropolis of the Islamic world.

title: Magtymguly Pyragy and Turkmen poetry
summary: The poet Magtymguly Pyragy (1724–c. 1807) wrote in the Turkmen language and called for the unity of the tribes; he is revered as the father of Turkmen literature and national identity.

title: Russians found Krasnovodsk
summary: A Russian military force landed on the eastern Caspian coast and founded the port of Krasnovodsk (now Türkmenbaşy), opening the conquest of the Transcaspian region.

title: Battle of Geok Tepe
summary: General Mikhail Skobelev stormed the Teke Turkmen fortress of Geok Tepe by detonating a mine under its walls; the assault and ensuing massacre of thousands broke Turkmen resistance and secured Russian control of Transcaspia.

title: Russian annexation completed
summary: Following Geok Tepe, the Transcaspian region was annexed as part of the Russian Empire, completing the conquest of the lands of modern Turkmenistan.

title: Creation of the Turkmen SSR
summary: In the Soviet national delimitation of Central Asia, the Transcaspian and Turkmen lands were combined to form the Turkmen Soviet Socialist Republic, with Ashgabat as its capital.

title: Collectivisation and cotton
summary: Forced collectivisation seized herds and land and ended Turkmen pastoral nomadism amid fierce resistance, while Soviet planning imposed cotton monoculture across the republic's irrigated land.

title: Ashgabat earthquake
summary: A devastating earthquake struck Ashgabat, destroying the city and killing tens of thousands of people in one of the deadliest seismic disasters in Soviet history.

title: The Kara-Kum Canal
summary: Construction began on the Kara-Kum Canal, which carried water from the Amu Darya across the desert to irrigate the cotton lands — a vast project that opened new farmland at heavy environmental cost.

title: Independence declared
summary: Turkmenistan declared independence from the Soviet Union, with Saparmurat Niyazov as its first president; the United States recognised the new state in December 1991 and opened relations in 1992.

title: Permanent neutrality recognised by the UN
summary: The UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 50/80 welcoming Turkmenistan's declared permanent neutrality, the basis of its non-aligned foreign policy and a status unique in being recognised by a UN resolution.

title: Niyazov declared president for life
summary: Parliament declared Saparmurat Niyazov ('Türkmenbaşy') president for life, the apex of a personality cult that included renaming the calendar and making his Ruhnama compulsory reading.

title: Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow elected
summary: Following Niyazov's death in December 2006, Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow was elected president, beginning fifteen years of rule that retained tight one-party control and the neutral, gas-export policy.

title: Serdar Berdimuhamedow succeeds his father
summary: In an early election, Serdar Berdimuhamedow won the presidency over 70 percent of the vote, succeeding his father in a managed dynastic transfer of power, with the elder Berdimuhamedow remaining head of the People's Council.

title: Society of the liurai
summary: Timor is organized into numerous small kingdoms ruled by hereditary chiefs, the liurai, whose authority rests on kinship, ritual, and the sacred houses central to Timorese culture.

title: The sandalwood trade
summary: Timor's prized aromatic sandalwood is traded across maritime Asia to China, India, and beyond, drawing Malay, Chinese, and other merchants and giving the island wide renown.

title: Portuguese arrival and missions
summary: Portuguese traders seeking sandalwood and Dominican missionaries reach Timor and the Solor archipelago, beginning Catholic conversion and a loose Portuguese presence.

title: Capital established at Dili
summary: The Portuguese move their administrative seat from Lifau in Oecusse to Dili on the north coast, which becomes the lasting capital of Portuguese Timor.

title: Partition of the island
summary: A Portuguese-Dutch treaty divides Timor between Dutch West Timor and Portuguese East Timor, leaving Portugal the eastern half plus the Oecusse enclave; the border is finalized in the early 20th century.

title: Decolonization begins
summary: After Portugal's Carnation Revolution, Lisbon moves to decolonize Timor; rival Timorese parties, the pro-independence Fretilin and pro-integration Apodeti, vie over the colony's future.

title: Declaration of independence
summary: Fretilin unilaterally proclaims the independent Democratic Republic of East Timor in Dili as Portugal withdraws and an Indonesian invasion looms.

title: Indonesian invasion
summary: Indonesia launches a full-scale air and sea invasion of Dili, beginning an occupation marked from the start by mass civilian killing.

title: Annexation as 27th province
summary: Indonesia formally annexes the territory as its 27th province, Timor Timur; the United Nations refuses to recognize the annexation and affirms Timorese self-determination.

title: Santa Cruz massacre
summary: Indonesian troops fire on a peaceful pro-independence procession at Dili's Santa Cruz cemetery, killing at least 250; smuggled video footage brings the occupation to global attention.

title: Capture of Xanana Gusmao
summary: Indonesian forces capture resistance commander Xanana Gusmao in Dili; tried and sentenced to a long prison term in Jakarta, he continues to lead the movement from prison.

title: Nobel Peace Prize
summary: Bishop Carlos Belo and Jose Ramos-Horta share the Nobel Peace Prize for their work toward a just and peaceful solution to the conflict in East Timor.

title: Independence referendum
summary: In a UN-supervised popular consultation, 78.5 per cent of Timorese reject autonomy within Indonesia and choose a transition to independence.

title: Post-ballot violence and INTERFET
summary: Pro-Indonesian militias unleash killings and destruction, displacing some 500,000 people; the Australian-led INTERFET deploys from 20 September to restore order.

title: UN administration established
summary: Security Council Resolution 1272 creates UNTAET, granting the United Nations full authority to govern East Timor through the transition to independence.

title: Restoration of independence
summary: UNTAET hands over sovereignty; Timor-Leste restores its independence with Xanana Gusmao as first president and soon joins the United Nations.

title: The 2006 crisis
summary: The dismissal of disaffected soldiers triggers fighting in Dili that kills dozens and displaces tens of thousands, topples the prime minister, and brings back international peacekeepers.

title: Attack on the president
summary: Rebel soldiers shoot and gravely wound President Jose Ramos-Horta and attack Prime Minister Xanana Gusmao's convoy; both survive and the rebellion collapses.

title: Maritime boundary treaty with Australia
summary: Timor-Leste and Australia sign a treaty settling their disputed Timor Sea boundary, the first reached through UN conciliation, resolving claims over the Greater Sunrise gas field.

title: ASEAN membership
summary: Timor-Leste is admitted as the 11th member of ASEAN at the bloc's summit in Kuala Lumpur, its first enlargement in over two decades and the culmination of a years-long bid.

title: The first settlers reach the islands
summary: Archaic Ortoiroid peoples migrated from the South American mainland into Trinidad, the earliest of several waves of indigenous settlement that populated the twin islands over millennia.

title: Arawak and Carib peoples established
summary: By the time of European contact the islands were home to Arawakan-speaking groups such as the Nepoya and Suppoya and Cariban speakers such as the Yao, peoples whose roots lay in the Orinoco region.

title: Columbus sights Trinidad and Tobago
summary: On his third voyage Christopher Columbus reached Trinidad, naming it after the Holy Trinity, and sighted Tobago — the first European contact with islands then inhabited by Arawak and Carib peoples.

title: Spain founds San José de Oruña
summary: Antonio de Berrio took possession of Trinidad and founded San José de Oruña (St Joseph), establishing the first effective Spanish settlement on an island the crown had claimed but long neglected.

title: Raleigh raids the Spanish settlement
summary: Sir Walter Raleigh attacked the Spanish settlement while searching for El Dorado, underscoring how weak and exposed the Spanish colony on Trinidad remained.

title: The Cédula de Población
summary: King Charles III's Cédula de Población offered free land and tax breaks to Roman Catholic settlers, drawing French planters with their enslaved Africans and free coloureds and remaking Trinidad as a plantation society.

title: Britain captures Trinidad
summary: A British expedition under Sir Ralph Abercromby took Trinidad from Spain almost without a fight; the last Spanish governor, Chacón, signed the capitulation at the Valsayn estate.

title: Trinidad ceded to Britain by treaty
summary: The Treaty of Amiens confirmed Trinidad as a British colony, beginning more than a century and a half of British rule over the island.

title: Tobago ceded to Britain
summary: After centuries of being fought over by the Dutch, Courlanders, French, and British, Tobago was finally awarded to Britain by the Treaty of Paris of 1814.

title: Abolition of slavery
summary: Under Britain's Slavery Abolition Act, slavery ended in Trinidad and Tobago on 1 August 1834, though a transitional 'apprenticeship' kept the freed people tied to the estates.

title: Full emancipation
summary: The apprenticeship system ended on 1 August 1838, granting the formerly enslaved full freedom and leaving the colony's planters scrambling for new sources of labour.

title: Arrival of the Fatel Razack
summary: The ship Fatel Razack landed the first indentured Indian labourers in Trinidad; over 147,000 Indians would arrive under indenture by 1917, transforming the colony's population and culture.

title: Tobago united with Trinidad
summary: Britain amalgamated Tobago with the wealthier colony of Trinidad to cut administrative costs; in 1899 Tobago became a ward, creating the single colony of Trinidad and Tobago.

title: Commercial oil production begins
summary: The first commercial oil flowed near the Pitch Lake at La Brea, beginning the petroleum industry that would dominate Trinidad and Tobago's economy for over a century.

title: End of Indian indentureship
summary: The indentured labour system was abolished in 1917, by which time roughly 147,000 Indians had come to Trinidad, the majority remaining to build the Indo-Trinidadian community.

title: The 1937 labour revolution
summary: An oilbelt strike led by Tubal Uriah 'Buzz' Butler spread into riots across the colony, leaving at least fourteen dead and giving birth to Trinidad and Tobago's modern trade-union and nationalist movements.

title: Eric Williams founds the PNM
summary: The historian Dr Eric Williams founded the People's National Movement and won office, beginning a dominance of Trinidad and Tobago's politics that would carry the colony to independence.

title: Independence from Britain
summary: Trinidad and Tobago became an independent state within the Commonwealth, with Eric Williams as first prime minister; the United States recognised the nation the same day.

title: The Black Power uprising
summary: Mass marches and protests over racial and economic inequality, with a mutiny in the army, forced Eric Williams to declare a state of emergency in the most serious challenge to his government.

title: Trinidad and Tobago becomes a republic
summary: A new constitution replaced the British monarch with a president as head of state; the last governor-general, Sir Ellis Clarke, became the republic's first president.

title: The Jamaat al-Muslimeen coup attempt
summary: The Islamist group Jamaat al-Muslimeen seized Parliament and the state television station, taking the prime minister and others hostage for six days in a failed coup that left more than twenty people dead.

title: Atlantic LNG begins exports
summary: The Atlantic LNG plant at Point Fortin started production, confirming Trinidad and Tobago's shift from oil to natural gas and making it a major global LNG exporter.

title: Birth of the steelpan
summary: Musicians in Port of Spain fashioned the steelpan from oil drums after colonial bans on African drumming — the only acoustic instrument invented in the 20th century and now the national instrument.

title: Persad-Bissessar returns as prime minister
summary: In the April 2025 general election the United National Congress defeated the PNM and Kamla Persad-Bissessar was sworn in as prime minister, another peaceful transfer of power in the republic.

title: Foundation of Carthage
summary: Phoenician settlers from Tyre establish Carthage, which grows into a dominant Mediterranean trading power.

title: Hannibal's war on Rome
summary: In the Second Punic War Hannibal invades Italy with elephants and wins at Cannae, before defeat at Zama in 202 BCE.

title: Rome destroys Carthage
summary: Roman armies raze Carthage in the Third Punic War; its lands become the province of Africa.

title: Augustus refounds Carthage
summary: Carthage is rebuilt as the capital of Africa Proconsularis, a prosperous grain-exporting Roman province.

title: Amphitheatre of El Djem
summary: The colossal amphitheatre of Thysdrus is built, the largest Roman amphitheatre in Africa and a later UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: Vandals take Carthage
summary: Gaiseric's Vandals seize Carthage, making it the capital of a kingdom in North Africa.

title: Byzantine reconquest
summary: Belisarius restores Carthage to the Eastern Roman Empire, ending Vandal rule.

title: Founding of Kairouan
summary: Uqba ibn Nafi establishes Kairouan with its Great Mosque, the first Arab-Muslim capital of the Maghreb.

title: Aghlabid dynasty
summary: The Aghlabids rule Ifriqiya from Kairouan, rebuild the Great Mosque in stone, and conquer Sicily.

title: Fatimid Caliphate
summary: The Shia Fatimids overthrow the Aghlabids; after moving to Cairo in 972 they leave the Zirids to govern locally.

title: Hafsid dynasty rules from Tunis
summary: The Hafsids make Tunis a prosperous capital of trade and learning until the Ottoman conquest.

title: Ottoman conquest of Tunis
summary: The Ottomans take Tunis from Spain, making Tunisia an autonomous province of the empire.

title: Husaynid dynasty founded
summary: Al-Husayn ibn Ali is proclaimed bey, founding the dynasty that rules Tunisia until 1957.

title: First written constitution
summary: Tunisia adopts the Arab world's first written constitution amid attempts at modernising reform.

title: Treaty of Bardo
summary: The bey signs the Treaty of Bardo, placing Tunisia under a French protectorate.

title: Neo-Destour founded
summary: Habib Bourguiba and colleagues break from the Destour to form the Neo-Destour, the engine of the independence movement.

title: Tunisian independence
summary: France recognises Tunisian sovereignty; Bourguiba becomes prime minister.

title: Republic proclaimed
summary: The monarchy is abolished and Tunisia becomes a republic with Bourguiba as first president.

title: Code of Personal Status
summary: Bourguiba's government bans polygamy and expands women's rights, a landmark reform in the Arab world.

title: Ben Ali takes power
summary: Zine El Abidine Ben Ali removes Bourguiba in a bloodless coup, beginning twenty-three years of authoritarian rule.

title: Mohamed Bouazizi self-immolation
summary: A street vendor sets himself alight in Sidi Bouzid, triggering nationwide protests.

title: Jasmine Revolution ousts Ben Ali
summary: Ben Ali flees the country; the uprising sparks the wider Arab Spring and a Tunisian democratic transition.

title: The Neolithic town of Çatalhöyük
summary: On the Konya plain, the streetless settlement of Çatalhöyük flourished for over a millennium (c. 7100–5700 BCE), one of the world's best-preserved Neolithic towns, with roof-access houses and elaborate wall art.

title: Hattusa becomes the Hittite capital
summary: King Hattusilis I established Hattusa in north-central Anatolia as the capital of the Hittite kingdom, the seat of a Bronze Age empire that would rival Egypt.

title: Battle of Kadesh and the Hittite–Egyptian treaty
summary: The Hittites under Muwatalli II fought Ramesses II of Egypt at Kadesh; the conflict ended in one of history's earliest surviving peace treaties between the two empires.

title: Troy of the Iliad
summary: The fortified city at Hisarlık (Troy VI–VII) corresponds to the era of the Trojan War remembered in Homer's Iliad; the layered ruins were excavated from 1870 and inscribed by UNESCO in 1998.

title: Bronze Age collapse
summary: Around 1200–1180 BCE the Hittite state and Hattusa were destroyed amid the wider collapse of eastern Mediterranean civilisations, ending Anatolia's first great imperial age.

title: Fall of Lydia and Croesus
summary: The wealthy Lydian kingdom of western Anatolia, credited with pioneering coined money, fell to Cyrus the Great of Persia, bringing Anatolia under Persian rule.

title: Constantine refounds Constantinople
summary: Constantine the Great dedicated the rebuilt city of Byzantium as Constantinople, a new Christian capital on the Bosporus that would anchor the Roman and then Byzantine state for over a millennium.

title: Justinian completes the Hagia Sophia
summary: Emperor Justinian I inaugurated the great domed church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, the masterpiece of Byzantine architecture and for centuries the largest cathedral in the world.

title: Battle of Manzikert
summary: The Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan defeated and captured the Byzantine emperor Romanos IV at Manzikert, breaking Byzantine control of the interior and opening Anatolia to Turkish settlement.

title: Sultanate of Rûm at Konya
summary: Seljuk Turks established the Sultanate of Rûm in Anatolia, with Konya as its centre, fostering a rich Islamic culture associated with the mystic poet Rumi.

title: Foundation of the Ottoman emirate
summary: Osman I, leader of a frontier emirate in north-western Anatolia, is traditionally regarded as founder of the Ottoman dynasty around 1299, giving his name to the empire.

title: Battle of Kosovo
summary: Ottoman forces under Murad I defeated a Serbian-led coalition at Kosovo, cementing Ottoman dominance in the Balkans even as Murad died on the field.

title: Battle of Ankara and the Interregnum
summary: Timur (Tamerlane) crushed and captured Sultan Bayezid I at Ankara, plunging the Ottoman state into a decade of civil war before it recovered.

title: Fall of Constantinople
summary: After a 53-day siege, Sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople, ending the Byzantine Empire; the city became the Ottoman capital and Hagia Sophia was converted to a mosque.

title: Reign of Süleyman the Magnificent
summary: Süleyman I presided over the Ottoman Empire at its territorial and cultural height, from Hungary to the Arab lands, codifying law and patronising the architecture of Sinan.

title: First Siege of Vienna
summary: Ottoman armies under Süleyman besieged Vienna, marking the high-water mark of Ottoman expansion into central Europe before withdrawing.

title: Treaty of Karlowitz
summary: After the failed 1683 siege of Vienna, the Treaty of Karlowitz ceded Hungary and other lands to the Habsburgs, the first major Ottoman territorial retreat in Europe.

title: The Tanzimat reforms
summary: A wave of modernising reforms reorganised Ottoman law, taxation, education and the military in an effort to halt the empire's decline and integrate its diverse subjects.

title: Young Turk Revolution
summary: The Young Turk movement forced Sultan Abdülhamid II to restore the constitution, ushering in a turbulent constitutional era dominated by the Committee of Union and Progress.

title: The Armenian Genocide
summary: From 24 April 1915 the Ottoman government deported and massacred its Armenian population in death marches and killings across Anatolia and into the Syrian desert; most historians recognise these events as genocide, with deaths estimated from roughly 600,000 to 1.5 million.

title: Gallipoli campaign
summary: Ottoman forces repelled an Allied attempt to seize the Dardanelles; the defence brought the officer Mustafa Kemal to national prominence.

title: Treaty of Sèvres
summary: The Allied treaty with the defeated Ottoman government proposed partitioning Anatolia among Greece, Armenia, Italy, France and others; rejected by the nationalists, it triggered the War of Independence.

title: Turkish War of Independence
summary: Mustafa Kemal led a national resistance and a new Grand National Assembly in Ankara, defeating Greek, Armenian and French forces and ending the Allied occupation of Anatolia.

title: Treaty of Lausanne
summary: Replacing the Treaty of Sèvres, the Lausanne treaty secured international recognition of Turkey's sovereignty and borders, the legal foundation of the modern state.

title: Abolition of the caliphate
summary: The Grand National Assembly abolished the Ottoman caliphate and separated religion from the state, a cornerstone of Atatürk's secular reforms; a new constitution followed in April 1924.

title: The alphabet and language reforms
summary: Turkey replaced the Arabic script with a new Latin-based Turkish alphabet in 1928, part of reforms that sharply raised literacy and reoriented the nation toward Europe.

title: First multiparty election
summary: The Democrat Party won a landslide in the 1950 election, ending nearly three decades of one-party rule and marking Turkey's first peaceful transfer of power.

title: Turkey joins NATO
summary: Turkey became a member of NATO in 1952, cementing its strategic alignment with the West throughout the Cold War.

title: Registered at the UN as 'Türkiye'
summary: At the government's request, the United Nations registered the country's official name as 'Türkiye' in June 2022, replacing 'Turkey' in international usage.

title: Dutch found Fort Zeelandia
summary: The Dutch East India Company establishes a fortified trading base, Fort Zeelandia, on the southwestern coast near present-day Tainan, beginning roughly four decades of Dutch commercial rule over parts of the island.

title: Spanish settle the northern coast
summary: Spanish forces from the Philippines occupy northern Taiwan, building forts at Keelung and Tamsui in response to the Dutch presence in the south.

title: Dutch expel the Spanish
summary: A Dutch expedition drives the Spanish from their northern outposts, leaving the Dutch East India Company as the dominant European power on the island.

title: Koxinga expels the Dutch
summary: After a siege begun in 1661, the Ming-loyalist commander Zheng Chenggong (Koxinga) forces the surrender of Fort Zeelandia, ending Dutch rule and founding the Zheng (Tungning) regime on Taiwan.

title: Qing conquest of the Zheng regime
summary: A Qing fleet defeats the Zheng (Tungning) forces, ending the Ming-loyalist kingdom; Taiwan is annexed the following year and attached to Fujian province as a prefecture.

title: Taiwan made a Qing province
summary: The Qing government raises Taiwan to the status of a separate province, with Liu Mingchuan as reforming first governor promoting railways and modernisation.

title: Treaty of Shimonoseki cedes Taiwan to Japan
summary: Ending the First Sino-Japanese War, the treaty obliges the Qing empire to cede Taiwan and the Pescadores to Japan, beginning fifty years of Japanese colonial rule.

title: Japanese colonial administration
summary: Japan develops Taiwan with railways, ports, public health and expanded agriculture while suppressing resistance and, from the late 1930s, pursuing intensive assimilation campaigns.

title: ROC takes over Taiwan
summary: After Japan's surrender, the Republic of China under the Nationalists (Kuomintang) takes over the administration of Taiwan from Japan.

title: February 28 Incident
summary: Protests against Nationalist rule, triggered by a violent monopoly-enforcement episode in Taipei, are crushed by troops; thousands are killed, beginning the long repression known as the White Terror.

title: People's Republic of China proclaimed
summary: Having defeated the Nationalists in the Chinese Civil War, Mao Zedong proclaims the People's Republic of China on the mainland; Chiang and his forces withdraw toward Taiwan.

title: ROC government relocates to Taiwan
summary: Chiang Kai-shek's Republic of China central government relocates to Taipei after defeat in the civil war, founding the present self-governing polity on the island; this was not a declaration of independence.

title: UN seat transferred to the PRC
summary: The UN General Assembly votes to seat the People's Republic of China in China's place at the United Nations; the ROC's representatives lose the seat. The resolution does not address Taiwan's sovereignty.

title: Shanghai Communiqué
summary: During President Nixon's visit to China, the United States and the PRC issue the Shanghai Communiqué; the U.S. acknowledges the position that there is but one China, beginning normalisation.

title: U.S. switches recognition to the PRC
summary: The United States establishes formal diplomatic relations with the PRC as the sole legal government of China and ends recognition of the ROC; Congress passes the Taiwan Relations Act to sustain unofficial ties.

title: National Palace Museum opens in Taipei
summary: A permanent home opens in Taipei for a vast collection of Chinese imperial art and antiquities, much of it relocated from the mainland around 1948 to 1949.

title: Martial law lifted
summary: President Lee Teng-hui ends nearly four decades of martial law and the ban on travel to the mainland, opening the way to democratic reform.

title: First direct presidential election
summary: Lee Teng-hui wins Taiwan's first direct, popular presidential election, becoming its first democratically elected president and completing the democratic transition.

title: Ongoing cross-strait dispute
summary: Into 2026 the dispute remains unresolved: the ROC governs Taiwan while the PRC claims it as a province without controlling it, and no peace treaty has settled the question.

title: Hominins leave footprints at Laetoli
summary: Early hominins, attributed to Australopithecus afarensis, cross a layer of fresh volcanic ash near Laetoli; their footprints harden and survive, giving direct evidence of upright walking.

title: Homo habilis and Oldowan tools at Olduvai
summary: Early members of the genus Homo at Olduvai Gorge make simple flaked-pebble tools of the Oldowan industry, among the earliest manufactured implements known.

title: Mary Leakey finds the Zinjanthropus skull
summary: At Olduvai Gorge, Mary Leakey uncovers the robust hominin skull OH 5 (Zinjanthropus / Paranthropus boisei), a landmark in the study of human evolution.

title: Discovery of the Laetoli footprints
summary: Mary Leakey's team excavates the trail of 3.6-million-year-old hominin footprints at Laetoli, confirming early bipedalism and cementing Tanzania's place in human prehistory.

title: Bantu farmers reach the coast
summary: Iron-using Bantu-speaking farmers settle the Tanzanian coast and interior, part of the wider Bantu expansion that reshaped eastern and southern Africa.

title: Rise of the Swahili coast
summary: Coastal communities trading across the Indian Ocean develop the Swahili language and an Afro-Islamic urban culture, founding settlements that grow into trading city-states.

title: Shirazi dynasty founds Kilwa
summary: According to the Kilwa Chronicle, the Shirazi line founds the ruling house of Kilwa Kisiwani; the city begins its rise as a Swahili trading power.

title: Kilwa dominates the gold trade
summary: Controlling the gold exported through Sofala, Kilwa reaches its peak of wealth, minting coins and building the Great Mosque, the largest in the region.

title: Ibn Battuta visits Kilwa
summary: The traveller Ibn Battuta describes Kilwa as a prosperous, devout and beautifully built Muslim city, attesting to the wealth of the medieval Swahili coast.

title: Vasco da Gama reaches the coast
summary: The Portuguese navigator Vasco da Gama arrives on the East African coast en route to India, opening an era of Portuguese intrusion that disrupted the Swahili city-states.

title: Said bin Sultan moves his capital to Zanzibar
summary: The Omani ruler Said bin Sultan transfers his capital from Muscat to Zanzibar, making the islands the commercial heart of the western Indian Ocean.

title: Clove plantations and the caravan trade
summary: Zanzibar and Pemba become the world's leading clove producers, while caravans reaching to Lake Tanganyika feed a vast and brutal trade in enslaved people and ivory.

title: Zanzibar becomes a separate sultanate
summary: On Said's death his domains are divided; his son Majid becomes the first sultan of Zanzibar, separating the islands from Oman.

title: Zanzibar bans the seaborne slave trade
summary: Under British pressure Sultan Barghash signs a treaty prohibiting the maritime slave trade and closing the Stone Town slave market, though domestic slavery endures for decades.

title: Germany establishes German East Africa
summary: Following Carl Peters's treaties, the German government charters his company, founding the colony of German East Africa over the Tanzanian mainland and the Great Lakes territories.

title: Maji Maji rebellion
summary: Inspired by the prophet Kinjikitile Ngwale, southern peoples rise against German rule, forced labour and cotton-growing; the revolt spreads widely before being crushed.

title: Scorched earth and the Great Hunger
summary: German forces suppress the rebellion by destroying crops and villages; the ensuing famine kills tens to hundreds of thousands of people, a catastrophe scholars term genocidal.

title: Tanganyika becomes a British mandate
summary: After the First World War the Treaty of Versailles strips Germany of the colony; Britain administers the mainland as the Tanganyika Territory under a League of Nations mandate from 1922.

title: Founding of TANU
summary: Julius Nyerere builds the Tanganyika African National Union, which campaigns for independence by constitutional means and comes to dominate the territory's politics.

title: Tanganyika gains independence
summary: Mainland Tanganyika becomes independent from Britain under Nyerere and TANU; it becomes a republic with Nyerere as president on 9 December 1962.

title: Zanzibar Revolution
summary: The African majority overthrows the Arab-led sultanate of Zanzibar in a bloody uprising, establishing a republic under Abeid Karume.

title: Union of Tanganyika and Zanzibar
summary: Tanganyika and Zanzibar unite to form the United Republic of Tanzania, with Nyerere as president and Karume as vice-president; Zanzibar keeps its own government.

title: The Arusha Declaration
summary: Nyerere proclaims Ujamaa, committing Tanzania to socialism and self-reliance, nationalising key sectors and launching the policy of collective villages.

title: Nyerere steps down
summary: Julius Nyerere voluntarily retires from the presidency, handing power to Ali Hassan Mwinyi in a peaceful transition and opening the way to economic liberalisation.

title: Return to multiparty politics
summary: Tanzania amends its constitution to permit multiple parties, ending decades of one-party rule; the first multiparty elections follow in 1995.

title: Dodoma confirmed as capital
summary: Tanzania advances the long-planned move of its capital to the central city of Dodoma, while Dar es Salaam remains the largest city and commercial centre.

title: Samia Suluhu Hassan becomes president
summary: On the death of President John Magufuli, Vice-President Samia Suluhu Hassan is sworn in as the first female president of the United Republic of Tanzania.

title: Bantu farmers settle the lakes region
summary: Iron-using Bantu-speaking agriculturalists spread into the interlacustrine region north and west of Lake Victoria, establishing the banana-farming societies that underlie the later kingdoms.

title: Rise of Bunyoro-Kitara
summary: The kingdom of Bunyoro-Kitara, ruled by the omukama and linked in tradition to the Bachwezi, emerges as the dominant power of the interlacustrine region.

title: Foundation of Buganda
summary: Buganda takes shape east of Bunyoro under its first kabakas; tradition credits its founding to Kintu or, in Bunyoro accounts, to Kato Kimera of the Babito dynasty.

title: Buganda expands at Bunyoro's expense
summary: Under a line of aggressive kabakas, the compact kingdom of Buganda annexes territory from Bunyoro-Kitara, growing into the largest state in the interlacustrine region.

title: Swahili-Arab traders reach Buganda
summary: A caravan led by Ahmed bin Ibrahim reaches the court of Kabaka Suna II, opening Buganda to the Zanzibar-based ivory and slave trade and to Islam.

title: Anglican missionaries arrive
summary: Agents of the Church Missionary Society reach Buganda after Stanley publicises Mutesa I's apparent interest in Christianity, beginning Protestant evangelism at the kabaka's court.

title: Catholic White Fathers arrive
summary: Roman Catholic missionaries of the White Fathers reach Buganda, adding a third faith to the rivalry of Muslim, Protestant and Catholic factions at court.

title: Martyrdom of Charles Lwanga
summary: Kabaka Mwanga II has Charles Lwanga and a group of Christian pages burned to death at Namugongo, the most notorious episode in the killing of the Uganda Martyrs of 1885–87.

title: Killing of the Uganda Martyrs
summary: Mwanga II executes some forty-five Catholic and Anglican converts who refuse to renounce their faith; twenty-two Catholic victims were later canonised as saints.

title: Uganda Protectorate declared
summary: Britain proclaims a protectorate over Buganda, soon extended across the wider territory, beginning sixty-eight years of colonial rule administered through the kingdoms.

title: The Uganda Railway is built
summary: The railway is driven from Mombasa to Kisumu on Lake Victoria by some 32,000 indentured Indian labourers, binding Uganda to the coast and bringing a lasting South Asian presence.

title: The Buganda Agreement
summary: Sir Harry Johnston and Buganda's regents sign the agreement recognising the kabaka and Lukiiko, creating the 'mailo' land system and entrenching Buganda's privileged status under indirect rule.

title: Path to independence negotiated
summary: Constitutional conferences in London settle a federal arrangement preserving Buganda's special status, clearing the way for Ugandan self-government and independence.

title: Uganda gains independence
summary: Uganda becomes independent from the United Kingdom with Milton Obote as prime minister; the constitution preserves a federal status for Buganda and the other kingdoms.

title: Mutesa II becomes first president
summary: Uganda becomes a republic and the kabaka of Buganda, Sir Edward Mutesa II, is elected its first president, a largely ceremonial post under the 1962 constitution.

title: Battle of Mengo and the fall of Buganda
summary: Obote suspends the constitution and orders the army under Idi Amin to storm the kabaka's palace; hundreds die and Mutesa II flees into exile, dying in London in 1969.

title: Kingdoms abolished
summary: A new republican constitution abolishes the kingdoms of Buganda, Bunyoro, Ankole and Toro and makes Obote executive president of a centralised, unitary Uganda.

title: Amin's coup
summary: While Obote is abroad, army commander Idi Amin overthrows the government in a military coup, beginning eight years of dictatorship.

title: Expulsion of the Asian community
summary: Amin orders the roughly 80,000 South Asians in Uganda to leave within about ninety days, seizing their property and businesses and devastating the economy.

title: Mass killings under Amin
summary: Amin's regime murders soldiers, professionals, clergy and dissidents through bodies such as the State Research Bureau; estimates of the dead run up to about 300,000.

title: Murder of Archbishop Luwum
summary: The Anglican archbishop Janani Luwum, who had protested against state violence, is killed; his death becomes a symbol of the regime's brutality.

title: Uganda–Tanzania War
summary: After Amin invades northern Tanzania, Julius Nyerere's forces and Ugandan exiles counter-attack and capture Kampala in April 1979, driving Amin into exile.

title: Obote returns to power
summary: After interim governments under Lule and Binaisa, disputed elections return Milton Obote and the UPC to power; opponents allege the vote was rigged.

title: The Ugandan Bush War
summary: Museveni's National Resistance Army wages guerrilla war against Obote's government from the Luwero Triangle; the army's counter-insurgency kills and displaces many thousands of civilians.

title: Museveni captures Kampala
summary: The National Resistance Army takes Kampala and Yoweri Museveni is sworn in as president, ending the post-Amin upheaval and beginning his long rule.

title: Rise of the Lord's Resistance Army
summary: Joseph Kony forms the Lord's Resistance Army in northern Uganda, launching an insurgency notorious for atrocities and the abduction of children.

title: Cultural kingdoms restored
summary: Museveni's government restores the kingdoms in a cultural, non-political form; a new kabaka of Buganda, Ronald Mutebi II, is enthroned.

title: Term limits removed
summary: Parliament removes presidential term limits from the constitution, and Uganda returns to multiparty politics; Museveni's tenure lengthens into one of Africa's longest.

title: LRA driven from Uganda
summary: After nearly two decades that displaced almost two million people and saw tens of thousands of children abducted, the Lord's Resistance Army is pushed out of northern Uganda.

title: The Baptism of Rus'
summary: Grand Prince Volodymyr the Great adopted Christianity in the Byzantine rite and had the people of Kyiv baptized, bringing Rus' into Eastern Christendom and shaping the culture of the East Slavs.

title: Reign of Yaroslav the Wise
summary: Yaroslav consolidated Kievan Rus', codified the Russkaya Pravda, promoted Christianity and learning, and built the Saint-Sophia Cathedral, marking the height of the realm.

title: Saint-Sophia Cathedral begun in Kyiv
summary: Built with Byzantine masters under Yaroslav the Wise as the main church of the Rus' capital, Saint-Sophia symbolised Kyiv as a 'new Constantinople'; it is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: Principality of Galicia-Volhynia formed
summary: Roman Mstyslavych united Galicia and Volhynia into a single powerful principality in the south-west, one of the major successor states to emerge as Kievan Rus' fragmented.

title: Mongol sack of Kyiv
summary: The Mongols of the Golden Horde stormed and destroyed Kyiv, ending its dominance and breaking the political unity of the Rus' lands.

title: Rus' lands pass to Lithuania and Poland
summary: Following the collapse of Galicia-Volhynia, most of the former Rus' lands were absorbed by the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, while Galicia in the west passed to the Kingdom of Poland.

title: Rise of the Cossacks
summary: On the southern steppe frontier free men known as Cossacks emerged, evolving by the mid-sixteenth century a democratic military organisation with an assembly, the rada, and elected hetmans.

title: The Zaporozhian Sich
summary: The Cossacks established the Zaporozhian Sich, a fortified camp on the lower Dnieper that became the political and military heart of Cossack Ukraine and a bastion of Orthodox resistance.

title: Union of Lublin brings Ukraine into the Commonwealth
summary: The union of Poland and Lithuania placed the bulk of the Ukrainian lands within the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, intensifying pressures of serfdom and Catholicism on the Orthodox population.

title: Khmelnytsky's uprising
summary: Bohdan Khmelnytsky led the Zaporozhian Cossacks, allied with the Crimean Tatars, in a great rebellion against Polish rule, founding a self-governing Cossack Hetmanate in the Ukrainian lands.

title: Council of Pereiaslav
summary: Khmelnytsky and the Cossack assembly swore allegiance to the tsar, placing the Hetmanate under Muscovite protection while seeking to retain its autonomy, and drawing Muscovy into war with Poland.

title: Partition along the Dnieper
summary: The Truce of Andrusovo and later settlements divided the Ukrainian lands between Russia and Poland, with the left bank and Kyiv under Russian control and the right bank remaining Polish.

title: Destruction of the Zaporozhian Sich
summary: Russian troops destroyed the Zaporozhian Sich, the bastion of Cossack self-government, completing the suppression of Cossack autonomy under the Russian Empire.

title: Galicia to Austria, right bank to Russia
summary: The partitions of Poland transferred Galicia to the Habsburg Empire in 1772 and most of the right-bank Ukrainian lands to the Russian Empire by 1795, dividing the Ukrainian people between two empires.

title: Shevchenko publishes 'Kobzar'
summary: The poet Taras Shevchenko, born a serf, published his collection Kobzar, giving voice to a distinct Ukrainian nation and laying the foundations of the modern Ukrainian literary language.

title: Ukrainian People's Republic proclaimed
summary: Amid the Russian Revolution, the Central Rada in Kyiv under Mykhailo Hrushevsky proclaimed the Ukrainian People's Republic, the first modern Ukrainian state.

title: Declaration of independence
summary: The Central Rada's Fourth Universal proclaimed the full independence of the Ukrainian People's Republic from Russia, as German, Bolshevik and other forces contested the country.

title: Defeat and Soviet incorporation
summary: After years of war between Bolshevik, Polish, White and Ukrainian forces, the People's Republic was defeated; most Ukrainian lands were incorporated into the Soviet state, while Galicia passed to Poland.

title: The Holodomor
summary: Soviet collectivisation and grain seizures caused a man-made famine that killed millions of Ukrainians; many states and, in 2022, the European Parliament have recognised it as a genocide.

title: Babyn Yar massacre
summary: German SS and police units shot 33,771 Jews at the Babyn Yar ravine outside Kyiv over two days; in all some 100,000 people were murdered there during the occupation.

title: Crimea transferred to the Ukrainian SSR
summary: The Presidium of the Supreme Soviet transferred the Crimean Peninsula from the Russian SFSR to the Ukrainian SSR, citing economic and geographic ties, an administrative change within the USSR.

title: Chernobyl disaster
summary: An explosion at the Chernobyl nuclear plant in northern Ukraine caused the worst nuclear accident in history, exposing Soviet failings and fuelling Ukrainian discontent in the final Soviet years.

title: Declaration of independence
summary: Amid the collapse of the Soviet Union, Ukraine's parliament declared independence on 24 August 1991, confirmed by referendum on 1 December with over 90 percent voting in favour.

title: Budapest Memorandum
summary: Ukraine agreed to surrender its nuclear arsenal and join the Non-Proliferation Treaty; Russia, the US and the UK pledged to respect its sovereignty and existing borders and to refrain from the use of force against it.

title: The Orange Revolution
summary: Mass protests against a fraudulent presidential election forced a court-ordered re-run that brought the pro-Western Viktor Yushchenko to the presidency over Viktor Yanukovych.

title: Revolution of Dignity (Euromaidan)
summary: Protests sparked by the rejection of an EU association agreement grew into the Revolution of Dignity; after deadly clashes President Yanukovych fled the country in February 2014.

title: Russia annexes Crimea; UN Resolution 68/262
summary: Russia seized Crimea and declared its annexation after a referendum deemed illegal; the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 68/262, affirming Ukraine's territorial integrity and declaring the referendum without legal validity.

title: Full-scale invasion; UN Resolution ES-11/1
summary: Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine; the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution ES-11/1 deploring the aggression and demanding the immediate, complete and unconditional withdrawal of all Russian forces.

title: Purported annexation of four oblasts; UN Resolution ES-11/4
summary: Russia proclaimed the annexation of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson; the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution ES-11/4, condemning the attempted annexation as invalid and calling for non-recognition.

title: Indigenous peoples of the grasslands
summary: The Charrua and other hunting and gathering peoples occupy the plains north of the Rio de la Plata over many millennia, well before any European arrival.

title: Solis reaches the Rio de la Plata
summary: The Spanish navigator Juan Diaz de Solis explores the estuary and is killed near its eastern shore; finding no gold, Spain largely ignores the Banda Oriental for nearly two centuries.

title: Cattle turn the plains to wealth
summary: Cattle and horses introduced by early expeditions multiply across the grasslands into vast feral herds, drawing gauchos, hide-hunters and contrabandists to the frontier.

title: Portugal founds Colonia del Sacramento
summary: Portuguese soldiers establish Colonia opposite Buenos Aires; it becomes a strategic outpost and smuggling centre, changing hands between the crowns for over a century.

title: Spain expels the Portuguese at Montevideo
summary: A Spanish force under Bruno Mauricio de Zabala drives out a Portuguese garrison that had begun fortifying the bay of Montevideo, opening the way for a Spanish town.

title: Founding of Montevideo
summary: Zabala formally establishes Montevideo as a fortified Spanish port to counter Portuguese expansion; it grows into the chief stronghold of the Banda Oriental.

title: Viceroyalty of the Rio de la Plata
summary: Spain creates the new viceroyalty centred on Buenos Aires, drawing the Banda Oriental into its administration and stoking eastern resentment of the centralising capital.

title: Colonia listed by UNESCO
summary: The historic quarter of Colonia del Sacramento, blending Portuguese, Spanish and post-colonial architecture, is inscribed as a World Heritage site.

title: Artigas and the Federal League
summary: Jose Gervasio Artigas leads the Orientals against Spain and builds a federal league of provinces, championing autonomy against Buenos Aires across the Banda Oriental and beyond.

title: Portuguese invasion and Artigas in exile
summary: Portuguese forces from Brazil invade the Banda Oriental; after three years of resistance Artigas is defeated in 1820 and goes into permanent exile in Paraguay.

title: The Thirty-Three Orientals declare independence
summary: Juan Antonio Lavalleja and the Thirty-Three Orientals, having landed that April, proclaim separation from Brazil and union with the United Provinces, reigniting the war for the province.

title: Treaty of Montevideo creates Uruguay
summary: Under British mediation, the Preliminary Peace Convention ends the Argentine-Brazilian war by establishing the contested territory as the independent buffer state of Uruguay.

title: First constitution sworn
summary: The Oriental Republic of Uruguay adopts its first national constitution, formally organising the new state.

title: Massacre of the Charrua at Salsipuedes
summary: Government forces ambush and massacre the Charrua at Salsipuedes, a campaign that destroyed them as a distinct people and is remembered as a foundational injustice.

title: The Guerra Grande
summary: The rivalry of Colorados and Blancos erupts into the Guerra Grande; the Blanco Oribe besieges Montevideo for nine years while the Colorados, aided by foreign legions, hold the city.

title: End of the long war
summary: The Guerra Grande ends without outright victory, leaving Uruguay exhausted but independent and its two-party rivalry entrenched.

title: Cattle economy and immigration
summary: Booming exports of hides, beef and wool, British-built railways, and waves of Italian and Spanish immigrants remake Montevideo and the countryside.

title: Batlle y Ordonez becomes president
summary: Jose Batlle y Ordonez of the Colorado Party wins the presidency, beginning the reform era that would make Uruguay an early welfare-state democracy.

title: The great reforms
summary: In his second term Batlle enacts the eight-hour day, free education, pensions, nationalisations, abolition of the death penalty and church-state separation, founding the model welfare state.

title: A new welfare constitution
summary: A reformed constitution entrenches the secular, democratic and social character of the Batllista republic, including a plural executive to check one-man power.

title: Terra's authoritarian interlude
summary: Amid the Great Depression President Gabriel Terra suspends the constitution in a self-coup; constitutional democracy is restored later in the decade.

title: Rise of the Tupamaros
summary: The leftist urban guerrilla movement of the Tupamaros forms under Raul Sendic, turning to robberies, kidnappings and assassinations amid economic decline.

title: Military takes power
summary: With the Tupamaros crushed and the country in crisis, the president dissolves parliament with military backing, beginning a civic-military dictatorship.

title: Return to democracy
summary: After elections in 1984, Julio Maria Sanguinetti is inaugurated president, restoring civilian rule and freeing political prisoners under an amnesty.

title: Frente Amplio breaks the duopoly
summary: The left-wing Frente Amplio coalition wins the presidency for the first time, ending nearly two centuries of Colorado and Blanco dominance.

title: Cannabis and progressive reform
summary: Under President Jose Mujica, Uruguay legalises same-sex marriage and becomes the first country in the world to fully legalise and regulate cannabis.

title: Peopling of the Americas
summary: Humans were established across the Americas by at least 13,000–15,000 years ago, having entered via the Beringian land bridge and Pacific coast from Asia during the last Ice Age.

title: Cahokia at its height
summary: The Mississippian city of Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, reached its peak as one of the largest urban centres north of Mexico, anchored by monumental earthen mounds.

title: Columbus reaches the Caribbean
summary: Christopher Columbus's landfall opened sustained contact between Europe and the Americas, beginning an era of conquest, colonisation, and devastating disease for Indigenous peoples.

title: Founding of Jamestown
summary: English settlers established Jamestown in Virginia, the first permanent English settlement in North America, financed by the Virginia Company of London.

title: First Africans landed in Virginia
summary: An English ship brought roughly twenty enslaved Africans to Point Comfort, Virginia, marking the beginning of African slavery in the English mainland colonies.

title: Pilgrims found Plymouth
summary: Separatist Pilgrims aboard the Mayflower established Plymouth Colony, the first enduring European settlement in New England.

title: French and Indian War
summary: Britain's victory in the North American theatre of the Seven Years' War expelled France from the continent but left Britain heavily indebted, prompting new colonial taxes.

title: Declaration of Independence
summary: The Second Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence, formally announcing the separation of the thirteen colonies from Great Britain.

title: Treaty of Paris
summary: Great Britain recognised the independence of the United States, ending the Revolutionary War and ceding territory east of the Mississippi.

title: Constitution ratified
summary: With New Hampshire's ratification the Constitution took effect; the federal government began operating on 4 March 1789 and Washington was inaugurated that April.

title: Louisiana Purchase
summary: The United States bought France's Louisiana territory for $15 million, roughly doubling the nation's size and opening the trans-Mississippi West.

title: Trail of Tears
summary: Under the Indian Removal Act, the United States forcibly marched the Cherokee and other southeastern nations west of the Mississippi; thousands died en route.

title: American Civil War
summary: War between the Union and the secessionist Confederacy, ignited at Fort Sumter, became the deadliest conflict in U.S. history and decided the fate of slavery.

title: Emancipation Proclamation
summary: President Lincoln declared enslaved people in the rebelling states 'forever free,' redefining the war's purpose and clearing the way for Black enlistment in the Union army.

title: Thirteenth Amendment abolishes slavery
summary: Ratified after the Union victory, the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery and involuntary servitude throughout the United States.

title: Fourteenth Amendment
summary: Ratified during Reconstruction, it granted citizenship to all persons born in the United States and guaranteed equal protection of the laws.

title: Transcontinental railroad completed
summary: The joining of the rails at Promontory, Utah, linked the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, accelerating settlement, commerce, and industrial growth.

title: Great Depression
summary: The stock market crash of 1929 triggered a decade-long economic collapse, answered by Roosevelt's New Deal programmes of relief, recovery, and reform.

title: Attack on Pearl Harbor
summary: Japan's surprise attack on the U.S. naval base in Hawaii brought the United States into the Second World War.

title: Brown v. Board of Education
summary: The Supreme Court ruled that racial segregation in public schools was unconstitutional, a landmark in the legal assault on Jim Crow.

title: Civil Rights Act
summary: Signed by President Johnson, the Act outlawed discrimination based on race, colour, religion, sex, or national origin in employment and public accommodations.

title: Voting Rights Act
summary: The Act banned racial discrimination in voting and authorised federal oversight of elections, dramatically expanding Black political participation.

title: Apollo 11 Moon landing
summary: American astronauts became the first humans to walk on the Moon, a defining achievement of the Cold War space race.

title: End of the Cold War
summary: The dissolution of the Soviet Union left the United States as the world's sole superpower and reshaped the international order.

title: Sogdiana settled and under Achaemenid rule
summary: The Zeravshan valley of Sogdiana, centred on Maracanda (Samarkand), is settled and passes under the Achaemenid Persian Empire; Bukhara grows as a Silk Road trade and crafts centre.

title: Alexander the Great conquers Sogdiana
summary: Alexander the Great captures Maracanda (Samarkand) and advances to the Jaxartes, overcoming two years of fierce Sogdian resistance under Spitamenes.

title: Alexander marries Roxana of Bactria
summary: To cement his conquest, Alexander marries Roxana, daughter of the Bactrian chieftain Oxyartes, symbolising the union of Macedonian and Central Asian peoples.

title: Sogdians dominate Silk Road trade
summary: Sogdian merchants from Samarkand and Bukhara become the leading caravan traders of the Silk Road, their language a lingua franca of Inner Asian commerce and culture.

title: Arab conquest of Bukhara and Samarkand
summary: The Umayyad commander Qutaybah ibn Muslim takes Bukhara and Samarkand and annexes Transoxiana, beginning the Islamisation of the region beyond the Oxus.

title: Battle of Talas
summary: Abbasid Arab forces defeat the army of Tang China at the Battle of Talas, confirming Islam's hold on Central Asia and, by tradition, spreading papermaking westward.

title: Samanid Bukhara, a centre of the Islamic Golden Age
summary: The Persian Samanid dynasty makes Bukhara its capital, a rival to Baghdad whose court fosters Persian literature, science and the refined art and architecture of the Islamic Golden Age.

title: Imam al-Bukhari and the Sahih
summary: Muhammad al-Bukhari, born in Bukhara, compiles the Sahih, accepted by Sunni Muslims as the most authoritative collection of the Prophet's sayings after the Qur'an.

title: Genghis Khan sacks Bukhara and Samarkand
summary: The Mongol armies of Genghis Khan storm Transoxiana, destroying Bukhara and Samarkand in a devastation from which the oasis cities took generations to recover.

title: Timur takes power and makes Samarkand his capital
summary: Timur (Tamerlane) seizes control of Transoxiana and makes Samarkand the capital of an empire reaching from Anatolia to India, adorning it as the cultural heart of Central Asia.

title: The Bibi-Khanym mosque and Timurid Samarkand
summary: Timur summons artisans from across his conquests to build the monumental Bibi-Khanym mosque and other masterpieces, making Samarkand one of the great cities of the medieval world.

title: Ulugh Beg builds his observatory
summary: Timur's grandson Ulugh Beg, ruler and astronomer, builds a great observatory at Samarkand and compiles star tables so accurate they were used in Europe two centuries later.

title: Shaybanid Uzbeks conquer Transoxiana
summary: Muhammad Shaybani Khan leads the Uzbeks south, expelling the last Timurids from Samarkand and Herat and founding the Shaybanid dynasty ruling from Bukhara.

title: The khanate of Khiva is founded
summary: A branch of the Shaybanid dynasty establishes the khanate of Khiva in the Khwarezm oasis, one of the three Uzbek states that would endure until the Russian conquest.

title: The khanate of Kokand emerges
summary: A third Uzbek state, the khanate of Kokand, rises in the fertile Fergana Valley, completing the trio of khanates of Bukhara, Khiva and Kokand.

title: Islamic monuments of Bukhara and Khiva
summary: The khanates raise the madrasas, minarets and palaces that survive in the historic centres of Bukhara and the walled Itchan Kala of Khiva, today UNESCO World Heritage sites.

title: Russia takes Tashkent
summary: Russian imperial forces storm Tashkent, beginning the conquest of the Uzbek lands; Samarkand falls in 1868 as the empire pushes into Central Asia.

title: Khanates absorbed into Russian Turkestan
summary: Bukhara (1868) and Khiva (1873) become Russian protectorates and Kokand is annexed in 1876, completing the conquest and the creation of Russian Turkestan.

title: Creation of the Uzbek SSR
summary: The Soviet national delimitation of 1924 carves Central Asia into ethnic republics; the Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic is created and becomes a union republic of the USSR in 1925.

title: Cotton monoculture and the death of the Aral Sea
summary: Soviet irrigation for cotton diverts the Amu Darya and Syr Darya, and the Aral Sea shrinks drastically from the 1960s — a notorious man-made environmental catastrophe.

title: Uzbekistan declares independence
summary: The Supreme Council of the Uzbek SSR declares independence on 31 August 1991; 1 September becomes Independence Day, and a December referendum confirms it with Islam Karimov as first president.

title: The Andijan events
summary: Government forces open fire on protesters in the city of Andijan; rights groups estimate that hundreds of civilians were killed, drawing international condemnation of Karimov's rule.

title: Mirziyoyev succeeds Karimov and opens reforms
summary: After Islam Karimov's death, Shavkat Mirziyoyev becomes president and launches a 'New Uzbekistan' programme of economic liberalisation and cautious political opening.

title: End of systemic forced labour in cotton
summary: After sustained reforms and international monitoring, civil-society groups conclude that Uzbekistan has dismantled the systemic state-imposed forced labour in its cotton harvest.

title: Martyrdom of Saint Peter
summary: According to tradition the apostle Peter was martyred in Rome during the persecution under Nero and buried on the Vatican Hill beside the circus, around 64 CE.

title: The Trophy of Gaius marks the grave
summary: About a century after Peter's death a small funerary monument, later known as the Trophy of Gaius, was built over the burial site and became a place of veneration.

title: Constantine builds Old St Peter's Basilica
summary: The emperor Constantine raised a great basilica over the traditional tomb of Peter on the Vatican Hill, enclosing the shrine and making the site the chief sanctuary of Western Christendom.

title: The bishops of Rome and apostolic succession
summary: The popes were regarded as successors of Peter as bishops of Rome, a claim founded on the doctrine of apostolic succession that linked their authority to the apostle buried at the Vatican.

title: The Donation of Pepin creates the Papal States
summary: After Pepin the Short forced the Lombards to surrender their conquests, he restored the lands of central Italy to the pope, creating the Papal States and the basis of papal temporal power.

title: The Avignon papacy
summary: The popes moved their residence to Avignon in France, where seven popes ruled for nearly seventy years away from Rome.

title: Gregory XI returns the papacy to Rome
summary: Pope Gregory XI brought the papacy back to Rome from Avignon, against French opposition, ending the Avignon period.

title: The Western Schism
summary: Rival popes in Rome and Avignon divided the Church for four decades until the Council of Constance restored a single papacy in 1417.

title: The Sistine Chapel completed
summary: Built under Pope Sixtus IV, the Sistine Chapel was consecrated in 1483; it became the place where cardinals meet in conclave to elect the pope.

title: First stone of the new Saint Peter's
summary: Pope Julius II laid the foundation stone of an entirely new Saint Peter's Basilica to replace the failing fourth-century church; it was completed in 1626.

title: Michelangelo paints the Sistine ceiling
summary: Commissioned by Julius II, Michelangelo painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel between 1508 and 1512, one of the supreme achievements of Renaissance art.

title: Origins of the Vatican Museums
summary: The Vatican Museums trace their founding to 1506, when Julius II displayed the newly excavated ancient sculpture of the Laocoon, beginning the papal collections.

title: The Kingdom of Italy claims Rome
summary: The new Kingdom of Italy, proclaimed in 1861, regarded Rome as its capital, leaving the pope's remaining territory protected only by a French garrison.

title: The capture of Rome
summary: Italian troops breached the walls at the Porta Pia and took Rome, ending more than a thousand years of papal temporal rule and completing the unification of Italy.

title: Pius IX, 'prisoner in the Vatican'
summary: Refusing to accept the loss of Rome, Pope Pius IX withdrew into the Vatican and declared himself a prisoner, a position his successors held until 1929.

title: The Roman Question
summary: For nearly six decades the popes refused to recognise the Italian state's seizure of Rome, leaving the church-state dispute known as the Roman Question unresolved.

title: Signing of the Lateran Treaty
summary: The Holy See and Italy signed the Lateran Treaty, signed by Mussolini for Italy and Cardinal Gasparri for the papacy, recognising the Holy See's sovereignty and creating the State of Vatican City.

title: The State of Vatican City comes into being
summary: With the exchange of ratifications on 7 June 1929 the State of Vatican City formally came into existence as an independent sovereign state of about 44 hectares.

title: The Roman Question resolved
summary: The Lateran Treaty ended the nearly sixty-year dispute over the popes' loss of Rome, reconciling the papacy to the Italian state in return for a sovereign territory.

title: Wartime neutrality and the liberation of Rome
summary: Vatican City kept to neutrality under Pius XII during the Second World War; though Rome was occupied and then liberated by the Allies on 4 June 1944, the Vatican itself was not occupied.

title: The Second Vatican Council
summary: Opened by John XXIII on 11 October 1962 in Saint Peter's and concluded under Paul VI in 1965, Vatican II reformed the worship, self-understanding and outward relations of the Roman Catholic Church.

title: The Holy See becomes a UN permanent observer
summary: The Holy See established a Permanent Observer Mission to the United Nations in 1964, choosing observer status to preserve its neutrality, distinct from the territory of Vatican City State.

title: Vatican City inscribed as a World Heritage Site
summary: UNESCO inscribed the entire State of Vatican City as a World Heritage Site, recognising Saint Peter's, the Sistine Chapel and the Vatican Museums as a cultural patrimony of universal value.

title: Diplomatic relations with the United States
summary: The United States and the Holy See established full diplomatic relations on 10 January 1984, more than a century after the loss of the Papal States had ended earlier ties.

title: Indigenous peoples of coast, plains and Andes
summary: Carib and Arawak peoples settle the Caribbean coast and the Orinoco basin, while the Timoto-Cuica farm the western Andes, long before European contact.

title: Columbus reaches the Gulf of Paria
summary: On his third voyage Christopher Columbus enters the Gulf of Paria near the Orinoco, the only South American mainland he ever set foot on.

title: The naming of 'little Venice'
summary: Navigators of the Ojeda expedition, on which Amerigo Vespucci sailed, name the coast around Lake Maracaibo 'Venezuela', or 'little Venice', after its stilt dwellings.

title: Founding of Coro
summary: Coro is founded as one of the first lasting Spanish towns on the mainland; its earthen colonial quarter is later inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site.

title: Founding of Caracas
summary: Diego de Losada founds Santiago de Leon de Caracas, which grows into the colony's principal city and the future national capital.

title: A cacao-and-slave economy
summary: Coastal plantations growing cacao, worked by enslaved Africans, enrich a creole planter elite, the mantuanos, and shape colonial society.

title: Captaincy General of Venezuela created
summary: A royal decree unites the scattered provinces into the Captaincy General of Venezuela, with Caracas as capital, giving the territory the outline of the future nation.

title: Junta deposes the captain general
summary: The cabildo of Caracas removes the Spanish captain general and forms a governing junta, the opening act of the independence movement.

title: First declaration of independence in Spanish America
summary: A congress at Caracas declares Venezuela independent of Spain and founds the First Republic, the first such declaration in the region.

title: Death of Francisco de Miranda
summary: The 'Precursor' of independence, handed to the Spanish after the fall of the First Republic, dies a prisoner in a fortress at Cadiz.

title: Battle of Carabobo
summary: Bolivar's victory over the Spanish army at Carabobo, won with Paez's llaneros and foreign volunteers, virtually secures Venezuelan independence.

title: Separation from Gran Colombia
summary: As Gran Colombia dissolves and Bolivar dies, Jose Antonio Paez leads Venezuela to declare itself a separate republic and becomes its first president.

title: The Federal War
summary: A devastating civil war between Liberal federalists and Conservative centralists ravages the country and ends with the Treaty of Coche and a federal constitution.

title: The era of Guzman Blanco
summary: The Liberal caudillo Antonio Guzman Blanco dominates Venezuela, modernising Caracas and centralising power while ruling through personal authority.

title: The dictatorship of Juan Vicente Gomez
summary: Gomez seizes power in 1908 and rules until 1935, presiding over the rise of the oil industry while suppressing opposition.

title: Oil gusher at Lake Maracaibo
summary: A massive blowout at La Rosa on Lake Maracaibo reveals vast reserves; foreign companies pour in and by 1929 Venezuela is a leading oil exporter.

title: Fall of Perez Jimenez and the Punto Fijo pact
summary: A civil-military uprising ousts the dictator Marcos Perez Jimenez; party leaders sign the Punto Fijo pact, founding four decades of power-sharing democracy.

title: Nationalisation of the oil industry
summary: Venezuela nationalises its oil industry and creates the state company Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA), the financial engine of the petro-state.

title: The Caracazo
summary: Austerity measures amid economic crisis trigger days of rioting in Caracas that are violently suppressed, with heavy loss of life, shaking the political order.

title: Chavez's failed coup
summary: Lieutenant Colonel Hugo Chavez leads a failed military coup against the government; jailed and later pardoned, he becomes a national political figure.

title: Chavez elected president
summary: Hugo Chavez wins the presidency promising to sweep aside the old two-party order, launching the Bolivarian project.

title: The Bolivarian Constitution
summary: A new constitution, approved by referendum, renames the country the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela and enlarges presidential and state power.

title: Death of Chavez; Maduro elected
summary: Hugo Chavez dies of cancer in March 2013, and his chosen successor Nicolas Maduro narrowly wins the ensuing election.

title: Economic collapse and exodus
summary: A deep contraction, hyperinflation and shortages drive a mass emigration that, by UN estimates, exceeds 7.7 million people by late 2024.

title: Disputed interim presidency
summary: Opposition leader Juan Guaido declares himself interim president and is recognised by dozens of states, while Maduro retains control of the government.

title: Disputed presidential election
summary: The electoral authority declares Maduro re-elected; the opposition rejects the result and the United States and many governments dispute it.

title: Legendary founding of Van Lang
summary: Vietnamese tradition dates the kingdom of Van Lang and its line of Hung kings to 2879 BCE; the historical Bronze Age Dong Son culture of the Red River delta flourished in the first millennium BCE.

title: Kingdom of Au Lac and Co Loa
summary: An Duong Vuong overthrows the last Hung king and unites the land as Au Lac, building the fortified capital of Co Loa north of modern Hanoi.

title: Han conquest begins Chinese rule
summary: The Chinese Han dynasty conquers the region, opening more than a thousand years of direct Chinese administration, taxation, and cultural influence.

title: Revolt of the Trung sisters
summary: Trung Trac and Trung Nhi lead a rebellion that briefly drives out the Chinese before being defeated in 43 CE; they become lasting symbols of Vietnamese resistance.

title: Battle of Bach Dang and independence
summary: Ngo Quyen destroys a Southern Han fleet at the Bach Dang River using hidden iron-tipped stakes, ending Chinese rule; he proclaims himself king in 939.

title: Founding of the Ly dynasty
summary: Ly Cong Uan takes the throne and founds the Ly dynasty, moving the capital to Thang Long (Hanoi) in 1010 and establishing the enduring institutions of independent Dai Viet.

title: Tran defeat of the Mongol invasions
summary: Under Tran Hung Dao the Tran dynasty repels three invasions by Kublai Khan's Mongols, climaxing in the 1288 victory at the Bach Dang River where the Mongol fleet is destroyed on hidden stakes.

title: Ming China occupies Dai Viet
summary: The Chinese Ming dynasty conquers Dai Viet and imposes two decades of harsh direct rule, provoking widespread resistance.

title: Le Loi expels the Ming and founds the Le dynasty
summary: After a ten-year war of liberation, Le Loi drives out the Ming, restores independence, and establishes the Le dynasty, which would rule, nominally, for centuries.

title: Conquest of Champa's capital
