summary: Emperor Le Thanh Tong's forces capture Vijaya, the capital of Champa, accelerating the southward expansion (Nam tien) of Vietnamese settlement.

title: Tay Son rebellion
summary: A peasant-led uprising overthrows the Nguyen and Trinh lords and the Le dynasty, and in 1789 routs an invading Chinese Qing army near Thang Long.

title: Gia Long founds the Nguyen dynasty
summary: Nguyen Anh defeats the Tay Son, reunifies the country, and is crowned emperor as Gia Long at Hue, founding Vietnam's last imperial dynasty.

title: The name Vietnam adopted
summary: The unified realm is recognized under the name Vietnam, with its capital at Hue and a centralized administration modeled on Qing China.

title: Reign of Minh Mang
summary: Emperor Minh Mang consolidates the Confucian state, completes administrative reforms, and intensifies suspicion of European traders and Catholic missionaries.

title: French attack on Da Nang
summary: A French and Spanish naval force assaults Da Nang, beginning the military conquest that would bring Vietnam under colonial rule.

title: France annexes Cochinchina
summary: Following the capture of Saigon, France secures the southern provinces of Cochinchina as a colony, its first permanent foothold in Vietnam.

title: French Indochina established
summary: France unites Cochinchina, Annam, Tonkin, and Cambodia into the Indochinese Union; Laos is added in 1893, binding Vietnam into a colonial federation centered on Hanoi.

title: Founding of the Indochinese Communist Party
summary: Ho Chi Minh helps unite rival communist groups into the Indochinese Communist Party, which becomes the organizational core of the independence struggle.

title: Great Vietnamese Famine
summary: Under Japanese occupation and wartime mismanagement, famine strikes northern Vietnam, killing an estimated one to two million people and deepening revolutionary discontent.

title: Declaration of independence
summary: As Japan surrenders, the Viet Minh seize power in the August Revolution and Ho Chi Minh proclaims the Democratic Republic of Vietnam in Hanoi's Ba Dinh Square.

title: First Indochina War
summary: War between France and the Viet Minh ends with the French defeat at Dien Bien Phu on 7 May 1954, terminating French colonial rule in Vietnam.

title: Geneva Accords divide Vietnam
summary: The Geneva Conference partitions Vietnam at the 17th parallel into a communist North and an anti-communist South pending reunification elections that are never held.

title: Gulf of Tonkin and U.S. escalation
summary: The Gulf of Tonkin incident leads Congress to pass a resolution authorizing the vast escalation of direct U.S. military involvement in the war.

title: Tet Offensive
summary: A coordinated communist surprise offensive across South Vietnam, though costly militarily, undermines American public support and shifts the war toward U.S. withdrawal.

title: Fall of Saigon and reunification
summary: North Vietnamese forces capture Saigon, ending the war; the country is formally reunified as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam on 2 July 1976.

title: Sino-Vietnamese War
summary: China invades northern Vietnam in response to Vietnam's ousting of the Khmer Rouge in Cambodia; the brief but bloody border war deepens Vietnam's isolation.

title: Doi Moi reforms launched
summary: The Communist Party's Sixth Congress adopts Doi Moi, replacing central planning with a socialist-oriented market economy and opening Vietnam to private enterprise and foreign investment.

title: Normalization with the U.S. and ASEAN membership
summary: Vietnam restores diplomatic relations with the United States and joins the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, ending decades of isolation.

title: Accession to the World Trade Organization
summary: Vietnam joins the WTO, cementing its integration into the global economy and accelerating an export-driven manufacturing boom.

title: Lapita seafarers settle the archipelago
summary: Austronesian voyagers of the Lapita culture reached northern Vanuatu, carrying their distinctive pottery, crops and animals on one of history's great oceanic migrations.

title: The Teouma cemetery on Efate
summary: The burial ground at Teouma on Efate, dated to about 3,000 years ago, is the oldest known cemetery in the Pacific and preserves the remains of the first settlers.

title: Reign of the paramount chief Roi Mata
summary: Oral tradition records Roi Mata as a great chief of central Vanuatu who ended inter-clan warfare and whose burial on Artok is honoured by lasting prohibitions on his sites.

title: Quirós reaches Espiritu Santo
summary: Pedro Fernández de Quirós, leading a Spanish expedition, landed on the largest island, named it La Austrialia del Espíritu Santo and claimed it for Spain before his short-lived colony failed.

title: Bougainville sails through the group
summary: The French navigator Louis-Antoine de Bougainville charted parts of the archipelago and showed that Quirós's 'southern continent' was a group of islands.

title: Cook names the New Hebrides
summary: On his second voyage James Cook surveyed and charted the islands, naming them the New Hebrides — a name they kept until independence in 1980.

title: Missionaries arrive; Williams killed at Erromango
summary: Christian missions began in the islands; the LMS missionary John Williams was killed at Erromango, the first of several martyrdoms as Christianity slowly took hold.

title: The blackbirding labour trade
summary: Recruiters carried over forty thousand islanders to Queensland and others to Fiji and New Caledonia for plantation labour, by indenture, deception and force.

title: Depopulation by introduced disease
summary: Measles, dysentery, influenza and other introduced diseases, together with the labour trade, devastated island populations across the colonial period.

title: Anglo-French Condominium established
summary: Britain and France agreed to govern the New Hebrides jointly, creating a famously duplicated administration with two of nearly everything.

title: U.S. wartime bases on Efate and Santo
summary: American forces built major bases in the islands during the Pacific War, flooding them with goods and personnel and transforming local society.

title: Rise of the John Frum movement
summary: On Tanna the John Frum cargo cult emerged, awaiting a messianic 'John from America' who would bring cargo and restore custom against missionary and colonial control.

title: Vanua'aku Pati founded under Walter Lini
summary: The party that became the Vanua'aku Pati, led by the Anglican priest Walter Lini, was formed to demand independence and the return of alienated land.

title: The Coconut War on Espiritu Santo
summary: Jimmy Stevens's Nagriamel movement declared the breakaway 'State of Vemerana' on Espiritu Santo; the lightly armed revolt was suppressed soon after independence.

title: Republic of Vanuatu proclaimed
summary: The New Hebrides became the independent Republic of Vanuatu, with Walter Lini as first prime minister; Papua New Guinean troops then crushed the Santo secession.

title: Chief Roi Mata's Domain joins World Heritage List
summary: UNESCO inscribed the residence, death site and burial of Chief Roi Mata on Efate, Lelepa and Artok — Vanuatu's first World Heritage property.

title: Cyclone Pam devastates the islands
summary: Tropical Cyclone Pam, the most destructive storm in Vanuatu's history, damaged the great majority of buildings and a vast share of national output.

title: UN asks the ICJ on climate obligations
summary: A Vanuatu-led campaign, begun by Pacific law students, won a UN General Assembly resolution requesting an ICJ advisory opinion on states' climate-change obligations.

title: ICJ delivers landmark climate opinion
summary: The International Court of Justice found that states have binding legal duties to protect the climate and that failure to act may be an internationally wrongful act.

title: The kingdom of Saba flourishes at Marib
summary: Saba, the biblical Sheba, emerged as the dominant South Arabian kingdom, with its capital at Marib controlling the lucrative caravan trade in frankincense and myrrh.

title: Construction of the Great Dam of Marib
summary: The Sabaeans built the Great Dam of Marib to harness the seasonal floods of the Wadi Adhanah, irrigating a vast oasis and underpinning the kingdom's wealth for over a thousand years.

title: Rise of the Himyarite kingdom
summary: The Himyarites rose in the southern highlands and gradually absorbed Saba, Qataban and Hadramawt, uniting much of South Arabia under a single dynasty.

title: Aksumite conquest and the viceroy Abraha
summary: An Ethiopian (Aksumite) invasion overthrew the Himyarite kingdom; the Christian viceroy Abraha later ruled from Yemen before the Sasanian Persians seized the region around 570.

title: Yemen embraces Islam
summary: Yemen adopted Islam in the 7th century, within the Prophet Muhammad's lifetime, and Sanaa became a major centre for the spread of the new faith in the 7th and 8th centuries.

title: Founding of the Zaidi imamate
summary: The scholar Yahya ibn al-Husayn, invited from Medina to arbitrate tribal disputes around Saada, founded the Zaidi imamate, binding the northern highlands to Zaidi Shia Islam for over a thousand years.

title: Ottomans claim Yemen
summary: From around the 1520s the Ottoman Empire asserted control over Yemen's ports and lowlands, contesting the highlands with the Zaidi imams in a struggle that recurred for centuries.

title: Zabid recognised as a centre of Islamic learning
summary: The historic town of Zabid, capital of Yemen under the Rasulids and a celebrated centre of Islamic scholarship from the 13th to 15th centuries, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: Britain captures Aden
summary: The British East India Company seized the port of Aden, establishing a coaling station on the route to India that grew into one of the world's busiest ports after the Suez Canal opened in 1869.

title: Ottoman return to the highlands
summary: The Ottomans reoccupied northern Yemen in the 19th century, meeting sustained resistance from the Zaidi tribes and imams of the mountainous interior.

title: Imam Yahya wins highland autonomy
summary: Imam Yahya Hamid al-Din, leader of Zaidi resistance, secured by treaty a degree of autonomy from the Ottomans over the Zaidi highlands, foreshadowing full independence.

title: Aden becomes a Crown Colony
summary: The port of Aden, previously governed as part of British India, was made a separate Crown Colony, with the surrounding territories organised as the Aden Protectorate.

title: Independent kingdom of North Yemen
summary: With the Ottoman defeat in the First World War and withdrawal from Yemen, Imam Yahya established the independent Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen across the northern highlands.

title: Revolution founds the Yemen Arab Republic
summary: Army officers under Abdullah al-Sallal overthrew the imam and proclaimed the Yemen Arab Republic, igniting a civil war that drew in Egyptian and Saudi forces until 1970.

title: The Aden Emergency
summary: Nationalist groups led by the National Liberation Front waged a guerrilla and urban insurgency against British rule in Aden and its protectorate, hastening Britain's decision to withdraw.

title: Independence of South Yemen
summary: After the British withdrawal, the People's Republic of Southern Yemen declared independence with Aden as its capital, later becoming the Marxist People's Democratic Republic of Yemen.

title: Unification of the Republic of Yemen
summary: North and South Yemen merged into the Republic of Yemen with Sanaa as capital and Ali Abdullah Saleh as president, ending more than two decades of partition.

title: Civil war and the defeat of southern secession
summary: Southern leaders declared secession, but northern forces took Aden in July 1994 and crushed the breakaway attempt, consolidating Saleh's control over a unified Yemen.

title: Old City of Sanaa joins the World Heritage List
summary: UNESCO inscribed the Old City of Sanaa, inhabited for more than 2,500 years and renowned for its multi-storey rammed-earth tower-houses and early mosques.

title: Shibam, the 'Manhattan of the desert', is listed
summary: The Old Walled City of Shibam, famed for its towering mud-brick high-rise houses in the Wadi Hadramawt, was inscribed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site.

title: Arab Spring uprising and Saleh's removal
summary: Mass protests against corruption and Saleh's three decades in power, part of the regional Arab Spring, led to a Gulf-brokered transition under which Saleh ceded power and Hadi became president in 2012.

title: Houthi forces seize Sanaa
summary: The Houthi movement, allied with former president Saleh, captured the capital Sanaa and went on to force President Hadi from the country, collapsing the post-2011 transition.

title: Saudi-led coalition intervenes
summary: A coalition led by Saudi Arabia and the UAE began military intervention to restore the recognised government, opening a prolonged war marked by air strikes, ground combat and blockade.

title: UN estimates 377,000 war-related deaths
summary: A United Nations Development Programme report projected that the war would have caused roughly 377,000 deaths by the end of 2021, most from indirect causes such as hunger and disease.

title: UN-mediated nationwide truce
summary: A two-month UN-brokered truce took effect on 2 April 2022, easing fighting, allowing fuel ships into Hodeidah and flights from Sanaa; it was extended and, though it later lapsed, largely held.

title: The Cradle of Humankind
summary: The Sterkfontein and Swartkrans caves preserve hominin fossils spanning millions of years, including Mrs Ples and Little Foot, marking southern Africa as a key site of human origins; the area was inscribed by UNESCO in 1999.

title: San and Khoekhoe of the subcontinent
summary: The San, hunter-gatherers present for tens of thousands of years, were joined around two thousand years ago by the herding Khoekhoe, together forming the long-established Khoisan societies of the region.

title: Bantu-speaking farmers spread south
summary: Bantu-speaking communities bringing iron-working, cattle and cultivated crops settled the eastern half of southern Africa, ancestors of the region's Nguni, Sotho-Tswana, Venda and Tsonga peoples.

title: The kingdom of Mapungubwe
summary: Near the Limpopo, Mapungubwe rose as southern Africa's first state-level society, trading gold and ivory to the Indian Ocean coast and producing famed gold artefacts before its decline around 1300.

title: Van Riebeeck founds the Cape station
summary: Jan van Riebeeck landed at Table Bay and established a Dutch East India Company refreshment station, the beginning of permanent European settlement in South Africa.

title: Slavery at the Cape
summary: The Company began importing enslaved people from Madagascar, East Africa, India and the Indonesian archipelago, founding a slave society whose labour underpinned the colony for nearly two centuries.

title: Smallpox devastates the Khoekhoe
summary: A smallpox epidemic introduced by passing ships killed great numbers of Khoekhoe, accelerating the loss of their land, herds and independence as the colony expanded.

title: First Cape Frontier War
summary: As trekboers reached the Great Fish River they clashed with the Xhosa, beginning a century-long series of frontier wars along the colony's eastern edge.

title: Britain seizes the Cape
summary: British forces occupied the Cape Colony during the Napoleonic Wars, beginning lasting British rule confirmed by the Congress of Vienna in 1815.

title: Rise of the Zulu kingdom and the Mfecane
summary: Shaka built the Zulu into a powerful centralised kingdom with a reorganised army; the wars and migrations of the Mfecane reshaped the political map of southern Africa.

title: Abolition of slavery at the Cape
summary: Slavery was abolished across the British Empire, freeing enslaved people at the Cape and deepening Boer discontent that helped spark the Great Trek.

title: The Great Trek
summary: Thousands of Voortrekkers left the Cape Colony for the interior, seeking independence from British rule and founding new Boer communities on lands occupied by African peoples.

title: Battle of Blood River
summary: A Voortrekker commando under Andries Pretorius defeated a large Zulu army at the Ncome (Blood) River, a battle long mythologised in Afrikaner nationalism and preceding the rise of Boer republics.

title: Diamonds discovered at Kimberley
summary: The discovery of diamonds near the Vaal and Orange rivers triggered a rush to Kimberley, beginning the mineral revolution and drawing capital and migrant labour into the region.

title: Gold found on the Witwatersrand
summary: The discovery of the world's largest goldfield on the Witwatersrand created Johannesburg, transformed the Transvaal's wealth, and entrenched a segregated migrant-labour system.

title: The South African War
summary: War between Britain and the Boer republics featured guerrilla campaigns and British concentration camps in which tens of thousands of Boer and Black civilians died.

title: Treaty of Vereeniging
summary: The peace signed at Pretoria ended the South African War, bringing the Transvaal and Orange Free State under British sovereignty with promises of eventual self-government.

title: Union of South Africa
summary: The four British colonies were united into the self-governing Union of South Africa under the South Africa Act, a white-controlled state that excluded the Black majority from political power.

title: National Party institutes apartheid
summary: The National Party won the 1948 election and began enacting apartheid, including the Population Registration Act and Group Areas Act of 1950, codifying racial classification, segregation and forced removals.

title: Sharpeville massacre
summary: Police fired on a peaceful anti-pass-law protest at Sharpeville, killing at least 69 people and wounding scores more; the atrocity drew global condemnation and led to the banning of the ANC and PAC.

title: Rivonia Trial imprisons Mandela
summary: Nelson Mandela and fellow leaders of the ANC's armed wing were convicted of sabotage and sentenced to life imprisonment, beginning Mandela's 27 years behind bars.

title: Soweto uprising
summary: Student protests against compulsory instruction in Afrikaans were met with police gunfire in Soweto, killing many, including children, and igniting nationwide resistance.

title: Mandela freed and the ANC unbanned
summary: President F. W. de Klerk unbanned the ANC, PAC and other organisations and released Nelson Mandela from prison, opening the way to negotiations that would dismantle apartheid.

title: First democratic election
summary: South Africans of all races voted together for the first time; the ANC won about 62.65 percent of the vote on an 86.9 percent turnout, ending apartheid rule. The main polling day, 27 April, is marked as Freedom Day.

title: Mandela inaugurated as president
summary: Nelson Mandela was sworn in as the first president of a democratic South Africa, leading a Government of National Unity and symbolising reconciliation across the country's racial divide.

title: Truth and Reconciliation Commission
summary: Chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, the TRC began public hearings into apartheid-era human rights abuses, offering conditional amnesty in exchange for full disclosure as a model of transitional justice.

title: A new Constitution
summary: South Africa's final Constitution, with its justiciable Bill of Rights, was signed into law in 1996 and took effect in February 1997, widely regarded as among the most progressive in the world.

title: ANC loses its majority
summary: In the 2024 general election the ANC lost the outright parliamentary majority it had held since 1994, leading to a multiparty government of national unity and a new phase of coalition politics.

title: Bantu farmers settle the plateau
summary: Bantu-speaking migrants bringing iron-working, cattle, and agriculture spread across the region over the first millennium CE, gradually settling land held by Khoisan and Batwa hunter-gatherers.

title: The Tonga of the Zambezi
summary: On the southern plateau the Tonga and related Ila peoples established dispersed farming communities along the middle Zambezi, organised by lineage rather than centralised kingship.

title: Trade at Ingombe Ilede
summary: The Iron Age settlement of Ingombe Ilede near the Zambezi yielded copper crosses, gold, and imported beads and cloth, showing the region's links to the Indian Ocean trade in gold and ivory.

title: Rise of the Lozi kingdom
summary: On the upper Zambezi floodplain the Luyana (Aluyi) people, of Lunda origin, built the Lozi (Barotse) kingdom ruled by a king titled the Litunga, with capitals that shifted with the annual flood.

title: Founding of the Kazembe kingdom
summary: An offshoot of the Lunda crossed the Luapula River, subdued the Shila, and established the kingdom of the Mwata Kazembe, which grew wealthy on Lake Mweru fisheries and trade in copper, salt, and ivory.

title: Lacerda reaches Kazembe
summary: A Portuguese expedition under Francisco de Lacerda reached the court of the Mwata Kazembe seeking to open trade links across the continent, an early European contact with the Luapula kingdom.

title: Gamitto's mission to Kazembe
summary: A second Portuguese expedition, led by António Gamitto, visited the Mwata Kazembe, leaving a detailed account of a Lunda state deeply engaged in the regional trade in ivory, copper, and captives.

title: Kololo conquest of the Lozi
summary: The Kololo, a Sotho people fleeing the wars of the Mfecane under Sebitwane, crossed the Zambezi and conquered the Lozi kingdom, imposing their rule and language on the floodplain.

title: Ngoni incursions from the south
summary: Ngoni warbands driven north by the upheavals of the Mfecane crossed the Zambezi under leaders such as Zwangendaba, raiding and absorbing peoples and settling in the east of the region.

title: Livingstone reaches Victoria Falls
summary: Guided by local people, David Livingstone became the first European recorded to see the falls the inhabitants called Mosi-oa-Tunya, renaming them Victoria Falls and drawing European attention to the region.

title: Swahili-Arab and Chikunda slave trade
summary: Swahili-Arab traders from the coast and Chikunda raiders from the Zambezi, with Bisa and Yao intermediaries, exchanged guns and cloth for ivory and captives, bringing violence and depopulation to the plateau.

title: Lozi restoration under Sipopa
summary: A Lozi rebellion overthrew Kololo rule and restored the kingdom under Sipopa, reviving the indigenous monarchy of the upper Zambezi floodplain.

title: The Lochner Concession
summary: The Lozi king Lewanika granted mineral rights to Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company in exchange for promises of protection, opening the territory to company rule.

title: Creation of Northern Rhodesia
summary: The British South Africa Company amalgamated North-Western and North-Eastern Rhodesia into a single territory named Northern Rhodesia, administered under royal charter.

title: Northern Rhodesia becomes a Crown protectorate
summary: Administration passed from the British South Africa Company to the Colonial Office, making Northern Rhodesia a British protectorate; the capital later moved to Lusaka in 1935.

title: Copperbelt copper proven
summary: Rich copper sulphide ores were proven beneath the Copperbelt, and large-scale mining from the 1930s built the industrial economy that came to dominate the territory.

title: Copperbelt mineworkers' strike
summary: African mineworkers struck over taxes and conditions; six men were shot dead during the disturbances, an early sign of the labour grievances that would fuel nationalist politics. Further strikes followed in 1940.

title: Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland
summary: Britain joined Northern Rhodesia, Southern Rhodesia, and Nyasaland into a federation dominated by white settlers, provoking widespread African opposition and galvanising nationalist politics.

title: Kaunda founds ZANC
summary: Breaking with Harry Nkumbula's ANC, Kenneth Kaunda founded the radical Zambia African National Congress; it was banned in 1959 and Kaunda imprisoned, but the movement continued as UNIP.

title: The Cha-cha-cha campaign
summary: Under Kaunda, UNIP launched a campaign of mass civil disobedience known as the Cha-cha-cha against colonial rule and the Federation, intensifying pressure for African self-government.

title: Federation dissolved
summary: Sustained African opposition and shifting British policy brought the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland to an end, opening the way to independence for its territories.

title: Independence of Zambia
summary: Northern Rhodesia became the independent Republic of Zambia, named after the Zambezi, with Kenneth Kaunda as its first president.

title: One-party state and Humanism
summary: Kaunda made Zambia a one-party state under UNIP, formalised in the 1973 constitution, governing under his philosophy of Humanism, a blend of African communal values and socialism.

title: Copper collapse and economic decline
summary: Copper, which provided the bulk of export earnings, fell sharply on the world market from the mid-1970s, triggering a long economic decline, rising debt, and austerity.

title: Frontline state for liberation
summary: Zambia hosted and supported southern African liberation movements, including the ANC, ZANU, ZAPU, and SWAPO, becoming a frontline state that bore retaliatory raids and economic costs.

title: Return to multiparty democracy
summary: After food riots and mounting pressure, Kaunda lifted the ban on opposition parties; Frederick Chiluba and the Movement for Multiparty Democracy won the elections, and Kaunda handed over power peacefully.

title: Sovereign debt default
summary: Burdened by debt and falling revenues, Zambia became the first African country of the COVID-19 era to default on its Eurobonds after missing a coupon payment.

title: Hichilema elected president
summary: Opposition leader Hakainde Hichilema won the presidency in a decisive, peaceful election, taking office with a mandate to restructure the national debt and revive the copper-dependent economy.

title: Great Zimbabwe is built
summary: Ancestors of the Shona began raising the mortarless granite walls of Great Zimbabwe, which would become the largest stone city in sub-Saharan Africa and give the modern nation its name.

title: Apex of the gold trade
summary: At its height the city held perhaps 10,000–18,000 people and controlled a gold and ivory trade reaching the Swahili coast at Sofala and Kilwa; Chinese porcelain, Persian glass and a Kilwa coin have been excavated there.

title: Decline and abandonment
summary: Great Zimbabwe was abandoned, probably owing to resource exhaustion and shifting trade routes, as the centre of power moved north toward the Zambezi and successor states.

title: Inscribed as a World Heritage Site
summary: UNESCO inscribed Great Zimbabwe National Monument as a World Heritage Site, recognising it as a unique testimony to the Bantu civilisation of the Shona between the 11th and 15th centuries.

title: Rise of the Mutapa empire
summary: The Mutapa (Mwenemutapa) empire emerged toward the Zambezi, inheriting Great Zimbabwe's gold trade and ruling much of the northern plateau and parts of present-day Mozambique.

title: Portuguese intervention in the gold trade
summary: Portuguese traders based at Sofala and on the Zambezi pressed into the interior, establishing fairs and interfering in Mutapa politics, steadily weakening the empire over the next century.

title: The Torwa state and Khami
summary: In the south-west the Torwa state built its capital at Khami near present-day Bulawayo, continuing the stone-walling tradition in decorated terraces; Khami is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: The Rozvi state under Changamire Dombo
summary: Changamire Dombo founded the Rozvi state, absorbing the Torwa and expelling Portuguese fairs from the plateau around the 1690s; Rozvi power dominated the region until the Mfecane in the 1830s.

title: The Ndebele settle the south-west
summary: Mzilikazi led the Ndebele north during the Mfecane and established a centralised military kingdom around Bulawayo, dominating the south-western plateau and its Shona inhabitants.

title: Rudd Concession and the Pioneer Column
summary: Lobengula signed the 1888 Rudd Concession granting mining rights to Rhodes's agents; Rhodes won a royal charter in 1889 and in 1890 the British South Africa Company's Pioneer Column occupied Mashonaland, raising the flag at Fort Salisbury on 13 September.

title: First Matabele War
summary: Company forces invaded and destroyed the Ndebele kingdom; Lobengula fled and soon died, and the British South Africa Company annexed Matabeleland.

title: First Chimurenga risings
summary: The Ndebele and Shona rose against Company rule in revolts inspired in part by spirit mediums such as Nehanda and Kaguvi; the risings were crushed and their leaders executed.

title: Southern Rhodesia becomes a self-governing colony
summary: After a settler referendum, Company rule ended and Southern Rhodesia became a self-governing British colony, with land and political power reserved for the white minority.

title: Land Apportionment Act
summary: Settler legislation formalised racial division of land, reserving the most productive areas for the white minority and restricting African landholding, a grievance that fuelled later nationalism.

title: Founding of ZANU and ZAPU
summary: African nationalism crystallised in two movements: ZAPU under Joshua Nkomo and the breakaway ZANU, soon led toward armed struggle by figures including Robert Mugabe.

title: Unilateral Declaration of Independence
summary: Ian Smith's Rhodesian Front declared independence from Britain to preserve white-minority rule; Britain and the UN refused recognition and imposed sanctions.

title: The liberation war (Second Chimurenga)
summary: Guerrilla forces of ZANU (ZANLA) and ZAPU (ZIPRA), based in Mozambique and Zambia, waged an escalating war against the Rhodesian state through the 1970s.

title: Lancaster House Agreement
summary: Talks in London produced an agreement providing for a ceasefire, a new constitution and British-supervised elections, ending the war and opening the path to majority rule.

title: Independence under Robert Mugabe
summary: Zimbabwe became an internationally recognised independent state, with Mugabe's ZANU(PF) in power after winning the February 1980 election.

title: The Gukurahundi massacres
summary: The army's Fifth Brigade carried out massacres in Matabeleland and the Midlands targeting ZAPU supporters and Ndebele civilians; estimates of the dead range from several thousand to over twenty thousand. The campaign ended with the 1987 Unity Accord.

title: Fast-track land reform
summary: The government backed often-violent seizures of white-owned commercial farms; the disruption, with drought and sanctions, helped trigger a severe economic collapse.

title: Hyperinflation and dollarisation
summary: Inflation reached among the highest rates ever recorded, peaking in late 2008; in 2009 Zimbabwe abandoned its own currency for foreign ones such as the US dollar.

title: Mugabe forced from power
summary: After a military intervention and the threat of impeachment, Robert Mugabe resigned after thirty-seven years in power, and Emmerson Mnangagwa became president.
